How to write answers that earn partial marks

  1. Write the formula or rule first (e.g. confidence = support(I ∪ {j}) ÷ support(I)). Even if the arithmetic goes wrong, you keep the method mark.
  2. Substitute the numbers visibly (e.g. 2 ÷ 4) — do not jump to the answer.
  3. Show intermediate tables (counts per item, counts per pair, mapper output, reducer output, distances to centroids). Markers award marks per correct intermediate result.
  4. State the final answer clearly, with units and a one-line interpretation ("not interesting because interest < 0.5").
  5. For "describe / explain" questions: use short numbered steps that mirror the algorithm's steps on the slides, then add one sentence on why (e.g. "monotonicity: if a set is frequent, all its subsets are frequent"). Keywords from the slides earn marks.
  6. If you get stuck, state the assumption you will make and continue — follow-through marks are common.

The big picture of Lectures 1–5

Three questions to ask about every algorithm in this course
  1. What is the bottleneck? (network, disk passes, main memory, CPU)
  2. What is the trick that removes it? (move computation to data, combiner, monotonicity, hash-bitmap, summary statistics, representatives …)
  3. What does the trick cost? (extra pass, false positives, assumption about the data)

The big-data era: why everybody cares

Lecture 1 · Slides 1–4

Slide 1 is the cover page. It names the course (EECS 4415 Big Data Systems: Course Introduction), the instructor (Jarek Szlichta) and one important acknowledgement: the course is built on the textbook Mining of Massive Datasets (MMD) by Jure Leskovec, Anand Rajaraman and Jeff Ullman. When a topic in these notes feels thin, MMD is the place to read more. The lab web address on the slide is a link, not exam material.

Data is exploding

Lecture 1 · Slides 2–3

Beginner intuition

Every tap, scroll, like, purchase and GPS ping leaves a small record behind. One record is tiny. Billions of people leaving records all day, every day, adds up to more data than any single computer, or any single person, could ever look at. That pile of records is what people call big data.

Slide 2 (a picture of a data-centre aisle). Rows of server racks, blue network cables and a technician inspecting a rack: this is where big data physically lives. The caption gives one scale statistic: 15 out of 17 sectors in the United States have more data stored per company than the US Library of Congress. The Library of Congress is used as a yardstick for "a very large amount of data". The slide gives no year or source.

Beyond the slides: the statistic comes from a 2011 McKinsey Global Institute report on big data. Treat that as background only; the exam point is the message, "almost every industry holds huge amounts of data".

Slide 3 (Big Data-Driven Era) makes two separate points:

  1. Supply: a massive data explosion. Social networks produce statuses, shared content and click streams (the continuous record of every click a user makes). The slide's example is "Platform X", which receives about 500 million posts per day. Check: 500,000,000 ÷ 86,400 seconds ≈ 5,787 posts every second, around the clock.
  2. Demand: everyone is interested. Business organizations, governments and hospitals all want to use data, and the trade press and popular press shout "Big Data!".

Lots of data plus lots of interest is the reason this course exists: we need methods and systems that can cope.

Slide erratum

Slide 3 says "500 millions of posts daily". Correct English is "500 million posts daily". Also, "Platform X" is the social network formerly called Twitter (beyond the slides); the slide gives no source or year for the figure.

"Data contains value"

Lecture 1 · Slide 4

Slide 4 shows the cover of a Popular Science special issue titled "Data is power: how information is driving the future", with the caption "Data contains value". The cover headlines list what data is used for: feeding the world, solving cold cases, battling malware, predicting our fate, and even asking whether a crime can be prevented before it begins ("Officer Algorithm"). The headlines are only a visual list; the slide does not discuss them.

Key idea

The value is not in the raw bytes. It is in what you can learn from the data and decide using it. Raw data that nobody analyses is just a cost (storage, electricity). That thought leads straight to the next section.

What is data analytics?

Lecture 1 · Slides 5–11

One-sentence definition

Lecture 1 · Slide 5

Slide 5 is a section divider (it carries no printed number). Its subtitle is the shortest definition you can memorise:

Definition — Data analytics

Discovering knowledge and actionable insights from data. Two ingredients: knowledge (you understand something new) and actionable (you can make a decision or take an action because of it).

Store, manage, analyse: where this class sits

Lecture 1 · Slide 8

Slide 8 says that to extract knowledge, data needs to be stored, managed and analyzed, and points at the last one: "ANALYZED ← this class". The centred statement is Big Data Analytics ≈ Data Science.

  • Stored: the data must be kept somewhere (disks, a distributed file system).
  • Managed: organised so it can be found, kept consistent and retrieved (databases).
  • Analyzed: turned into patterns and models. This is the focus of the course.
  • "≈" means "roughly equivalent": in this course the terms big data analytics and data science are used as near-synonyms. The slide does not define "data science" further.

Good news: demand for big data skills

Lecture 1 · Slide 9

This is the "why take this course" slide. It makes three claims:

  • The data science market is expected to grow from $220 billion in 2026 to $975 billion in 2034. Check: 975 ÷ 220 ≈ 4.43 times in 8 years, which is a compound growth of about 20.5% per year.
  • 80% of firms across the globe are investing in building a skilled data analytics division.
  • Salaries in data analytics and AI are surging; a data scientist earns about $190K.

None of these figures has a source or a definition of units on the slide. They are motivation, not exam content.

What is data analytics? The four properties (V-U-U-U)

Lecture 1 · Slide 10

Beginner intuition

Imagine you ask a very fast but very naive assistant to "find something interesting" in a spreadsheet of a million sales. It will hand you hundreds of "findings". Most are junk: coincidences, things everybody already knows, or tangled formulas no one can read. The four properties below are the filter that separates a real finding from junk.

Definition — Data analytics (slide 10)

Given lots of data, discover patterns and models that are Valid, Useful, Unexpected and Understandable.

PropertySlide wordingWhat it meansExample
Validhold on new data with some certaintyThe pattern generalises to new data, not only the data you looked at. "Some certainty" means with high probability, not 100%."Customers who buy A also buy B" still holds next month.
Usefulshould be possible to act on the itemYou can do something with it (the "item" is the discovered pattern).Put A and B on the same shelf.
Unexpectednon-obvious to the systemThe system did not already know it; it tells you something new.A surprising link between two products.
Understandablehumans should be able to interpret the patternA person can read it and see why it makes sense.A short rule, not 10,000 coefficients.
Exam tip

"Name and explain the properties of a good discovered pattern" is a standard short answer. Give the four words and one sentence each (the table above). A pattern failing Valid is the Bonferroni problem of the next sections: it was just noise that will not reappear.

Common mistake

Writing "novel" or "new" for Unexpected is acceptable as a paraphrase, but do not confuse Valid (true on new data) with "true on the data we have". Almost any pattern is true on the data used to find it.

  • A recommender system predicts how much a user will like an item they have not seen yet. Slide 19 lists it as a real-world problem and slide 20 puts it in the "Apps" column.
Exam tip

Distinguish by the question: descriptive describes what is in the data; predictive estimates something not yet known. Always add the slide's example for each.

Meaningfulness of analytics: Bonferroni's principle

Lecture 1 · Slides 12–14

The risk and the principle

Lecture 1 · Slide 12

Beginner intuition

Look at enough clouds and you will see a face in one of them. The more places you look, the more "faces" you find, and none of them means anything. A data analyst searching a mountain of data for "interesting" patterns is in the same position: if the search is wide enough, pure randomness will produce patterns that look real.

Slide 12 says: "A risk with Data Analytics is that an analyst can 'discover' patterns that are meaningless. Statisticians call it Bonferroni's principle:" and then stops. The statement itself is missing.

Slide erratum

Slide 12 ends with a colon and an empty slide body: the actual statement of Bonferroni's principle never appears in the slides. Supply it yourself (next box) and quote it in the exam.

Definition — Bonferroni's principle (Beyond the slides: standard statement, MMD §1.2.3)

Calculate the expected number of occurrences of the events you are looking for, on the assumption that the data is random. If this number is significantly larger than the number of real instances you hope to find, then you must expect that almost anything you find is bogus, that is, a statistical artifact rather than evidence of what you are looking for.

Informal version: if you look in more places for interesting patterns than your amount of data can support, you are bound to find noise.

The recipe in three steps
  1. Pretend the data is completely random (nobody is doing anything special).
  2. Compute how many "interesting" matches that random world would still give.
  3. If that number is much bigger than the number of true cases you expect, the matches are not trustworthy evidence.

The hotel example

Lecture 1 · Slides 13–14

The task (slide 13). Find (unrelated) people who at least twice have stayed at the same hotel on the same day. Suppose such meetings are a sign of wrongdoing. The data:

Definition — C(n, 2) and expected number

C(n, 2) = n(n−1)/2 is the number of ways to choose 2 things from n, order ignored. Example: 4 people give 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6 pairs; for huge n this is about n²/2. Expected number = the average count you would see over many random repetitions; for N chances, each with probability p, the expected number of successes is N × p (this holds even when the chances are not independent). Example: 600 rolls of a die are expected to give 600 × 1/6 = 100 sixes.

The same numbers in four lines (full derivation in Quiz L1-Q1):

  1. One day: P(both people are in some hotel) = 0.01 × 0.01 = 10⁻⁴; P(same hotel | both in hotels) = 1/10⁵; so P(same hotel on one given day) = 10⁻⁹.
  2. Two given days: 10⁻⁹ × 10⁻⁹ = 10⁻¹⁸.
  3. Pairs of people ≈ (10⁹)²/2 = 5 × 10¹⁷; pairs of days ≈ (1000)²/2 = 5 × 10⁵.
  4. Expected = 5 × 10¹⁷ × 5 × 10⁵ × 10⁻¹⁸ = 250,000 innocent pairs.
QuantitySlide valueConsequence
People tracked10⁹about 5 × 10¹⁷ pairs of people
Days1,000about 5 × 10⁵ pairs of days
Chance a person is in a hotel on a given day1% (1 day in 100)10⁹ × 1% = 10⁷ people in hotels each day
Hotel capacity100 people10⁷ ÷ 100 = 10⁵ hotels

The slide asks: if everyone behaves randomly (no terrorists at all), will the analytics detect anything suspicious? Common sense says "no: nothing is going on". The surprising answer, on slide 14, is yes.

The result (slide 14). The expected number of "suspicious" pairs of people is 250,000. The slide continues: that is too many combinations to check, so we need additional evidence to find suspicious pairs more efficiently.

Why does it happen? Each individual coincidence is fantastically unlikely, but there are a staggering number of pairs of people and pairs of days that could produce one. Multiply a tiny probability by an enormous number of chances and you get a large expected count. It is the same reason someone wins a lottery most weeks even though your own ticket almost never wins.

Quick check of the setup: 10⁹ × 0.01 ÷ 100 = 10⁵ hotels (matches slide 13). Exact arithmetic gives about 249,750 expected pairs, which rounds to the slide 14 answer of 250,000. The slide prints only the final answer; the full derivation is walked through in the quiz below.

Key idea — what the lesson is

250,000 innocent pairs would be flagged by pure chance. The suspicious-pair rule is therefore meaningless on its own (it fails Valid and Useful from slide 10). To catch real wrongdoers we need additional evidence (more conditions that random behaviour would almost never satisfy), and a more efficient way than examining 250,000 pairs by hand.

Exam tip

For a hotel-style question write: (1) probability for one pair of people on one day, (2) on two days, (3) number of pairs of people, (4) number of pairs of days, (5) multiply, (6) interpret ("far more than the handful of real cases, so most are bogus"). Each step carries marks. Remember that "pairs" means C(n, 2) ≈ n²/2, not n².

Common mistake

Do not conclude "the data is fine, the algorithm found suspects". The point is the opposite: when the random expectation is already large compared to the true cases, the finding says nothing. Another slip: using n² instead of n²/2 for pairs, which doubles the count.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution of Quiz L1-Q1, state the principle, derive 250,000 and say what it means, then check your steps against the solution.

Quiz L1-Q1Bonferroni’s principle: the hotel example Lecture 1 · Slides 12–14
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 12. “A risk with ‘Data Analytics’ is that an analyst can ‘discover’ patterns that are meaningless. Statisticians call it Bonferroni’s principle:” (the slide text stops at this colon; nothing follows it in the PDF).

Slide 13 — Example. We want to find (unrelated) people who at least twice have stayed at the same hotel on the same day. Data:

  • 109 people being tracked;
  • 1,000 days;
  • each person stays in a hotel 1% of the time (1 day out of 100);
  • hotels hold 100 people (so 105 hotels).

If everyone behaves randomly (i.e., no terrorists) will the data analytics detect anything suspicious?

Slide 14. “Expected number of ‘suspicious’ pairs of people: 250,000 … too many combinations to check – we need to have some additional evidence to find ‘suspicious’ pairs of people in some more efficient way.”

The slides print only the final number 250,000, so the derivation is yours to show. Parts (a)–(c) split the slide question into pieces that can each earn marks:

(a) State Bonferroni’s principle.
(b) If everyone behaves randomly, will the analytics detect anything suspicious? Derive the expected number of “suspicious” pairs of people: the probability that two given people are in the same hotel on one given day and on two given days, the number of pairs of people, the number of pairs of days, and the product.
(c) Explain what this number means: why it is meaningless as evidence of wrongdoing, and what lesson we draw.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Think of a lottery. Your own ticket almost never wins, yet somebody wins most weeks because so many tickets are sold. Here a “ticket” is a pair of people together with a pair of days. Each ticket has an absurdly small chance (10−18) of showing the coincidence, but there are about 2.5 × 1023 tickets, so a great many “win” by luck alone. Those lucky pairs look suspicious, yet nobody did anything wrong.

Beyond the slides — the birthday paradox has the same shape: among 23 people there are C(23, 2) = 253 pairs, each with only a 1-in-365 chance of sharing a birthday, but the chance that some pair matches is about 51%. Bonferroni’s principle says: before you believe a pattern, ask how many such patterns pure randomness would give you.

Part (a) — Definition: Bonferroni’s principle

What the slide says (Lecture 1 · Slide 12): “A risk with ‘Data Analytics’ is that an analyst can ‘discover’ patterns that are meaningless. Statisticians call it Bonferroni’s principle.”

Beyond the slides (the standard statement, close to the wording of the textbook Mining of Massive Datasets, §1.2.3): calculate the expected number of occurrences of the events you are looking for, on the assumption that the data is random. If this number is significantly larger than the number of real instances you hope to find, then you must expect almost anything you find to be bogus, i.e. a statistical artifact rather than evidence of what you are looking for.

In beginner language: if you look in more places for interesting patterns than your amount of data can support, you are bound to “find” patterns that are only noise. (The underlying statistical theorem is called the Bonferroni correction; the informal rule above is Bonferroni’s principle.)

Slide erratum

Slide 12 ends with “Statisticians call it Bonferroni’s principle:” followed by an empty slide body. The statement the colon promises is missing from the PDF (the page text is empty below the colon and the only images are the title banner). The slides therefore define the principle only as “the risk that an analyst ‘discovers’ meaningless patterns”; use the textbook statement above for a complete definition in an exam. Also, slide 14 prints the answer 250,000 with no derivation; steps 1–8 below are the standard textbook derivation and they reproduce the slide’s number.

  1. (b) Formula / idea — what are we counting? Assume everyone behaves randomly. A “suspicious event” is a combination of four things: two different people X and Y and two different days d1 and d2, such that X and Y were in the same hotel on d1 and in the same hotel on d2 (the hotel on d1 may differ from the hotel on d2). If we cannot predict the exact count we can still predict its average (expected) value:
    Formula

    E = (number of pairs of people) × (number of pairs of days) × P(one given pair of people is together on both given days)

    Beyond the slides: this is linearity of expectation — the expected number of “yes” events is the sum of their probabilities; every event here has the same probability, so we multiply (how many events) × (probability of each).

  2. (b) Random model, and a check of “105 hotels”. “Behaves randomly” means: independently on each day, a person is in some hotel with probability 1/100 (= 1%), and if so is equally likely to be in any of the hotels. Check of slide 13’s “so 105 hotels”: people in hotels on one day = 109 × 1100 = 107; each hotel holds 100 people, so the number of hotels is 107 ÷ 100 = 105 ✓ (not 109 ÷ 100, which would ignore that only 1% are away on a given day).
  3. (b) P(both people are in some hotel on a given day). Each person independently has probability 1/100, and for independent events we multiply probabilities: 1100 × 1100 = 10−2 × 10−2 = 10−4.
  4. (b) P(they are in the same hotel on a given day). Given that both are in hotels, fix X’s hotel; Y picks one of the 105 equally likely hotels, so the chance Y picks X’s hotel is 1/105 = 10−5. Rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B given A), so P(same hotel, one given day) = 10−4 × 10−5 = 10−9 (one chance in a billion).
  5. (b) P(same hotel on two given days). Different days are independent, so multiply the two one-day probabilities: (10−9)2 = 10−18. (We need X and Y together on each of the two days, not the same hotel on both days.)
  6. (b) Number of pairs of people. Choose 2 people out of 109, order not mattering (the pair {X, Y} is the same as {Y, X}): C(109, 2) = 109 × (109 − 1)2 ≈ (109)22 = 10182 = 5 × 1017. (Check the formula on a tiny case: 4 people give 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6 pairs. For huge n, n − 1 ≈ n, so C(n, 2) ≈ n²/2.)
  7. (b) Number of pairs of days. C(1000, 2) = 1000 × 9992 = 499,500 ≈ 100022 = 5 × 105.
  8. (b) Multiply everything. E = (5 × 1017) × (5 × 105) × 10−18. Multiply the numbers: 5 × 5 = 25. Add the exponents: 17 + 5 − 18 = 4. So E = 25 × 104 = 250,000, exactly the slide’s answer. (Python check with the exact C(n, 2) values: 4.99999999 × 1017 × 499,500 × 10−18 = 249,749.99975 ≈ 249,750; the slide’s 250,000 is the rounded n²/2 version, a difference of 0.1%.)
  9. (b) Sanity check from the other direction. One given pair of people looks suspicious with probability ≈ 499,500 × 10−18 ≈ 5 × 10−13 (about 1 in 2 trillion). Multiplying by the 5 × 1017 pairs of people gives 2.5 × 105 again. (Beyond the slides: an exact binomial calculation that counts each pair of people once, however often they coincide, gives 249,749.83 — the same to within 0.2 out of 250,000.)
  10. (c) Answer to the slide’s question. “Will the data analytics detect anything suspicious if everyone behaves randomly?” Yes: about 250,000 pairs of people will look suspicious (involving at most 500,000 different people, since a pair has two members), although nobody in the data is a terrorist. By assumption every one of these hits is a pure coincidence, a false alarm.
  11. (c) Why the number is meaningless as evidence. Apply Bonferroni’s principle: compare the expected number of chance matches (250,000) with the number of real cases we hope to find. Beyond the slides — suppose, for illustration, there were about 10 real pairs of evil-doers. They would be buried among about 250,010 flagged pairs, so only 10 ÷ 250,010 ≈ 0.004% (about 1 flagged pair in 25,000) would be real. Because chance matches vastly outnumber real ones, being flagged tells us almost nothing, and nobody can investigate 250,000 pairs — slide 14’s “too many combinations to check”.
  12. (c) The lesson (Slide 14). Do not trust a pattern merely because the data shows it. Either (i) show that the expected number of chance occurrences is much smaller than the number found, or (ii) bring additional evidence that shrinks the set of candidate pairs before you look (“some more efficient way”), for example examine only pairs of people already linked by other clues, or demand a stronger pattern. The “stronger pattern” table further below shows how this removes the chance matches.
QuantitySlide-style roundingExact
Pairs of people C(109, 2)5 × 1017499,999,999,500,000,000
Pairs of days C(1000, 2)5 × 105499,500
Expected suspicious pairs250,000249,749.99975 ≈ 249,750
Key idea

The same formula in symbols: with N people, D days, a fraction p of days spent in a hotel and H hotels, E = C(N, 2) × C(D, 2) × (p2/H)2. Here p2/H = 10−4/105 = 10−9, which is why one day gives 10−9 and two days give 10−18. The expected count is huge because the number of candidate combinations (≈ 2.5 × 1023) is far bigger than 1 ÷ (chance probability) = 1018. Beyond the slides: searching more data finds more noise — double the number of people while keeping the 105 hotels and the number of pairs quadruples, so the expected number of chance matches is about 4 times larger (≈ 1,000,000).

Beyond the slides — how a stronger pattern changes the answer. Same data, but now we demand that the two people were together on k given days: Ek = C(109, 2) × C(1000, k) × (10−9)k (all computed exactly in Python).

Coincidences demandedExpected chance-only pairsReading
k = 1 day≈ 5 × 1011hopeless: half a trillion pairs
k = 2 days (the slide)≈ 2.5 × 105 (249,750 exact)too many to check
k = 3 days≈ 0.083about an 8% chance that even one random pair shows up
k = 4 days≈ 2 × 10−8essentially never by chance

This is also why “at least twice” is practically the same as “exactly twice” on the slide: pairs that meet three or more times by luck number only about 0.08 in total, so the 250,000 is not inflated by them.

Common mistake
  • Skipping a factor in the one-day probability. “Both in a hotel” (10−4) is not “same hotel” (10−9). Leaving out the 1/105 makes the answer 1010 times too large (≈ 2.5 × 1015); using only 10−5 (leaving out the 10−4) gives an absurd 2.5 × 1013.
  • Using n² instead of n(n − 1)/2 for the pairs (ordered instead of unordered pairs): each of the two counts is doubled, so the result becomes 106 instead of 250,000, four times too big. The “÷ 2” appears twice (people and days).
  • Computing the number of hotels as 109 ÷ 100 = 107. The slide’s 105 is the number of hotels needed for the 1% of people who are away on a given day.
  • Requiring the same hotel on both days. The hotels on the two days may differ; only “together on each day” is needed.
  • Stopping at 10−18 and calling the event “practically impossible”. You must multiply by the number of opportunities.
  • Reading 250,000 as a probability or as “250,000 guilty pairs found”. It is the expected number of innocent pairs that look guilty in data that contains no terrorists.
  • Concluding “data mining is useless”. The lesson is to calibrate (compare with the chance level) and to add evidence, not to stop analysing.
Exam tip

Write the formula first (pairs of people × pairs of days × probability), then show each probability and each power of ten in order: 10−9 → 10−18 → 5 × 1017 pairs of people → 5 × 105 pairs of days → 250,000. Use the word “expected”, say that all of them are false positives because the behaviour was random, and finish with one sentence: “The expected number of chance matches, 250,000, is far larger than the number of real cases we hope to find, so by Bonferroni’s principle almost every match is bogus; we need additional evidence or a smaller candidate set.” Even if you slip on one power of ten, the earlier lines keep their marks.

Practice (self-made, not from the course)
  • Same setup but only 100 days are recorded. Pairs of days ≈ 1002/2 = 5 × 103, so E ≈ 5 × 1017 × 5 × 103 × 10−18 = 2,500 (exact 2,475).
  • Original data but hotels hold only 10 people (so 107 ÷ 10 = 106 hotels): P(same hotel, one day) = 10−4/106 = 10−10; two days 10−20; E ≈ 5 × 1017 × 5 × 105 × 10−20 = 2,500 (exact 2,497.5).
Final answer: (a) Bonferroni’s principle — an analyst who looks for patterns in a huge amount of data will “discover” meaningless ones; compute the expected number of chance occurrences under random data, and if it is much larger than the number of real cases hoped for, expect nearly everything found to be bogus. (b) P(same hotel, one given day) = 10−4 × 10−5 = 10−9; two given days = 10−18; pairs of people ≈ 5 × 1017; pairs of days ≈ 5 × 105; expected “suspicious” pairs = 5 × 1017 × 5 × 105 × 10−18 = 250,000 (exact C(n, 2) version 249,750). (c) Even when everyone behaves randomly the analytics still flags about 250,000 pairs; they are chance coincidences, so being flagged is not evidence of wrongdoing and the list is far too long to check — we need additional evidence or a much smaller candidate set.
Where the marks come from: (1) State Bonferroni’s principle: expected chance occurrences vs. number of real cases, so most findings are bogus. (2) Identify the event (pair of people + pair of days) and the formula: expected number = count × probability. (3) P(both in a hotel on a day) = 10−4. (4) Divide by 105 hotels to get 10−9 for one day. (5) Square it for two days: 10−18. (6) Pairs of people ≈ 5 × 1017 (n²/2, unordered). (7) Pairs of days ≈ 5 × 105. (8) Product = 250,000, called an expected number. (9) Interpretation: all false alarms because behaviour was random, too many to check, so we need additional evidence or a smaller search space.
Slide check: the final number 250,000 matches the slide (Slide 14; it is the n²/2 approximation, the exact C(n, 2) value is 249,750). Slide erratum: Slide 14 gives no derivation, and Slide 12 is missing the statement of Bonferroni’s principle after its colon. Both are supplied above (the definition from the textbook, labelled “Beyond the slides”; the derivation re-computed in Python).

What matters when dealing with data? Challenges, modalities, operators

Lecture 1 · Slide 15

Slide 15 is a conceptual diagram with three arrows meeting at a point, like the x, y and z axes of a 3-D graph. Any big-data problem sits at some point in this 3-D space: you choose one value on each axis.

AxisValues on the slidePlain meaning
Challenges (what makes it hard)Quality · Streaming · ScalabilityQuality: data is dirty, missing or inconsistent (recall China's 3.9M and the "Unavailable" countries on slide 7). Streaming: data arrives continuously and must be handled on the fly (see click streams, slide 3). Scalability: too big for one machine, so the method must grow with the data.
Data modalities (what form the data takes)Ontologies · Structured · Graphs · Text · MultimediaOntologies: formal descriptions of concepts and their relations. Structured: tables with fixed columns. Graphs: nodes and links (social networks, the web). Text: documents. Multimedia: images, audio, video.
Data operators (steps from raw data to insight)Collect · Prepare · Model · Reason · VisualizeGather the data; clean and reshape it; build a model of it; draw conclusions from the model; show the results to people. (The slide does not explain "Reason"; read it as drawing inferences from the model.)

Beyond the slides: the plain-meaning column is this guide's own explanation; slide 15 prints only the labels.

The slide does not explain the axes or how they interact; it is a framework to remember. The course samples it: the later lectures attack scalability (MapReduce and Spark, frameworks for computing on many machines, Lectures 2–3; SON, a frequent-itemsets algorithm, Lecture 4), streaming (infinite data), and several modalities (high-dimensional data, graphs).

Exam tip

If asked for "the challenges when dealing with big data", answer with the three on the slide (quality, streaming, scalability) and one sentence each. Mention the other two axes (modalities and operators) to show you understand the framework.

Data science and its cultures

Lecture 1 · Slides 16–17

Where data science comes from

Lecture 1 · Slide 16

Data science is not a single old field. It sits where three older fields overlap, and each contributes one ingredient:

FieldWhat it contributes (slide 16)
DatabasesLarge-scale data: storing and querying huge data collections
Machine Learning (ML)Complex models learned from data
CS TheoryAlgorithms: efficient procedures with provable behaviour

Different cultures, same job

Lecture 1 · Slide 16

  • Database person: data science is an extreme form of analytic processing, that is, queries that examine large amounts of data. Beyond the slides: this means scan and aggregate, as opposed to quick look-ups of single records.
  • ML person: data science is the inference of models: fitting a model (rules, parameters, clusters) to the data so that it can predict or describe.
  • Slide verdict: "In this class we will do all!" You will see the database view (queries and big scans via MapReduce and Spark), the ML view (clustering, models) and the algorithm view (hashing, sampling, streaming algorithms).
Slide note

Minor label inconsistency: the bullets say "Databases" but the circle says "Database systems". They mean the same thing.

What this class stresses

Lecture 1 · Slide 17

Slide 17 redraws the Venn diagram with Statistics replacing CS Theory (the circles are now Statistics, Machine Learning, Database systems, with Data Science in the middle). The text says the class overlaps with databases, statistics, machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI), but puts more stress on four things:

EmphasisMeaningQuestion it asks
ScalabilityThe method still works when the data grows by a large factor.Does it still run when data grows 1000 times?
AlgorithmsEfficient procedures, not merely correct ones.How much time and memory does it need?
Computing architecturesThe hardware and software setup: clusters, distributed file systems, MapReduce and Spark style frameworks.Where does the data live and who computes what?
Automation for handling large dataThe system, not a person, deals with the size (the slide does not elaborate; think of automatic parallelisation, fault tolerance and data placement).Who does the heavy lifting?

In short: less proving statistical theory, more making things run on huge data.

What will we learn? Data types, computation models, problems, tools

Lecture 1 · Slides 18–21

Two axes: types of data and models of computation

Lecture 1 · Slide 18

Types of data (the shape)What it means
High dimensionalEach item has very many attributes (for example a document described by thousands of word counts). Distances and similarity become tricky. Beyond the slides: a document described by 10,000 word counts is a point in 10,000 dimensions, and in such spaces almost all points look about equally far apart, which is why special tools are needed. LSH and dimensionality reduction appear on the course map but are not part of Lectures 1–5; Lecture 5 covers scalable clustering.
GraphItems are nodes connected by links (web pages, friends). Ranking and community finding use the link structure.
Infinite / never-endingA data stream that never stops; you cannot store it all and may see each item only once.
LabeledExamples come with known answers (for example emails marked spam or not). This is the setting of supervised machine learning.
Models of computationWhat it meansBeyond the slides: where it comes in
Single machine, in memoryEverything fits in one computer's RAM; classic algorithms apply.Classic algorithms; also what each worker runs on its own share of the data
Distributed computingData and work are spread over many machines.Lecture 2 (MapReduce), Lecture 3 (Spark), Lecture 4 (SON), Lecture 5 (clustering with MapReduce)
Streams and online algorithmsData arrives over time; each item can be seen once or a few times with limited memory.Infinite data topics (filtering streams, Bloom filters)
Key idea

The right algorithm depends on the pair (type of data, model of computation). Same task, different setting, different method. This slide leaves that implicit.

Quick recap of slides 1–29
  • Data is exploding (slides 2–3) and contains value (slide 4); data analytics is discovering knowledge and actionable insights from data (slide 5).
  • Data must be stored, managed and analysed; this class is about analysis; big data analytics ≈ data science (slide 8).
  • Good patterns are Valid, Useful, Unexpected, Understandable (slide 10). Tasks are descriptive (clustering) or predictive (recommender systems) (slide 11).
  • Bonferroni's principle: if the expected number of matches under pure randomness is much larger than the real cases, most findings are bogus. Hotel example: about 250,000 innocent suspicious pairs (slides 12–14, Quiz L1-Q1).
  • Three challenges: quality, streaming, scalability; with data modalities and data operators they form the framework of slide 15.
  • Data science sits among databases, ML and CS theory/statistics; this class stresses scalability, algorithms, computing architectures, automation (slides 16–17).
  • Data types: high-dimensional, graph, infinite, labeled; computation models: single machine, distributed, streams (slide 18). Tools: MapReduce, Spark, LSH, Bloom filters, dynamic programming (slide 19). The course map is slide 20.
  • Logistics: prerequisites EECS 3421 and 3101; grading 20/35/10/35; read MMD Chapter 1 (slides 22–29).

Theory Q&A bank

Lecture 1 · Slides 1–29

Cover the answer, write your own, then compare. Each model answer is short enough to write in an exam; the numbered steps are the marking points.

Q1. What is data analytics? Why does it matter now?

Lecture 1 · Slides 2–5, 8

Data analytics is discovering knowledge and actionable insights from data. It matters now because (1) data is being produced at enormous scale (social networks, shared content, click streams), (2) demand is high from business, government and hospitals, and (3) the value is not in storing the data but in analysing it. Data must be stored, managed and analysed; this course concentrates on the last step. Big data analytics ≈ data science.

Q2. Name and explain the four properties of a good discovered pattern.

Lecture 1 · Slide 10

  1. Valid: it holds on new data with some certainty, not only on the data it was found in.
  2. Useful: it is possible to act on it.
  3. Unexpected: it is non-obvious to the system, so it adds knowledge.
  4. Understandable: humans can interpret it.

A pattern produced by pure chance fails Valid; that is the Bonferroni problem.

Q3. Compare descriptive and predictive data analytics methods.

Lecture 1 · Slide 11

DescriptivePredictive
GoalFind human-interpretable patterns that describe the dataUse some variables to predict unknown or future values of other variables
QuestionWhat is in the data I have?What is not known yet / will happen?
Slide exampleClusteringRecommender systems

Q4. State Bonferroni's principle.

Lecture 1 · Slide 12 (statement supplied beyond the slides, MMD §1.2.3)

Calculate the expected number of occurrences of the events you are looking for, assuming the data is random. If this number is significantly larger than the number of real instances you hope to find, then almost anything you find is bogus: a statistical artifact, not evidence. In short: if you search in more places than the data can support, you will find noise. Slide 12 itself only names the risk (an analyst "discovers" meaningless patterns); its statement is missing.

Q5. Explain the hotel example and its conclusion.

Lecture 1 · Slides 13–14

Task: find (unrelated) people who stayed at the same hotel on the same day at least twice. Data: 10⁹ people, 1,000 days, each person in a hotel 1% of days, hotels hold 100 people, so 10⁹ × 1% ÷ 100 = 10⁵ hotels. Assume everyone behaves randomly.

  1. Both people in some hotel on a given day: 0.01 × 0.01 = 10⁻⁴.
  2. Same hotel (Y picks X's hotel among 10⁵): 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁹.
  3. Same hotel on two given days: (10⁻⁹)² = 10⁻¹⁸.
  4. Pairs of people ≈ (10⁹)²/2 = 5 × 10¹⁷; pairs of days ≈ 1000²/2 = 5 × 10⁵.
  5. Expected pairs = 5 × 10¹⁷ × 5 × 10⁵ × 10⁻¹⁸ = 250,000.

Conclusion: even with nobody doing anything wrong, about 250,000 pairs look suspicious. Far more than the few real cases, so the rule is meaningless alone; we need additional evidence and a more efficient way than checking all pairs (slide 14).

Q6. Why does a very unlikely coincidence still happen many times?

Lecture 1 · Slides 13–14

Each single event is rare (10⁻¹⁸ for one pair of people and one pair of days), but the number of opportunities is huge (5 × 10¹⁷ × 5 × 10⁵ ≈ 2.5 × 10²³). Expected count = probability × number of opportunities = 2.5 × 10²³ × 10⁻¹⁸ = 250,000. A tiny probability times an enormous number of trials gives a large expected number of false positives.

Q7. What are the three challenges, the data modalities and the operators in the framework "What matters when dealing with data?"

Lecture 1 · Slide 15

  • Challenges: quality (dirty or missing data), streaming (data arrives continuously), scalability (too big for one machine).
  • Data modalities: ontologies, structured data, graphs, text, multimedia.
  • Data operators: collect, prepare, model, reason, visualize.

A problem is a point in this 3-D space: one choice on each axis.

Q8. What fields does data science overlap with? Contrast the database and the machine-learning view.

Lecture 1 · Slides 16–17

It overlaps databases (large-scale data), machine learning (complex models) and CS theory (algorithms); slide 17 also names statistics and AI. To a database person data science is an extreme form of analytic processing: queries that examine large amounts of data. To an ML person it is the inference of models from data. The slide's verdict: "in this class we will do all".

Q9. What does this class stress compared with the neighbouring fields?

Lecture 1 · Slide 17

More stress on: (1) scalability (still works when data grows hugely), (2) algorithms (efficient, not just correct), (3) computing architectures (clusters, distributed file systems, MapReduce and Spark), (4) automation for handling large data (the system, not a person, copes with the size).

Q10. What types of data and models of computation does the course cover?

Lecture 1 · Slide 18

  • Data: high dimensional, graph, infinite/never-ending, labeled.
  • Computation: single machine in memory, distributed computing, streams and online algorithms.

The best algorithm depends on the pair (data type, computation model).

Q11. List the real-world problems and tools named in the course introduction.

Lecture 1 · Slide 19

Problems: recommender systems, link analysis, spam detection, duplicate document detection. Tools: MapReduce and Spark (distributed computing), Locality Sensitive Hashing and Bloom filters, dynamic programming.

Q12. Describe how the course topics are organised ("how it all fits together").

Lecture 1 · Slide 20

Five columns. High-dimensional data: LSH, clustering, dimensionality reduction. Graph data: PageRank/SimRank, community detection, spam detection. Infinite data: filtering data streams, web advertising, queries on streams. Machine learning: decision trees, neural networks, deep learning. Apps: recommender systems, association rules, duplicate document detection. Columns carry the meaning; rows are unrelated.

Q13. Why is a statement such as "these 250,000 pairs are suspects" not reliable, and what would make findings more trustworthy?

Lecture 1 · Slides 10, 12–14

Under pure randomness we already expect about 250,000 such pairs, so being one of them is not evidence. Findings become more trustworthy when (1) additional evidence is required, i.e. more conditions that random behaviour would almost never satisfy, (2) the pattern is checked on new data (Valid), and (3) the expected number of random matches is computed first and compared with the number of real cases hoped for.

Q14. Where does this class sit in the data pipeline, and how are big data analytics and data science related?

Lecture 1 · Slide 8

The pipeline is store → manage → analyse. This class is the analyse step. The slide writes Big Data Analytics ≈ Data Science: roughly equivalent terms in this course.

Hotel example — the whole calculation (slides 13–14)

Hotels = 10⁹ × 0.01 ÷ 100 = 10⁵. P(same hotel, one day) = 0.01 × 0.01 × 10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁹. P(two days) = (10⁻⁹)² = 10⁻¹⁸.

Pairs of people ≈ n²/2 = 5 × 10¹⁷. Pairs of days ≈ 1000²/2 = 5 × 10⁵ (exact 499,500).

Expected suspicious pairs = 5 × 10¹⁷ × 5 × 10⁵ × 10⁻¹⁸ = 250,000 (exact arithmetic gives 249,749.99975).

Bonferroni recipe in 3 steps
  1. Assume the data is random (nothing special happens).
  2. Compute the expected number of "interesting" matches = (number of possible combinations) × (probability each matches).
  3. If this is much larger than the number of real cases you hope for, treat findings as bogus; demand more evidence.

1%chance in hotel on a day100hotel capacity
10⁵hotels250,000expected false "suspicious" pairs

Common mistakes & traps

Lecture 1 · Slides 10–20

  • Writing the formula but not the principle. Slide 12 gives no statement of Bonferroni's principle; you must supply "expected number under random data ≫ real cases ⇒ bogus".
  • Using n² instead of C(n, 2) ≈ n²/2 for pairs of people or days. That quadruples the hotel answer to 10⁶ instead of 250,000 (twice for people, twice for days).
  • Forgetting that only 1% of people are in a hotel on a given day: the number of hotels is 10⁹ × 1% ÷ 100 = 10⁵, not 10⁹ ÷ 100 = 10⁷.
  • Forgetting a step in the probability: both in a hotel (10⁻⁴) and the same hotel (10⁻⁵) give 10⁻⁹ per day; skipping the first factor gives 10⁻⁵ and a wrong answer.
  • Not squaring for two days. Two days means (10⁻⁹)² = 10⁻¹⁸, not 2 × 10⁻⁹.
  • Concluding that 250,000 pairs are real suspects. The point is the opposite: they are false alarms in a world with no wrongdoers.
  • Confusing Valid with "true on the current data". Valid means it holds on new data.
  • Mixing up descriptive and predictive. Clustering is descriptive; recommender systems are predictive (slide 11).
  • Listing the wrong axis values. Challenges are only quality, streaming, scalability; "structured" and "text" are modalities; "visualize" is an operator.
  • Mixing slide 16 and 17. Slide 16's Venn has CS Theory; slide 17's has Statistics; the four "more stress" items are on slide 17.
  • Treating the logistics and statistics (3 billion users, $975 billion) as exam content. They are motivation; do know the prerequisites and grading split.

Lecture 2Distributed Computing: Distributed File Systems & Map-Reduce

Roadmap — what this lecture is about
  • The problem (Slides 4–16): one computer needs about 46 days just to read 200 TB, so big data is stored and processed on a cluster of commodity nodes (racks, switches, a backbone). Clusters bring two hard facts: machines fail every day (about 1,000 a day at 1M machines) and moving data over the network is slow (10 TB at 1 Gbps takes about a day).
  • The three ideas of Map-Reduce (Slide 16): store data redundantly, move computation close to the data, and give the programmer a simple model that hides the complexity.
  • Storage (Slides 17–25): the distributed file system (GFS / HDFS): huge files cut into 16–64 MB chunks, each replicated 2× or 3× on different chunk servers (different racks if possible), a master / Name Node that holds only metadata, and a client library that reads straight from the chunk servers.
  • Computation (Slides 26–57): the four stages Map → group by key (sort and shuffle) → Reduce → write result; the programmer writes only Map and Reduce. Worked examples: word count, host size, 5-word sequences. Then how it runs in parallel, where data lives, the master, and failure handling.
  • Refinements and extras (Slides 58–80): many small tasks and pipelining, combiners (sum, average, median), the partition function, backup tasks for stragglers, how many map and reduce tasks, the join, cost measures, implementations (Hadoop, Hive, Pig) and cloud computing (EC2, S3, EMR).
  • No code is examined: the pseudo-code on Slides 41–42 is explained in words only. (Lecture 2 has no BFR content; BFR belongs to Lecture 5.)

Exam checklist — by the end of this lecture you can:

  • reproduce the 200 TB calculation (2 × 10⁸ MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 4 × 10⁶ s ≈ 46 days) and its 1,000-disc version (4,000 s), and say which assumption the speed-up needs;
  • draw and explain the cluster architecture (16–64 nodes per rack, 1 Gbps in a rack, 2–10 Gbps backbone) and rank same node < same rack < other rack by cost;
  • derive the failure rate (1,000 servers ÷ 1,000 days = 1 a day; 1M machines = 1,000 a day) and the 10 TB / 1 Gbps transfer time (80,000 s ≈ 0.93 day);
  • state the three ideas of Map-Reduce and match each to the problem it solves;
  • describe the DFS: chunks, replication, never two copies on one server, master/Name Node (metadata only), client library, recovery from failure, data locality;
  • write the Map and Reduce signatures, say how many calls of each occur, and design key and value for word count, host size, 5-word sequences and the natural join;
  • trace a small job by hand through map, partition, shuffle, sort and group, and reduce, and explain what the environment (not the programmer) handles;
  • say where input, intermediate and output data are stored, what the master does, and what is redone after a map-worker, reduce-worker or master failure (and why);
  • explain fine-granularity tasks, M and R, combiners (when legal, the average trick, why median fails), the partition function, and backup tasks;
  • define communication cost, computation cost, total cost and elapsed cost, and name the implementations and cloud services on Slides 76–77.
