Why one computer is not enough

Lecture 2 · Slides 1–4

Where this lecture sits

Lecture 2 · Slides 1–3

Slide 1 is only the title card: Distributed Computing: Map-Reduce (EECS 4415 Big Data Systems, Jarek Szlichta). Slide 2 is the agenda, which is also the map of the whole lecture:

  1. Distributed File System (DFS): how to store data that is too big for one machine, safely. This part is Slides 4–25 and is the subject of this half of the chapter.
  2. Computational model: Map-Reduce: how to compute on that data with a very simple programming model.
  3. Refinements: improvements to the basic model.

Slide 3 (titled “MapReduce”) states the whole motivation in four lines. The goal is large-scale computing for data analytics, meaning running analyses over data far bigger than one machine can hold. There are two challenges: how to distribute the computation, and the fact that distributed/parallel programming is hard. Map-Reduce is presented as the answer to both: it is Google’s computational/data-manipulation model and an “elegant way to work with big data”. The slide only makes the claim; the rest of the lecture justifies it.

Beginner intuition

Imagine you must count every word in every book of a national library. One person can do it, but it will take a lifetime. Hiring 1,000 people helps, but now you must decide who gets which books, hand the books out, collect the partial counts, and cope with people who fall ill halfway. Map-Reduce is a system that does that boring management for you, so you only describe what to count.

Naming note: the slides write “MapReduce”, “Map-reduce” and “Map-Reduce”. They all mean the same thing.

The single-node (classical) architecture

Lecture 2 · Slide 4

Slide 4 shows the picture every programmer has in mind: one machine (a “node”) made of three parts, stacked top to bottom: the CPU (the processor that executes instructions), memory (RAM, fast but small and temporary) and the disk (large and permanent, but much slower). The slide labels this picture “Classical” data mining and machine learning: traditional methods assume the data fits on this one machine, so you simply load it and compute.

Definition: node

A node is one computer in a cluster: a CPU, some memory and a disk. “Single-node” means everything happens on one such computer.

Everything that follows is about what breaks when the data no longer fits this picture. The next four slides give the first and most dramatic reason: the disk is too slow.

Motivating example: reading the web

Lecture 2 · Slides 5–8

The question (Slide 5) and the answer (Slide 6)

Lecture 2 · Slides 5–6

Slide 5 sets the scene with a calculation you should be able to do from memory. There are 10+ billion web pages and the average page is 20 KB, so the data is 10 × 10⁹ × 20 KB = 2 × 10¹¹ KB = 200 TB (terabytes). A single computer reads from its disk at 30–50 MB/sec; the slide says to assume a modern figure of 50 MB/sec. The question: how long does it take to read 200 TB at 50 MB a second?

Formula

time = data sizeread bandwidth  (“time = distance ÷ speed”). Convert the data size into the unit of the rate first (here 1 TB = 10⁶ MB), so that the units cancel and leave seconds.

Slide 6 gives the answer: 4 million seconds = 46+ days (exactly 4 × 10⁶ s ÷ 86,400 s/day = 46.3 days). Just reading the data once, doing nothing with it, takes over six weeks. The full derivation with every unit conversion is in Quiz L2-Q1 below, so it is not repeated here.

Common mistake

The slide’s numbers are best-case. It uses the top of the 30–50 MB/s range and treats “10+ billion” and “200+ TB” as exact. With 30 MB/s the time would be larger still, so 46 days is a lower bound for one disk. Do not forget that 1 TB = 10⁶ MB (decimal prefixes, as on the slides); using 10³ or 10⁹ gives answers that are off by factors of 1,000.

Commodity cluster and the idea of striping (Slides 7–8)

Lecture 2 · Slides 7–8

Slide 7 makes two points. First, reading is only the beginning: it “takes even more to do something useful with the data” (parsing, counting, joining, ranking). Second, the industry settled on a standard architecture: a cluster of commodity nodes joined by a commodity network (Ethernet).

Definition: commodity hardware

Commodity machines are ordinary, cheap, off-the-shelf computers (not a custom supercomputer). A cluster is a large group of such machines wired together and used as one big computer. Ethernet is the standard cheap network technology that connects them.

Slide 8 gives the obvious fix: split the data into chunks, have multiple discs and CPUs, stripe (spread) the data across the discs, and process in parallel. With 1,000 discs and CPUs the 4 million seconds become 4,000,000 ÷ 1,000 = 4,000 seconds (about 67 minutes). Each disc now reads only 200 TB ÷ 1,000 = 0.2 TB = 200 GB.

Beginner intuition

One garden hose empties a swimming pool slowly, and a cleverer person holding the hose does not help. A thousand hoses, each draining its own slice of the pool at the same time, empty it a thousand times faster. The disk is the hose; the CPU speed hardly matters.

Common mistake

4,000 s is an ideal speed-up. It assumes the data is split perfectly evenly, every disc runs at full speed independently, and nothing fails or waits. It ignores moving results around and combining them. The next slides are exactly about those ignored costs, so do not quote “1,000 discs = 1,000× faster” without stating the assumption.

Slide wording note: Slide 8 says “a 1,000 discs”, which should read “1,000 discs”, and it spells “discs” while Slide 4 says “Disk”. Both mean the same device.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution and compute the read time for one computer, then for 1,000 discs, before you look.

Quiz L2-Q1How long to read 200 TB from disk? Lecture 2 · Slides 5–8
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 5 — “Motivation: Google Example”. 10+ billion web pages × 20 KB = 200+ TB. The average size of a web page is 20 KB, so 10 billion × 20 KB = 200 TB. One computer reads 30–50 MB/sec from disk; assume a modern read bandwidth of 50 MB/sec. How long does it take to read 200 TB at 50 MB a second?

Slides 6–8 (the slides’ own answers, which the parts below turn into questions). Slide 6: “Time to read = 4 million seconds = 46+ days!” Slide 7: “Takes even more to do something useful with the data! Standard architecture for such problems is emerging: cluster of commodity nodes; commodity network (ethernet) to connect them.” Slide 8: “The obvious thing is to split the data into chunks: have multiple discs and CPUs, stripe the data across multiple discs, process in parallel. For example, if you had 1,000 discs and CPUs: 4 million seconds divided by 1,000, which is 4,000 seconds.”

(a) How long does one computer take to read the 200 TB at 50 MB/s? Show every unit conversion (1 TB = 106 MB) and give the answer in seconds, minutes, hours and days. (This is the question printed on Slide 5.)
(b) How long if you have 1,000 discs and CPUs reading in parallel? State the assumption this needs. (Slide 8 as a question.)
(c) Explain why this calculation motivates a cluster of commodity nodes joined by a commodity network. (Slides 7–8 as a short explain-question, so you can earn the marks for it.)
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Picture emptying a huge swimming pool through one garden hose. It does not matter how clever you are (the CPU): the hose (the disk’s read speed) limits how fast the water (data) comes out. To empty the pool quickly you do not look for a magic hose, you connect 1,000 hoses and let each one drain its own slice of the pool at the same time. That is what the slides propose: cut the data into pieces, give each piece its own disk and CPU, and read all the pieces in parallel.

Unit ladder (decimal prefixes, as the slide’s numbers imply)Conversion factor
1 MB, 1 GB, 1 TB1 MB = 103 KB; 1 GB = 103 MB; 1 TB = 103 GB, so 1 TB = 106 MB = 109 KB (the one to remember)
Time1 min = 60 s; 1 h = 3,600 s; 1 day = 24 × 3,600 = 86,400 s

Part (a) — one computer reads 200 TB

  1. Formula / idea: reading is a “rate × time = amount” problem, so t = data size Dread bandwidth R (the same as “time = distance ÷ speed”). Here D = 200 TB and R = 50 MB/s. Only the disk’s read speed matters, because it is the bottleneck. The units must match: if D is in MB and R in MB/s, the MB cancel and t comes out in seconds.
  2. Check the data size (Slide 5’s “200 TB”): 10 billion = 10 × 109 = 1010 pages. Total = 1010 × 20 KB = 2 × 1011 KB. With 1 TB = 109 KB: 2 × 1011 KB ÷ 109 KB/TB = 200 TB, exactly as on the slide.
  3. Convert D into the unit of the rate (MB): the rate is in MB/s, so convert TB to MB first, otherwise the units will not cancel. 200 TB × 106 MB/TB = 2 × 108 MB = 200,000,000 MB. (Same result from the other side: 2 × 1011 KB ÷ 103 KB/MB = 2 × 108 MB.)
  4. Substitute and divide: t = 2 × 108 MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 4,000,000 s, because (MB) ÷ (MB/s) leaves seconds. In powers of ten: 2 × 108 ÷ (5 × 101) = 0.4 × 107 = 4 × 106 s = 4 million seconds (the number on Slide 6).
  5. Convert seconds to human units: minutes: 4,000,000 ÷ 60 = 66,666.7 min; hours: 66,666.7 ÷ 60 = 1,111.1 h (= 4,000,000 ÷ 3,600); days: 1,111.1 ÷ 24 = 46.296 days (= 4,000,000 ÷ 86,400). Exact breakdown: 46 days = 46 × 86,400 = 3,974,400 s; the remainder 25,600 s = 7 h (25,200 s) + 400 s = 6 min 40 s, so 4,000,000 s = 46 d 7 h 6 min 40 s ≈ 6.6 weeks ≈ 1½ months. This is the slide’s “46+ days”. Answer to (a): 4 × 106 s ≈ 46.3 days for one computer, just to read the data once.

Part (b) — 1,000 discs and CPUs in parallel

  1. Idea (Slide 8): split the data into chunks, stripe (spread) it evenly over n = 1,000 discs, give every disc its own CPU, and let all of them read their own chunk at the same time, each at 50 MB/s.
  2. Assumptions (write them down for marks): (i) the data is spread evenly, so every disc has the same amount to read; (ii) each disc still delivers its full 50 MB/s; (iii) the discs work independently: no waiting for the network, no failures, no time to combine results; (iv) only reading is timed. This is the ideal case (perfect linear speed-up).
  3. Method 1 — divide the data: each disc holds D/n = 200 TB ÷ 1,000 = 0.2 TB = 200 GB = 2 × 105 MB. All discs run at once, so the whole job takes the time of one chunk: t = 2 × 105 MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 4,000 s.
  4. Method 2 — divide the time (the slide’s shortcut): 4,000,000 s ÷ 1,000 = 4,000 s. Both methods agree. Cross-check with the combined bandwidth: 1,000 × 50 MB/s = 50,000 MB/s = 50 GB/s, and 2 × 108 MB ÷ 5 × 104 MB/s = 4,000 s. In words: 1,000 discs behave like one imaginary disc that is 1,000 times faster.
  5. Convert: 4,000 s ÷ 60 = 66.7 min = 1 h 6 min 40 s ≈ 1.11 h (4,000 ÷ 3,600). The speed-up is 4,000,000 ÷ 4,000 = 1,000 (the number of discs). Answer to (b): 4,000 s ≈ 66.7 min ≈ 1.1 h, instead of 46.3 days.

Part (c) — why this motivates clusters of commodity nodes

  1. The bottleneck is the read speed of one disc, not the arithmetic. One computer reads only 30–50 MB/s (Slide 5), so its time grows in direct proportion to the data: 200 TB takes 46 days. “Classical” data mining and machine learning run on one node of CPU, memory and disc (Slide 4). We cannot make one disc 1,000 times faster, but we can use 1,000 discs.
  2. Reading is only the minimum. Slide 7: “Takes even more to do something useful with the data!” (parsing, counting, ranking …). So we need the CPUs, memory and discs of many machines together, not only many discs.
  3. The fix is parallelism (Slide 8): split the data into chunks, use multiple discs and CPUs, stripe the data across the discs, and process in parallel. With 1,000 nodes the read drops from 46 days to about an hour.
  4. Hence the standard architecture (Slide 7): a cluster of commodity nodes (ordinary, inexpensive, off-the-shelf machines, each with CPU, memory and disc) connected by a commodity network (ethernet). Slides 9–10 show it: racks of 16–64 nodes, 1 Gbps between any pair of nodes in a rack through a switch, a 2–10 Gbps backbone between racks, and Google was guesstimated to have about 1 million machines. Beyond the slides: thousands of cheap machines give far more total disc bandwidth, CPU power and storage per dollar than one very expensive machine (“scale out” instead of “scale up”), and capacity grows simply by adding nodes.
  5. The price (what the rest of Lecture 2 solves): distributed / parallel programming is hard (Slide 3); machines fail (one server stays up about 1,000 days, so 1,000 servers lose about 1 per day and 1 million machines about 1,000 per day, Slide 12); data must stay available and long computations must survive failures (Slide 13); and the network is a bottleneck (1 Gbps: moving 10 TB takes about 1 day, Slide 14). So we need a framework that does not move data around much: the distributed file system and Map-Reduce.
Ideal speed-up: what the slide assumes

The “4,000 seconds” is an ideal number: perfectly even chunks, every disc reading at full speed, no time spent moving data over the network, no failures, and only reading counted. Beyond the slides: in practice the data must first be spread over the discs, chunks may be unequal (the job waits for the slowest node), failed work must be redone, and partial results must be combined, so the real time is longer and the 1,000-fold speed-up is an upper limit. The slide itself only gives the ideal division by 1,000.

Common mistake
  • Wrong power of ten: using 1 TB = 103 MB gives 4,000 s instead of 4,000,000 s; using 109 MB gives 4 × 109 s. TB to MB needs two steps of 1,000 (TB → GB → MB), so 1 TB = 106 MB. Always check against the slide: 4 million seconds.
  • Bits versus bytes: disc speed is in MB/s (bytes); the network figures on Slides 9–10 are in Gbps (bits). Beyond the slides: 1 byte = 8 bits, so 50 MB/s = 400 Mbps and 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s at best.
  • Stopping at “4 million seconds”: 4 × 106 is seconds, not days. Divide by 86,400 to get 46.3 days.
  • Multiplying instead of dividing by n: more discs means less time. The speed of each disc stays 50 MB/s; only the amount each disc must read shrinks.
  • Saying “buy a faster CPU”: the bottleneck here is disc read bandwidth, so the answer is more discs working at the same time.
Exam tip

Write the formula (time = size ÷ rate), convert the size into the unit of the rate (MB), show the units cancelling (MB ÷ MB/s = s), then convert seconds to days with ÷ 86,400. For the parallel case state the assumption (even striping, independent reads) and the shortcut t ÷ n. If the exam changes the numbers, the method is identical: t = (number of items × size per item) ÷ (rate per disc × number of discs). Part (c) is normally 3–4 sentences: disc speed is the bottleneck, parallelism on many cheap nodes gives the speed-up, and the cost is failures and the network, which the distributed file system and Map-Reduce handle.

Practice variants (same method; not from the slides)

Discs / CPUs nTime = 4,000,000 s ÷ nIn friendlier units
14,000,000 s46.3 days
10400,000 s111.1 h = 4.63 days
10040,000 s11.1 h
1,000 (the slide)4,000 s66.7 min ≈ 1.11 h
10,000400 s6.7 min
  • Slower end of the quoted range (30 MB/s): t = 2 × 108 ÷ 30 = 6,666,667 s ≈ 77.2 days on one computer. Only the rate changes.
  • Backwards: discs needed to read 200 TB in 1 hour = 4,000,000 s ÷ 3,600 s = 1,111.1, so at least 1,112 discs (round up; 1,111 discs would need 3,600.4 s).
  • Binary prefixes (1 TB = 240 B, 1 MB = 220 B) would give 4,194,304 s ≈ 48.5 days. The slides use powers of ten, so use 4 × 106 s ≈ 46.3 days.
Final answer:
(a) One computer: 200 TB = 2 × 108 MB, so t = 2 × 108 MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 4 × 106 s (4 million seconds) ≈ 66,667 min ≈ 1,111 h ≈ 46.3 days (46 d 7 h 6 min 40 s; the slide’s “46+ days”).
(b) 1,000 discs and CPUs in parallel: each reads 200 GB = 2 × 105 MB, so t = 4,000,000 s ÷ 1,000 = 4,000 s ≈ 66.7 min ≈ 1.1 h, a 1,000-fold speed-up (ideal case: even striping, independent reads, only reading counted).
(c) One disc’s read speed is the bottleneck (46 days just to read, more to process), so the data is striped over a cluster of cheap commodity nodes joined by commodity ethernet that read and process the chunks in parallel; the price is node failures, a network bottleneck and hard programming, which the distributed file system and Map-Reduce are designed to handle.
Where the marks come from: (1) formula time = data size ÷ read rate, with D = 200 TB and R = 50 MB/s; (2) data size and unit conversion: 10 billion × 20 KB = 200 TB and 200 TB = 200 × 106 MB = 2 × 108 MB; (3) correct division, units cancelling: 2 × 108 ÷ 50 = 4 × 106 s; (4) conversion to days with 86,400 s/day: 46.3 days (and minutes/hours if asked); (5) parallel case: divide the data (200 GB per disc) or the time by 1,000, giving 4,000 s, with the even-striping / no-overhead assumption stated; (6) conversion 4,000 s ≈ 66.7 min; (7) explanation: disc bandwidth is the bottleneck, so use many discs and CPUs in parallel, built from cheap commodity nodes and commodity ethernet, and mention the cost (failures, network, programming). Even if the final number is wrong, steps (1), (2), (5) and (7) can still earn marks.
Slide check: matches the slide’s answers. Slide 5 says “200+ TB”, Slide 6 says “4 million seconds = 46+ days” (exact: 4,000,000 s = 46.296 days = 46 d 7 h 6 min 40 s), and Slide 8 says 4 million ÷ 1,000 = 4,000 seconds. The “+” in “10+ billion”, “200+ TB” and “46+ days” means “at least”; with exactly 10 billion pages the figures are exactly 200 TB, 4,000,000 s and 46.3 days. Notes (not errors): Slide 5 quotes a 30–50 MB/s range but then assumes the optimistic 50 MB/s (30 MB/s would give 77.2 days); the slides do not convert 4,000 s into minutes (66.7 min), which is added above. No slide erratum.

Cluster architecture

Lecture 2 · Slides 9–11

One rack (Slide 9)

Lecture 2 · Slide 9

Slide 9 draws the basic building block. A rack is a physical frame that holds 16–64 nodes; each node is the CPU + memory + disk of Slide 4. All nodes in the rack plug into one switch (a network device that forwards data between the machines plugged into it). The slide labels the link speed: 1 Gbps between any pair of nodes in a rack.

Definition: rack, switch, Gbps

A rack = 16–64 nodes behind one rack switch. Gbps = gigabits per second (10⁹ bits per second). Network speeds are quoted in bits, disk speeds in bytes; 1 byte = 8 bits, so 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s.

Common mistake

Gbps is not GB/s. Lower-case b is a bit, capital B is a byte. Forgetting the factor of 8 makes every network calculation 8 times too fast.

Many racks: the data centre (Slides 10–11)

Lecture 2 · Slides 10–11

Slide 10 (“Modern Data Centers”) repeats the rack and joins the racks through higher-level switches. Traffic between two racks must climb through a backbone of 2–10 Gbps. The slide adds that “it was guestimated that Google had ~1M machines”. Slide 11 is a photograph of rows of server racks packed with cables: it shows what “a cluster of commodity nodes” physically looks like and contains nothing to memorise.

The result is a tree: nodes at the leaves, rack switches above them, a backbone above those. The numbers needed to read this picture (how many racks 1M machines need, what 1 Gbps and 2–10 Gbps mean in MB/s) are worked out in Quiz L2-Q2 below, together with a labelled diagram of the hierarchy.

Where is the data?Link usedSpeed (slides)Network cost
On the same node’s diskno network at alldisk read ≈ 50 MB/s (Slide 5)cheapest: no network
On another node in the same rackrack switch1 Gbps (125 MB/s) per pair (Slide 9)cheap
On a node in another rackrack switches + backbone2–10 Gbps, shared (Slide 10)most expensive

This ranking (same node < same rack < other rack) is the reason the rest of the lecture keeps talking about locality. The “network cost” column is the standard reading of the slides’ picture. The ranking is by network use and sharing, not raw bandwidth: a local disk (50 MB/s) is slower per reader than a 1 Gbps link (125 MB/s), but it uses no shared network and scales with the number of nodes.

Beyond the slides

The slides do not say whether “2–10 Gbps” is per rack or the total capacity. In Mining of Massive Datasets (Section 2.1.1) the point is that many nodes may want to use the inter-rack links simultaneously, so each gets only a share. Quiz L2-Q2 works out the fair-share numbers.

Cluster computing challenges

Lecture 2 · Slides 12–14

Challenge 1: machines fail (Slides 12–13)

Lecture 2 · Slides 12–13

Cheap machines break. Slide 12: one server may stay up 3 years (1,000 days). If you have 1,000 servers, expect to lose 1 a day; if Google had ~1M machines, then 1,000 machines fail every day.

Formula: expected failures per day

failures/day ≈ (number of machines) ÷ (average lifetime in days). Check: 1,000 ÷ 1,000 = 1 per day; 1,000,000 ÷ 1,000 = 1,000 per day. This assumes failures are independent and happen at a steady average rate.

Slide erratum (minor)

Slide 12 has the typo “loose” for “lose”. Also “3 years (1,000 days)” is a rounding: 3 × 365 = 1,095 days. The conclusion is unchanged. The quiz below derives rates per hour and the average gap between failures.

Beginner intuition

A building with 1,000 light bulbs that each last about 1,000 days sees one bulb die on an average day. Nobody panics; spare bulbs are kept. A data centre with a million bulbs sees a thousand die every day, so replacing them is routine, not an emergency. The software, not the hardware, must absorb failure.

Slide 13 turns this into two design questions, and they are the two halves of the lecture:

  • Storage: how do we store data persistently (not lost) and keep it available (readable) if nodes can fail? Answer: the distributed file system (Slides 17–24).
  • Computation: how do we deal with node failures during a long-running computation? Answer: the Map-Reduce framework re-runs lost work instead of starting over (second half of the lecture).

(Slides 12 and 13 both carry the title “Challenges (1)”: the numbering groups challenges, not slides.)

Challenge 2: the network bottleneck (Slide 14)

Lecture 2 · Slide 14

Slide 14 (“Challenges (2)”) asks how do you distribute computation? and names the obstacle: the network bottleneck. Network bandwidth is 1 Gbps and moving 10 TB takes approximately 1 day. (Exactly: 10 TB = 8 × 10¹³ bits ÷ 10⁹ bit/s = 80,000 s = 0.93 days; the quiz derives it.) The conclusion on the slide: we need a framework that does not move data around so much during computation.

Key idea

Data is heavy and the network is slow, but a program is small. So send the program to the data, not the data to the program. This single idea shapes the whole design of the DFS and Map-Reduce.

Beginner intuition

You can carry an entire library through one narrow door to a reader (slow), or you can send the reader, with a page of instructions, into the library. The data is the library; the program is the reader.

Try it yourself first: before opening the solution, write down the expected failures per day for 1,000 and for ~1M machines, and the time to move 10 TB at 1 Gbps.

Quiz L2-Q2Cluster failures and the network bottleneck (the numbers) Lecture 2 · Slides 9–14
Question (built from the numbers on the slides)

Slides 9–14 state facts about how a cluster is built and what goes wrong with it; they do not pose a numbered question. The four parts below are practice-style questions built directly from those numbers. You must be able to derive every number and explain what it implies. Data given on the slides:

SlideWhat it says
9 (Cluster Architecture)Each node has a CPU, memory (Mem) and a disk. Each rack contains 16–64 nodes; a switch gives 1 Gbps between any pair of nodes in a rack.
10 (Modern Data Centers)Rack switches are joined through a higher switch by a 2–10 Gbps backbone between racks. “It was guestimated that Google had ~1M machines.”
11A photograph of racks of servers only. No text, no numbers.
12 (Challenges 1)Machines fail (node failures). One server may stay up 3 years (1,000 days). If you have 1,000 servers, expect to lose 1/day, so 1 failure/day. People estimated Google had ~1M machines, so 1,000 machines fail every day.
13How to store data persistently and keep it available if nodes can fail? How to deal with node failures during a long-running computation?
14 (Challenges 2)Network bottleneck: network bandwidth = 1 Gbps; moving 10 TB takes approximately 1 day. Need a framework that does not move data around so much during computation.
(a) About how many racks does a cluster of ~1M machines need, and what are the in-rack and between-rack speeds expressed in MB/s?
(b) A server lasts about 1,000 days. Derive the expected number of failures per day for 1,000 servers and for ~1M machines (also per hour, and the average time between two failures).
(c) Derive exactly how long it takes to move 10 TB over a 1 Gbps link, showing every unit conversion, and compare with the slide's “approximately 1 day”. How would the answer change if the 2–10 Gbps backbone speed were available?
(d) Explain why the numbers in (b) and (c) motivate (i) storing data redundantly and (ii) moving the computation to the data instead of the data to the computation.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Failures. A building has 1,000 light bulbs and each bulb lasts about 1,000 days on average. Then, on an average day, one bulb burns out. Nobody is alarmed; you keep spare bulbs and replace it. A data centre with a million cheap machines is a building with a million bulbs: about a thousand burn out every day, so failure is part of normal operation, not an emergency.

Network. To get a huge pile of books read, you can carry the whole library through one narrow door to the reader (slow), or you can send the reader (a few pages of instructions) to the library. The data is the library, the program is the reader. A 10 TB “library” through a 1 Gbps “door” takes about a day.

Unit facts used in this quiz (decimal prefixes, as on the slides)Value
Network speed is quoted in bits per second1 Gbps = 109 bit/s. 1 byte = 8 bits, so 1 Gbps = 1.25 × 108 byte/s = 125 MB/s
Data sizes are quoted in bytes1 TB = 1012 bytes = 106 MB, so 10 TB = 1013 bytes = 8 × 1013 bits
Time1 h = 3,600 s; 1 day = 24 h = 86,400 s
Common mistake

Gbps is not GB/s. The lower-case “b” means bit, the capital “B” means byte. Forgetting the factor 8 gives 1013 ÷ 109 = 104 s ≈ 2.8 h, which is 8 times too small. Also: “1 failure per 1,000 days” is the rate of one server, not of the whole cluster, and “1 failure per day” is an average, not a timetable.

Part (a): the architecture numbers (Slides 9–10)

  1. Formula / idea: number of racks = (number of machines) ÷ (nodes per rack). Machines ≈ 1M = 106 (Slide 10; a guess, hence “guestimated”). Nodes per rack = 16 to 64 (Slides 9–10). More nodes per rack means fewer racks.
  2. Compute both ends: 106 ÷ 64 = 15,625 racks (fullest racks) and 106 ÷ 16 = 62,500 racks (smallest racks). So roughly 1.6 × 104 to 6.3 × 104 racks; a middle value of 32 nodes per rack gives 31,250 racks. The picture on Slide 10 (nodes, rack switches, a higher switch) is repeated tens of thousands of times: the cluster is a hierarchy.
  3. Convert the speeds into one unit (bits to bytes, ÷ 8): inside a rack, any pair of nodes talks at 1 Gbps = 109 ÷ 8 = 1.25 × 108 B/s = 125 MB/s. The backbone between racks is 2–10 Gbps = 250–1,250 MB/s. For scale, one local disk reads about 50 MB/s = 400 Mbps (Slide 5).
  4. Beyond the slides: the backbone is shared. The slides do not say whether “2–10 Gbps” is per rack or in total; take it as the capacity available for traffic that leaves a rack (this is the picture in Mining of Massive Datasets, Section 2.1.1: inter-rack bandwidth is only somewhat larger than the in-rack Ethernet, yet many node pairs may need it). All nodes of a rack must then share it, so if every node of a rack sends to other racks at the same time, each gets only its fair share:
    Nodes per rackFair share at 2 GbpsFair share at 10 Gbps
    162,000 Mbps ÷ 16 = 125 Mbps10,000 Mbps ÷ 16 = 625 Mbps
    642,000 Mbps ÷ 64 = 31.25 Mbps10,000 Mbps ÷ 64 = 156.25 Mbps
    The demand-to-capacity ratio is (nodes × 1 Gbps) ÷ backbone = 16 ÷ 10 = 1.6 up to 64 ÷ 2 = 32. Conclusion: moving data between racks is the most expensive kind of network use, which is one more reason to keep computation near its data.

Part (b): failures (Slide 12)

  1. Model and formula: if one server lasts on average L = 1,000 days, then on average it fails at a rate of 1/L = 1/1,000 = 10−3 failures per server per day (a 0.1 % chance on any given day). Why multiply? Expected values simply add up across servers, so N identical servers give N times the single-server rate. We assume, as the slide does, that the rate is constant over time.
    Formula

    expected failures per day F = N × (1 ÷ L) = NL   (here L = 1,000 days). Average time between failures = 1 day ÷ F = L ÷ N days.

  2. 1,000 servers: F = 1,000 × 10−3 = 1,000 ÷ 1,000 = 1 failure per day. This is exactly the slide's “expect to lose 1/day”. Unit check: servers × (failures ÷ (server · day)) = failures per day. Per hour: 1 ÷ 24 ≈ 0.042. Average gap between failures = 86,400 s ÷ 1 = 86,400 s = 24 h.
  3. ~1M machines: F = 106 × 10−3 = 106 ÷ 103 = 1,000 failures per day (slide: “1,000 machines fail every day!”). Shortcut: the cluster is 1,000 times larger, so there are 1,000 times as many failures. Per hour: 1,000 ÷ 24 ≈ 41.7; per minute: 1,000 ÷ 1,440 ≈ 0.69. Average gap = 86,400 s ÷ 1,000 = 86.4 s, i.e. one machine dies every minute and a half, around the clock (1,000 × 365 = 365,000 per year).
  4. Scaling table (same formula, more or fewer servers):
    Servers NFailures per day = N ÷ 1,000Failures per hourAverage time between failures
    16 (a small rack)0.0160.0006762.5 days
    64 (a full rack)0.0640.002715.6 days
    1,00010.04224 h
    10,000100.422.4 h (8,640 s)
    1,000,0001,00041.786.4 s
    The more machines, the more often something fails: the failure rate grows in direct proportion to the cluster size.
  5. Precision check on “3 years (1,000 days)”: 3 × 365 = 1,095 days, so the slide rounds 1,095 down to 1,000 (about 9 % lower) to keep the arithmetic easy. With 1,095 days: 1,000 servers give 1,000 ÷ 1,095 ≈ 0.91 failures/day and 106 machines give 106 ÷ 1,095 ≈ 913 failures/day. Same order of magnitude, so the conclusion is unchanged. In an exam, quote the slide's 1,000 days.
  6. Beyond the slides: what failures mean for a long computation (Slide 13, second question). Expected failures during a job = N × (job length in days) ÷ 1,000. Assuming independent failures at a constant rate, the chance of at least one failure is 1 − e−λ, where λ is that expected number:
    JobExpected failures λP(at least one failure) = 1 − e−λ
    1,000 servers, 4,000 s (the parallel read of Slide 8)1,000 × (4,000 ÷ 86,400) ÷ 1,000 = 0.046≈ 4.5 %
    1,000 servers, 1 day11 − e−1 ≈ 63.2 %
    1,000 servers, 10 days10≈ 99.9955 %
    106 machines, 1 hour106 ÷ 24 ÷ 1,000 = 41.7≈ 100 %
    The longer the job and the bigger the cluster, the more certain a failure becomes. A method that restarts the whole job after every failure would almost never finish.
Slide erratum

Slide 12 writes “expect to loose 1/day”: this is a typo for “lose”. Also “3 years (1,000 days)” is a rounding (3 years = 1,095 days), and “1,000 servers: 1 failure/day” is an average (expected value), not a guarantee. Slide 14 does not say which link the 1 Gbps refers to (presumably the in-rack, per-node figure of Slides 9–10; the slide does not say) or how “approximately 1 day” was obtained; part (c) derives it. None of this changes the argument.

Part (c): the network bottleneck (Slide 14)

  1. Formula / idea: time = amount of data ÷ rate. Both must be in the same units: bits and bit/s, or bytes and byte/s. Network speeds are quoted in bits, data sizes in bytes, so convert first: t = data size D (bits)bandwidth B (bits/s).
  2. Data size in bits: 10 TB = 10 × 1012 bytes = 1013 bytes. Multiply by 8 bits per byte: 1013 × 8 = 8 × 1013 bits.
  3. Bandwidth in bits per second: 1 Gbps = 1 giga-bit per second = 109 bit/s (Slide 14).
  4. Divide (units cancel: bits ÷ (bits/s) = s): t = 8 × 1013 ÷ 109 = 8 × 104 s = 80,000 s.
  5. Convert to human units: 80,000 ÷ 60 = 1,333.3 min; 80,000 ÷ 3,600 = 22.2 h (exactly 22 h 13 min 20 s); 80,000 ÷ 86,400 = 0.926 day. So the slide's “approximately 1 day” is correct as an order-of-magnitude statement: it is about 22 hours. Cross-check in bytes: 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s and 10 TB = 107 MB, so t = 107 ÷ 125 = 80,000 s, the same answer. Sanity check: in one day a 1 Gbps link at full speed carries 125 MB/s × 86,400 s = 1.08 × 107 MB = 10.8 TB, so 10 TB fills almost exactly one day.
  6. This is a best case: it assumes the link runs at full line rate with no other traffic and no protocol overhead. Beyond the slides: at a realistic 70–80 % efficiency the time is 80,000 ÷ 0.8 to 80,000 ÷ 0.7 s = 27.8–31.7 h, i.e. more than a day. If “TB” meant binary tebibytes (240 bytes), then 10 TiB = 8.80 × 1013 bits would take 87,961 s ≈ 24.4 h ≈ 1.02 days, almost exactly the slide's “1 day”. Either way: “about a day”.
  7. What-if table (the faster backbone): same data, bigger bandwidth, t = 8 × 1013 ÷ B.
    Link speed BTime for 10 TBIn hoursIn days
    1 Gbps (Slide 14)80,000 s22.2 h0.93
    2 Gbps (Slide 10, low end)40,000 s11.1 h0.46
    10 Gbps (Slide 10, high end)8,000 s2.2 h0.093
    Even the best case is hours. Beyond the slides: these rows are optimistic lower bounds, because the backbone is shared by many nodes (part a) and one node's own 1 Gbps connection caps what it can send or receive. Scale up: the 200 TB of Slide 5 over one 1 Gbps link = 200 × 1012 × 8 ÷ 109 = 1.6 × 106 s ≈ 18.5 days just to copy it.

Part (d): why these numbers lead to the ideas of Map-Reduce (Slides 13, 14, 16)

  1. (i) Failures lead to redundancy (answers Slide 13).
    • If every chunk of data lived on one machine, then because ~1,000 machines die per day, the data on them would be lost or unavailable every day, and a petabyte-scale data set would always have holes. (Beyond the slides: one year of 1 failure/day on 1,000 servers is 365 failures, about 31 % of the servers once a dead server cannot die twice, since 1 − 0.999365 ≈ 0.306.) The data must therefore be stored redundantly on multiple nodes (Slide 16). A distributed file system (Slide 17: GFS, HDFS) keeps each chunk (16–64 MB, Slide 19) on 2 or 3 different machines (Slide 20), never two copies on the same chunk server (Slide 22), and tries to keep replicas in different racks (Slide 20). When a node dies, the copies on other nodes are still readable (Slide 23: “seamless recovery from disk or machine failure”).
    • Beyond the slides: a rough calculation. With a failure chance of p = 1/1,000 per node per day and independent failures, the chance that all r copies of a chunk are lost in the same day is pr: 10−3 for 1 copy, 10−6 for 2 copies, 10−9 for 3 copies. Each extra copy makes loss 1,000 times less likely, at the price of using r times more disk. Different racks matter because a rack switch or power failure takes out a whole rack at once, which breaks the “independent” assumption.
    • Long-running computation: by the table in part (b), a failure during a long job on a large cluster is almost certain, so the framework must detect it and re-run only the lost pieces of work on other machines instead of starting over. This is Map-Reduce's “handling machine failures” (Slide 53): the master pings workers (Slide 56) and resets the tasks of a failed worker to idle so they are rescheduled elsewhere (Slide 57).
  2. (ii) A slow network leads to moving the computation to the data (answers Slide 14). Compare the two ways of processing the same 10 TB. Beyond the slides (illustration with assumed numbers): a program of 1 MB, the 10 TB spread evenly over 1,000 nodes, each node reading its own disk at 50 MB/s (Slide 5), processing time ignored.
    StrategyWhat travels, and the arithmeticTime
    Move the data to the computation10 TB = 8 × 1013 bits through a 1 Gbps link (part c)80,000 s ≈ 22.2 h
    Move the program to the data~1 MB = 8 × 106 bits per node: 8 × 106 ÷ 109 = 0.008 s per node, so 1,000 × 0.008 = 8 s from one source≈ 8 s
    …then each node reads its own share from its local disk, all in parallel10 TB ÷ 1,000 nodes = 10 GB per node; 10 GB ÷ 50 MB/s = 1010 ÷ (5 × 107) = 200 s200 s ≈ 3.3 min
    The data is 10 TB ÷ 1 MB = 107 times larger than the program. Total with code shipping ≈ 8 + 200 = 208 s versus 80,000 s: 80,000 ÷ 208 ≈ 385 times faster (≈ 400 times if the 8 s is ignored, since 80,000 ÷ 200 = 400). Equivalent view: 1,000 disks give 1,000 × 50 MB/s = 50 GB/s = 400 Gbps of combined local read bandwidth, 400 times one 1 Gbps link.
    Common mistake

    The gain does not come from a disk being faster than a link: one disk (50 MB/s = 400 Mbps) is actually slower than a 1 Gbps link, and reading all 10 TB from a single disk would take 1013 ÷ (5 × 107) = 200,000 s ≈ 55.6 h. The gain comes from parallelism: every node reads its own data locally, so nothing has to squeeze through the one scarce, shared resource, the network.

    Hence Slide 14: “Need a framework that does not move data around so much during computation”, and Slides 16, 23 and 25: “Move computation close to data to minimize data movement”, “Bring computation directly to the data! Chunk servers also serve as compute servers”, and “Issue: copying data over a network takes time. Idea: bring computation close to the data”. In Map-Reduce the scheduler even tries to schedule map tasks close to the physical location of their input (Slide 55).
  3. Putting it together: the two numbers give two design rules, and Map-Reduce (Slide 16) adds a third:
    Number (slide)Problem it causesDesign response
    1,000 failures/day for 1M machines; 1 per day for 1,000 (Slide 12)Data lost or unavailable; long jobs interrupted (Slide 13)Store data redundantly (2–3 replicas, in different racks); re-run only failed tasks
    10 TB over 1 Gbps ≈ 22 h ≈ 1 day (Slide 14); 1 Gbps in rack, 2–10 Gbps between racks (Slides 9–10)Copying data across the network dominates the run timeMove computation close to data; minimise data movement
    Both of the above make programming hard (Slide 15)Programmers should not handle failures and data placement by handA simple programming model (Map-Reduce) that hides the complexity
Exam tip

For any “how long to move or read X” question, write the three lines: (1) formula t = D ÷ B; (2) convert both numbers to the same unit (write “× 8” for bytes to bits explicitly); (3) divide with units and convert seconds to hours or days. Each line earns marks even if the arithmetic slips. For failure questions, state the assumption (average lifetime 1,000 days, constant rate) and say the answer is an expected value. For “why does it motivate X”, always link one number to one consequence to one design rule: “1,000 failures/day → data and tasks are lost all the time → replicate the data and re-run only failed tasks”, and “10 TB takes ~1 day over 1 Gbps → copying data is the bottleneck → move the program to the data”.

Final answer:
(a) ~106 machines ÷ (16 to 64 nodes per rack) = 15,625 to 62,500 racks. In-rack 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s per pair; backbone 2–10 Gbps = 250–1,250 MB/s, shared between racks.
(b) Expected failures per day F = N ÷ 1,000: 1,000 servers → 1 failure/day (one every 24 h); ~1M machines → 1,000 failures/day ≈ 41.7 per hour ≈ one every 86.4 s.
(c) 10 TB = 8 × 1013 bits ÷ 109 bit/s = 8 × 104 s = 80,000 s ≈ 22.2 h ≈ 0.93 day ≈ “about 1 day” (best case); 2 Gbps → 11.1 h, 10 Gbps → 2.2 h.
(d) Frequent failures ⇒ store each chunk redundantly (2–3 replicas on different machines and racks) and re-run only the lost tasks. A slow, shared network ⇒ move the small computation to where the big data already is, instead of moving the data (about 200 s versus 80,000 s in the illustration).
Where the marks come from: (1) Rack count: formula machines ÷ nodes per rack and both values 15,625 and 62,500; speeds converted to MB/s (125 and 250–1,250). (2) Failure rate per server = 1/1,000 per day and F = N ÷ 1,000. (3) 1 failure/day for 1,000 servers and 1,000/day for 1M machines (with the per-hour or 86.4 s interpretation as bonus detail). (4) Unit conversion for the network: TB → bytes → bits (× 8) and Gbps = 109 bit/s. (5) Division 8 × 1013 ÷ 109 = 8 × 104 s and conversion to about 22 h ≈ 1 day; the backbone comparison (11.1 h, 2.2 h). (6) Explanation (i): failures are certain at scale, so store data redundantly (replication, different racks) and recover/re-run only lost tasks. (7) Explanation (ii): the network is the bottleneck, so move the small program to the large data and minimise data movement.
Slide check: matches the slides' answers (1 failure/day for 1,000 servers; 1,000 failures/day for ~1M machines; 10 TB over 1 Gbps = 22.2 h = 0.93 day, which is “approximately 1 day”). Slide erratum (minor, no answer changes): “loose” should read “lose” (Slide 12); “3 years (1,000 days)” is a rounding of 1,095 days; Slide 14 gives no derivation and no unit convention (decimal TB assumed; binary TB gives 24.4 h). See the Slide erratum box above.

The three ideas of Map-Reduce

Lecture 2 · Slides 15–16

Slide 15 (“Large-scale Computing (3)”; the “(3)” is a leftover from an older deck) restates the goal: large-scale computing for data analytics problems on commodity hardware. The question it poses is the programmer’s problem: how can we make it easy to write distributed programs? Distributed programming is hard (you must split data, schedule work, move data, survive failures, combine results), so we need a simple model that hides most of the complexity.

Slide 16 answers with the three bullets that summarise the lecture. Memorise them; “What challenges does Map-Reduce address and how?” is a classic short-answer question.

Idea (Slide 16)Problem it answersWhere it is realised
Store data redundantly on multiple nodes for persistence and availabilityMachines fail (Slide 12)Distributed file system: chunks and replicas (Slides 19–23)
Move computation close to data to minimise data movementNetwork bottleneck (Slide 14)Chunk servers double as compute servers (Slide 23)
Simple programming model to hide the complexity of all this “magic”Distributed programming is hard (Slides 3, 15)Map and Reduce functions; the framework handles the rest (second half of the lecture)
Definitions

Persistence: data is not lost when a machine or disk dies. Availability: the data can still be read while some machines are down. Programming model: the style of program you must write for a system; here, you supply two functions (Map and Reduce) and the system runs them on the cluster.

The distributed file system

Lecture 2 · Slides 17–24

What a DFS is (Slide 17)

Lecture 2 · Slide 17

Slide 17 (“Storage Infrastructure”) states the problem: if nodes fail, how do we store data persistently? And the answer: a Distributed File System (DFS).

Definition: distributed file system

A file system that stores your data across a cluster but stores each piece of data multiple times. It provides redundancy (extra copies) and availability (data stays readable when some nodes are down). Two implementations are named on the slide: GFS (Google File System) and HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System).

Beginner intuition

A library has one book on a shelf. If the shelf collapses, the book is gone. Now photocopy every chapter of every book, put the copies in different rooms and different buildings, and keep a catalogue saying where each chapter is. Losing any one room loses nothing. A DFS is that library, with disks instead of shelves and the cluster instead of buildings.

Beyond the slides: GFS was described in a 2003 Google paper; HDFS is the open-source clone and follows the same design, so the vocabularies map one to one (see the table in the master-node section).

Typical usage pattern (Slide 18)

Lecture 2 · Slide 18

Slide 18 lists the assumptions the DFS is designed for. They explain its design:

  • Huge files (hundreds of GB to TB): a file cannot fit on one machine, so it must be cut into pieces spread over machines.
  • Data is rarely updated in place (“in place” = overwriting bytes in the middle of an existing file).
  • Reads and appends are common: files are mostly scanned and extended at the end, like logs, web crawls and click streams.
Why this matters

If copies are never edited in the middle, keeping several copies identical is easy and cheap: you only ever add new data. A DFS is therefore not a general-purpose file system for many small, frequently edited files. Beyond the slides: that is why HDFS is a poor fit for lots of tiny files or for low-latency random updates.

Chunks and chunk servers (Slide 19)

Lecture 2 · Slide 19

Slide 19 introduces the building blocks, with a picture of empty dashed boxes named “Chunk server 1, 2, 3, … N”. Data is kept in chunks spread across machines, and each chunk is typically 16–64 MB.

Definitions

A chunk is one fixed-size piece of a big file (16–64 MB). A chunk server is a machine (node) whose disk stores chunks. N is just “the large number of chunk servers”. In HDFS a chunk is called a block.

Tiny example: a 1 TB file (10⁶ MB) in 64 MB chunks is 10⁶ ÷ 64 = 15,625 chunks; in 16 MB chunks it is 10⁶ ÷ 16 = 62,500 chunks. (With binary units, 1 TB = 1,048,576 MB, you get 16,384 and 65,536; the order of magnitude is the same.) Different chunks of the same file normally land on different servers, so many servers can read the file at once, which is exactly the striping of Slide 8.

Beyond the slides: chunks are large (not 4 KB) so that the master’s list of chunks stays small, and so a program can read a chunk with one long sequential read instead of many slow disk seeks.

Replication (Slide 20)

Lecture 2 · Slide 20

Slide 20 adds the rule that makes the system reliable: each chunk is replicated on different machines, usually 2× or 3×, which ensures persistence and availability. The slide also says: try to keep replicas in different racks.

Definition: replication factor

The replication factor is the number of copies of each chunk (2× or 3×). A replica is one of the copies.

Why different racks? All 16–64 nodes of a rack share one switch (and often one power feed). If that switch fails, the whole rack disappears at once. If every copy of a chunk lived in that rack, the chunk would be unreachable. Replicas in different racks survive a rack failure.

  • Cost: 3× replication stores 3× the raw data. A 1 TB file occupies 3 TB (46,875 chunk copies at 64 MB).
  • Best effort: “try to” means the rack rule is a goal, not a guarantee. “2× or 3×” is a typical, configurable range.
Beyond the slides

Why replication works. Suppose, simplifying, that a chunk’s copies sit on random machines and 1,000 of 1,000,000 machines die in a day (Slide 12). One machine dies with probability 1,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 10⁻³. A chunk with 2 copies loses both with probability about (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶; with 3 copies about 10⁻⁹. Over the 15,625 chunks of the 1 TB file that is about 1.6 % per day at 2× (15,625 × 10⁻⁶) but only 0.0016 % at 3× (15,625 × 10⁻⁹), if no lost copy were ever rebuilt. Re-creating lost copies quickly (next sections) is what keeps the real risk tiny. This is a simplified independent-failure model, not from the slides.

A file placed on the cluster (Slides 21–22)

Lecture 2 · Slides 21–22

Slide 21: File 1 (named C) is divided into six chunks C0–C5. (The letter C is the file’s name and the subscript is the chunk index.) The picture scatters the chunks over chunk servers, one copy each: server 1 holds C0, C1, C5, C2; server 2 holds C3; server 3 holds C4; server N is empty. They need not be in order or evenly spread.

This is not safe: lose server 1 and C0, C1, C2 and C5 are gone. Slide 22 repeats the picture and adds the fix: “You need copies of these chunks (e.g., C1). Copies are never on the same chunk server.” The replicated layout (2×) is:

ChunkC0C1C2C3C4C5
Copies on servers1, N1, 21, 32, N3, N1, 2

Check: every chunk has exactly two copies, 6 × 2 = 12 boxes (4 on server 1 + 3 on server 2 + 2 on server 3 + 3 on server N = 12), and no server holds two copies of the same chunk.

Key idea: never the same server

Two copies on the same machine would die together and give no protection. The stronger wish of Slide 20 (different racks) is a further layer: servers 1 and 2 above both hold C1 and C5, so if they shared a rack, a rack failure would destroy both chunks. The figure shows only the machine-level rule; it does not show racks.

Slide erratum (typos only)

Slide 22 reads “copies of this chunks (e.g, C1)”; it should be “these chunks (e.g., C1)”. The labels C3 and C4 are faint and identified only by colour; the placement above was read from the figure and cross-checked by counting boxes.

Seamless recovery from failure (Slide 23)

Lecture 2 · Slide 23

Slide 23 calls this a reliable distributed file system with seamless recovery from disk or machine failure. “Seamless” means the application using the file does not notice and does not need special code. Here is the mechanism, using Figure L2p1-5:

  1. Failure. Chunk server 1 crashes. Its four chunks C0, C1, C2, C5 each lose one copy.
  2. Reads continue. Each lost chunk still has a second copy elsewhere (C0 on N, C1 and C5 on server 2, C2 on server 3), so a reader is simply directed to a surviving copy. Nothing is unavailable.
  3. Re-replication. The system notices that these chunks are down to one copy and makes a new copy of each on a server that does not already hold it, restoring 2×.
  4. Back to normal. Every chunk again has two copies on two different servers.

(Beyond the slides: the master node of the next section is the component that notices the failure, because it knows where every chunk is. The slides do not show this step; they only promise the outcome.)

Exam tip

If asked how the DFS tolerates a machine failure, write the chain: chunks are replicated on different machines (2×/3×, different racks if possible) → data stays readable from another replica → the system re-creates the lost copies → no data loss and no interruption. Without the re-creation step, repeated failures would eventually destroy all copies.

Computation moves to the data (Slide 23)

Lecture 2 · Slide 23

The lower half of Slide 23 carries the second Map-Reduce idea in two banners: “Bring computation directly to the data!” and “Chunk servers also serve as compute servers.” The same machines that store the chunks also run the computation, so a task can run on a server that already holds its chunk and read from its local disk with no network transfer. This is called data locality.

The figure also shows that one cluster holds many files: the slide adds a second file D divided into two chunks D0 and D1 (pink and light green) next to file C.

Common mistake

Do not read replica counts off Slide 23. It is an illustration, not a consistent 2×/3× layout: C3 and D1 appear once, C5 four times, C4 not at all. The servers between 3 and N are hidden behind the “…” and may hold the missing copies. Colours also differ from Slides 21–22 (C3 is bright green here, dark green there).

If a computation cannot run on a node holding the chunk, the next best choice is a node in the same rack (link at 1 Gbps), and the worst choice is a node in another rack (shared 2–10 Gbps backbone); see the distance table in the cluster section. Beyond the slides: the Map-Reduce scheduler uses exactly this preference order when it assigns tasks.

Master node and client library (Slide 24)

Lecture 2 · Slide 24

Someone must remember where every chunk is. Slide 24 introduces two components:

  • Master node (in the Google File System; a.k.a. Name Node in Hadoop’s HDFS). It stores metadata about where files are stored and might be replicated.
  • Client library for file access. It talks to the master to find chunk servers, then connects directly to the chunk servers to access data without going through the master.
Definition: metadata

Metadata is “data about data”: which chunks make up file C and which chunk servers hold each chunk’s copies. The master stores this catalogue; it does not store the file’s bytes.

How a read works, step by step

Lecture 2 · Slide 24

  1. The application asks the client library to open file C.
  2. The library asks the master: “where are the chunks of C?”
  3. The master replies with, for each chunk, the list of chunk servers holding a copy (a small message).
  4. The library connects directly to a chunk server for each chunk and reads the bytes. The master is no longer involved, so it never becomes a bottleneck for the terabytes of data traffic.
Beginner intuition

The master is the library catalogue; the chunk servers are the shelves. You ask the catalogue once (“which shelf holds chapter 3?”), then walk to the shelf and read yourself. The librarian never carries the books.

Common mistake

“Without master node” on the slide means the data transfer bypasses the master, not that the master is never contacted. Also, “might be replicated” is vague: a single, un-replicated master would be a single point of failure, which is why it may have standby copies. Beyond the slides: chunk servers report the chunks they hold to the master, which is how it learns locations.

RoleGFS (Google) termHDFS (Hadoop) termWhat it does
Catalogue of locationsMaster nodeName NodeStores metadata only; may be replicated (Slide 24)
Machine storing dataChunk serverData Node (beyond the slides)Stores chunks on its disk; also runs computation
Piece of a fileChunk (16–64 MB)BlockReplicated 2×–3× on different servers (different racks if possible)
Application interfaceClient libraryAsks the master, then reads/writes chunk servers directly

Closing the storage story: issue, idea, solution

Lecture 2 · Slide 25

Slide 25 (“Idea and Solution”) ties it together in three beats:

  • Issue: copying data over a network takes time (the 10 TB ≈ 1 day of Slide 14).
  • Idea: bring computation close to the data (Slide 23: chunk servers are compute servers).
  • Map-Reduce addresses these problems. It is Google’s computational/data-manipulation model, an elegant way to work with big data, and a programming model: you supply the two functions Map and Reduce and the system runs them on the cluster.

The slide does not yet define Map or Reduce; the next slides do, starting with the word-count warm-up. Beyond the slides: Map-Reduce was introduced by Google (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004) and Hadoop MapReduce is its open-source implementation. Note the slight circularity of the slide’s wording (“Programming model → Map-Reduce”): Map-Reduce is the programming model.

Quick recap
  • One node reading 200 TB at 50 MB/s needs 4 × 10⁶ s ≈ 46 days; 1,000 discs in parallel (ideal case) need 4,000 s.
  • Standard architecture: a cluster of commodity nodes (CPU + memory + disk), 16–64 per rack, 1 Gbps in a rack, 2–10 Gbps backbone between racks; ~1M machines at Google.
  • Challenge 1: failures are daily routine (1,000 machines a day at 1M). Challenge 2: network bottleneck (10 TB ≈ 1 day at 1 Gbps). Challenge 3: distributed programming is hard.
  • Three ideas: store data redundantly, move computation close to data, simple programming model.
  • DFS (GFS/HDFS): huge files, rare in-place updates, reads and appends; chunks of 16–64 MB; replicated 2×–3× on different servers and, if possible, racks.
  • Chunk servers also compute (data locality). The master/Name Node holds only metadata; clients ask it once, then talk directly to chunk servers.
Practice: check yourself (self-made, not from the course)
  1. Why is a replica never placed on the same chunk server as another copy of the same chunk? (Both would die together; Slide 22.)
  2. A 640 GB file uses 64 MB chunks and 3× replication. How many chunks and how many chunk copies? (640,000 MB ÷ 64 = 10,000 chunks; × 3 = 30,000 copies; 1.92 TB of raw storage.)
  3. Does the master node ever see the file’s bytes during a read? (No: metadata only; data flows between client and chunk servers.)

The warm-up task: counting words

Lecture 2 · Slide 26

Slides 1–25 explained why big data needs many machines and where the data lives (a distributed file system, DFS, with chunks replicated on chunk servers). Slide 26 now asks how to compute on it. The lecture uses one problem to teach the whole programming model:

Warm-up task (Slide 26)

We have a huge text document. Count the number of times each distinct word appears in the file. This is word count, the "hello world" of Map-Reduce.

Slide 26 lists two sample applications that have exactly the same shape:

  • Term search statistics: count how often each search term was queried (the "word" is a query term).
  • Web-server logs: count the hits per URL to find the popular URLs (the "word" is a URL).
Beginner intuition

On one machine this is easy: read the words one by one and keep a tally table (the → 1204, big → 87, …). The difficulty is purely one of scale: the file is stored as chunks on hundreds of machines, no single machine can read it all in reasonable time (Slides 5–8), and machines fail (Slides 12–13). Map-Reduce is a way to describe this tally so that the system can run it on all the chunks at the same time.

Slide 26 only poses the task. The solution is built step by step on Slides 27–42; try to predict it as you read. The complete practice problem is Quiz L2-Q3, placed after Slide 42.

Map-Reduce overview: four stages

Lecture 2 · Slides 27–28

Every Map-Reduce job, whatever the problem, follows the same four stages (Slide 27):

  1. Map. Scan the input file record-at-a-time. For each record, extract (output) "something you care about" as (key, value) pairs. A record is one unit of input, for example one line of a text file or one row of a log.
  2. Group by key (sort and shuffle). Collect all pairs that have the same key and bring them together.
  3. Reduce. For each key, aggregate, summarise, filter or transform the values collected for it.
  4. Write the result (to the distributed file system, as Slide 55 later states).
Definitions
  • Key-value pair (k, v): a two-part item. The key says what the item is about (a word, a host name); the value is the data attached to it (a count, a size). Everything that flows through Map-Reduce is a key-value pair.
  • Shuffle: moving the pairs across the network so that equal keys end up on the same machine. Sort: ordering the pairs by key so equal keys sit next to each other.

Slide 28 is a one-sentence take-away in a black box: "Outline stays the same, Map and Reduce change to fit the problem." The four-stage skeleton is fixed and supplied by the framework; the only things you change from problem to problem are the two functions you plug in.

Programmer providesFramework (the "environment") provides
Mapthe Map function: what to extract from each recordreading the chunks, running many Map calls in parallel
Group by keynothingpartitioning, shuffling over the network, sorting and grouping
Reducethe Reduce function: how to combine the values of one keyrunning many Reduce calls in parallel
Write the resultnothingstoring the output in the DFS (Slide 55)
Everything elsenothingscheduling, communication, failure handling (Slide 53, below)
Key idea

Think of Map-Reduce as an assembly line (the fixed skeleton) with two interchangeable tools (Map and Reduce) that you clip in. The programmer writes only Map and Reduce; the grouping step is not written by the programmer.

Exam tip

"Who writes what?" is a classic short question. Answer: the programmer supplies Map and Reduce (and names the input files); the framework does the group-by-key (sort and shuffle) and everything about machines. The slides state this explicitly through the "Provided by the programmer" captions on Slides 36–38, which sit over Map and Reduce but not over Group by key.

The data model: Map step and Reduce step

Lecture 2 · Slides 29–35

Slides 29–35 draw the same pipeline abstractly, with shapes instead of words. Shape and colour are only a drawing convention: colour = key identity (a purple key stays purple from column to column) and shape = type (triangle/rectangle for input keys/values, diamond/parallelogram for intermediate, diamond/octagon for output). Figure L2-7 redraws the whole sequence with the types written out and a word-count instance underneath.

The Map step

Lecture 2 · Slides 29–31

  • Slide 29: input key-value pairs. The input is a (typically huge) set of pairs. What k and v mean depends on the application, for example (document name, document text) or (position in file, one line of text).
  • Slide 30: the first map application. The function map is applied to one input pair and produces intermediate key-value pairs. On the slide, one input pair becomes two intermediate pairs. Map may emit zero, one or many pairs; it is not "one in, one out". The new keys are chosen by the programmer and need not resemble the input key (for word count: input key = document name, intermediate key = a word). "Intermediate" simply means "not the final answer yet".
  • Slide 31: map is applied to every input pair. The intermediate collection is the union of what all the map calls emitted. It is still unorganised: the same key may appear many times, from different inputs.
Key idea: independence gives parallelism

Each map call looks at its own input pair only. So the calls can run on different machines at the same time, and if one fails it can simply be run again without affecting the others. This independence is the source of Map-Reduce's parallelism and of its easy failure recovery (Slide 57, below).

The Reduce step: group by key, then reduce

Lecture 2 · Slides 32–35

  • Slide 32: group by key. Starting from the intermediate pairs, the next operation brings together all pairs that share a key. It is performed by the system. (The slide title says "Reduce Step" because the lecture treats grouping as the front part of the reduce phase.)
  • Slide 33: key-value groups. The flat list becomes a list of (key, list of all its values). Each distinct key appears exactly once, with a variable-length list: three values for the purple key, two for ochre, one for yellow. The order of values inside a group carries no meaning. All values of one key must arrive at one machine, which is why the shuffle is expensive.
  • Slide 34: first reduce. Reduce is applied once per key group. It receives the key and all its values and emits an output key-value pair, typically (key, one combined value) such as a sum, count or maximum. The shape changes from parallelogram to octagon to signal that the output value is a different kind of value.
  • Slide 35: the complete picture. Intermediate pairs → (group by key) → key-value groups → (reduce, once per key) → output pairs. The sizes shrink to the right: 3 values → 1, 2 values → 1, 1 value → 1.
Slide erratum (minor, schematic figures)

Slides 33 and 35 are drawings, not literal traces: the purple group has three values although only one purple pair is visible in the left column (the rest hide in the "…"), and the light-teal key of the intermediate column has no group or output. The yellow group also has an output pair but no drawn "reduce" arrow. Do not try to match the figure pair for pair; read it as a picture of the types.

Quick recap (Slides 29–35)
  • Input (k, v) → map (once per input pair, zero or more outputs) → intermediate (k', v').
  • Intermediate pairs → group by key (by the system) → one group (k', list of v') per distinct key.
  • Each group → reduce (once per key) → output pair (k', v'').

Word count, step by step

Lecture 2 · Slides 36–40

Slides 36–40 build one picture in five steps, using a "Big document" that begins "The crew of the space shuttle Endeavor recently returned to Earth as ambassadors, harbingers of a new era of space exploration …". Three coloured lists appear from left to right: teal (Map output), amber (after Group by key), green (after Reduce).

SlideWhat is addedWhat it shows
36Map box, caption "Provided by the programmer"; teal list (The,1) (crew,1) (of,1) (the,1) (space,1) (shuttle,1) (Endeavor,1) (recently,1) …For every word occurrence Map emits (word, 1): "I saw this word once." Map does not count anything; the counting happens later. The eight pairs are exactly the first eight words of the document.
37Group by key box ("Collect all pairs with same key"), amber list (crew,1) (crew,1) (space,1) (the,1) (the,1) (the,1) (shuttle,1) (recently,1) …Equal keys become adjacent. No "Provided by the programmer" caption: the system does this.
38Reduce box, second "Provided by the programmer" caption; green list (crew,2) (space,1) (the,3) (shuttle,1) (recently,1) …Reduce sums the 1s of each key: two 1s for crew give 2, three 1s for the give 3. Output = (word, number of occurrences).
39Three pairs of red lines cutting the document and the Map output into four piecesThe big document is cut into pieces (chunks); each piece produces its own part of the Map output. Separate machines (map tasks) read their pieces at the same time. This is where parallelism enters. (The slide gives no words for the red lines; this is the natural reading.)
40Red lines around the three (the,1) pairs and the one (the,3); big arrow "Only sequential reads"One key group (the) is handled as a unit and can be reduced independently, possibly on another machine. The whole pipeline needs only sequential reads.

Why "only sequential reads" matters

Lecture 2 · Slide 40

A sequential read streams through a file from start to end; random access jumps around it. Disks are fast at the first and slow at the second (every jump costs a seek). Map scans its chunk from start to end, and the sort-and-group works on whole files of pairs, so nothing needs to leap around. Beyond the slides: that is the standard reasoning; the slide only states the take-away. It fits the lecture's earlier assumption of a disk read speed of 30–50 MB/s (Slides 5–8): the job should always read at that streaming speed.

Slide erratum (Slides 36–38: the lists are schematic)
  • The Map list contains both (The,1) and (the,1) (capital T), but the grouped and reduced lists show only the with three pairs. Either the figure is schematic or case is ignored. The pseudo-code on Slides 41–42 does no lower-casing, so under that code The and the are two different keys. Remember: a key is compared exactly, so normalising case is the Map function's job.
  • The grouped list omits (of,1) and (Endeavor,1) from the Map list, its keys are in no particular order, and counts such as (crew,2) and (the,3) cannot be derived from the visible excerpt alone (it has crew once). The "…" hides the rest of the document. Treat the three lists as an illustrative selection, not an exact trace.
  • Slide 38 says Reduce "collects all values belonging to the key and outputs". Strictly, the collecting was done by Group by key; Reduce combines the collected values (here by addition).
  • Slide 36 says "Read input and produces" (should be "produce"); the document text contains the typo "man/mache" (probably "man/machine"). Harmless.

The word-count pseudo-code

Lecture 2 · Slides 41–42

Not examined — code (understand, don't memorise)

Slides 41–42 give pseudo-code for word count. Explained in words, no code to learn:

  • Map receives one input pair: the document name (key) and the document text (value). It walks over every word w of the text and, for each occurrence, emits the pair (w, 1). The key (document name) is not used. This produces exactly the teal list of Slides 36–40.
  • Reduce receives one word (the key) and an iterator over all the counts collected for it. It starts a running total at 0, adds each count to it, and finally emits (word, total) once, after the loop. For key the with counts [1,1,1] the total is 3, so it emits (the, 3), as on Slide 38.
  • The whole program is these two short functions. Grouping and everything else is done by the framework.

Not specified by the pseudo-code: how text is split into words, whether punctuation is removed and whether case is normalised. On Slide 42 the comment says "value: an iterator over counts" while the parameter is named values; a typo.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution, decide the key and value for word count, then trace the pipeline on the practice input with two mappers and two reducers.

Quick maths: mod, hash, straggler, partition (used before they are explained)

x mod R is the remainder after dividing x by R (7 mod 3 = 1). A hash function turns a key into a big number, so hash(key) mod R is always one of 0, …, R−1, i.e. a reduce-task number. A partition function is exactly this key-to-reduce-task rule (details in the partition-function section of Part 3). A straggler is a task that runs unusually slowly (defined in the backup-tasks section of Part 3).

The slides pose no numbered question, so this block turns Slides 26–42 into five exam-style parts. Practice: the 3-line input in (b) is invented for this guide (it is not on the slides), and so are the task numbers and the toy partition rule stated in (b).

(a) State precisely what the programmer provides and what the framework does. Which key and which value do you choose for word count, and why?
(b) Trace the whole pipeline Map → Group by key (sort & shuffle) → Reduce on this practice input, with 2 mappers and 2 reducers:
