1The crew of the space shuttleMap task 0
2crew recently returned to EarthMap task 1
3the Earth is blueMap task 1
Set-up for this practice: Map writes every word in lower case; there are R = 2 reduce tasks; if no partition rule is given, use the toy rule “reduce task = (number of letters in the key) mod 2”.
(c) Reproduce the slide’s example counts (crew,2) (space,1) (the,3) (shuttle,1) (recently,1) from the grouped pairs of Slides 37–38 and show where each one comes from.
(d) Explain the slide pseudo-code (Slides 41–42) in words.
(e) What does the red arrow “Only sequential reads” on Slide 40 mean, and why is it good?
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Counting votes in a huge election. A mountain of ballot papers must be tallied by candidate. Many volunteers each take a small stack. For every ballot they read, they write one slip “(candidate, 1)” — they do not add anything up yet. That is Map. Then the post office sorts all slips of all volunteers into piles, one pile per candidate, and delivers every pile to a counting desk; the same candidate’s slips always land at the same desk. That is Group by key (nobody on the staff has to write this part: it is the framework’s job). Finally each desk adds up the 1s in each pile and writes “(candidate, total)”. That is Reduce. You only describe how to make a slip (Map) and how to add up a pile (Reduce).

Key idea

The four-stage outline (Map, Group by key, Reduce, Write the result) never changes; only Map and Reduce change to fit the problem (Slide 28). For word count: the key is the word, the value is 1, and Reduce adds. Every item is a (key, value) pair. “Same key ⇒ same place”: that single rule is what makes the final counts correct. The same outline solves the sample applications of Slide 26: to find popular URLs in web server logs, Map outputs (URL,1) for every log line and Reduce is unchanged; for term search statistics, Map outputs (search term,1).

Part (a) — who provides what (Slides 27, 28, 36–38, 44, 53–55, 66–67)

  1. Formula / idea — the four stages (Slide 27): Map (scan the input record-at-a-time; output something you care about from each record, as keys and values) → Group by key (Sort and Shuffle) → Reduce (aggregate, summarise, filter or transform) → write the result. Why two functions are enough: Map says “what do I extract from one record?” and Reduce says “what do I do with everything that shares a key?”. Everything else is routine plumbing that is identical for every job.
  2. Choose the key and the value (the one design decision of this job). To know how often a word occurs, all its occurrences must be brought to one place and added up. Group by key brings together everything that shares a key, so the key must be the word. Each time a word is seen its tally goes up by exactly one, so the value is 1; adding the 1s later gives the total. This is exactly what Slide 36 shows: (crew,1), (space,1), …
  3. The shape of the data at each stage (Slides 29–35). Everything is a (key, value) pair. Input pairs go through map and become intermediate pairs (one input pair can produce any number of them, Slides 30–31); group by key gathers all intermediate values that share a key into one group (Slides 32–33); reduce turns each group into one output pair (Slides 34–35).
    StageSlidesWhat it holdsWord count
    Input key-value pairs29(k, v), one per record(line number, text of the line)
    Intermediate key-value pairs30–31(k’, v’), many per input pair(the,1) — one for each word occurrence
    Key-value groups32–33(k’, v’ v’ v’ …): all values of one key(the,[1,1,1])
    Output key-value pairs34–35(k’, v’’), one per group(the,3)
  4. The two programmer-written functions, in the slides’ notation (Slide 44):
    Formula

    Map(k, v) → <k’, v’>*    (one input pair in; a set of zero or more key–value pairs out; one Map call for every input pair)

    Reduce(k’, <v’>*) → k’, v’’    (a key and the list of all its values in; the key and one result out; one Reduce call per unique key k’)

    For word count: Map(line id, line text) → a pair (word, 1) for every word occurrence; Reduce(word, list of 1s) → (word, sum of the list). (Slide 44’s example: “value is a single line in the file”, so one Map call per line. Slide 44 also says all values with the same key are “reduced together and processed in v’ order”; for addition the order is irrelevant, Slide 62.)
  5. Division of labour — table:
    PieceWhoWhat it does (slide wording) and the word-count meaningSlides
    Mapprogrammer“Read input and produces a set of key-value pairs.” Word count: for each word w in the record, output (w, 1).27, 36, 41
    Group by keyframework“Collect all pairs with same key” — Sort and Shuffle (also named “Hash merge, Shuffle, Sort, Partition”). Not labelled “Provided by the programmer” on the slides.27, 37, 51
    Reduceprogrammer“Collect all values belonging to the key and output.” Word count: add up the 1s of one word and output (word, total).27, 38, 42
    Input filesprogrammer“Programmer specifies: Map and Reduce and input files.”54
    Everything elseframework“Map-Reduce environment takes care of”: scheduling the program’s execution across a set of machines; managing required inter-machine communication; partitioning the data; performing the group by key step; handling machine failures.53
    Optional extrasprogrammerA combiner that pre-adds on the mapper (Slides 59–62); a custom partition function — the default is hash(key) mod R (Slides 66–67).59–67
  6. Where the data lives (Slide 55): the input and the final output are on the distributed file system (DFS); the scheduler tries to place map tasks “close” to the physical location of their input data (the Slide 25 idea: bring the computation to the data); intermediate pairs are kept on the local file system of the mapper’s machine until the reducers fetch them.

Part (b) — trace on the practice input (Slides 36–40, 51–54, 66)

Three set-up decisions (state them in your answer)

1. Which words are “the same”? We let Map write each word in lower case (so “The” and “the” are one word) and our input has no punctuation (a real Map would also strip it). The slide’s final (the,3) only works if “The” and “the” are merged (see the erratum below). 2. How many tasks? The file is cut into 2 chunks (one DFS chunk per Map task is common, Slide 69), so there are 2 map tasks, and we use R = 2 reduce tasks. Real jobs use many more (Slide 69: far more map tasks than nodes, and usually R smaller than the number of map tasks); two of each just keeps the picture small. We number tasks from 0 as Slide 54 does. 3. Which reducer gets which key? The real default is hash(key) mod R (Slide 66), which cannot be computed by hand, so we use a simple toy rule instead (Step 3).

  1. Step 1 — split the input (framework). The framework partitions the data into chunks and hands one chunk to each Map task (Slide 53: “partitioning the data”; Slide 39 shows the document cut into pieces). Chunk 0 = line 1 (goes to Map task 0). Chunk 1 = lines 2 and 3 (goes to Map task 1). Chunk boundaries fall between records, so no line is cut in half. Why: each Map call needs only its own record, so chunks can be processed on different machines at the same time.
  2. Step 2 — Map (programmer’s function; one call per line). Rule: for every word occurrence w output (lower-case w, 1). Map does not count: if “the” occurs twice in a line it simply outputs two (the,1) pairs.
    Map taskMap call (input record)Pairs output (in reading order)#
    0line 1: “The crew of the space shuttle”(the,1) (crew,1) (of,1) (the,1) (space,1) (shuttle,1)6
    1line 2: “crew recently returned to Earth”(crew,1) (recently,1) (returned,1) (to,1) (earth,1)5
    line 3: “the Earth is blue”(the,1) (earth,1) (is,1) (blue,1)4
    Total intermediate pairs = 6 + 5 + 4 (one per word occurrence; the input has 15 words)15
    There were 3 Map calls (one per input record, Slide 44) — 1 on Map task 0 and 2 on Map task 1.
  3. Step 3 — Group by key, part A: partition (framework). Every pair must be sent to the reduce task that is responsible for its key, and the rule must give the same task for the same key, whichever mapper produced the pair (Slide 66: “records with the same intermediate key end up at the same worker”; Slide 52 draws a “Partitioning Function” at the end of every Map task). In this example we use the simple toy rule below.
    Formula

    Reduce task number = (number of letters in the key) mod R, with R = 2. (Any rule that looks only at the key would do; what matters is that the same key always gets the same number.)

    Keythespaceshuttleearthcrewofrecentlyreturnedtoisblue
    letters35754288224
    mod 2 → task11110000000
    Pairs on each route: Map 0 → Reduce 0: crew, of (2); Map 0 → Reduce 1: the, the, space, shuttle (4); Map 1 → Reduce 0: crew, recently, returned, to, is, blue (6); Map 1 → Reduce 1: earth, the, earth (3). Check: 2 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 15. Notice crew and the are each made by both mappers, yet each ends up on a single reducer. Why must the rule look at the key only? If the three (the,1) pairs could be split between two reducers (say 2 at one and 1 at the other), the output would contain (the,2) and (the,1) — two partial counts instead of (the,3). With any key-only rule the final counts are the same; only the split of the words between the two output files changes.
  4. Step 4 — Group by key, part B: shuffle, then sort and group (framework). Shuffle = copy the pairs across the network from the mappers’ local disks to the reducers: every Map task sends to every Reduce task (the all-to-all arrows of Slide 54), and the master tells the reducers where each mapper’s files are (Slide 56). Each reducer then sorts its pairs by key, which puts equal keys next to each other, and groups them into one list per key (Slide 52: “Sort and Group”). The result is the “key-value groups” of Slides 33–35:
    Reduce taskPairs receivedAfter sort & group: (key, list of values)#keys
    08(blue,[1]) (crew,[1,1]) (is,[1]) (of,[1]) (recently,[1]) (returned,[1]) (to,[1])7
    17(earth,[1,1]) (shuttle,[1]) (space,[1]) (the,[1,1,1])4
    Within one reducer the keys come out in alphabetical order; there is no global order across the two reducers, because they hold different sets of words. Pairs received: 8 + 7 = 15, none lost.
  5. Step 5 — Reduce (programmer’s function; one call per key). Rule: result = sum of the values in the list; output (key, result).
    Reduce taskReduce calls (key: sum)Output pairs
    0blue: 1 · crew: 1+1 · is: 1 · of: 1 · recently: 1 · returned: 1 · to: 1(blue,1) (crew,2) (is,1) (of,1) (recently,1) (returned,1) (to,1)
    1earth: 1+1 · shuttle: 1 · space: 1 · the: 1+1+1(earth,2) (shuttle,1) (space,1) (the,3)
    There are 7 + 4 = 11 Reduce calls, one per distinct word (Slide 44: “one Reduce function call per unique key”), not one per pair (there are 15 pairs).
  6. Step 6 — write the result (Slides 27, 54, 55). Each reduce task writes its own output file to the DFS (“Out 0” and “Out 1” on Slide 54): output file 0 holds 7 pairs, output file 1 holds 4 pairs. Together they are the answer. (Output is often the input of another Map-Reduce job, Slide 55.)
  7. Step 7 — sanity checks (quick marks-savers). (i) pairs output by Map = words in the input: 15 = 15. (ii) the final counts add up to the same number: (1+2+1+1+1+1+1) + (2+1+1+3) = 8 + 7 = 15. (iii) Reduce calls = distinct words: 11. (iv) Map calls = input records: 3. (v) count by hand from the text: “the” occurs 2 + 0 + 1 = 3 times (lines 1, 2, 3), “crew” 2 (lines 1 and 2), “earth” 2 (lines 2 and 3), and the other eight words once each, which matches the Reduce output. If any check fails, a pair was lost or double-counted.
Common mistake
  • Adding inside Map. Writing (the,2) for a line that contains “the” twice is wrong for this Map: Map outputs one (w,1) per occurrence (Slide 41); adding is Reduce’s job. (Pre-adding on the map side is a separate, optional optimisation, the combiner of Slides 59–62.)
  • Reduce is called once per distinct key, not once per pair (Slide 44): 11 calls here, not 15.
  • One key, one reducer. The final list is per key, so a word that appears in two lines or on two mappers must still appear only once in the output.
  • Mappers never talk to each other. Intermediate data travels only from the map side to the reduce side, through the shuffle.
  • Case and punctuation. “The” and “the” are two different keys unless Map lower-cases the word; decide, and say so in your answer.

Part (c) — reproducing the slide’s counts (Slides 36–38)

  1. Formula / idea: final count of a word = sum of the values in its group = number of times Map output that word (because every value is 1). count(w) = ∑ of the list for key w = number of (w,1) pairs.
  2. Read the Map box of Slide 36. It is Map applied to the first words of the document, “The crew of the space shuttle Endeavor recently”: 8 words give 8 pairs, (The,1) (crew,1) (of,1) (the,1) (space,1) (shuttle,1) (Endeavor,1) (recently,1); the dots “….” stand for the pairs of the rest of the document.
  3. Take the Group-by-key box of Slides 37–38 (8 grouped pairs) and apply Reduce to each group (Slide 38):

    crew(crew,1) (crew,1)[1, 1]1 + 1 = 2(crew,2) ✓Reduce 0 (both mappers contribute)
    space(space,1)[1]1(space,1) ✓Reduce 1
    the(the,1) (the,1) (the,1)[1, 1, 1]1 + 1 + 1 = 3(the,3) ✓Reduce 1 (both mappers contribute)

Why the practice input of (b) was chosen this way: it contains “the” three times (twice in line 1, once in line 3) and “crew” twice (lines 1 and 2), and “space”, “shuttle”, “recently” once each, so the same five results appear in our trace; the extra words (of, returned, to, earth, is, blue) make the group-by-key step more interesting. The slide’s “…” means more pairs exist in the real big document; we only see a sample of them.
Slide erratum (minor — the slide figures are illustrative)
  • “The” vs “the”. Slide 36 lists (The,1) and (the,1) as two separate pairs, but Slides 37–38 then show only lower-case (the,1) pairs and the result (the,3). With the pseudo-code of Slides 41–42 taken literally (each word w is used exactly as written, no case conversion) “The” and “the” are different keys and would be counted separately. Correct version: the slide’s result is right only if Map first converts every word to lower case; that is what we did. If you want case-insensitive counts, lower-case the word inside Map and say so.
  • The numbers are schematic. The text excerpt visible on Slide 36 already contains lower-case “the” five times, “The” twice (seven “the” in all, ignoring case), “crew” once and “space” at least twice (“space shuttle”, “era of space exploration”), so (the,3) and (crew,2) cannot be counts of the visible text; also (of,1) and (Endeavor,1) disappear between the Map box and the Group box. Treat the slide’s lists as a picture of the pattern (many (w,1) → groups → sums), not as numbers to re-derive from the photo of the document.
  • Order. The groups on Slides 37–38 are in order of appearance (crew, space, the, shuttle, recently), not alphabetical. This does not matter: group by key only guarantees that equal keys are together.

Part (d) — the pseudo-code explained in words (Slides 41–42)

Not examined — code (understand, don't memorise)

Slide 41 shows the first function, Slide 42 adds the second (the code is the slide’s; no code will be asked in the exam):

map(key, value):
// key: document name; value: text of the document
  for each word w in value:
     emit(w, 1)

reduce(key, values):
// key: a word; value: an iterator over counts
      result = 0
      for each count v in values:
            result += v
      emit(key, result)

In words — map: it is handed one input record (a document name, or in our trace a line number, as the key, and the text as the value). It looks at every word in the text, one after the other, and for each word it writes down the pair (word, 1) with emit (“emit” = hand one output pair to the framework). It keeps no tally. The input key (the document name) is not used. reduce: it is handed one word and an iterator (a one-by-one walk through the list) over all the counts the Map calls produced for that word. It starts a running total at 0, adds each count to it, and finally emits (word, total). Because Map only produces 1s, total = how many times the word occurred. The two emit lines are the only way these functions hand their results back to the framework; grouping is not in the code at all because the framework does it. (Slide 41 says the value is “text of the document”, Slide 44 says “a single line in the file”: both are fine, because Map is called once per input record, whatever a record is.)

Part (e) — Slides 39–40: the red lines and “Only sequential reads”

  1. What the slides show. On Slide 39 red lines cut the document, and the Map output next to it, into bands; on Slide 40 more red lines fence off the three (the,1) pairs in the group box and the matching result (the,3), and a big red arrow pointing down carries the words “Only sequential reads”. The slides do not label the red lines; our reading is that each band is a piece of work that a different task can handle (document pieces by different Map tasks, Slides 52 and 69; all the pairs of one key — here “the” — as one independent unit of Reduce work).
  2. Meaning of “Only sequential reads”. Every phase works through its data from top to bottom in one pass, never jumping to random positions: Map scans its input record-at-a-time (Slide 27); the group step streams the pairs and puts equal keys together; Reduce walks through each group’s values once (the “iterator over counts” of Slide 42).
  3. Why that is good (Slides 18–19). The data are huge files (hundreds of GB to TB) that are mostly read and appended to and rarely updated in place (Slide 18), stored as large chunks of 16–64 MB (Slide 19). Reading big blocks in order is the access pattern that disks and distributed file systems handle best, so no phase needs an expensive random lookup into the big file. Beyond the slides: a disk seek to a random position is far slower than streaming the same amount of data in order, which is why large-scale systems are built around scans and sorting rather than random access.
Exam tip

For a “trace Map-Reduce on this input” question, draw the three columns of Slides 36–38: (1) Map output, one (w,1) per word occurrence; (2) after group by key: each key with the list of its values; (3) Reduce output, one pair per key. Say which key and value you chose, and label which part is written by the programmer (Map, Reduce) and which by the framework (group by key). Finish with the sanity checks of Step 7 (sum of counts = number of words; Reduce calls = distinct words); partial marks are given for each column even if a later one is wrong. Slogan: programmer = Map + Reduce; framework = everything in between, plus scheduling, failures and I/O.

Preview (Slides 59–62) — what a combiner would change here

If each mapper pre-added its own pairs before sending (a combiner; for word count it is the same function as Reduce), Map task 0 would send (the,2) instead of two (the,1), and Map task 1 would send (earth,2) instead of two (earth,1): 13 pairs (5 + 8) would travel instead of 15, but the final answer is identical. That is why Reduce must add its values and never just count the list length once a combiner is used.

Final answer: key = word, value = 1. Programmer = Map (one call per input pair: output (w,1) for every word occurrence) + Reduce (one call per distinct key: (w, [1,…,1]) → (w, ∑ list)) + the input files; framework = splitting, scheduling, group by key (partition, shuffle, sort and group), communication, failure handling, writing the output. Practice input: Map outputs 15 pairs (6 + 9) in 3 calls; Reduce 0 gets 8 pairs and outputs (blue,1) (crew,2) (is,1) (of,1) (recently,1) (returned,1) (to,1); Reduce 1 gets 7 pairs and outputs (earth,2) (shuttle,1) (space,1) (the,3) (11 distinct words = 11 Reduce calls; counts sum to 15). Slide counts: (crew,2) (space,1) (the,3) (shuttle,1) (recently,1) = sums of the groups [1,1], [1], [1,1,1], [1], [1]. “Only sequential reads” = every phase streams its data in one ordered pass, with no random access into the huge file.
Where the marks come from: (1) Choosing key = word and value = 1, with the reason (equal words must meet to be added). (2) Correct roles: programmer writes Map and Reduce (and names the input files), framework does splitting, scheduling, group by key, data movement, failures; Map(k,v) → <k’,v’>* and Reduce(k’,<v’>*) → k’,v’’ with one Map call per input pair and one Reduce call per key. (3) Map output is (word, 1) per occurrence with the right 15 pairs. (4) Group by key: same key to the same reducer, shuffle across mappers, sort and group into lists (the list for “the” is [1,1,1]). (5) Reduce sums each list, one call per distinct key (11). (6) Final counts correct, including the five slide counts. (7) Diagram or table in the order Map → Group → Reduce with the stage owners labelled. (8) Explaining the pseudo-code in words (map outputs (w,1); reduce adds up). (9) “Only sequential reads” explained. (A typical split only — marking schemes vary.)
Slide check: matches the slide’s answer — the five counts (crew,2) (space,1) (the,3) (shuttle,1) (recently,1) are reproduced, and the Map → Group by key → Reduce structure is exactly that of Slides 36–38. Slide erratum (minor): the slide’s “The”/“the” handling and its schematic counts, explained in the box above.

The programming model, more specifically

Lecture 2 · Slides 43–44

Slides 43–44 restate the model in general notation. The input is a set of key-value pairs, and the programmer specifies two methods:

Signatures (Slides 43–44)

Map(k, v) → <k', v'>*: takes one key-value pair and outputs a set (list) of key-value pairs.
Reduce(k', <v'>*) → k', v'': takes one key k' and the list of all values v' emitted for it, and outputs (k', v'') where v'' is the aggregated value.

In one line: Map: (k, v) → list of (k', v'). Reduce: (k', list of v') → (k', v'').

Reading the notation: the star * means "zero or more" (a list); <k', v'> is one pair; primes mark that the type changed (k to k', v to v' to v''). For example, value is a single line in the file is one possible record choice (Slide 43).

MapReduce
Inputone pair (k, v)one key k' with the list of all its v'
Outputany number of pairs (k', v'), including nonethe aggregated pair (k', v'')
How many callsone Map call for every (k, v) pairone Reduce call per unique key k'
Depends on other calls?no: every call is independentno: every key is independent
Worked example — counting calls Lecture 2 · Slides 43–44, 51

Take the document "a rose is a rose" as one input pair. That is 1 Map call. It emits 5 intermediate pairs. They contain 3 distinct keys (a, rose, is), so there are 3 Reduce calls, one per key: a gets [1, 1], rose gets [1, 1], is gets [1]. Output: (a,2) (rose,2) (is,1). If the input were instead split into the two lines "a rose" and "is a rose" as separate input pairs, there would be 2 Map calls, but still 3 Reduce calls: the number of Reduce calls depends on distinct keys, not on how the input is cut.

Common mistake: call versus task

A call is one invocation of the Map or Reduce function. A task is a unit of work run by a worker machine, and it makes many calls. "One Reduce call per unique key" does not mean one Reduce task per key: on Slide 52 Reduce task 1 handles keys k2, k4 and k5, i.e. three Reduce calls.

Slide erratum (Slide 44)
  • "All values v' with same key k' are reduced together and processed in v' order" is ambiguous. Beyond the slides: Map-Reduce sorts the keys (Slide 52, "Sort and Group") but does not guarantee any order for the values of one key. A Reduce function must therefore not depend on value order (summing, counting and maximum do not).
  • Map's output is written as a list <k', v'>* but Reduce's output as k', v'', with no star. A Reduce call may in general emit several pairs; the word-count code on Slide 42 emits exactly one.

Example: host size

Lecture 2 · Slides 45–47

Problem (Slide 45). A large web corpus has a metadata file with one record per page: (URL, size, date, …). For each host, find the total number of bytes. There may be many URLs for the same host name.

The host is the machine-name part of a URL. In the sample URL http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QhcwLyyEjOA the protocol is http://, the host is www.youtube.com, the path is /watch and v=QhcwLyyEjOA is the video id. (The odd spaces in the slide's rendering, "http:// www. youtube.com /watch", are a typesetting artefact; real URLs contain no spaces.) The task is "group by host, SUM(size)" over a corpus too big for one machine.

Answer (Slides 46–47). The hint on the slide, "many URLs for the same host", says: records with the same host must be brought together and added. That is group-by-key plus reduce.

  1. Map: for each record, output (hostname(URL), size). hostname(URL) is a helper that cuts the host out of the URL. The key is the host; the value is the page size; date and other fields are dropped. The choice of key is what makes the grouping collect "all pages of one host".
  2. Group by key: done by the framework; for each host it builds the list of all its sizes.
  3. Reduce: sum the sizes for each host and output (host, total bytes).
Worked example — three records Lecture 2 · Slides 46–47

Three invented records: (http://www.youtube.com/a, 3000), (http://www.yorku.ca/b, 500), (http://www.youtube.com/c, 2000). Map: (www.youtube.com,3000), (www.yorku.ca,500), (www.youtube.com,2000). Group: (www.youtube.com,[3000,2000]), (www.yorku.ca,[500]). Reduce: (www.youtube.com, 5000), (www.yorku.ca, 500). Check: 3000 + 2000 + 500 = 5500 bytes in, 5000 + 500 = 5500 out.

Exam tip

For any "compute X per Y" question, ask: "what must meet in one place to compute one answer?" That thing is the key. Here one answer = one host, so key = host. Then Map = emit (key, the number you need), Reduce = combine the numbers. Slide 47 lists the three steps; write all three, and say that Group by key is done by the framework.

Try it yourself first: design the job, then trace it on the 8-record practice file with two mappers and two reducers.

(d) Can a combiner be used in this job? Why is it legal here? Show its effect on the practice input.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition — receipts sorted by shop

Imagine a giant heap of receipts and a team of helpers. Each helper takes a few receipts and, for each receipt, writes one slip: “shop name – amount”. Everything else on the receipt (date, items) is ignored. The slips are then sorted into trays, one tray per shop, so every slip of one shop ends up in the same tray whichever helper wrote it. Finally one accountant per tray adds up the amounts. Here the “shop” is the host (www.youtube.com), the “amount” is the page size in bytes; helpers = Map, sorting into trays = Group by key (done by the framework), accountants = Reduce.

Steps are tagged (a)–(d) to match the four parts of the question.

  1. (a) Idea: decide the key and the value. The question asks for one number per host: the sum of the sizes of all pages of that host. As a formula, for one host h:
    Formula — what we compute

    total(h) = ∑ size(r) over all records r whose hostname(URLr) = h

    The sizes of one host's pages sit at different places of the file (possibly on different machines), so they must first be brought together and only then added. “Bring equal things together, then combine them” is exactly the outline of Slide 27 (Map, Group by key, Reduce), and what decides which items are brought together is the key. So: key = host name (what we group by), value = size (what we add up; we assume the size field is in bytes, as the question asks for bytes). The date and all other fields are not needed, so Map drops them. This is the word-count template of Slides 41–42 with one change: word count emits (word, 1) and adds the 1s; here we emit (host, size) and add the sizes.
    Common mistake

    Using the whole URL as the key. Then every URL forms its own group, sizes of different URLs of the same host are never brought together, and you get a size per page, not per host. That is why the slide stresses “there might be many URLs for the same host name”.

  2. (a) Map (Slide 46). In the slide's notation Map(k, v) → <k', v'>* (Slide 44). The input pair is (k, v) with v = one record (URL, size, date, …) (Slide 44: “value is a single line in the file”); k is just a position or record number that this job ignores. Map computes hostname(URL) and outputs exactly one pair per record:

    Map: (URL, size, date, …) → (hostname(URL), size)

    There is one Map call for every input pair (Slide 44), i.e. one per record: 8 calls for our 8 records. Each page belongs to exactly one host and adds its bytes to that host only, hence one pair. (Beyond the slides: a Map call may also emit zero pairs, for example for a malformed record with no URL, because the output is “a set of key-value pairs”.) Notice that Map does no adding: it sees one record at a time and knows nothing about the other records of the host.
  3. (a) Group by key (Slide 47). Done by the framework, not by the programmer (Slides 27, 51, 53). It collects all pairs with the same key using “Hash merge, Shuffle, Sort, Partition” (Slide 51): a partition function decides which reducer owns each key (default hash(key) mod R, Slide 66, where R = number of reducers), the pairs are moved across the network (the shuffle, Slide 54) and sorted so that equal keys sit together. Result: for every host one list host → [size, size, …]. Because the destination depends only on the key, all pairs of one host reach the same reducer, which is what makes a correct total possible.
  4. (a) Reduce (Slide 47: “Sum the sizes for each host”). Reduce(k', <v'>*) → k', v'' (Slide 44). It receives one host and the list of all sizes for that host, and outputs (host, ∑ sizes). There is one Reduce call per unique key (Slide 44): one per distinct host, so 3 calls in our example, not 8. Here k' = host, v' = size of one page, v'' = total bytes of the host. (Slide 44 says the values of a key are “processed in v' order”; for a sum the order does not matter.)
  5. (b) Where the host sits in a URL. A URL is built from parts: scheme://host[:port]/path?query. For the slide's sample the parts are http:// (scheme, i.e. protocol), www.youtube.com (host name) and /watch?v=QhcwLyyEjOA (path and query, which pick one page on that host). hostname(URL) must return only the middle part. This is why many URLs share one host: the host part stays the same while the path and the video ID change.
  6. (b) Recipe for hostname(URL) (the slides use the function without defining it, so this is the standard definition):
    1. Remove the scheme: everything up to and including ://.
    2. Keep the characters up to the first / (or ? or #); if there is none, keep everything to the end.
    3. Beyond the slides: if present, also drop a port number (:80) and any user@ prefix, and write the result in lower case (host names are not case-sensitive).
    Map only cuts a string: no web access is needed. Examples:
    URLhostname(URL) = keyComment
    http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QhcwLyyEjOAwww.youtube.comthe slide's sample
    http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=mapreducewww.youtube.comdifferent page, same host, so the same group
    http://www.yorku.ca/index.htmlwww.yorku.capath dropped
    http://en.wikipedia.org:80/wiki/Big_dataen.wikipedia.orgport :80 dropped
    HTTP://WWW.YouTube.com/watch?v=abcwww.youtube.comlower-cased, so the same key as the sample
    https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QhcwLyyEjOAwww.youtube.comthe scheme is not part of the host, so http and https pages share a key
    http://youtube.com/watch?v=abcyoutube.coma different string, hence a different key from www.youtube.com
    Convention to state in your answer: two host spellings are the same host only if the strings are equal after this clean-up, so www.youtube.com, youtube.com and m.youtube.com are three keys. If the question wanted them merged you would have to say so (for example “strip a leading www.”); the Map-Reduce structure does not change, only hostname() does. In practice a standard URL-parsing routine does this job; no code is examined.
  7. (c) Split the input; Map task versus Map call. The real file is cut into blocks and each block is read by one Map task (Slide 69: “one DFS chunk per map task is common”; DFS = distributed file system). Here records 1–4 go to Mapper M1 and records 5–8 to Mapper M2. A Map task is a process; a Map call is one invocation of the Map function (Slide 44: one per record). So M1 makes 4 calls, M2 makes 4 calls, 8 in total.
  8. (c) Map phase (Slide 46). For each record compute hostname(URL) and keep the size. Repeated hosts are not merged here.
    RecordMapperhostname(URL)sizeMap output pair
    1M1www.youtube.com52400(www.youtube.com, 52400)
    2M1www.youtube.com61700(www.youtube.com, 61700)
    3M1www.yorku.ca18300(www.yorku.ca, 18300)
    4M1www.youtube.com47100(www.youtube.com, 47100)

    6M2www.youtube.com58800(www.youtube.com, 58800)

    Total Map output = 8 pairs, one per record (the dates were dropped). Notice that M1 alone produced three www.youtube.com pairs and M2 one more.
  9. (c) Group by key, part 1: partition (Slides 47, 51, 66). Every mapper sorts its pairs into one bucket per reducer using a partition function of the key only. The default is reducer = hash(key) mod R with R = 2 (Slide 66); here we simply use the assignment given in the question (R0: www.youtube.com; R1: en.wikipedia.org and www.yorku.ca). A real hash could split the three hosts differently; the only guarantee is that one host always goes to one reducer. Why only the key? If the YouTube pairs were split between two reducers, each would output a partial total and the answer for the host would be wrong.
    FromBucket for R0 (www.youtube.com)Bucket for R1 (en.wikipedia.org, www.yorku.ca)
    M1(www.youtube.com, 52400) (www.youtube.com, 61700) (www.youtube.com, 47100) — 3 pairs(www.yorku.ca, 18300) — 1 pair
    M2(www.youtube.com, 58800) — 1 pair(en.wikipedia.org, 33900) (www.yorku.ca, 12600) (en.wikipedia.org, 29700) — 3 pairs
    Check: 3 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 8 pairs, none lost.
  10. (c) Group by key, part 2: shuffle and sort (Slides 27, 51, 54). Each reducer fetches its bucket from every mapper (the all-to-all “Shuffle” of Slide 54, where data crosses between machines) and sorts the pairs so that equal keys sit together. The pairs of one key become one group host → [list of sizes].
    ReducerPairs receivedAfter sort and group (key → list of values)
    R03 (from M1) + 1 (from M2) = 4www.youtube.com → [52400, 61700, 47100, 58800]
    R11 (from M1) + 3 (from M2) = 4en.wikipedia.org → [33900, 29700]; www.yorku.ca → [18300, 12600]
    Check: 4 + 4 = 8. The YouTube list mixes sizes written by two different mappers; only the shuffle brings them together. (The order of the numbers inside a list does not matter for a sum.)
  11. (c) Reduce phase (Slide 47; one call per unique key, Slide 44). Add up each list, v'' = ∑ v'. Three distinct hosts give 3 Reduce calls.
    ReducerKey (host)Value listSumOutput pair
    R0www.youtube.com[52400, 61700, 47100, 58800]52400 + 61700 = 114100; 114100 + 47100 = 161200; 161200 + 58800 = 220000(www.youtube.com, 220000)
    R1en.wikipedia.org[33900, 29700]33900 + 29700 = 63600(en.wikipedia.org, 63600)
    R1www.yorku.ca[18300, 12600]18300 + 12600 = 30900(www.yorku.ca, 30900)
    R0 writes (www.youtube.com, 220000) to its output file; R1 writes (en.wikipedia.org, 63600) and (www.yorku.ca, 30900) (two output files, like “Out 0” and “Out 1” on Slide 54).
  12. (c) Sanity check (always do this). Go back to the raw table and add by hand. YouTube = records 1, 2, 4, 6: 52400 + 61700 + 47100 + 58800 = 220000. York U = records 3, 7: 18300 + 12600 = 30900. Wikipedia = records 5, 8: 33900 + 29700 = 63600. All three match the Reduce output. The grand total of all 8 sizes is 52400 + 18300 + 61700 + 33900 + 47100 + 12600 + 58800 + 29700 = 314500 = 220000 + 30900 + 63600, so no byte was lost or counted twice. Also: 8 pairs entered the groups, and 3 distinct hosts gave 3 Reduce calls and 3 output pairs. Figure L2-Q4-2 shows the whole run.
  13. (d) The problem a combiner solves (Slide 59). “Often a Map task will produce many pairs of the form (k, v1), (k, v2), … for the same key k.” Here mapper M1 emits three separate pairs for www.youtube.com, and with a real web corpus a mapper reads very many pages of a popular host. Sending every one of these pairs over the network is wasteful, because the reducer is only going to add them anyway.
  14. (d) What a combiner does (Slides 60–61). It “pre-aggregates values in the mapper”: combine(k, list(v1)) → v2. It runs on the same machine as one mapper, takes all pairs of that single mapper and merges the pairs of each key into one pair before anything is shuffled. “Much less data needs to be copied and shuffled!” For this job the combiner simply adds the sizes per host, the same code as Reduce (Slide 62: “Combiner is usually same as the reduce function”).
    MapperMap output (before)After the combiner (sent to the shuffle)Pairs
    M1(www.youtube.com, 52400) (www.youtube.com, 61700) (www.yorku.ca, 18300) (www.youtube.com, 47100)(www.youtube.com, 161200) (www.yorku.ca, 18300)
    since 52400 + 61700 + 47100 = 161200    		4 → 2
    M2(en.wikipedia.org, 33900) (www.youtube.com, 58800) (www.yorku.ca, 12600) (en.wikipedia.org, 29700)(en.wikipedia.org, 63600) (www.youtube.com, 58800) (www.yorku.ca, 12600)
    since 33900 + 29700 = 63600    		4 → 3
    The shuffle now moves 5 pairs instead of 8 ((8 − 5) ÷ 8 = 37.5% fewer): R0 receives (www.youtube.com, 161200) from M1 and (www.youtube.com, 58800) from M2 (2 pairs); R1 receives 1 pair from M1 and 2 pairs from M2 (3 pairs). Reduce then finishes the job: www.youtube.com 161200 + 58800 = 220000; www.yorku.ca 18300 + 12600 = 30900; en.wikipedia.org = 63600. The final answer is identical to the one without a combiner.
  15. (d) Why a combiner is legal here (Slide 62). A combiner may be used only when the reduce function is commutative and associative, because the framework does not control how the values of a key are split among mappers or in which order they are added. Sum has both properties: a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). Check on the YouTube numbers: adding per mapper first gives (52400 + 61700 + 47100) + 58800 = 161200 + 58800 = 220000, which equals 52400 + (61700 + 47100 + 58800) = 52400 + 167600 = 220000. A partial sum is just a regrouping of the same addends. A second requirement is that the combiner's output pairs have the same form as the map output, a pair (host, number of bytes), so Reduce cannot tell whether a number is one page or the sum of several pages and simply adds. Beyond the slides: the framework may run a combiner zero, one or several times, so the job must give the right answer with or without it; for a sum it does. The combiner is only an optimisation for the network; the reducer is still required.
    Common mistake — a combiner is not allowed for every reducer (Slides 63–65)

    Suppose the question asked for the average page size per host. Average is not commutative and associative (Slide 63), so reusing the reducer as combiner would be wrong. On YouTube: M1's local average = (52400 + 61700 + 47100) ÷ 3 = 53733.33, M2's = 58800; the average of the two averages is (53733.33 + 58800) ÷ 2 = 56266.67, but the true average is 220000 ÷ 4 = 55000. Fix (Slide 64): ship (sum, count) pairs, M1: (161200, 3) and M2: (58800, 1); add them to (220000, 4) and divide only at the very end: 220000 ÷ 4 = 55000. The median cannot be repaired this way at all (Slide 65). Our job only sums, so the plain combiner is safe.

  16. Link to Slides 66–67 (partitioning). The default partition function hash(key) mod R (Slide 66) already sends all pairs of one host to the same reducer here, because the key is the host. Slide 67 shows the override hash(hostname(URL)) mod R, which ensures “URLs from a host end up in the same output file” even when the key is something finer, such as the full URL (Beyond the slides: that reading of the slide is our interpretation). Beyond the slides: a very popular host such as www.youtube.com makes one reducer receive many more pairs than the others (skew); the combiner eases this too, since each mapper sends at most one pair per host.
Common mistakes
  • Key = URL instead of host (step 1): you must group by the host to add up pages of the same host.
  • Adding inside Map. Map emits one pair per record and does no summing; totals appear after grouping. (Pre-adding inside the mapper is a separate optimisation, the combiner, which comes on top and does not replace Reduce.)
  • Reduce is called once per host (3 calls here), not once per record (8).
  • Keeping the date or other fields in the value. Only the size is needed; extra fields would also have to be shuffled.
  • Inconsistent hostname(). WWW.YouTube.com and www.youtube.com would become two keys unless hostname() lower-cases; and youtube.com is not www.youtube.com unless you say so.
  • Using a combiner for a function that is not commutative and associative (average, median) without the (sum, count) fix.
  • Confusing combiner and reducer. The combiner is local (one mapper), optional, and only cuts network traffic; the reducer receives the data of all mappers and produces the final answer.
Exam tip

For any “find the total per X” question write: (1) key = X, value = the number to add, with one reason; (2) Map in one line, e.g. (URL, size, date) → (hostname(URL), size); (3) “Group by key” is done by the framework; (4) Reduce: sum; (5) a small table Map output → groups → Reduce output with a sanity check (here 314500 = 220000 + 30900 + 63600); (6) one line on the combiner: “same as Reduce, legal because sum is commutative and associative, shuffles 5 instead of 8 pairs”. Each item is separate partial credit. If the question asked for the number of URLs per host instead, only the value changes: emit (hostname(URL), 1) and sum, exactly as in word count.

Final answer: key = hostname(URL), value = size. Map: for each record output (hostname(URL), size) (one call per record). Group by key (framework): collect all sizes of each host at one reducer. Reduce: sum the sizes of each host (one call per host). hostname(URL) = the text between :// and the next / (port dropped, lower-cased), e.g. www.youtube.com for http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QhcwLyyEjOA. Practice input: Map emits 8 pairs; R0 gets 4 and outputs (www.youtube.com, 220000); R1 gets 4 and outputs (en.wikipedia.org, 63600) and (www.yorku.ca, 30900); grand total 314500 bytes. A combiner (same code as Reduce) is legal because sum is commutative and associative; it cuts the shuffle from 8 to 5 pairs and leaves the totals unchanged.
Where the marks come from: (1) key = host, value = size, with the reason (pages of one host must be brought together; URL as key would not work); (2) Map: one call per record outputs (hostname(URL), size), other fields dropped; (3) Group by key is a separate step done by the framework, all pairs of a host reach the same reducer; (4) Reduce: sum per host, one call per unique key; (5) explanation of hostname(URL): drop the scheme, keep up to the next “/”, ignore path and query; (6) Map output table (8 pairs); (7) groups after shuffle and sort; (8) correct sums 220000, 63600, 30900 and the check 314500; (9) combiner named as pre-aggregation in the mapper, same as Reduce, with the reason (sum is commutative and associative) and its effect (8 → 5 pairs); (10) optionally, why average or median would break it. (Typical split only; marking schemes vary.)
Slide check: matches the slide's answer. Map outputs (hostname(URL), size), then Group by key, then Reduce sums the sizes for each host (Slides 46–47). No slide erratum on Slides 45–47. The slides stop at this outline: they give no data, do not define hostname(URL), do not name the key and value explicitly and do not apply a combiner to this example (combiners appear on Slides 59–62 with word count); those parts were solved here as an extension of the outline. The gaps in the sample URL “http:// www. youtube.com /watch?v=…” on Slide 45 are only typesetting.

Example: language model (5-word sequences)

Lecture 2 · Slides 48–49

Problem (Slide 48). Count the number of times each 5-word sequence occurs in a large corpus of documents. A 5-word sequence (Beyond the slides: a "5-gram") is any run of 5 consecutive words; the windows overlap, one starting at every word position. Such counts are the raw material of a language model (used for autocomplete, speech recognition and machine translation), which is why the slide has that title.

Answer (Slide 49). It is word count where the thing counted is a 5-word window instead of a single word.

  1. Map: slide a 5-word window along each document and, for each position, emit (5-word sequence, count), where the count is 1 per occurrence (the slide leaves the 1 implicit).
  2. Group by key: the framework collects the counts of each 5-word sequence, for example (the cat sat on the, [1, 1, 1]).
  3. Reduce: combine the counts by adding them up: (the cat sat on the, 3).

The key is the 5-word sequence, and that choice alone decides what is counted. Compare the three examples so far:

ExampleSlidesKeyValue emitted by MapReduce does
Word count26, 36–42a word1sum
Host size45–47host namepage size in bytessum
Language model48–495-word sequence1 (count)sum

This is Slide 28 in action: the outline stays the same; Map and Reduce change to fit the problem.

Try it yourself first: write down the key and value, then work the two-document trace and the "n − 4 windows" counting argument.

Quiz L2-Q5Counting 5-word sequences in a large corpus (language model) Lecture 2 · Slides 48–49
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 48 — “Example: Language Model”. “Count number of times each 5-word sequence occurs in a large corpus of documents.” Slide 49 (“Answer: Language Model”) gives the outline of the answer: cover it and try first.

The slides give one question and a three-line answer, with no data and no numbered parts, so this block turns them into four exam-style parts. Part (a) is what the slides ask. Parts (b)–(d), the two documents in (b) and the sentence in (d) are Practice written for this guide (invented, not on the slides). Assumptions: words are separated by spaces, the text is already lower-case with punctuation removed, and one Map call reads one document, so a 5-word sequence never runs across the end of a document.

(a) Design the Map-Reduce job: what are the key and the value, what does Map emit, what does Group by key do and what does Reduce compute?
(b) Practice: trace the job on two short documents with 2 mappers (M1 reads D1, M2 reads D2) and 2 reducers. Show the sliding windows, the Map output, the group by key (shuffle) step and the Reduce output.
DocTextRead by
D1the quick brown fox jumps over the dogMapper M1
D2yesterday the quick brown fox jumps highMapper M2
(c) Practice: explain why a document of n words yields exactly n − 4 five-word sequences. What happens if n < 5?
(d) Practice: what is a combiner? Show on the sentence to be or not to be or not to be how it helps in this job, and explain why it is allowed here.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition — a keyhole that is 5 words wide

Word count (Slides 36–42) counted single words. Here the thing we count is a phrase of exactly five consecutive words. Picture reading the text through a keyhole that shows five words at a time. You note down the five visible words on an index card with a tally mark “1”, slide the keyhole one word to the right, note down again, and so on until the keyhole runs off the end. That is Map. Then you put all cards with the same phrase into one pigeonhole: that is Group by key. Finally you add up the tally marks in each pigeonhole: that is Reduce. Nobody ever needs the whole book at once, which is why the job can be split over thousands of machines.

Beyond the slides: the slide is titled “Language Model” because a table of 5-word-sequence counts lets a program estimate how likely a word is to follow the four words before it, roughly P(w5 | w1 w2 w3 w4) ≈ count(w1 … w5) ÷ count(w1 … w4). Such tables (built from billions of web pages) are used in machine translation, speech recognition and auto-complete. That is why the corpus is huge and the counting must be distributed.

Steps are tagged (a)–(d) to match the four parts of the question.

  1. (a) Idea: what must be brought together (Slides 27–28, 44). To know how often one 5-word sequence occurs, all its occurrences, which may sit in documents on many different machines, must meet in one place and be added. “Bring equal things together, then combine them” is exactly the Map-Reduce outline of Slides 27–28 (“Outline stays the same, Map and Reduce change to fit the problem”). It is the same pattern as word count (Slides 36–42) and host size (Slides 45–47), with a 5-word sequence in place of a single word. The programmer supplies only Map(k, v) → <k′, v′>* and Reduce(k′, <v′>*) → k′, v″ (Slide 44); the system does Group by key. So three decisions remain:
    • Key = the whole 5-word sequence (all five words, in order, treated as one string).
    • Value = 1 (one sighting; Slide 49 calls it “count”).
    • Reduce = add the values of each key.
    Why the whole sequence is the key: Group by key gathers pairs whose keys are equal. Only if the key is the complete sequence do two sightings of the same sequence land in the same group; sequences that differ in even one word are different keys and are counted separately.
  2. (a) Map (Slide 49: “Extract (5-word sequence, count) from document”). Let a document have words w1, w2, …, wn. One Map call reads one document (Slide 44: one Map call per (k, v) pair; in word count the pair is (document name, text), Slide 41). It slides a window of 5 words along the text, one word at a time, and for each start position s = 1, 2, …, n − 4 emits (“ws ws+1 ws+2 ws+3 ws+4”, 1).
    Why one word at a time, not five: a sequence may start at any word, so stepping by 5 would miss 4 out of every 5 sequences. Why Map does no adding: a Map call sees only its own document and cannot know the global total; totals are Reduce’s job. (The “count” on Slide 49 is 1 per window; it becomes a partial sum only if a combiner has already run, see (d).)
  3. (a) Group by key (Slide 49; done by the framework, the programmer writes nothing). The system collects the pairs from all mappers and sends every pair with the same key to the same Reduce worker (“hash merge, shuffle, sort, partition”, Slide 51; the default rule is hash(key) mod R, Slide 66; the environment does this for you, Slide 53). Result: one group (5-gram, [1, 1, …, 1]) per distinct 5-word sequence, with as many 1s as the sequence has occurrences. (Beyond the slides: a 5-word sequence is also called a 5-gram; the guide uses both names.)
  4. (a) Reduce (Slide 49: “Combines the counts (adds them up)”). There is one Reduce call per unique key (Slide 44). For key g with value list [v1, …, vm] it outputs (g, v1 + … + vm), i.e. count(g) = ∑ vi. All Reduce outputs together form the table of counts the question asks for. Why we write “add the values” and not “count the list items”: with a combiner (step 11) a value can be larger than 1, and adding is still right.
    Key idea

    Every Map call looks only at one document and every Reduce call looks only at one 5-gram, so no machine ever needs the whole corpus or the whole table of counts. Only the Group by key step moves data between machines. That is why the job scales to a “large corpus of documents”.

  5. (b) Step 1: the sliding windows. A document of n words gives windows starting at word 1, 2, …, n − 4 (reason in (c)). D1 has n = 8 words, so 8 − 4 = 4 windows. D2 has n = 7 words, so 7 − 4 = 3 windows. Figure 1 shows D1.
    Doc (n)Window sWords used5-word sequence

    The shaded 5-gram the quick brown fox jumps is window 1 of D1 but window 2 of D2: a repeated sequence does not need to sit at the same position in both documents.
  6. (b) Step 2: Map output. Every window becomes a pair (window, 1):
    MapperPairs emittedCount
    M1 (D1)(the quick brown fox jumps, 1) · (quick brown fox jumps over, 1) · (brown fox jumps over the, 1) · (fox jumps over the dog, 1)4 = 8 − 4
    M2 (D2)(yesterday the quick brown fox, 1) · (the quick brown fox jumps, 1) · (quick brown fox jumps high, 1)3 = 7 − 4
    Total Map output = 4 + 3 = 7 pairs. Note that (the quick brown fox jumps, 1) was produced twice, on two different machines; neither mapper can know that the other one saw it too.
  7. (b) Step 3: Group by key (sort and shuffle). The framework sorts the 7 pairs by key and puts equal keys into one group. The groups are shared out among the 2 reducers; a real system uses hash(key) mod R (Slide 66), so the R0/R1 split below is only an illustration. Any split that keeps a whole key on one reducer is correct.

Figure 2 follows the repeated key through the whole job.

    quick brown fox jumps over1(quick brown fox jumps over, 1)
    the quick brown fox jumps1 + 1 = 2(the quick brown fox jumps, 2)
    yesterday the quick brown fox1(yesterday the quick brown fox, 1)
    Sanity checks. (i) Pairs emitted = (8 − 4) + (7 − 4) = 4 + 3 = 7. (ii) The output counts add up to 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7 = number of Map pairs, so nothing was lost or invented (Reduce only adds). (iii) Distinct 5-grams = 7 − 1 = 6 = number of groups = number of Reduce calls = number of output lines (one 5-gram was seen twice, so one pair “disappears” in the grouping).
  9. (c) Why n − 4: argument 1, count the start positions. Number the words 1 to n. A window is fixed by the position s of its first word. It then occupies words s, s+1, s+2, s+3, s+4 (five words), so its last word is word s + 4, which must exist: s + 4 ≤ n, i.e. s ≤ n − 4. Also s ≥ 1. The legal starts are 1, 2, …, n − 4, and a list of the integers 1 up to m has m members, so there are n − 4 windows. In words: the last 4 words of a text can never start a window, because there are not enough words after them.
  10. (c) Argument 2, count the new words; the case n < 5. The first window uses the first 5 words. Each later window is the previous one moved one word to the right, so it adds exactly one new word at the end. The words left after the first five are n − 5, giving 1 + (n − 5) = n − 4 windows. Both arguments agree:
    n (words)Possible start positions s (need s + 4 ≤ n)Windows
    ≤ 4none (no room for even one window)0
    5s = 11
    6s = 1, 22
    7 (D2)s = 1, 2, 33
    8 (D1)s = 1, 2, 3, 44
    9s = 1, …, 55
    10 (sentence in (d))s = 1, …, 66
    ns = 1, 2, …, n − 4n − 4
    Checks against part (b): D2 (n = 7) → 3 ✓, D1 (n = 8) → 4 ✓. If n < 5 the document emits 0 pairs, so the count is max(0, n − 4), never negative. Beyond the slides: for windows of k words the count is n − k + 1; for k = 5 that is n − 4.

    Consequence for the whole corpus: Map emits ∑ over documents of max(0, nd − 4) pairs, i.e. almost one pair per word of the corpus. Each pair carries a 5-word key, so (Beyond the slides) the Map output holds about five times as much text as the input. Shuffling it is expensive, which is why a combiner matters (d).

    Common mistake

    Cutting the text into non-overlapping blocks of five (about n ÷ 5, rounded down: D1 would give only 1) misses almost all 5-grams. The window must slide by one word. Another frequent slip is the off-by-one answer n − 5, which gives 0 for a 5-word document that clearly contains one 5-gram.

  11. (d) What a combiner is (Slides 59–62). A Map task often produces many pairs with the same key (Slide 59). A combiner is a mini-Reduce that runs on the mapper’s own machine, before the shuffle: combine(k, list(v1)) → v2 (Slide 60). It “combines the values of all keys of a single mapper (single machine)”, so “much less data needs to be copied and shuffled” (Slide 61). For this job the combiner is the same function as Reduce: add the counts (Slide 62: “Combiner is usually same as the reduce function”). Pairs leaving a mapper then carry partial counts instead of 1s.
  12. (d) Worked example. to be or not to be or not to be has n = 10 words, so 10 − 4 = 6 windows (shaded rows = 5-grams that occur twice):
    sWindow (words s to s+4)Map emits
    1to be or not to(to be or not to, 1)
    2be or not to be(be or not to be, 1)
    3or not to be or(or not to be or, 1)
    4not to be or not(not to be or not, 1)
    5to be or not to (repeat of s = 1)(to be or not to, 1)
    6be or not to be (repeat of s = 2)(be or not to be, 1)
    Without a combiner this mapper ships 6 pairs over the network. With the combiner it adds the 1s per key first and ships only 4 pairs: (to be or not to, 2), (be or not to be, 2), (or not to be or, 1), (not to be or not, 1). The counts still add up (2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6) and the traffic drops by (6 − 4) ÷ 6 = 33 %. Figure 3 shows the data flow.
  13. (d) Effect on the trace in (b). M1 emits 4 different keys and M2 emits 3 different keys, so a combiner has nothing to merge: still 7 pairs. The repeated key sits on two different mappers, and a combiner only merges within one machine (Slide 61); the Reducer is still needed to add the two partial counts. If one mapper had read both documents, the combiner would turn the two pairs into (the quick brown fox jumps, 2) and ship 6 pairs instead of 7. On a real corpus, frequent phrases occur thousands of times per mapper, so the saving is large.
  14. (d) Why it is allowed (Slide 62). A combiner may be used only if the reduce function is commutative and associative: a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). Summation is both, so adding the 1s in groups first (per mapper) and the partial sums later gives the same total as adding all the 1s at once, in any order. Example: if a second mapper also emitted (to be or not to, 1), the Reducer would receive [2, 1] and add 2 + 1 = 3, the same as 1 + 1 + 1. (Counting the list length would wrongly give 2, which is why Reduce adds the values.) The combiner is only an optimisation: the final output is identical with or without it. Beyond the slides: the framework may run a combiner zero, one or several times, so the program must still be correct without it. Contrast: the average is not commutative and associative (Slides 63–64) and the median cannot be split into such functions (Slide 65), so they cannot use the combiner trick directly. That is not an issue here because we only add.
Exam tip

Write the answer under the three slide headings Map / Group by key / Reduce, each with its exact key–value format: (1) Map → (5-word sequence, 1) for every sliding window, one word at a time, giving n − 4 pairs per document; (2) Group by key → (5-word sequence, [1, 1, …]), all pairs with the same 5-gram at the same reducer; (3) Reduce → (5-word sequence, sum). Then add a short trace (2 documents, one repeated 5-gram) and one line on the combiner: same function as Reduce, runs on the mapper, valid because + is commutative and associative, saves network traffic. Each of these is a separate partial mark.

Common mistakes
  • Using the word as the key (that is word count, not 5-word-sequence count), or the document name as the key.
  • Treating quick brown fox jumps over and quick brown fox jumps high as “the same” because four words agree. The whole sequence is the key.
  • Stepping the window by 5 words instead of 1, or the off-by-one slips n, n − 5 and n − 3 instead of n − 4.
  • Adding up counts inside Map: one Map call sees one document only; the global total exists only after Group by key.
  • Letting Reduce count the list length instead of adding the values (breaks as soon as a combiner is used).
  • Thinking the combiner replaces the Reducer: equal keys on different mappers can only be added together after the shuffle.
Final answer: (a) Map: for every document slide a window of 5 consecutive words one word at a time and emit (5-word sequence, 1), giving n − 4 pairs for a document of n ≥ 5 words (0 if n < 5). Group by key (framework): all pairs with the same 5-word sequence go to the same reducer as (5-gram, [1, 1, …]). Reduce: add the list and output (5-gram, total count), one call per distinct 5-gram. (b) D1 gives 4 windows and D2 gives 3, so 7 Map pairs → 6 groups → 6 Reduce calls with output (brown fox jumps over the, 1), (fox jumps over the dog, 1), (quick brown fox jumps high, 1), (quick brown fox jumps over, 1), (the quick brown fox jumps, 2), (yesterday the quick brown fox, 1); counts add up to 7. (c) Start positions are s = 1, …, n − 4 (because s + 4 ≤ n), so n − 4 windows, and 0 if n < 5. (d) A combiner is a mapper-side pre-sum (same function as Reduce, allowed because addition is commutative and associative) that cuts the data shuffled without changing the result, e.g. 6 pairs → 4 for to be or not to be or not to be.
Where the marks come from: (1) Map: key = the 5-word sequence (sliding window of 5 consecutive words, step of one word), value = 1 (“count”); (2) Group by key: all pairs with the same 5-gram are brought to the same reducer, a framework step; (3) Reduce: add the values per key → (5-gram, count), one call per distinct key; (4) trace: correct overlapping windows (4 for D1, 3 for D2), 7 Map pairs, 6 groups, the repeated 5-gram the quick brown fox jumps with list [1, 1] and final count 2, every other count 1, and the check that the counts add up to 7; (5) n − 4 with a reason (the last window starts at word n − 4, or the first window uses 5 words and each further word adds one) and 0 when n < 5; (6) combiner: pre-aggregation on the mapper, same as Reduce, valid because the sum is commutative and associative, less data shuffled, plus a small example (6 → 4 pairs). The exact mark split is set by the instructor; the list shows where each step can earn credit.
Slide check: matches the slide’s answer. Slide 49 gives only the outline (Map: extract (5-word sequence, count) from document; Group by key; Reduce: combine the counts, i.e. add them up) and this solution agrees with it. No slide erratum. The outline leaves implicit (omissions, not errors) that the “count” emitted by Map is 1 per window, that the extraction is a sliding window with a one-word step giving n − 4 pairs per n-word text, and that a combiner can be used (combiners are on Slides 59–62); these are filled in above. Slide 48 gives no data and does not say why 5-grams are counted; the language-model background is marked “Beyond the slides”.

Other uses of Map-Reduce

Lecture 2 · Slide 50

Slide 50 is a one-line list of further problems that fit the model: link analysis and graph processing, machine-learning algorithms, mining frequent itemsets and clustering. The slide gives no detail; you only need to quote these four areas. They preview the course: frequent itemsets are the subject of Lecture 4 and clustering of Lecture 5 (Beyond the slides: PageRank is the classic link-analysis computation, and it is iterative, which is why "output is input to another job" on Slide 55 matters).

The Map-Reduce picture, and how it runs in parallel

Lecture 2 · Slides 51–52

Slide 51: the single-flow diagram

Lecture 2 · Slide 51

Slide 51 shows the whole job top to bottom. A "Big document" is cut into 7 input pieces. Each piece goes through one M (a Map call). The "Intermediate" row holds the emitted pairs, written key:value; one Map call emitted nothing (the empty second cell). One box Group by Key regroups them into the "Grouped" row, and one R per key writes the "Output" row.

Piece1234567
Intermediatek1:v k1:v k2:v(empty)k1:vk3:v k4:vk4:v k5:vk4:vk1:v k3:v

Count it: 11 pairs in total; k1 four times, k2 once, k3 twice, k4 three times, k5 once (4 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 11). The Grouped row is therefore k1:v,v,v,v | k2:v | k3:v,v | k4:v,v,v | k5:v: 5 distinct keys = 5 Reduce calls, while there are 7 Map calls (one per input piece). The slide's three coloured call-outs repeat what you know: MAP reads input and produces key-value pairs; Group by key collects all pairs with the same key (and names the machinery "Hash merge, Shuffle, Sort, Partition"); Reduce collects all values belonging to the key and outputs.

Terms on the group-by-key call-out (Slide 51)

The slide lists the words without defining them. Beyond the slides: partition = decide which reduce task receives a given key, typically hash(key) mod R where R is the number of reduce tasks; shuffle = move the pairs over the network from map workers to reduce workers; sort / hash merge = order or merge the arrived pairs so that equal keys are adjacent.

Slide 52: in parallel

Lecture 2 · Slide 52

Slide 51 draws Group by Key as one box in the middle, which hides that this step is itself distributed. Slide 52 draws the same job the way it runs on a cluster, with the caption "All phases are distributed with many tasks doing the work." The 7 pieces are shared among 3 Map tasks (3 + 2 + 2 Map calls). At the end of each Map task a Partitioning Function looks only at the key of each pair and decides which of the 2 Reduce tasks must receive it. Each Reduce task receives parts from every Map task (3 × 2 = 6 arrows: the shuffle), sorts and groups them by key and calls R once per key.

Worked example — follow key k4 Lecture 2 · Slide 52

k4 occurs three times: twice in Map task 2 (cells "k3 k4" and "k4 k5") and once in Map task 3. Each Map task's partitioning function sends its k4 pairs to Reduce task 1, so Reduce task 1 receives k4:v,v,v and makes one R call that sees all three values. Whichever Map task made them, they cannot be split between the two Reduce tasks; otherwise the total would be wrong. Likewise all four k1 pairs (Map task 1 twice in cell 1 and once in cell 3, Map task 3 once) land in Reduce task 2: k1:v,v,v,v.

So group-by-key is done by the combination partition at the map side + shuffle across the network + sort and group at the reduce side. The key-to-task assignment in the figure (k2, k4, k5 → Reduce 1; k1, k3 → Reduce 2) is illustrative; the slide does not give the partitioning rule (typically hash(key) mod R, Beyond the slides).

What the environment takes care of

Lecture 2 · Slide 53

Slide 53 lists, in five items, what you do not have to write. The Map-Reduce environment (the runtime, such as Google's system or Hadoop) takes care of:

#The environment takes care ofIn plain words
1Scheduling the program's execution across a set of machinesdecides which task runs on which machine and when
2Managing required inter-machine communicationmoves data between machines
3Partitioning the datasplits the input into pieces so that many Maps can run in parallel (and, per Slide 52, divides the intermediate keys among reduce tasks)
4Performing the group by key stepthe sort and shuffle between Map and Reduce
5Handling machine failuresdetects dead machines and re-runs their tasks (Slide 57)

This is the answer to the challenge of Slides 15–16: distributed programming is hard, so give the programmer a simple model that hides the complexity. The slide's "partitioning the data" is ambiguous (input splitting versus key partitioning); both are done by the system.

Exam tip

"What does the Map-Reduce environment take care of?" has a five-item answer: scheduling, communication, partitioning the data, group by key, failures. Learn the list as S-C-P-G-F.

Slide 54: the programmer's view of the workflow

Lecture 2 · Slide 54

Slide 54 condenses the same idea to a small picture. Programmer specifies: Map, Reduce and the input files. Workflow: Map → sort and shuffle → Reduce. All phases are distributed with many tasks doing the work. The picture has three inputs (Input 0, 1, 2) feeding Map 0, 1, 2; a wide band labelled Shuffle; two reduce tasks Reduce 0 and Reduce 1, each receiving one arrow from every Map (6 shuffle arrows); and one output each, Out 0 and Out 1. The shuffle is an all-to-all exchange, so it is the most network-heavy step (Beyond the slides).

  • The number of Map tasks follows the number of input pieces (3 here); the number of Reduce tasks (2 here) is chosen by the user (Beyond the slides).
  • The "Input 0/1/2" circles are input pieces (splits), not necessarily separate files.
  • One Reduce task produces one output piece, so a job with R reduce tasks writes R output pieces.
Slide erratum (minor, Slides 51–54)
  • Slide 51 draws Group by Key as one central box; Slide 52 shows it is distributed. Use Slide 52's version when you explain the system.
  • Slide 52 numbers tasks from 1 (Map task 1, Reduce task 1); Slide 54 numbers from 0 (Map 0, Reduce 0). Same idea, different labels; some diagonal arrows on Slide 52 also start slightly outside their boxes (drawing glitch).
  • Slide 54 writes "Sorts & Shuffles" (grammar); Slide 27 calls the same stage "Group by key (sort and shuffle)". It also omits that the programmer may choose the number of reducers.
TermMeaningExample on the slides
Map callone invocation of Map on one input pairthe 7 M circles of Slide 51
Map taska worker's job over one input piece; makes many Map callsMap task 1 on Slide 52 (3 M calls)
