Where the data lives: data flow

Lecture 2 · Slide 55

Three rules, one per bullet:

  1. Input and final output are stored on the distributed file system (DFS), the replicated, fault-tolerant GFS/HDFS of Slides 17–24. The scheduler tries to schedule map tasks "close" to the physical storage location of their input chunk: "bring the computation to the data" (Slides 16, 23, 25). (Beyond the slides: "close" means the same machine first, then the same rack.)
  2. Intermediate results (the Map output) are stored on the local file system of the map worker, not in the DFS. Beyond the slides: they are temporary and can be recomputed, so replicating them would be wasted work. The consequence, that they vanish with the machine, drives the failure rules below.
  3. Output is often input to another Map-Reduce task, so large problems are solved by chains or iterations of jobs.
DataStored onReplicated?Survives a worker crash?
Input chunksDFSyes (2x or 3x)yes
Intermediate (Map output)local disk of the map workernono
Final outputDFSyesyes

Coordination: the master

Lecture 2 · Slide 56

A job has one master node (the coordinator) and many worker nodes that run map and reduce tasks. The master takes care of coordination:

  • Task status: every task is idle (waiting to be assigned), in-progress or completed.
  • Idle tasks get scheduled as workers become available.
  • When a map task completes, it sends the master the location and sizes of its intermediate files (Beyond the slides: one file region per reduce task). The data itself stays on the map worker's local disk.
  • The master pushes this information to the reducers. (Beyond the slides: only the locations are pushed; the reducers then read the data from the map workers' disks.)
  • The master pings workers periodically to detect failures. A worker that does not answer is declared failed.
Practice (beyond the slides) — one map task finishes Lecture 2 · Slide 56

Map task 0 (state idle) is assigned to a free worker, becomes in-progress, reads its chunk (ideally from that machine's own disk) and writes its intermediate pairs into R local files, one per reduce task (R = 2 here, so 2 files). On completion it tells the master "done; my 2 files are here, with these sizes". The master marks it completed and passes the file locations to Reduce 0 and Reduce 1. The reducers fetch their file from every map worker (3 maps × 2 reducers = 6 fetches).

Dealing with failures

Lecture 2 · Slide 57

Jobs run for a long time on thousands of cheap machines, where failures are routine (Slides 12–13), so the framework must recover automatically. Slide 57 gives three cases, from least to most serious. The master finds failed workers by its periodic pings (Slide 56); a worker that does not answer is dead.

FailureWhat the slide saysWhy (the reason the slide leaves implicit)
Map worker failsMap tasks completed or in-progress at that worker are reset to idle; idle tasks are eventually rescheduled on other workers.A map task's output is on the local disk of that worker and is lost with the machine. A completed map task is therefore not done any more: reducers still need its output.
Reduce worker failsOnly in-progress tasks are reset to idle; the idle reduce task is restarted on other workers.The output of a completed reduce task was already written to the distributed file system, which is replicated, so it survives. Nothing needs redoing.
Master failsThe Map-Reduce job is aborted and the client is notified.The master holds all the task states. There is a single master (a single point of failure). Beyond the slides: a failure of one machine during any single job is unlikely (Dean and Ghemawat). The client must resubmit.
Key idea: why completed map tasks are redone but completed reduce tasks are not

It is a question of where the output lives. A map task's output is written to the local disk of its worker (Slide 55); when the worker dies, the disk is unreachable, so the work is lost even though the task was "completed", and reducers that have not yet fetched that output need it. A reduce task's output goes to the distributed file system (Slide 55), which keeps replicas on other machines, so once completed it is safe and need not be redone. In-progress tasks, of either kind, have produced nothing durable yet and are always redone.

Worked example — a map worker dies Lecture 2 · Slide 57

Worker W ran map task A (completed) and was running map task B (in-progress) when it stopped answering pings. The master resets both A and B to idle, and gives them to other workers as they become free. Reduce tasks that still needed A's files are told the new location after A reruns (Beyond the slides). If instead W had been a reduce worker running reduce task X (completed) and Y (in-progress), only Y would be reset to idle.

Common mistakes
  • Saying "completed tasks are never redone". For map tasks they are, because their output is on the failed worker's local disk.
  • Saying "reduce tasks are redone if the reduce worker fails" without the qualifier only the in-progress ones.
  • Forgetting that master failure is not recovered: the job is aborted and the client notified.
  • Writing that intermediate data is stored in the DFS. It is on the local FS; only input and final output are in the DFS.
Exam tip

For a "what happens when worker X fails?" question, answer in the order: (1) the master detects it by missing pings, (2) which tasks are reset to idle (map: completed and in-progress; reduce: in-progress only), (3) the reason (local disk versus DFS), (4) idle tasks are rescheduled on other workers as they become available. Slide wording note: "Idle Reduce task is restarted" is loose; the task is started afresh because it was reset to idle.

Quick recap (Slides 26–57)
  • Word count is the model example: Map emits (word, 1) per word; the framework groups by key; Reduce sums.
  • Four stages: Map, group by key (sort and shuffle), Reduce, write result. The programmer writes only Map and Reduce; the outline stays the same.
  • Signatures: Map(k, v) → list of (k', v'), one call per input pair; Reduce(k', list of v') → (k', v''), one call per unique key.
  • Choose the key as "what must meet to give one answer": word, host, 5-word sequence.
  • Parallel run: Map tasks → partitioning function → shuffle (every map to every reduce) → sort and group → Reduce tasks.
  • The environment handles scheduling, communication, partitioning, group by key and failures.
  • Input and final output are in the DFS (map tasks scheduled close to the data); intermediate data is on local disks.
  • The master tracks task states (idle, in-progress, completed), receives file locations and sizes from finished map tasks, and pings workers.
  • Map worker fails: completed and in-progress map tasks redone. Reduce worker fails: only in-progress reduce tasks redone. Master fails: job aborted.

Fine-granularity tasks and pipelining

Lecture 2 · Slide 58

The previous slides showed how the master hands out work and what happens when a worker fails (Slide 57). Slide 58 asks a design question: how big should one task be? Its single bullet gives the answer: fine granularity tasks: map tasks >> machines. In words: cut the job into many more map tasks than there are machines, each task small.

Beginner intuition

Four removal workers must empty a house. If you give each worker one whole floor, the worker with the cluttered attic finishes last while the others stand around. If you instead cut the work into 40 small jobs ("this room", "that cupboard") on a whiteboard, whoever finishes grabs the next job, and everybody is busy until the very end. Small tasks = good load balancing. And if one worker falls ill, only a small job has to be redone.

Reading the Gantt chart on Slide 58

Lecture 2 · Slide 58

The slide has no legend, so here is how to read it. Time runs left to right. The User Program calls MapReduce() and then simply waits. The Master assigns tasks to four worker machines. Green bars are map work, red bars are "reads", blue bars are reduce work. Read i.j means "reduce task i reads (fetches) the output of map task j" (this is the shuffle, seen from the reducer's side).

Three things to notice:

  1. More tasks than machines. Worker 1 runs Map 1 and then Map 3, while Worker 2 runs the long Map 2. Three map tasks share two machines. The machine that finished early took the next task instead of idling.
  2. Pipelining. Reads begin as soon as the matching map task ends. Read 1.1 and Read 2.1 start when Map 1 ends; Read 1.3 starts when Map 3 ends; Read 1.2 starts when Map 2 ends. So network copying overlaps with map computation still going on elsewhere. The shuffle does not wait for all maps to finish.
  3. The reduce barrier. A Reduce bar starts only after all of that reduce task's reads are done (Reduce 1 after Read 1.2, Reduce 2 after Read 2.3), because the reduce function needs every value of a key.

The white gaps in Worker 3's row are idle time waiting for the next map output. Worker 4's Read 2.2 starts later than Map 2 ends because Worker 4 is still busy with the long Read 2.1 (it reads one output at a time).

Definition: fine granularity and pipelining

Fine granularity: splitting a job into many small tasks (number of map tasks M much larger than the number of machines). Pipelining: overlapping stages, so that the shuffle of finished map outputs runs while other map tasks are still computing. Only the reduce function has to wait for the group-by-key barrier.

Exam tip

"Why use many more map tasks than machines?" Give two reasons: (1) dynamic load balancing (fast machines simply take more tasks), (2) fast recovery (a failed worker loses only small tasks, and they can be re-run in parallel on many other machines). Slide 69 repeats both; see the rule of thumb later in this part.

Common mistake

Do not write that reduce tasks start computing before all maps finish. Only the copying (reads) starts early. The reduce function itself needs all values for each key.

Refinement: combiners

Lecture 2 · Slides 59–65

Slides 59 to 65 form one story: what a combiner is (59–61), when it is allowed (62), and why it works for sum, needs a trick for average and fails for median (62–65).

The problem: many pairs for the same key

Lecture 2 · Slide 59

Slide 59: "Often a Map task will produce many pairs of the form (k,v1), (k,v2), … for the same key k, e.g. popular words in the word count example." Think of a chunk of English text: the word "the" appears hundreds of times, so the mapper emits hundreds of ("the", 1) pairs. Each pair is written to local disk, sent across the network (the bottleneck, Lecture 2 Slide 14) and sorted at the reducer, although they could have been added up locally first.

The slide's figure is the generic data flow: three map tasks (each calls the map function M several times and has a "Partitioning Function" that decides the target reduce task), arrows crossing to two reduce tasks (each does "Sort and Group", then calls the reduce function R once per key). No combiner is drawn. The point is the repeated keys. Counting the pairs in that figure:

Map taskPairs emitted (keys)Pairs without combinerPairs with a combiner (one per distinct key)
Map Task 1k1, k1, k2, k142 (k1, k2)
Map Task 2k3, k4, k4, k543 (k3, k4, k5)
Map Task 3k4, k1, k333
Total shuffledk1 ×4, k4 ×3, k3 ×2, k2 ×1, k5 ×1118

The right-hand column is Practice (assuming the values of one key can be merged, which Slide 59 itself does not claim). The left column is read off the figure; the key counts agree with the reduce side of the figure (Reduce Task 2 receives k1:v,v,v,v and k3:v,v; Reduce Task 1 receives k2, k4:v,v,v and k5). Note also that a map call may emit zero pairs: the empty second cell of Map Task 1.

Definition: the combiner

Lecture 2 · Slide 60

Slide 60: "Can save network time by pre-aggregating values in the mapper: combine(k, list(v1)) → v2."

Definition: combiner

A combiner is a mini-reducer that runs on the mapper's own machine, right after the map function and before anything is sent over the network. For each key k that this one mapper produced, it takes the mapper's list of values for k and replaces it by a single value. It cuts the number of pairs to be shuffled, which saves network time, disk I/O and sorting work.

  • Where it runs: on the mapper machine, on the output of that machine's map tasks only. It never sees values from other mappers.
  • What it is: an optimisation, not part of the logic. The final answer must be identical with or without it.
  • Beyond the slides: the framework is free to run the combiner zero, one or several times on any subset of a key's values. Your program must therefore be correct whatever happens. The combiner's output must have the same type as the map output value (the reducer receives combiner outputs in place of, or mixed with, raw map outputs).

Worked example: word count with a combiner

Lecture 2 · Slide 61

Slide 61 draws two input blocks, each with its own Mapper and Combiner (each green frame is one machine), then Shuffle and Reducer. The mapper turns each input pair into (its second item, 1). Follow Block 1:

  1. Input: (A,B) (A,C) (A,D) (B,E) (B,D) (C,B).
  2. Mapper output (6 pairs): (B,1) (C,1) (D,1) (E,1) (D,1) (B,1).
  3. Combiner: the key B occurs twice, D twice, C and E once. Output (4 pairs): (B,2) (C,1) (D,2) (E,1).

Block 2 gives mapper output (D,1) (A,1) (A,1) (C,1) (B,1) (D,1) and combiner output (D,2) (A,2) (C,1) (B,1). The Shuffle groups the 8 combined pairs by key: (A,[2]) (B,[2,1]) (C,[1,1]) (D,[2,2]) (E,[1]). The Reducer adds each list: (A,2) (B,3) (C,2) (D,4) (E,1).

Slide 61's conclusion: much less data needs to be copied and shuffled. Here 12 pairs shrink to 8 (a third fewer); with real text and very skewed word frequencies the saving is far larger. The reducer's job did not change; it just adds a few bigger numbers (B: 2 + 1 instead of 1 + 1 + 1).

Slide erratum (minor)

Slide 61 calls this "our word counting example", but the mapper emits only the second item of each input pair ((A,B) gives (B,1)). So it counts how often each letter occurs in the second position, not all words. It is a schematic; every number on the slide is internally consistent (checked above).

When is a combiner legal? Commutative and associative

Lecture 2 · Slide 62

Slide 62: "Combiner is usually the same as the reduce function. Works only if the reduce function is commutative and associative." Example: Sum, where a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).

Why this condition? The framework may combine any subset of a key's values, in any grouping and any order, and then the reducer finishes with the partial results. The final answer is guaranteed to be unchanged only if "combine the pieces" equals "combine everything at once".

  • Commutative (order does not matter): values arrive from different mappers in arbitrary order.
  • Associative (grouping does not matter): lets you pre-add one part, e.g. (1+2+3) + 4 = 1 + (2+3+4).

Slide 62's hand drawing shows exactly this: the row of values of one key is cut in two, each half is added separately (a circled "+"), and the two partial sums are added. For word count the combiner and the reducer are the same function: sum.

Beyond the slides: other functions with both properties include count (a sum of 1s), maximum, minimum, product and set union. They all work as their own combiner.

Average: not combinable directly, but fixable

Lecture 2 · Slides 63–64

Slide 63 states "Average is not commutative and associative" and draws the wrong idea: each mapper averages its part (ave1, ave2) and the reducer computes (ave1 + ave2) / 2, marked with a big X. It is wrong because an average forgets how many values stand behind it. Numeric check (Practice): the values 1, 2, 3 on mapper 1 and 4 on mapper 2 give averages 2 and 4, and (2 + 4)/2 = 3, but the true average of 1, 2, 3, 4 is 10/4 = 2.5. See Figure L2-13 (middle row).

Slide erratum (wording)

The slide's phrase is shorthand. Strictly, the two-argument average (a+b)/2 is commutative; what fails is associativity, and more importantly that merging partial averages ignores their sizes. The correct statement: an average cannot be computed by combining partial averages.

Slide 64 gives the fix: carry (Sum, count) pairs, then ave = Sum / count.

  1. Map: emit (k, (value, 1)), not the bare value.
  2. Combiner: for each key add the pairs component-wise: (s1, c1) + (s2, c2) = (s1+s2, c1+c2). This operation is commutative and associative, so it is a legal combiner. No division here.
  3. Reducer: add all pairs the same way, then divide once: Average = (Sum1 + Sum2 + Sum3) / (count1 + count2 + count3) (the slide's three-part drawing).

Check: {1,2,3} gives (6, 3); {4} gives (4, 1); combined (10, 4); 10/4 = 2.5, correct.

Key idea

Any function can use a combiner if it can be rewritten as a commutative and associative merge of small partial summaries, followed by a cheap final step (for average: merge by adding (sum, count), finish by dividing). Note that here the combiner is not the same as the reducer (the reducer divides, the combiner must not), so "combiner = reduce function" on Slide 62 holds literally only for sum-like functions.

Median: no combiner trick

Lecture 2 · Slide 65

Slide 65: for the median "there is actually a mathematical proof that it is impossible to split it into commutative and associative functions, so we cannot use the combiner trick." (The proof is asserted, not shown; you only need the conclusion.) Intuition: no small, fixed-size summary of a part of the data lets you recover the overall middle value. Practice check: parts {1,2,3} and {10} have medians 2 and 10; the median of those medians is 6, but the true median of {1,2,3,10} is 2.5. So for a median the reducer must receive all the values of the key (full shuffle, no combiner).

Reduce functionCombiner allowed?What the mapper-side combiner keeps
Sum, count, max, min (slide: sum)Yesthe partial sum / count / max / min
AverageYes, with the trickthe pair (sum, count); divide only in the reducer
MedianNonothing smaller than all the values
Exam tip: the 3-question test

Before using a combiner ask: (1) Is the reduce operation commutative and associative? (2) Does the combiner output have the same type as the map output value? (3) Is the answer the same with or without it (it may run 0, 1 or many times)? If you must justify "average cannot be combined directly", use a two-part counterexample with different part sizes (as above). Never answer "average is not associative" without showing the numbers.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution of the next block, then write down what a combiner is, what it saves on Slide 61's data, and what happens for sum, average and median. Compare with the model solution.

Quiz L2-Q7Combiners: sum vs average vs median Lecture 2 · Slides 59–65
Question (as on the slides)

Refinement: Combiners (Slides 59–65). These seven slides contain no numbered exercise; they build one argument: what a combiner is, when the reduce function may be reused as one, and why that works for sum, fails for average (but can be repaired) and is impossible for median. Any link of this chain can be asked in an exam, so this block solves the whole chain. What the slides give:

  • Slide 59: “Often a Map task will produce many pairs of the form (k,v1), (k,v2), … for the same key k; e.g. popular words in the word count example.” The figure shows three Map tasks feeding two Reduce tasks; Map Task 1 itself emits k1:v three times and Reduce Task 2 receives k1:v,v,v,v.
  • Slide 60: “Can save network time by pre-aggregating values in the mapper: combine(k, list(v1)) → v2”.
  • Slide 61: “Back to our word counting example: Combiner combines the values of all keys of a single mapper (single machine) … Much less data needs to be copied and shuffled!” plus the figure whose data are tabulated below.
  • Slide 62: “Combiner is usually same as the reduce function. Works only if reduce function is commutative and associative.” Sum: a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). A hand-drawing shows the row of values of one key cut by a vertical line into two parts, each part fed into a circled “+”, and the two partial results joined again.
  • Slide 63: “Average is not commutative and associative.” Hand-drawing: the two parts give ave1 and ave2, and (ave1 + ave2)/2 is circled and marked with a big X (wrong).
  • Slide 64: Average: (Sum, count); ave = sum / count. Drawing with three parts, each giving a circled (Sumi, counti): Average = (Sum1 + Sum2 + Sum3) / (count1 + count2 + count3).
  • Slide 65: Median: “There is actually a mathematical proof that it is impossible to split it into commutative and associative functions. So we cannot use the combiner ‘trick’.”

Data printed in the Slide 61 figure (two input blocks, each processed by its own Mapper and Combiner; then Shuffle and Reducer):

Input recordsMapper outputCombiner output
Block 1(A,B) (A,C) (A,D) (B,E) (B,D) (C,B)(B,1) (C,1) (D,1) (E,1) (D,1) (B,1)(B,2) (C,1) (D,2) (E,1)
Block 2(C,D) (C,A) (D,A) (E,C) (E,B) (E,D)(D,1) (A,1) (A,1) (C,1) (B,1) (D,1)(D,2) (A,2) (C,1) (B,1)

Reading the figure: each Mapper turns a record such as (A,B) into (its second letter, 1), so the job simply counts how often each letter occurs in the second position; the five letters A–E play the role of “words”. The slides give no numbers for the average and median discussions beyond the hand-drawings, so the numbers used in parts (b)–(e) are Practice values written for this guide: the same five numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are used for sum, average and median so that the three can be compared.

(a) What is a combiner, where does it run and what does it save? Apply it to the two blocks of Slide 61: how many key–value pairs have to be shuffled with and without the combiner, and what does the Reducer output?
(b) When can the reduce function be used as a combiner? Show that sum satisfies the condition, using word count (a mapper that emits (the,1) three times).
(c) Show that average does not satisfy it: give a numerical counterexample (the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 split as {1,2} and {3,4,5}) and prove the failure in general.
(d) Show how the average can be computed correctly with a combiner (Slide 64).
(e) Why can the median not use the combiner trick (Slide 65)?
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Imagine a school election. Each classroom (a “mapper”) first tallies its own ballots and sends one slip per candidate to the central office (the “reducer”), instead of carrying every single ballot across town (the “network”). That is a combiner. It is safe for counting votes: partial tallies simply add up, in any order and any grouping. It is not safe for “the average age of the voters”: a class of 2 students and a class of 3 students must not be averaged as if they were equal, because an average has forgotten how many people stand behind it; the fix is to send “total age and head-count” instead. And for the median age, no small slip from a classroom is ever enough: the central office needs the actual ages. Throughout, the rule is: the answer must not change, only the traffic may.

  1. Idea — what a combiner is and where it runs (Slides 59–60). In the Map-Reduce flow (Slides 36–44, 51) every Map call emits (key, value) pairs, the system moves them over the network to the reducers (the shuffle = group by key) and one Reduce call processes all values of one key. A Map task often emits the same key many times (Slide 59): in word count it emits (the,1) every single time it reads “the”. In the Slide 59 figure Map Task 1 emits k1:v three times, so Reduce Task 2 receives k1:v,v,v,v (three values from Task 1 and one from Task 3), and each of those pairs crossed the network separately. A combiner is a small “mini-reduce” that runs on the same machine as the map task, on that map task’s own output, before anything is sent. Slide 60 writes it combine(k, list(v1)) → v2: for one key k it takes the list of values this one mapper produced and returns one value v2 that stands for the whole list (“pre-aggregating values in the mapper”).
    Slide 59 check (counting only; the figure’s values are just “v”, so assume they can be added): the three Map tasks emit 4 + 4 + 3 = 11 pairs. With a combiner Task 1 sends k1, k2 (2 pairs), Task 2 sends k3, k4, k5 (3 pairs) and Task 3 sends k4, k1, k3 (3 pairs) = 8 pairs; Reduce Task 2 would then receive 2 values for k1 instead of 4.
  2. Part (a): apply the combiner to the Slide 61 data and count pairs. A combiner groups its own mapper’s pairs by key and adds the values of each key. For the two blocks:
    BlockMapper output (raw)What the combiner doesCombiner outputpairs: raw → combined
    1(B,1) (C,1) (D,1) (E,1) (D,1) (B,1)B twice → 1+1 = 2; D twice → 1+1 = 2; C, E once(B,2) (C,1) (D,2) (E,1)6 → 4
    2(D,1) (A,1) (A,1) (C,1) (B,1) (D,1)D twice → 2; A twice → 2; C, B once(D,2) (A,2) (C,1) (B,1)6 → 4
    Total pairs sent to the shuffle12 → 8
    Shuffle (group by key) of the 8 combined pairs: A: [2]; B: [2,1] (2 from Block 1, 1 from Block 2); C: [1,1]; D: [2,2]; E: [1]. Reducer (adds the values of each key; one Reduce call per unique key, Slide 44): A = 2; B = 2+1 = 3; C = 1+1 = 2; D = 2+2 = 4; E = 1. Output (A,2) (B,3) (C,2) (D,4) (E,1), exactly the Slide 61 result. Check: 2+3+2+4+1 = 12 = number of Mapper output pairs ✓. Without the combiner the Reducer would receive (B,[1,1,1]), (D,[1,1,1,1]), … (12 pairs) and print the same five totals.
    • Where it runs: on the machine of each map task, on that task’s output only (“a single mapper (single machine)”, Slide 61). It cannot merge Block 1’s B with Block 2’s B: the two partial values 2 and 1 still travel, so the reducer must still do the final addition (B: 2+1 = 3). The combiner does not replace the reducer.
    • What it saves: network time (Slide 60) and shuffle work (copying, sorting, grouping): “much less data needs to be copied and shuffled” (Slide 61). Here 4 of 12 pairs (one third, 33.3 %) disappear; for a really popular word the saving is enormous (1,000,000 pairs (the,1) from one mapper become the single pair (the,1000000)). At most one pair per distinct key per mapper is ever sent.
    • What it does not change: the number of Map calls (the map work is still done), the number of Reduce calls (one per unique key) and, when the combiner is legal (next steps), the final output. It is a pure optimisation.
  3. Part (b), formula / idea: the condition “commutative and associative” (Slide 62). The combiner is “usually the same as the reduce function”. The system, not the programmer, decides how the values of a key are split between mappers and in what order the partial results are merged. The final answer must not depend on those accidents. So for every way of cutting the values v1, …, vn of a key into groups we need
    reduce(v1, …, vn) = reduce( combine(group 1), combine(group 2), … ).
    Writing the two-value operation as f(a, b), this holds when f is
    Formula

    Commutative (the order does not matter): f(a, b) = f(b, a).   Associative (the grouping / brackets do not matter): f(f(a, b), c) = f(a, f(b, c)).   For sum, f(a, b) = a + b: a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) (Slide 62).

    Commutative = values from different mappers may arrive in any order; associative = it does not matter which values were pre-combined together on which machine. Slide 62 draws exactly this: the row of values of key k is cut by a vertical line into two parts (two mappers); each part is “added” (circled +) and then the two partial sums are added again.
    Slide erratum (omission, not an error)

    Slide 62 gives the commutative/associative test but does not mention two practical rules. Beyond the slides: in Hadoop the combiner is optional and the system may run it zero, one or several times on a map task’s output, and its output must have the same type as the Map output (the reducer cannot tell whether a combiner ran). So correctness must never depend on whether, or how often, it ran; this is the real reason for the condition above, and it is why the average (part d) needs the mapper to emit (value, 1) pairs from the start. Also, “usually the same as the reduce function” is not “always the same” (see part d).

    Common mistake

    Do not write “the combiner must be identical to the reducer” or “the combiner may be anything”. The test is: would the final answer be the same however the values were split and ordered?

  4. Part (b): show that sum works (word count). For “+” on numbers, a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), so any order and any bracketing of the same numbers give the same total. Hence total = (sum of group 1) + (sum of group 2) + …, and “sum” can serve as combiner and reducer.
    The required example: a mapper emits (the,1), (the,1), (the,1). The combiner replaces them by (the, 1+1+1) = (the,3) (3 pairs → 1). The brackets do not matter: (1+1)+1 = 2+1 = 3 and 1+(1+1) = 1+2 = 3. The same check on Slide 61, key B: it occurs twice at mapper 1 and once at mapper 2, combiner 1 gives 1+1 = 2, combiner 2 leaves 1, the reducer adds 2+1 = 3 = 1+1+1 ✓.
    A complete small example (Practice, written for this guide): Map task 1 reads “the cat the dog the” and Map task 2 reads “the sat on the mat”.
    Map taskRaw Map outputAfter combinerpairs
    1(the,1) (cat,1) (the,1) (dog,1) (the,1)(the,3) (cat,1) (dog,1)5 → 3
    2(the,1) (sat,1) (on,1) (the,1) (mat,1)(the,2) (sat,1) (on,1) (mat,1)5 → 4
    Total pairs over the network10 → 7
    The reducer receives the: [3,2] and adds 3 + 2 = 5; the other words appear once. Without any combiner it would add 1+1+1+1+1 = 5: the same result. Other bracketings agree: (1+1)+(1+1+1) = 5 = 1+(1+1+1+1).
    Same idea with the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (the values of one key, Slide 62 drawing): mapper 1 holds {1,2}, mapper 2 holds {3,4,5}. Partial sums 1+2 = 3 and 3+4+5 = 12; the reducer adds 3 + 12 = 15 = 1+2+3+4+5 ✓. (Beyond the slides: count, which is a sum of 1’s, and also max, min and product are commutative and associative, so they can use their own reduce function as combiner too.)
  5. Part (c): average fails. First the numerical counterexample (Slide 63). Suppose we naively use “average” as the combiner (combiner = reduce = average) for the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 of one key, split as in the Slide 62/63 drawings: mapper 1 gets {1,2}, mapper 2 gets {3,4,5}.
    QuantityComputationResult
    ave1 (combiner at mapper 1)(1 + 2) / 21.5
    ave2 (combiner at mapper 2)(3 + 4 + 5) / 3 = 12 / 34
    Average of the averages (the crossed-out recipe of Slide 63)(ave1 + ave2) / 2 = (1.5 + 4) / 2 = 5.5 / 22.75
    True average of all five values(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5) / 5 = 15 / 53
    Since 2.75 ≠ 3, using average as the combiner gives a wrong answer. The result also depends on how the values happened to be split, which the programmer does not control:
    Split of {1,2,3,4,5}ave1ave2(ave1 + ave2)/2true averagecorrect?
    {1} | {2,3,4,5}13.52.253✗
    {1,2} | {3,4,5} (Slide 63 style)1.542.753✗
    {1,2,3} | {4,5}24.53.253✗
    {1,2,3,4} | {5}2.553.753✗
    {1,5} | {2,3,4}3333✓ (by luck)
    Four splits give four different wrong answers; the fifth is right only by luck, because both group averages happen to equal 3. A correct combiner must give 3 for every split.
  6. Part (c): proof that “average of averages” is wrong in general. Let mapper 1 hold n1 values with average a1 (so their sum is n1a1) and mapper 2 hold n2 values with average a2. Then
    true average T = n1a1 + n2a2n1 + n2  (a weighted average: each group counts in proportion to its size)
    average of averages W = a1 + a22  (both groups get equal weight)
    Subtract, using the common denominator 2(n1 + n2):
    T − W = 2(n1a1 + n2a2) − (n1 + n2)(a1 + a2)2(n1 + n2) = n1a1 + n2a2 − n1a2 − n2a12(n1 + n2) = (n1 − n2)(a1 − a2)2(n1 + n2).
    So W = T only when n1 = n2 (equal group sizes) or a1 = a2 (equal averages). In every other case the combiner is wrong, and since the system chooses the split we can guarantee neither. Numeric check with our data (n1 = 2, a1 = 1.5, n2 = 3, a2 = 4): (2−3)(1.5−4)/(2·5) = (−1)(−2.5)/10 = 0.25 = 3 − 2.75 ✓.
    Two more ways to see the same failure.
    • Not associative (Slide 63’s claim). The two-argument average avg(a,b) = (a+b)/2 is commutative (avg(1,2) = 1.5 = avg(2,1)) but it is not associative: avg(avg(1,2),3) = avg(1.5,3) = 2.25, whereas avg(1,avg(2,3)) = avg(1,2.5) = 1.75: two different answers for the same three numbers (and neither equals their true average 2). Different brackets = different ways of pre-combining on different machines, so the condition of the “Formula” box is violated.
    • An average forgets how many values it stands for. The pair of partial averages (1.5, 4) arises from {1,2} | {3,4,5} (true average 15/5 = 3) and equally from {1,2} | {4} (true average 7/3 ≈ 2.33). Same partial results, different correct answers, so no formula that uses only the partial averages can be right. The missing information is the count.
    Key idea

    A plain average has forgotten its weight. The average 1.5 stands for 2 values and the average 4 stands for 3 values, so they must not get equal weight. The fix is to carry the weight (the count) alongside.

    Slide erratum (wording)

    Slide 63 says “Average is not commutative and associative”. Read it as “average is not (commutative and associative)”: the failing property is associativity, while the two-argument average is commutative. A safe exam sentence: “averaging partial averages is wrong because it ignores how many values each partial average represents; equivalently avg is not associative.”

  7. Part (d): the fix, carry (sum, count) and divide at the very end (Slide 64). Sum and count are each commutative and associative, so carry both and compute the average only once, after everything has been merged: ave = sum / count.
    • Map: turn every value v into the pair (v, 1) = (sum, count) of a one-element group. (Beyond the slides: so the Map output values are already (sum, count) pairs; this keeps the combiner’s input type equal to its output type.)
    • Adding pairs means adding each coordinate separately: (s1,c1) + (s2,c2) = (s1+s2, c1+c2).
    • Commutative: (s1+s2, c1+c2) = (s2+s1, c2+c1), because ordinary + is commutative in each coordinate.
    • Associative: ((s1,c1) + (s2,c2)) + (s3,c3) = ((s1+s2)+s3, (c1+c2)+c3) = (s1+(s2+s3), c1+(c2+c3)) = (s1,c1) + ((s2,c2) + (s3,c3)), again because + is associative in each coordinate.
    • Combiner: add all pairs of the same key on the mapper’s machine and output one pair (no division!). Reducer: add all pairs it receives, then divide once: ave = sum/count.
    Run on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 split {1,2} | {3,4,5}: mapper 1: (1,1) + (2,1) = (3,2); mapper 2: (3,1) + (4,1) + (5,1) = (12,3). Reducer: (3,2) + (12,3) = (3+12, 2+3) = (15,5); then ave = 15/5 = 3 ✓, the true average (Figure L2-Q7-2, right panel).
    Other splits give the same pair. {1,2,3} | {4,5}: (6,3) + (9,2) = (15,5). Three mappers {1} | {2,3} | {4,5}: partial pairs (1,1), (5,2), (9,2). Left bracketing: ((1,1) + (5,2)) + (9,2) = (6,3) + (9,2) = (15,5). Right bracketing: (1,1) + ((5,2) + (9,2)) = (1,1) + (14,4) = (15,5). Reversed order: (9,2) + (5,2) + (1,1) = (15,5). All give 15/5 = 3. (Computer check for this guide: all 52 ways of splitting {1,…,5} into groups, in every order and bracketing, always give (15,5).) This is exactly the Slide 64 drawing: Average = (Sum1+Sum2+Sum3)/(count1+count2+count3).
    Link with the proof above: a pair (sum, count) is an average together with its weight, since sum = count × average. The formula for T is exactly the weighted average of the group averages: (2 × 1.5 + 3 × 4)/5 = 15/5 = 3.
    Common mistake

    (1) Dividing inside the combiner: that turns the pair back into a plain average and the weight is lost again. The division is the one step that is not commutative and associative, so it waits for the reducer, once, at the very end. (2) Concluding “combiner = reducer” for average: here the combiner outputs a (sum, count) pair while the reducer outputs a number; Slide 62’s “usually the same” is not “always the same”. The network still gains: each mapper ships one small pair per key instead of one pair per value.

  8. Part (e): the median cannot use the combiner trick (Slide 65). The median is the middle value of the sorted list (for an even number of values, the mean of the two middle ones). It depends on the rank (sorted position) of every value, not on a sum. For 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 the median is 3.
    (i) The naive attempt fails. Split {1,2} | {3,4,5}: partial medians 1.5 and 4; the median of these two is (1.5+4)/2 = 2.75 ≠ 3. Another example: 1, …, 9 split {1,2,9} | {3,4,5} | {6,7,8}: partial medians 2, 4, 7; the median of the medians is 4, but the true median of 1, …, 9 is 5.
    (ii) No rescue by adding a count (the fix that worked for the average). Compare two data sets whose two mappers send identical summaries (median, count), namely (2, 3) and (5, 3) (Practice values):
    Data setMapper 1 valuesMapper 2 valuespartial medianscountstrue median of all 6 values
    P{1, 2, 3}{4, 5, 6}2 and 53 and 3sorted 1 2 3 4 5 6 → (3+4)/2 = 3.5
    Q{1, 2, 3}{0, 5, 100}2 and 53 and 3sorted 0 1 2 3 5 100 → (2+3)/2 = 2.5
    The reducer would see exactly the same information, (2, 3) and (5, 3), in P and in Q, yet it must answer 3.5 for P and 2.5 for Q. No formula applied to (partial median, count) can be right for both, however cleverly the partial results are merged: the partial medians threw away the information that decides the answer.
    (iii) Conclusion (the slide’s claim). There is no way to split the median into commutative-and-associative pieces that each summarise a group by a small number of values; Slide 65 says a mathematical proof exists (the P/Q table shows the idea on a small example). So we cannot use the combiner “trick”: for the median every value of a key must be shuffled to the reducer, which sorts them and takes the middle one. The shuffle is not reduced (the combiner is simply left out).
    Beyond the slides: why no short summary can work

    Statisticians call aggregates like sum, count, max “distributive”, average “algebraic” (a fixed-size summary such as (sum, count) suffices) and median “holistic” (no fixed-size summary exists). Idea of the proof: take two different sorted lists of the same length n that first differ at position i. Add a second list made of enough very small and very large numbers (as the 0 and 100 in Q above) so that the overall median lands exactly on position i of the original list. The two overall medians then differ, so any valid summary must tell the two lists apart; hence it must distinguish all lists, i.e. it must be as large as the data itself. (The “union of the lists” is commutative and associative too, but it saves nothing.) In practice one uses approximate quantile summaries or extra Map-Reduce rounds, giving up the simple exact one-round trick.

  9. Summary: which reduce functions can use a combiner?
    FunctionCommutative & associative as is?Combiner sendsReducer doesOn 1–5 split {1,2} | {3,4,5}
    Sum, count (word count)yes (Slide 62)partial sum, e.g. (the,3)adds partial sums3 + 12 = 15 ✓
    Average, plainno (Slide 63)— (do not use)—(1.5 + 4)/2 = 2.75, true 3 ✗
    Average via (sum, count)yes, for the pairs (Slide 64)pair (sum, count), no divisionadds pairs, then divides once(3,2) + (12,3) = (15,5), 15/5 = 3 ✓
    Medianno, and no small summary exists (Slide 65)nothing useful: all values must gosorts all values, takes the middlemedians 1.5 and 4 cannot give 3 ✗
    Exam tip

    A full-mark answer has five sentences: (1) a combiner pre-aggregates a mapper’s values per key on the mapper’s own machine, saving network and shuffle; (2) the reduce function may be reused if it is commutative and associative, because the framework controls the split and order; (3) sum qualifies, e.g. (the,1)×3 → (the,3); (4) average does not: {1,2},{3,4,5} give (1.5+4)/2 = 2.75 ≠ 3; fix: send (sum,count), add, divide once at the end → 15/5 = 3; (5) median cannot be decomposed (proof exists), so no combiner trick. Always write the true answer next to the wrong one (2.75 versus 3): that is where the marks are.

    Common mistakes

    (1) Averaging the averages (Slide 63’s crossed-out recipe). (2) Dividing sum by count inside the combiner: only the very last step may divide. (3) Writing “the combiner replaces the reducer”: it only sees one mapper, so the reducer is still required. (4) Saying “the combiner saves computation in the map”: it saves network and shuffle work, not map work. (5) Thinking the median can be fixed with (sum, count): it cannot.

Final answer:
(a) A combiner is a mini-reduce, combine(k, list(v1)) → v2, run on each map machine on that mapper’s own output before the shuffle; it pre-aggregates per key and saves network and shuffle traffic (not map work). Slide 61: 12 pairs → 8 pairs shuffled (33.3 % fewer); the Reducer still adds the partial counts and outputs (A,2) (B,3) (C,2) (D,4) (E,1), the same as without a combiner.
(b) The reduce function can be reused as the combiner only if it is commutative and associative (f(a,b) = f(b,a) and f(f(a,b),c) = f(a,f(b,c))), because the system chooses the split and order. Sum is: (the,1) three times → (the,3); example 10 → 7 pairs, same final counts (the = 3 + 2 = 5).
(c) Average is not: {1,2} | {3,4,5} gives (1.5+4)/2 = 2.75 ≠ true average 3. In general T − W = (n1−n2)(a1−a2)/(2(n1+n2)) ≠ 0 unless the sizes or the averages are equal; avg is not associative (2.25 ≠ 1.75); a partial average forgets its count.
(d) Send (sum, count) pairs, which add coordinate-wise (commutative and associative): (3,2) + (12,3) = (15,5); divide once at the very end, in the reducer: ave = 15/5 = 3 ✓.
(e) The median cannot be split into commutative and associative functions (Slide 65): identical partial summaries (medians 2 and 5, counts 3 and 3) give true medians 3.5 (set P) and 2.5 (set Q). So there is no combiner trick: all values must be shuffled to the reducer, which sorts them and takes the middle one.
Where the marks come from: (1) definition of a combiner, where it runs (on the mapper’s machine, on that mapper’s output only, before the shuffle) and what it saves (network/shuffle); (2) Slide 61 numbers: 12 → 8 pairs, shuffle groups, Reducer output (A,2) (B,3) (C,2) (D,4) (E,1); (3) the condition: commutative and associative, with the two equations, and the reason (the system chooses split and order); (4) sum satisfies it, with the (the,1)×3 → (the,3) example and the final total unchanged; (5) average counterexample with numbers: 1.5, 4, 2.75 versus 3; (6) the reason it fails (partial averages lose the counts / avg is not associative), ideally with the weighted-average proof; (7) the fix: (sum, count) pairs, shown commutative and associative, (15,5), divide once at the very end, 15/5 = 3; (8) median: cannot be decomposed (Slide 65), so no combiner and all values go to the reducer, ideally with the (median, count) counterexample (3.5 versus 2.5).
Slide check: the slides give no numerical answers for this topic (they argue qualitatively), and everything above agrees with them: sum works (62), average does not (63) but works via (sum, count) (64), median cannot use the trick (65). The Slide 61 figure is reproduced exactly (12 → 8 pairs; output (A,2) (B,3) (C,2) (D,4) (E,1)); every Practice number was recomputed in Python. No numerical erratum. Slide erratum (wording and omission only): (1) Slide 63’s “not commutative and associative” should be read as “fails associativity” (the two-argument average is commutative); (2) Slide 62 omits that the combiner’s output type must equal the Map output type and that the system may run it zero, one or several times (beyond the slides); (3) Slide 62’s “works only if … commutative and associative” is the test for reusing the reduce function unchanged as combiner, and Slide 64 shows a failing function can still be combined after re-expressing it through (sum, count); (4) Slide 65’s “impossible” is exact only for small fixed-size partial results (the union of all values is trivially commutative and associative but saves nothing); in the exam quote the slide’s version.

Refinement: the partition function

Lecture 2 · Slides 66–67

Between map and reduce the framework must decide which reduce task gets which key. Slide 66: "Want to control how keys get partitioned": a partition is the set of keys that go to one reduce task, and the one hard requirement is that records with the same intermediate key end up at the same worker. If the values of one key were split over two reducers, each would compute a wrong, partial answer.

Definition: partition function

A function from an intermediate key to a number in 0, 1, …, R−1, the index of the reduce task that receives it. The system's default is hash(key) mod R, where R is the number of reduce tasks, hash turns the key into a (large) number and mod takes the remainder after division by R.

Why it works: same key gives the same hash and the same remainder, hence the same reduce task. Different keys are spread roughly evenly, which balances the load. Each map task applies the function to every pair it emits and writes its output into R buckets (the "Partitioning Function" bars of Slide 59), one per reduce task.

Tiny example (Practice, made-up hash values): with R = 3, a key with hash 7 goes to task 7 mod 3 = 1; a key with hash 9 goes to task 0; hash 20 goes to task 2.

Overriding the hash

Lecture 2 · Slide 67

Slide 67: "Sometimes useful to override the hash function: e.g. hash(hostname(URL)) mod R ensures URLs from a host end up in the same output file." The default would send yorku.ca/a, yorku.ca/b and yorku.ca/c to arbitrary reduce tasks. If you hash only the hostname part (yorku.ca), all of that site's URLs share one hash and therefore one reduce task and one output file (each reduce task writes its own output file; there are R in total). The key itself is unchanged (still the full URL); only the routing uses a function of the key.

Beyond the slides: hash partitioning balances load only on average. A very frequent key (such as "the") or one huge host sends all of its pairs to a single reduce task, which becomes a straggler. Each reduce task writes its own output file, so there are R output files (Slide 66's "reduce worker" means a reduce task).

Common mistakes
  • A custom partition function must still map equal keys to the same reducer. Any function of the key (such as its hostname) satisfies this, a random choice does not.
  • Beyond the slides: a custom partitioner can unbalance the load (one huge site means one slow reduce task), and a hash cannot split a single very popular key such as "the" across reducers.
  • Slide 66 says "reduce worker" and "set of keys" loosely; precisely, the unit is a reduce task, and a worker may run several.

Refinement: backup tasks (stragglers)

Lecture 2 · Slide 68

Slide 68 is organised as Problem, Solution, Effect.

  • Problem: slow workers significantly lengthen the job completion time. Reasons listed: other jobs on the machine, bad disks, "weird things". A machine that is alive but slow is a straggler. A phase (map phase or reduce phase) finishes only when its last task finishes, so one straggler delays everything. This is different from a failure (Slide 57): the worker still works, just slowly.
  • Solution: near the end of a phase, the master spawns backup copies of the tasks still in progress on other, idle machines. Whichever one finishes first "wins"; the other is discarded.
  • Effect: dramatically shortens job completion time.
Worked example (Practice, numbers invented): one straggler Lecture 2 · Slide 68

Three tasks should each take 10 minutes. Workers 1 and 2 do tasks A and B in 10 minutes. Worker 3 has a bad disk and needs 40 minutes for task C.

  1. Without backups: the phase ends when C ends, at 40 min; Workers 1 and 2 idle for 30 minutes.
  2. With a backup: at minute 10 the master starts a copy of C on idle Worker 1. A normal-speed copy needs 10 minutes, so it finishes at minute 10 + 10 = 20 min; the slow original is cancelled.
  3. Saving: 40 → 20 minutes. Cost: one extra copy of one task.

Why duplicating is safe: map and reduce functions are deterministic and tasks are independent, so running a task twice gives the same output; the master simply keeps the first. Beyond the slides: this is also called speculative execution; Dean and Ghemawat report that a sort job took about 44% longer with backup tasks disabled. The slide does not say how a straggler is recognised (the master watches progress near the end of a phase).

Exam tip

Typical question: "What is a straggler and how does Map-Reduce handle it?" Answer in three lines: slow-but-alive machine (other load, bad disk) delays the whole phase; near the end of the phase the master launches backup copies of the remaining tasks on other machines; the first copy to finish wins, shortening the job at a small extra cost. Do not confuse with failure recovery.

How many map and reduce tasks?

Lecture 2 · Slide 69

A job has M map tasks and R reduce tasks. Slide 69 gives the rule of thumb:

  • Make M much larger than the number of nodes in the cluster.
  • One DFS chunk per map task is common.
  • This speeds up recovery from worker failures and gives dynamic load balancing.
  • Usually R is smaller than M.
Worked example (Practice) Lecture 2 · Slide 69

Input 1 TB, chunk size 64 MB, cluster of 1,000 nodes. One map task per chunk: M = 1,000,000 MB / 64 MB = 15,625 (about 16,000 if 1 TB is counted as 220 MB: 16,384). That is roughly 16 map tasks per node, so the cluster stays busy and a dead node loses only about 16 small tasks that are re-run on many machines at once.

Why R < M? The slide gives no reason. Beyond the slides: every reduce task writes one output file, and many tiny output files are unwanted; the output is also usually smaller than the input. R is often a small multiple of the number of machines. Remember that R is the modulus in hash(key) mod R (Slide 66).

Slide erratum (minor)

The title says "jobs" but the content is about tasks: one Map-Reduce job consists of M map tasks and R reduce tasks. "Rule of a thumb" should read "rule of thumb".

Problems suited for Map-Reduce

Lecture 2 · Slide 70

Slide 70 is a section divider announcing two topics: "Problems Suited for Map-Reduce" and "Join by Map-Reduce". It carries no printed number and no further content; the join comes next. The slide itself lists no criteria, so the guidance below is Beyond the slides: a summary of the course background.

Well suitedPoorly suited
One huge input processed in one or a few passes (scan, filter, count, aggregate, join)Small data that fits on one machine (the cluster overhead dominates)
Work that splits into independent pieces (map) followed by a group-by-key and per-key aggregation (reduce)Jobs needing low latency or random access/updates to single records
Data that is written once and read many times (as for the DFS, Slides 17–18)Iterative algorithms with many rounds: each round re-reads and re-writes the DFS (the motivation for Spark in Lecture 3)
Examples in this lecture: word count, host size, language model, joinTasks where pieces must constantly exchange state with each other

Example: join by Map-Reduce

Lecture 2 · Slides 71–72

The problem

Lecture 2 · Slide 71

A relation is a table; a tuple is one row. Slide 71 asks for the natural join R(A,B) ⋈ S(B,C), where R and S are each stored in files and tuples are pairs (a,b) or (b,c). They are "stored in files" because they are huge and live in the DFS.

Definition: natural join

R(A,B) ⋈ S(B,C) glues every tuple (a,b) of R to every tuple (b,c) of S that has the same value of the shared attribute B, producing (a,b,c). A tuple whose b has no partner on the other side produces nothing.

Slide 71's data: R = {(a1,b1), (a2,b1), (a3,b2), (a4,b3)}, S = {(b2,c1), (b2,c2), (b3,c3)}. Value b1 occurs only in R (a1 and a2 vanish); b2 occurs once in R and twice in S (two result rows); b3 once on each side. The join has three tuples: (a3,b2,c1), (a3,b2,c2), (a4,b3,c3).

Slide erratum

The result table on Slide 71 has only the columns A and C (and the next slide outputs (a,b,c)). The natural join has schema (A,B,C). The slide's three rows are the (A,C) projection of the correct result, so its tuples are right but the column B is missing. Use (A,B,C) in your answer.

The algorithm

Lecture 2 · Slide 72

Idea: tuples that must be glued share the same b, and Map-Reduce's group-by-key brings equal keys together. So make b the key.

  1. Map: each R tuple (a,b) becomes the pair (b, (a, R)); each S tuple (b,c) becomes (b, (c, S)). The tag R or S records the origin, because a reducer receives a mixed bag and must know which side each value came from.
  2. Shuffle: every pair with key b goes to Reduce process h(b), where h is a hash function ("Hadoop does this automatically"). Beyond the slides: in Hadoop this is the default partition function hash(key) mod R of Slide 66.
  3. Reduce: for one key b, match every (a,R) with every (c,S) and output (a,b,c), a cross product per key.

Trace on the slide data: 4 + 3 = 7 pairs are shuffled. b1 has values [(a1,R), (a2,R)] and no S value, so no output; b2 pairs a3 with c1 and c2; b3 pairs a4 with c3. Result: 3 tuples, as above.

Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the tag; without it the reducer cannot tell R values from S values.
  • "Match all (b,(a,R)) with all (b,(c,S))" means for the same key b: a reducer for b2 never sees b3 pairs.
  • Outputting something for a key that appears on one side only (dangling tuples give nothing).
  • The slide says "process" where the rest of the lecture says "task"; one Reduce process handles many keys.

Cost measures for Map-Reduce algorithms

Lecture 2 · Slides 73–74

How do we compare two Map-Reduce algorithms? Slide 73: "In MapReduce we quantify the cost of an algorithm using":

Definition: the two cost measures (Slide 73)
  1. Communication cost = total I/O of all processes: how much data all map and reduce tasks read and write, i.e. how much data is moved around.
  2. (Elapsed) computation cost: analogous, but counting only the running time of the processes.

The note on the slide: "the big-O notation is not the most useful (adding more machines is always an option)". Classic analysis says "this takes n log n steps"; but with 1,000 machines the work simply divides, so what matters is how much data moves and how long you wait.

What the measures mean

Lecture 2 · Slide 74

  • Either the I/O (communication) cost or the processing (computation) cost dominates; ignore one or the other (analyse the bigger one).
  • Total cost tells what you pay in rent from "your friendly neighborhood cloud": the sum of work over all machines.
  • Elapsed cost is wall-clock time using parallelism: how long you wait.
Total costElapsed cost
What it adds upwork of all machines (machine-hours, bytes moved by all)the longest chain of dependent work (wall-clock time)
Pays forthe cloud billyour waiting time
Effect of adding machinesstays about the samegoes down
Worked example (Practice, assumed numbers): communication cost of a job Lecture 2 · Slide 73 and Slide 61

1,000 map tasks each read a 64 MB chunk, and (no combiner) each emits about as much as it reads, which the reducers then read.

  1. Map input: 1,000 × 64 MB = 64,000 MB.
  2. Reduce input (the shuffled data): about 64,000 MB.
  3. Communication cost, convention B (textbook: count each task's input only) ≈ 64,000 + 64,000 = 128,000 MB (about 128 GB). Convention A (literal Slide 73: every byte read or written) would also add the Map output written (about 64,000 MB) and the final output, so about 192,000 MB plus the output. State which convention you use; the cost is linear in the data either way.
  4. With a combiner that cuts the shuffled data tenfold: 64,000 + 6,400 = 70,400 MB.

Beyond the slides (textbook, Mining of Massive Datasets §2.3): convention B, the textbook, counts each task's input size and does not count the final output, and defines "elapsed" cost as the largest total along any chain of dependent tasks, since independent tasks run simultaneously. Slide 73's phrase "total I/O" is vague on this point; the same example is applied to the join in the quiz below.

Common mistake

Quoting big-O as "the" cost, or saying that more machines reduce total cost. They reduce elapsed cost; total cost stays (or even grows, because of communication overhead).

Try it yourself first: for the Slide 71 data, write the Map output, the groups and the Reduce output, then say what the communication cost is, before looking at the solution.

Quiz L2-Q6Natural join R(A,B) ⋈ S(B,C) with Map-Reduce Lecture 2 · Slides 70–74
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 71, “Example: Join By Map-Reduce” (Slide 70 is only the section divider “Join by Map-Reduce”). Compute the natural join R(A,B) ⋈ S(B,C). R and S are each stored in files. Tuples are pairs (a,b) or (b,c). The slide prints the two input tables and the result. (The slide writes a with subscript 1, b with subscript 1, and so on; here they are typed a1, b1, …)

result as printed on Slide 71

Slide 72, “Map-Reduce Join”, gives the method in words: a Map process turns each input tuple R(a,b) into the key-value pair (b,(a,R)) and each input tuple S(b,c) into (b,(c,S)); each key-value pair with key b is sent to Reduce process h(b) (“Hadoop does this automatically”); each Reduce process matches all the pairs (b,(a,R)) with all (b,(c,S)) and outputs (a,b,c). Slides 73–74 then define the cost measures of a Map-Reduce algorithm. The slides pose one task and give no numbers beyond the tables, so this block splits it into the parts an exam could ask:

(a) Give the result of R ⋈ S and check every tuple.
(b) Map: list the output pairs (b,(a,R)) and (b,(c,S)), tagged by relation.
(c) Shuffle and Reduce: show which pairs go to Reduce process h(b) and what every Reduce call outputs.
(d) Practice (written for this guide, not on the slides): explain why a join key that occurs on only one side (for example b1, which occurs only in R) produces no output.
(e) Slides 73–74: what is the communication cost (= total I/O of all processes), and how do the elapsed and total cost differ? Discuss briefly using this example.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Think of two lists at a university. List R says which student is in which tutorial group (student a, group b). List S says which room each group uses (group b, room c). “Join” means: work out, for each student, the room(s) where they must go, by gluing a student line and a room line together whenever the group is the same. Doing this on a huge pile of papers is easy if you first sort everything into one box per group: then the students of group b2 and the rooms of group b2 are in the same box, and you simply pair every student with every room in that box. Map-Reduce does exactly this. Map writes the group on the front of every paper; the shuffle posts each paper to the box (Reduce process) h(b) that owns that group; Reduce pairs things up inside each group. A coloured sticker (the tag R or S) tells the clerk whether a paper is a student line or a room line. A group that has students but no room (b1) gives no pairs at all.

  1. Formula / idea — what a natural join is. The natural join glues together every pair of tuples that agree on the attribute they share, B, and keeps that shared value only once:
    Formula

    R(A,B) ⋈ S(B,C) = { (a,b,c) : (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S }. The result has the three attributes (A,B,C). If the value b occurs rb times in R and sb times in S, it contributes rb × sb result tuples, so |R ⋈ S| = ∑b rb · sb.

    Why this suits Map-Reduce (Slides 32–35, 44): the framework’s Group by key step brings together all values that have the same key. Tuples that must be glued share the same b. So choose key = b, and the system itself delivers to one place exactly the tuples that have to meet.
  2. Part (a) — compute the expected answer directly (nested comparison). |R| = 4 and |S| = 3. Compare every R-tuple with every S-tuple (4 × 3 = 12 comparisons) and keep a pair only if the B values are equal. This gives the answer that Map-Reduce must reproduce, and it lets us check the slide:
    R-tuple ↓ / S-tuple →(b2,c1)(b2,c2)(b3,c3)
    (a1,b1)✗ b1 ≠ b2✗ b1 ≠ b2✗ b1 ≠ b3
    (a2,b1)✗ b1 ≠ b2✗ b1 ≠ b2✗ b1 ≠ b3
    (a3,b2)✓ (a3,b2,c1)✓ (a3,b2,c2)✗ b2 ≠ b3
    (a4,b3)✗ b3 ≠ b2✗ b3 ≠ b2✓ (a4,b3,c3)
    Three of the 12 pairs match, so the expected join has 3 tuples: (a3,b2,c1), (a3,b2,c2), (a4,b3,c3). The two R-tuples with b1 find no partner in S. Dropping the B column gives (a3,c1), (a3,c2), (a4,c3), which is the table printed on Slide 71. Beyond the slides: comparing all pairs is fine for 12 pairs but hopeless for billions of tuples; the Map-Reduce method below never compares tuples with different b.
  3. Part (b) — Map (Slide 72): one Map call per input tuple (Slide 43), key = the join attribute b, value = the other attribute plus a tag. Every R-tuple (a,b) becomes the pair (b,(a,R)); every S-tuple (b,c) becomes (b,(c,S)). Applied to the data:
    Input fileInput tupleMap output pair (key, (value, tag))
    R(a1,b1)(b1,(a1,R))
    (a2,b1)(b1,(a2,R))
    (a3,b2)(b2,(a3,R))
    (a4,b3)(b3,(a4,R))
    S(b2,c1)(b2,(c1,S))
    (b2,c2)(b2,(c2,S))
    (b3,c3)(b3,(c3,S))
    That is 7 Map calls and 7 output pairs (4 from R plus 3 from S). Why key = b? It is the only attribute shared by R and S, and Group by key gathers all pairs with equal b. Why the tag? The Reduce side receives a mixed bag of values such as a3, c1, c2 with no column names; without a tag it could not tell whether a value is an A-value (from R) or a C-value (from S), and it could wrongly glue two R-values together. Beyond the slides: in Hadoop a Map task knows which input file it is reading, so it can attach the right tag.
  4. Part (c) — Shuffle / group by key (Slide 72: “Send each key-value pair with key b to Reduce process h(b)”). The hash function h turns a key into the number of a Reduce process. Its defining property is that the same b always goes to the same Reduce process, so all R-pairs and S-pairs of one b meet. “Hadoop does this automatically”: the programmer writes nothing for it. (Slide 66 gives the default hash(key) mod R; Slide 69 defines R as the number of Reduce tasks; the system’s default partition function is hash(key) mod R, where R is the number of Reduce tasks.) The slides fix neither h nor the number of Reduce processes, so for the picture I assume R = 2 Reduce processes, numbered 0 and 1, with h(b1) = 0, h(b2) = 0, h(b3) = 1 (illustration only; any other h gives the same final join). Then:
    Reduce processKeys it ownsPairs it receives#pairs
    0b1, b2(b1,(a1,R)), (b1,(a2,R)), (b2,(a3,R)), (b2,(c1,S)), (b2,(c2,S))5
    1b3(b3,(a4,R)), (b3,(c3,S))2
    Inside each process the pairs are grouped by key, giving three key groups: b1 → [(a1,R), (a2,R)]; b2 → [(a3,R), (c1,S), (c2,S)]; b3 → [(a4,R), (c3,S)]. The pairs arrive in arbitrary order, mixed R and S, which is why the tag is needed.
    Common mistake

    Slide 72 says each Reduce process matches “all the pairs (b,(a,R)) with all (b,(c,S))”. Read this as pairs with the same b. Reduce process 0 holds two different keys (b1 and b2); it must not pair a b1-tuple with a b2-tuple. The unit of work is the Reduce call: one call per unique key (Slide 44), here 3 calls, even though there are only 2 Reduce processes. (Also: on Slides 66 and 69 the number of Reduce tasks is called R; it has nothing to do with relation R.)

  5. Part (c) — Reduce (Slide 72): inside one call, separate the values by tag and output every R–S combination. For key b, build the R-list (values tagged R, the a-values) and the S-list (values tagged S, the c-values), and output (a,b,c) for every a in the R-list together with every c in the S-list. That is rb × sb outputs for the key. The three Reduce calls:

    1 (process 0)b1a1, a2(empty)2 × 0 = 0nothing
    2 (process 0)b2a3c1, c21 × 2 = 2(a3,b2,c1), (a3,b2,c2)
    3 (process 1)b3a4c31 × 1 = 1(a4,b3,c3)
    Total33 tuples
  6. Part (a) again — collect the output and check it. The join is the union of all Reduce outputs: R ⋈ S = { (a3,b2,c1), (a3,b2,c2), (a4,b3,c3) }, as a table:
    ABC

    Three checks: (i) it equals the direct comparison in step 2; (ii) the count formula gives ∑ rb·sb = 2·0 + 1·2 + 1·1 = 3 ✓; (iii) removing the B column leaves exactly the three (A,C) rows of the table on Slide 71 ✓.
  7. Draw the data flow. Figure 1 shows the whole job: 7 input tuples → 7 tagged pairs → shuffle (arrow colour = key) → 3 Reduce calls on 2 Reduce processes → 3 result tuples.
  8. Part (d) — why a key found on one side only gives no output. Take b1. Both pairs with key b1 come from R: the Reduce call receives R-list = [a1, a2] but S-list = [ ] (empty). The number of combinations is rb1 × sb1 = 2 × 0 = 0, so there is nothing to glue and the call outputs nothing. Why this is the right answer: a natural join keeps (a,b,c) only if both (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S. There is no tuple (b1,c) in S, so (a1,b1) and (a2,b1) are dangling tuples (tuples with no join partner). A natural (inner) join discards them, which is why a1 and a2 are missing from the table on Slide 71. The same happens for a key that occurs only in S: its R-list is empty, so 0 × sb = 0 outputs. In general, if either list is empty the product is 0. (Padding the missing side with NULL would be a different operation, an outer join, not a natural join.) The price: the two b1 pairs were still read, shuffled and received before being thrown away, because Map cannot know in advance which keys have a partner. This wasted traffic counts in the communication cost below. Practice (self-made check): if S also contained (b1,c4), the b1 Reduce call would have R-list [a1, a2] and S-list [c4], so 2 × 1 = 2 outputs, (a1,b1,c4) and (a2,b1,c4), and the join would grow from 3 to 5 tuples.
  9. Part (e) — communication cost (Slide 73): count the total I/O (input/output, i.e. reading and writing data) of all processes. Slide 73 gives only the definition: communication cost = total I/O of all processes. To make it concrete, count every tuple or pair that a process reads or writes (unit: one tuple = one unit; the slide fixes no unit, so this tally is my illustration). With r = |R| = 4, s = |S| = 3 and o = |R ⋈ S| = 3:
    StageWhat is read or writtenGeneralHere
    Map tasks read their inputevery tuple of R and Sr + s7
    Map tasks write pairsexactly one pair per input tupler + s7
    Reduce tasks read pairsevery pair is shuffled to its reducerr + s7
    Reduce tasks write the resultone (a,b,c) per matcho3
    Total I/O of all processes7 + 7 + 7 + 33(r + s) + o24
    So the cost grows linearly with the size of the inputs plus the size of the output: the whole of both relations is read, shipped across the network once and received, including the dangling b1 pairs. Beyond the slides: a combiner (Slides 59–62) cannot shrink this traffic, because a join does not aggregate anything; every tuple must reach its reducer. Beyond the slides: the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets, Ch. 2) counts only the input size of each task, because one task’s output is the next task’s input; then the cost here is 7 (Map input) + 7 (Reduce input) = 14, or 17 if the final output of 3 tuples is also counted, i.e. O(r + s + o). Whichever convention you use, state it; the conclusion (linear in the data) is the same. Real systems count bytes rather than tuples.
  10. Part (e) — elapsed versus total cost (Slides 73–74). Slide 73 names two measures: (1) communication cost = total I/O of all processes, and (2) (elapsed) computation cost, which is analogous but counts only the running time of the processes. It adds that big-O notation is not the most useful measure here, because “adding more machines is always an option”. Slide 74 explains the meaning:
    Total costElapsed cost
    What it measuresthe work of all processes on all machines, added upwall-clock time from start to end when processes run in parallel; only the slowest chain counts
    Slide 74 wording“tells what you pay in rent from your friendly neighborhood cloud”“wall-clock time using parallelism”
    Effect of adding machinesabout the same (the work is only spread out)goes down, because tasks run at the same time
    Slide 74 also says that either the I/O (communication) cost or the processing (computation) cost dominates, so you can ignore one or the other. For this join the per-tuple processing is trivial (build a pair, compare two keys), so communication dominates and the communication cost is the number to look at (my reading of the example).
    Illustration (assumed cost model, made up for this guide): every pair costs 1 time unit to process in a task, shuffle time is ignored, and Reduce starts only when all Map tasks are done. The 2 Map tasks process 4 and 3 pairs; the 2 Reduce processes (our h) process 5 and 2 pairs (Figure 2).
    Number of Reduce processesPairs per Reduce processTotal costElapsed cost
    174 + 3 + 7 = 144 + 7 = 11
    2 (our h)5 and 2144 + 5 = 9
    3 (one per key)2, 3 and 2144 + 3 = 7
    Adding Reduce processes lowers the elapsed cost but leaves the total work unchanged (14 units); the elapsed cost is limited by the most heavily loaded process. This is the point of Slide 73’s note: since more machines can always be added, what you really trade off is money (total) against waiting time (elapsed). Here there are only 3 keys, so a 4th Reduce process would receive nothing and sit idle (Slide 69: usually R is smaller than M, the number of Map tasks). Beyond the slides: if one value of b is very common, its Reduce call receives huge lists and becomes the slowest task, so the elapsed time is set by that call (“skew”).
Slide erratum (minor)

(1) The result table on Slide 71 has only the columns A and C, but the natural join R(A,B) ⋈ S(B,C) has the schema (A,B,C), and Slide 72 itself says that Reduce outputs (a,b,c). The slide table is the join with column B dropped (a projection onto A and C). The A–C pairs are correct. In an answer, write the full tuples (a,b,c) and, if you also show the A–C table, say that B has been left out. (2) Slide 72’s “each Reduce process matches all the pairs (b,(a,R)) with all (b,(c,S))” is only correct per key: matching happens inside one Reduce call (one per unique key, Slide 44), never across different keys that happen to sit on the same process.

Exam tip

A full-marks answer has five visible parts: (1) key = join attribute B; (2) the two Map rules with tags: R(a,b) → (b,(a,R)) and S(b,c) → (b,(c,S)); (3) all 7 Map output pairs written out; (4) the shuffle statement “pairs with the same b go to the same Reduce process h(b)”, with the groups per key; (5) per key, the R-list × S-list combinations and the final tuples. If asked about cost, quote the definition (“communication cost = total I/O of all processes”) and the contrast “total = cloud rent, elapsed = wall-clock time with parallelism”. Even if the arithmetic goes wrong, each of these lines is a separate mark.

Common mistake
  • Forgetting the tags, so the Reduce side cannot tell a-values from c-values.
  • Choosing A or C as the key. The key must be the shared attribute B; otherwise tuples that should join go to different reducers and never meet.
  • Pairing an R-value with another R-value, or pairing values that belong to different keys just because they landed on the same Reduce process.
  • Outputting something for b1, for example (a1,b1,NULL). A natural join outputs nothing for unmatched keys.
  • Giving only (a,c). The Reduce output is (a,b,c); the (A,C) table is the same join with B left out.
  • Saying “one Reduce process per key”. There is one Reduce call per key; a process may own several keys.
Final answer:
(a) R ⋈ S = { (a3,b2,c1), (a3,b2,c2), (a4,b3,c3) } (3 tuples; on columns A,C only: (a3,c1), (a3,c2), (a4,c3), as on Slide 71).
(b) Map: R(a,b) → (b,(a,R)); S(b,c) → (b,(c,S)). 7 pairs: (b1,(a1,R)), (b1,(a2,R)), (b2,(a3,R)), (b3,(a4,R)), (b2,(c1,S)), (b2,(c2,S)), (b3,(c3,S)).
(c) Shuffle: every pair with key b goes to Reduce process h(b); groups: b1 → [a1,a2 from R], b2 → [a3 from R; c1,c2 from S], b3 → [a4 from R; c3 from S]. Reduce (one call per key, output = all R–S combinations): b1 → nothing (2 × 0); b2 → (a3,b2,c1), (a3,b2,c2) (1 × 2); b3 → (a4,b3,c3) (1 × 1).
(d) A key with only R-tuples (b1) or only S-tuples has an empty list on one side, so rb × sb = 0 and nothing is output; those tuples are dangling and do not appear in the join.
(e) Communication cost = total I/O of all processes. Convention A (literal Slide 73, every read and write counted): 3(r + s) + o = 24 tuple transfers here. Convention B (textbook, task inputs only): 14, or 17 with the output. State which convention you use; it grows linearly with input plus output size. Total cost (sum of all work, the cloud rent) is 14 units while elapsed cost (wall-clock with parallelism) is 9 units in the illustrative model; more Reduce processes lower elapsed but not total.
Where the marks come from: (1) The natural-join definition (a,b,c) with (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S, and the correct 3-tuple result — (a). (2) Key = the join attribute B; Map rule for R-tuples, (b,(a,R)), and for S-tuples, (b,(c,S)), including the tags; all 7 output pairs written correctly — (b). (3) Shuffle: same b → same Reduce process h(b); the grouped lists per key — (c). (4) Reduce rule: match every R-value with every S-value of the same key and output (a,b,c); correct per-key outputs (nothing for b1, two tuples for b2, one for b3) — (c). (5) A key present on one side only gives an empty list, a product of 0 and dangling tuples — (d). (6) Communication cost = total I/O of all processes, ideally with the count 24 or the formula 3(r + s) + o; total (rent) versus elapsed (wall-clock with parallelism) — (e). (This split is typical, not the examiner’s actual scheme; every step above is a separate credit opportunity.)
Slide check: matches the slide’s answer. The R and S tables were read from the Slide 71 image tuple by tuple and checked by hand and by computer; the result printed on Slide 71, (a3,c1), (a3,c2), (a4,c3), is exactly the A and C columns of the join computed here, and the method is the one on Slide 72. Notes: (i) minor erratum above (the slide result table omits column B although the join and Slide 72 output (a,b,c)); (ii) Slide 72’s “all the pairs … with all …” must be read as “with the same b”; (iii) the slides give no hash function, number of reducers, or cost numbers for this example, so h, the 2 Reduce processes, the count 24 and the 14 / 9 time units are my illustrative assumptions (Slides 73–74 give only the definitions).

Implementations and cloud computing

Lecture 2 · Slides 75–77

Slide 75 is the divider "Map-Reduce Implementations and Pointers" (unnumbered; "pointers" means references and links). Map-Reduce is a model; Slide 76 names the systems that implement it.

Implementations

Lecture 2 · Slide 76

SystemWhat it is (Slide 76)Storage
Google MapReduceGoogle's original; not available outside GoogleGFS (Google File System) for stable storage
HadoopAn open-source implementation in JavaHDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) for stable storage
Hive, PigProvide SQL-like abstractions on top of the Hadoop Map-Reduce layer(they run on Hadoop and HDFS)

Stable storage means storage that keeps data safe and available despite machine failures, because it is replicated (Slides 21–22), unlike a worker's local disk where intermediate map output lives and is lost with the machine. Hive and Pig let analysts write short queries or scripts instead of Java map and reduce programs; the system compiles them into Map-Reduce jobs. Beyond the slides: Hive's language HiveQL is SQL-like; Pig's language Pig Latin is a step-by-step data-flow script, so "SQL-like" fits Hive better than Pig.

Slide erratum (minor)

The download link on Slide 76 (lucene.apache.org/hadoop) and the wiki/Javadoc links on Slide 79 date from when Hadoop was a Lucene sub-project and are obsolete; Hadoop now has its own Apache site. They are not examinable. HDFS is not expanded on the slide (Hadoop Distributed File System).

Beyond the slides: GFS and HDFS terminology

The two file systems share one design (Lecture 2 Slides 17–25); the vocabulary differs. Defaults can vary by version, so treat sizes as typical.

Cloud computing

Lecture 2 · Slide 77

Slide 77: cloud computing is the "ability to rent computing by the hour", plus additional services such as persistent storage. You do not buy a cluster; you rent machines and release them when the job ends, which is why total cost (Slide 74) is literally your bill. Amazon's offering:

ServiceWhat it is
EC2, Elastic Compute Cloudrentable virtual machines (the compute)
S3stable storage for the data (Beyond the slides: Simple Storage Service)
EMR, Elastic Map Reduceready-made Hadoop Map-Reduce service

The slide adds: "Hadoop can be run on EC2" (you can install and run it yourself on rented machines). Beyond the slides: S3 and EMR are separate Amazon services used together with EC2, not parts of it, although the slide nests them under EC2.
