Exam tip: the single most useful hint of the lecture

Slide 80 says every worked example is a potential quiz question. In this lecture that means word count, host size, the language model, the combiner example (Slide 61) and the join (Slides 71–72). For each be able to state the Map function, the Reduce function and the key and value types, in words, and trace a small input by hand. (Slide 80 has a typo, "treat is as", which should read "treat them as".)

Quick recap (Slides 58–80)
  • Granularity: many more map tasks than machines (M ≫ nodes, one DFS chunk per map task) gives load balancing and fast recovery; R is usually smaller than M. Shuffle reads start as each map ends (pipelining); reduce waits for all its reads.
  • Combiner: runs on the mapper's machine before the shuffle; legal when reduce is commutative and associative (sum, count, max, min). Average: carry (sum, count), divide at the end. Median: impossible. Slide 61: 12 pairs become 8.
  • Partition function: default hash(key) mod R; equal keys must reach the same reducer; override such as hash(hostname(URL)) mod R keeps a site's URLs in one output file.
  • Backup tasks: near the end of a phase duplicate the slow tasks; the first copy to finish wins.
  • Join: map to (b,(a,R)) and (b,(c,S)); shuffle by h(b); reduce pairs R-values with S-values per key and outputs (a,b,c); one-sided keys give nothing.
  • Cost: communication cost = total I/O of all processes; computation cost = running time; total cost = the cloud bill, elapsed cost = wall-clock time; big-O is less useful because more machines are always an option.
  • Systems: Google MapReduce + GFS (not public); Hadoop + HDFS (open source, Java); Hive and Pig on top of Hadoop; Amazon EC2 + S3 + EMR; readings are the GFS and MapReduce papers.

Theory Q&A bank

Lecture 2 · Slides 1–80

Cover the answer, write your own, then compare. Each model answer is short enough to write in an exam; numbered steps are the marking points. The slides pose Q1 directly (Slide 5: how long to read 200 TB) and the two design questions behind Q3 (Slides 13 and 15). Slide 80 tells you to treat all the worked examples as quiz questions, which is why the worked-example questions are included. The rest are likely exam questions built from the slides.

Q1. How long does it take one computer to read 200 TB, and how do we speed it up?

Lecture 2 · Slides 5–8

  1. Data: 10+ billion pages × 20 KB = 2 × 10¹¹ KB = 200 TB = 2 × 10⁸ MB (1 TB = 10⁶ MB).
  2. Time = data ÷ bandwidth = 2 × 10⁸ MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 4 × 10⁶ s ≈ 46 days (4 × 10⁶ ÷ 86,400 = 46.3).
  3. Fix: split the data into chunks, stripe it over many discs and process in parallel. With 1,000 discs and CPUs: 4 × 10⁶ ÷ 1,000 = 4,000 s ≈ 67 minutes.
  4. The 4,000 s is ideal: it assumes an even split, independent discs at full speed, and no failures or result-combining cost. Reading is also only the start; useful work takes longer (Slide 7).

Q2. Describe the architecture of a compute cluster and rank the cost of moving data.

Lecture 2 · Slides 9–11

A node = CPU + memory + disk. A rack holds 16–64 nodes joined by one switch with 1 Gbps (= 125 MB/s) between any pair. Racks are joined through higher-level switches by a backbone of 2–10 Gbps; a data centre can hold ~1M machines (Google estimate). All of it is commodity hardware and Ethernet. Cheapest to read: data on the same node (no network); next: another node in the same rack; most expensive: another rack (shared backbone). This ranking is why the lecture stresses locality.

Q3. What challenges does cluster computing face, and how does Map-Reduce address them?

Lecture 2 · Slides 12–16

Challenge (slide)NumbersMap-Reduce idea (Slide 16)
Machines fail (12–13): how to store data persistently and keep it available, and how to survive failures during a long computation?1 server up ~1,000 days: 1,000 servers lose 1 a day; 1M machines lose 1,000 a dayStore data redundantly on multiple nodes (DFS replicas); the framework re-runs lost tasks
Network bottleneck (14)1 Gbps: moving 10 TB takes about a dayMove computation close to the data: chunk servers also compute
Distributed programming is hard (3, 15): how to make it easy?—Simple programming model: write Map and Reduce; the framework hides the complexity

Q4. What is a distributed file system? Explain chunks, replication, the master and how a read works.

Lecture 2 · Slides 17–24

  1. A DFS (GFS at Google, HDFS in Hadoop) stores files across a cluster and keeps each piece several times, for redundancy and availability. It is designed for huge files (100s of GB to TB), rarely updated in place, mostly read and appended.
  2. A file is cut into chunks of 16–64 MB stored on chunk servers. Each chunk is replicated 2× or 3× on different servers (never two copies on one server) and, if possible, in different racks.
  3. The master node (Name Node in HDFS) keeps only metadata: which chunks make up a file and where their copies are. It may be replicated.
  4. Read: the client library asks the master where the chunks are, then connects directly to the chunk servers to read the data. The data never passes through the master.
  5. Failure: if a server dies, each affected chunk still has another copy, so reads continue; the lost copies are re-created elsewhere (seamless recovery).

Q5. What are the four stages of a Map-Reduce job, who writes what, and what does the environment handle?

Lecture 2 · Slides 27–28, 53–54

Stages: (1) Map: apply the Map function to each input record, emitting (key, value) pairs; (2) Group by key (sort and shuffle): bring all pairs with the same key together; (3) Reduce: aggregate the values of each key; (4) write the result. The programmer supplies only the Map and Reduce functions (and the input files); "the outline stays the same, Map and Reduce change to fit the problem". The environment takes care of: scheduling, inter-machine communication, partitioning the data, the group-by-key step and machine failures.

Q6. State the signatures of Map and Reduce. How many calls of each are made?

Lecture 2 · Slides 29–35, 43–44

Map(k, v) → <k', v'>*: one call per input pair; emits zero or more intermediate pairs. Reduce(k', <v'>*) → (k', v''): one call per unique intermediate key, receiving all its values, emitting the aggregated pair. Example: "a rose is a rose" as one input pair gives 1 Map call, 5 pairs, 3 distinct keys and so 3 Reduce calls. A call is not a task: a task (run by a worker) makes many calls.

Q7. Design a Map-Reduce solution for (a) word count, (b) host size, (c) counting 5-word sequences.

Lecture 2 · Slides 26, 36–49

Method: ask "what must meet in one place to give one answer?"; that is the key.

ProblemMap emitsGroup by key (framework)Reduce
(a) Word count(word, 1) for every word occurrence(word, [1, 1, …])sum: (word, total)
(b) Host size(hostname(URL), size) per record(host, [sizes])sum: (host, total bytes)
(c) 5-word sequences(5-word window, 1) for each window position(sequence, [1, 1, …])sum: (sequence, count)

Same skeleton each time; only the key, the emitted value and the Reduce operation change.

Q8. Explain how a Map-Reduce job runs in parallel on a cluster.

Lecture 2 · Slides 51–52, 54

  1. The input is divided into pieces; each piece is processed by a Map task (many Map calls) on some worker.
  2. At the end of each Map task a partitioning function looks at each pair's key and sends it to one of the R Reduce tasks (typically hash(key) mod R), so equal keys always go to the same reducer.
  3. Shuffle: every Reduce task fetches its part from every Map task (all-to-all, M × R transfers).
  4. Each Reduce task sorts and groups by key and calls Reduce once per key. Each Reduce task writes its own output piece.

All phases are distributed, with many tasks doing the work.

Q9. Where is data stored during a Map-Reduce job, and what does the master do?

Lecture 2 · Slides 55–56

Input and final output are in the DFS (replicated); map tasks are scheduled close to their input chunk. Intermediate (map output) is on the local file system of the map worker (not replicated). Output is often the input of another job. The master tracks each task's state (idle, in-progress, completed), schedules idle tasks as workers become free, receives the location and sizes of intermediate files from each completed map task and pushes this information to the reducers, and pings workers periodically to detect failures.

Q10. What happens when a map worker, a reduce worker or the master fails? Why the difference?

Lecture 2 · Slide 57

FailureActionReason
Map workerAll its map tasks, completed and in-progress, reset to idle and rescheduled elsewhereOutput sits on the dead worker's local disk, so completed work is lost
Reduce workerOnly in-progress tasks reset to idle and restartedCompleted output is already in the replicated DFS
MasterJob aborted; client notifiedMaster holds all task state; Beyond the slides: with a single master, a failure during one job is unlikely

Detection is by the master's periodic pings.

Q11. Why should there be many more map tasks than machines? What about R?

Lecture 2 · Slides 58, 69

Rule of thumb: M much larger than the number of nodes, often one DFS chunk per map task; R usually smaller than M. Reasons: (1) dynamic load balancing: fast machines simply take more small tasks, so nobody idles while one machine is stuck with a big task; (2) faster recovery: a failed worker loses only small tasks, which are re-run in parallel on many other machines. Also, pipelining: the shuffle reads of a finished map task start while other maps still run; only the reduce function must wait for all its reads. Example: 1 TB in 64 MB chunks gives 15,625 map tasks, about 16 per node on 1,000 nodes. (Beyond the slides: R is small because each reduce task writes one output file.)

Q12. What is a combiner? When can it be used? How do you handle average and median?

Lecture 2 · Slides 59–65

  1. A combiner pre-aggregates the values of each key inside the mapper, before the shuffle: combine(k, list(v₁)) → v₂. It reduces the data copied and shuffled (Slide 61: 12 pairs become 8).
  2. It is usually the same as the reduce function and works only if reduce is commutative and associative (sum, count, max, min).
  3. Average is not (averaging averages ignores sizes: parts {1,2,3} and {4} give (2+4)/2 = 3, but the true average is 2.5). Fix: carry (sum, count) pairs; combiners add them component-wise; the reducer adds and divides once.
  4. Median: there is a proof that it cannot be split into commutative and associative functions, so no combiner trick; the reducer needs all the values.

The answer must be the same with or without the combiner.

Q13. What is the partition function and why override it?

Lecture 2 · Slides 66–67

It decides which reduce task receives each intermediate key. Requirement: records with the same key must end up at the same reducer. Default: hash(key) mod R (a number 0 … R−1). Override when you want related keys together: hash(hostname(URL)) mod R sends all URLs of one host to the same reduce task, hence the same output file. The key itself is unchanged; only the routing uses a function of the key. Risk (beyond the slides): load imbalance if one host is huge.

Q14. What is a straggler and how are stragglers handled?

Lecture 2 · Slide 68

Problem: a slow (not failed) worker, due to other jobs, a bad disk or "weird things", delays the whole phase because a phase ends when its last task ends. Solution: near the end of a phase the master launches backup copies of the remaining in-progress tasks on other machines; whichever copy finishes first wins and the other is discarded. Effect: job completion time drops dramatically for a small extra cost. Safe because tasks are independent and deterministic. Different from failure recovery: here the worker still works, just slowly.

Q15. Explain how to compute the natural join R(A,B) ⋈ S(B,C) with Map-Reduce.

Lecture 2 · Slides 71–72

  1. Key: the shared attribute b, because tuples to be glued share it.
  2. Map: R tuple (a,b) → (b, (a, R)); S tuple (b,c) → (b, (c, S)). The tag R or S lets the reducer tell the two sides apart.
  3. Shuffle: pairs with key b go to Reduce process h(b), h a hash function (Hadoop does this automatically).
  4. Reduce: for each b, pair every (a,R) with every (c,S) and output (a,b,c). A b present on one side only gives no output.

On the Slide 71 data: 4 + 3 = 7 pairs shuffled; b₁ has no S partner; output (a₃,b₂,c₁), (a₃,b₂,c₂), (a₄,b₃,c₃).

Q16. How do we measure the cost of a Map-Reduce algorithm? Why not big-O?

Lecture 2 · Slides 73–74

Communication cost = total I/O of all processes (how much data is read and written and moved). State your convention in an exam: counting every read and write (literal Slide 73), or counting only task inputs (textbook). (Elapsed) computation cost = analogous, but counting running time. Usually one of the two dominates and the other is ignored. Total cost (sum over all machines) is the bill from "your friendly neighborhood cloud"; elapsed cost is wall-clock time using parallelism. Adding machines lowers elapsed cost but not total cost. Big-O is "not the most useful" because adding more machines is always an option; what matters is how much data moves and how long you wait. (Slide 80 also advises treating all examples in the lecture as quiz questions: word count, host size, language model, combiner example and join.)

Machines at Google~1M (guesstimate)10, 12
Failuresmachines ÷ lifetime (1,000 days): 1,000 → 1 a day; 1M → 1,000 a day (≈ one every 86 s)12
Move 10 TB at 1 Gbps8 × 10¹³ bits ÷ 10⁹ = 80,000 s ≈ 22 h ≈ 0.93 day ("about 1 day")14
Chunk size, replication16–64 MB; 2× or 3×; 1 TB at 64 MB = 15,625 chunks19–20

Definitions

Algorithms in steps

Lecture 2 · Slides 26–72

AlgorithmSteps
Word count1. Map: emit (w, 1) for every word. 2. Framework groups by key. 3. Reduce: sum the 1s. Output (w, n).
Host size1. Map: (hostname(URL), size). 2. Group by host. 3. Reduce: sum sizes.
5-word sequences1. Map: slide a 5-word window, emit (window, 1) (n − 4 pairs for n words). 2. Group. 3. Reduce: sum.
Join R ⋈ S1. Map: (b,(a,R)) and (b,(c,S)). 2. Shuffle by h(b). 3. Reduce: all (a,R) × all (c,S) → (a,b,c).
Average with combiner1. Map: (k,(value,1)). 2. Combine: add (sum,count) component-wise. 3. Reduce: add, then sum ÷ count.
Read from the DFS1. Client library asks master for chunk locations. 2. Master replies with servers. 3. Client reads from chunk servers directly.
Parallel run1. Map tasks on input pieces. 2. Partition by hash(key) mod R. 3. Shuffle to R reduce tasks. 4. Sort and group. 5. Reduce, write to DFS.

Common mistakes & traps

Lecture 2 · Slides 1–80

  • Units: Gbps is bits per second, GB/s is bytes. 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s. Convert 1 TB = 10⁶ MB before dividing by MB/s; otherwise answers are off by 10³ or 8 (Slides 5, 9, 14).
  • The 4,000 s is ideal. Never write "1,000 discs = 1,000× faster" without the assumptions (even split, no failures, no combining cost) (Slide 8).
  • The master does not carry data. It stores metadata; clients read from chunk servers directly. It does not store file bytes (Slide 24).
  • Replicas on one server are useless. Copies must be on different servers, and racks if possible. Do not read replica counts from Slide 23, which is only an illustration (Slides 20–23).
  • Group by key is not written by the programmer. Only Map and Reduce are; the framework does sort and shuffle (Slides 28, 36–38, 53).
  • Calls versus tasks. One Reduce call per unique key, but one Reduce task handles many keys; Map is not "one in, one out" (zero or more pairs) (Slides 30, 44, 52).
  • Intermediate data is on the local disk, not in the DFS (Slide 55). Failure rules: a map worker failure redoes completed and in-progress map tasks; a reduce worker failure redoes only in-progress tasks; master failure aborts the job (Slide 57).
  • Combiner is only an optimisation. The answer must not change; reduce must be commutative and associative. Never average partial averages; never divide in the combiner (Slides 62–64). Median has no combiner (Slide 65).
  • Partition function must send equal keys to the same reducer. A random choice breaks the result (Slide 66).
  • Reducers do not compute before all maps finish (only the copying starts early, Slide 58). Stragglers are not failures: backups are launched near the end of a phase and the first copy to finish wins (Slide 68).
  • Join: forgetting the R/S tag, outputting rows for keys present on one side only, or writing the result as (A,C) instead of (A,B,C) (Slides 71–72).
  • Cost: more machines lower elapsed cost, not total cost; big-O is not the main measure (Slides 73–74).

Lecture 3Spark: Beyond Map-Reduce (RDDs, DataFrames, the Ecosystem)

Roadmap — what this lecture is about
  • Map-Reduce (Lecture 2) saved the day for scaling out, but it pays for disk I/O between every step and it does not compose: real programs need chains of jobs (slides 3–6).
  • The fix is a data-flow system: any number of stages, any functions, data moving in one direction only (a DAG, slide 7).
  • Apache Spark is the most popular one: a core engine plus Spark SQL, Streaming, MLlib and GraphX, connected to many data stores (slides 8–10).
  • Its key construct is the RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset): a partitioned, read-only collection cached in memory, changed only through lazy transformations and result-producing actions (slides 11–16).
  • The task scheduler runs general DAGs in stages, pipelining steps and avoiding shuffles (slide 17); DataFrames and Datasets add structure and SQL (slides 12, 18–19); the libraries are listed on slide 20.
  • Finally Spark is compared with Hadoop MapReduce and we ask which problems suit MapReduce at all (slides 21–23).

Exam checklist — by the end you can:

  • state what Map-Reduce gave us and its two limitations (performance, programmability), and explain "does not compose well";
  • define a data-flow system and a DAG, and say how they generalise Map-Reduce;
  • list what Spark adds to MapReduce (fast data sharing, general DAGs, richer functions, Hadoop compatibility) and the weakness each one fixes;
  • define an RDD (partitioned, read-only, cached with disk fallback, created from stored data or other RDDs) and explain "resilient" and lineage;
  • separate transformations from actions, and explain lazy evaluation and why it helps (trace a lineage graph);
  • explain what the task scheduler does: stages, shuffles, pipelining, cache and partition awareness;
  • contrast RDD, DataFrame and Dataset; name the Spark libraries and describe GraphX's graph type;
  • compare Spark and Hadoop MapReduce (with the memory caveat) and decide which problems suit MapReduce.

Scope note: no code is examined in Lectures 1–5. Slide code is explained in words only. This lecture contains no BFR material.

Where this lecture starts: Spark extends Map-Reduce

Lecture 3 · Slides 1–2

Slide 1 is the title card ("Spark and Tutorial", presenter Rafael Dolores). The large black block on it is an empty picture area, not content. The word "Tutorial" signals that a hands-on Spark session follows the theory; that part is outside this section. Slide 2 is a section divider with one line: "Spark: Extends Map Reduce".

That one line is the storyline of Slides 3–12. Spark is presented as a generalisation of the Map-Reduce model from Lecture 2, not as something unrelated. The slides follow a fixed argument:

  1. Recap what Map-Reduce gave us (Slides 3–4).
  2. Criticise it: two limitations (Slides 5–6).
  3. Generalise it: data-flow systems (Slide 7).
  4. Introduce Spark: its ecosystem, what it adds, its key data type (Slides 8–12).
Key idea

Every feature of Spark on Slides 10–12 is an answer to a specific weakness of Map-Reduce on Slides 5–6. When you study, always pair them: problem → Spark's fix. A table doing exactly this is at the end of this part.

Spelling note

The slides write "Map Reduce", "MapReduce" and "map-reduce" for the same thing. This guide uses "Map-Reduce" for the model and "MapReduce" when the slide does.

Map-Reduce recap: why we scale out

Lecture 3 · Slide 3

Search engines, scale up and scale out

Lecture 3 · Slide 3

Slide 3 opens with history. Search engines (the slide says "i.e. Google"; it should read "e.g.", because Google is just an example) created one of the earliest big-data problems. To answer a search query quickly, the engine must crawl (automatically download) billions of web pages and build an index over them. That volume does not fit on one computer.

The slide then asks: "Scale up or scale out?" It never answers in words; the colours do (scale up in red, scale out in green). The answer is scale out.

Definition: scale up vs scale out

Scale up (vertical scaling): make one machine bigger, with more CPU, RAM and disk. Scale out (horizontal scaling): add many ordinary (commodity) machines and let them work together as a cluster.

Beginner intuition

You must move 10 000 boxes. Scaling up is buying one gigantic truck: very expensive, there is a limit to how big a truck can be, and if it breaks down all work stops. Scaling out is hiring 100 ordinary vans: cheap, you can add a van any time, and one broken van only delays a little. The price is organisation: someone must decide which van takes which boxes.

Scale upScale out
HowOne bigger machineMany commodity machines in a cluster
CostGrows steeply; special hardwareGrows roughly in proportion to the machines added
LimitHard ceiling (biggest machine you can buy)Keep adding machines
FailureSingle point of failureFailures are normal, so software must tolerate them
Hard partCostStorage, coordination and programming across machines
Choice for big data✗✓

The Cost, Limit and Failure rows are background (Beyond the slides: standard cost and failure arguments from the textbook); the slide itself only gives the question and the colour hint. Scaling out creates three new hard problems, storage, coordination and programming, and the next bullet of the slide says who solves them.

What Map-Reduce gave us

Lecture 3 · Slide 3

"The MapReduce programming model saved the day." The slide lists four things it provides:

Slide bulletPlain meaningWhere it came from (Lecture 2)
Handles persistent storageFiles are stored safely across many machines and survive crashes.The distributed file system (HDFS/GFS): files split into chunks, each chunk replicated.
Handles distributed worker coordinationThe framework decides which worker does which task, notices failed workers, and restarts their tasks. (The slide has a stray "'s": "coordination's".)The master process.
Brings computation closer to the dataMove the small program to the machine that holds the data, not terabytes of data to the program. This is called data locality. (The slide says "Bring"; it should be "Brings".)The master schedules map tasks on the machines (or racks) that hold the input chunk.
Simpler to work with from the programmer's POV (point of view)The programmer writes only map and reduce functions; everything above is hidden.The Map-Reduce programming model.
Exam tip

A typical short question: "What problems does MapReduce solve for the programmer?" Answer with the four bullets above and add the one-line reason: scaling out creates storage, coordination and programming problems, and MapReduce hides all three.

The MapReduce execution overview

Lecture 3 · Slide 4

Slide 4 contains no text, only a diagram (it is the classic "execution overview" figure from the 2004 Google MapReduce paper by Dean and Ghemawat; the slide gives no citation). Our redrawing below keeps all its parts and its six numbered steps. Read the figure from the top (control) to the bottom (data).

The six steps, in words

Lecture 3 · Slide 4

  1. (1) fork. The User Program starts (forks) copies of itself: one Master and many workers.
  2. (2) assign map / assign reduce. The master hands tasks to idle workers: some get map tasks, some get reduce tasks.
  3. (3) read. A map worker reads its input split (one chunk of the input file; split 2 in the figure).
  4. (4) local write. It runs the user's map function and writes the resulting intermediate key-value pairs to its own local disk (not to the distributed file system).
  5. (5) remote read. Each reduce worker fetches ("pulls") the pieces it needs from every map worker's local disk. This all-to-all fan-out is the shuffle.
  6. (6) write. The reduce worker runs the reduce function and writes one output file.
Exam tip

Remember three counting facts: the number of map tasks follows the number of input splits; the number of reduce tasks (and so of output files) is chosen by the user; and intermediate data lives on local disks. Only the final output goes to the distributed file system. Only one path is drawn in black on the slide, but steps 3–6 happen for every task.

Common mistake

Do not confuse the control flow (dotted arrows 1 and 2, small messages) with the data flow (solid arrows 3–6, the actual data). Another frequent error is to say map output is written to HDFS; it is written to the mapper's local disk. This matters again on the next slide.

Problems with MapReduce

Lecture 3 · Slides 5–6

Limitation 1: disk I/O overhead

Lecture 3 · Slide 5

Slide 5 states the first problem: MapReduce incurs substantial overheads due to disk I/O (input/output). The sub-bullet explains where: the outputs of mappers (M) are saved on the disk and then read again by reducers (R).

The slide's figure shows a chain: Data on Disk (input from stable storage) → HDFS read → mappers M1–M3 → HDFS write → Tuples (on Disk) → HDFS read → reducers R1–R3 → HDFS write → Tuples (on Disk) → "…" (the chain goes on). HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) is the disk-based, replicated file system of Lecture 2. Every arrow into a box is a disk read, every arrow out is a disk write.

Beginner intuition

Imagine a team of clerks. After finishing each step of a task, every clerk must file the result in a basement archive, and the next clerk must walk down and fetch it before starting. The basement trips take far longer than the actual work. Keeping the paper on the desk (memory) between steps would be much faster. That is the whole difference between MapReduce and Spark.

Disks (and the network used to replicate files) are orders of magnitude slower than RAM. For a single pass over data this does not matter much. It matters hugely for multi-step work, for example iterative algorithms such as machine learning or PageRank, where the same data is processed again and again: every pass pays the disk price.

Worked example — counting the disk touches Lecture 3 · Slide 5

A job needs k successive MapReduce jobs, each reading its input from HDFS and writing its output to HDFS. (Practice example with made-up speeds, not from the slides.)

  1. Disk touches in a chain of k jobs: k reads + k writes = 2k. For k = 5 that is 10; for k = 10 it is 20.
  2. Minimum actually needed: read the original input once, write the final result once = 2, whatever k is.
  3. Time of one pass over 100 GB: at an assumed 100 MB/s disk speed, 100 000 MB ÷ 100 MB/s = 1000 s. At an assumed 10 000 MB/s memory speed, 100 000 ÷ 10 000 = 10 s, which is 100 times faster.

Result: 2k − 2 of the disk touches are wasted work; Spark's design removes them by keeping intermediate results in memory.

Slide erratum

Slide 5's figure (a) labels the map stage "Iteration-1" and the reduce stage "Iteration-2". In reality one MapReduce job already contains a map phase and a reduce phase; a second iteration is a second whole job. (b) It draws "HDFS write" after the mappers, while Slide 4 (and real Hadoop) puts map output on the mappers' local disks; HDFS is written only for reducer output. The text of the slide ("saved on the disk and then read again by reducers") is correct either way, and the conclusion (heavy disk I/O) stands. In the exam, follow the slide's message: mapper output goes to disk, reducers read it back.

The two major limitations, side by side

Lecture 3 · Slide 6

Slide 6 names two major limitations of MapReduce and then sums them up in one sentence:

LimitationSlide's explanationWhat it means in practice
1. Performance bottlenecksSaving to disk is typically much slower than in-memory work.The disk-I/O overhead of Slide 5. Each step pays for writes and reads.
2. Potential difficulty of programming directly in MapReduceSome big-data problems/algorithms are not easily described as map-reduce.The rigid shape "one map, then one reduce" does not fit many algorithms (iterative, multi-stage, graph, interactive). The programmer must force them into it.
Key idea: "does not compose well"

The summary line is: "MapReduce does not compose well for all large applications", because many times one needs to chain multiple map-reduce steps. "Compose" means building a big program out of small pieces. With MapReduce each piece is a separate job; the pieces can only be glued together through files on disk, so each link of the chain pays limitation 1, and the programmer carries limitation 2 (writing and managing the chain by hand).

Exam tip

"State the two limitations of MapReduce" is a likely question. Answer: (1) performance, because intermediate results go to disk which is much slower than memory; (2) programmability, because many problems do not naturally fit one map plus one reduce and need chains of jobs, so MapReduce does not compose well.

Data-flow systems

Lecture 3 · Slide 7

Slide 7 shows the abstract fix. Start with what Map-Reduce looks like from a distance: two "ranks" of tasks, one for Map and a second for Reduce, and data flows from the first rank to the second. ("Rank" is the slide's word; "stage" or "layer" is more common.)

Definition: data-flow system

A system in which a computation is a network of tasks and data flows through it. It generalises MapReduce in two ways: (1) it allows any number of tasks/ranks, and (2) it allows functions other than Map and Reduce. Data flows in one direction only, so the network is a DAG (directed acyclic graph). The slide leaves out the closing parenthesis after "directed acyclic graph".

Definition: DAG

A graph whose nodes are tasks and whose arrows are the data flowing from one task to the next (directed), with no way to start at a node and follow arrows back to it (acyclic, no loops).

Beginner intuition

MapReduce is an assembly line with exactly two stations. A data-flow system is an assembly line with as many stations as you need, and each station may do any job (filter, join, sort, group, ...). The only rule: a product never goes back to an earlier station.

Slide erratum

On Slide 7 the bullet "Data flow is in one direction only (DAG ...)" is printed under item 2, but it is a property of the whole generalisation (items 1 and 2 both), not of item 2 alone.

Beyond the slides: a DAG is what lets the system plan the whole computation in advance and, after a failure, re-run only the lost part rather than everything. Loops in an algorithm (iterations) are expressed by writing a longer acyclic graph, not by a cycle in the graph.

The Spark software stack

Lecture 3 · Slide 8

Slide 8 ("Data Analytics Software Stack") is one picture: four library boxes sitting on top of a single wide engine box. We redraw it with a plain explanation of each box.

BoxSlide's subtitleWhat it is for
Spark (core)Fast memory-optimized execution engine (Python/Java/Scala APIs)The engine that runs tasks over a cluster, keeping data in memory. You program it from Python, Java or Scala.
Spark StreamingStream processingProcessing live data that keeps arriving (clicks, sensor readings), (Beyond the slides: classic Spark Streaming processes the stream in small batches.)
GraphXGraph computationAlgorithms on graphs (Beyond the slides: for example PageRank).
MLlibUser-friendly machine learningReady-made machine-learning algorithms (classification, clustering, ...).
SparkSQLSQL APIQuery structured data with SQL; this is where DataFrames come in (Slide 12).
Key idea

One engine, many workloads. Streaming, graphs, machine learning and SQL all reuse the same fast core, so one system and one skill set covers jobs that used to need separate specialised systems. (That last comparison with Hadoop is background; the slide only shows the stack.)

Beyond the slides: Spark also has an R API, and newer versions add "Structured Streaming" next to Spark Streaming. The slide does not show the cluster managers or storage layers beneath Spark; the next slide covers the storage side.

Data lakes: Spark connects to everything

Lecture 3 · Slide 9

Slide 9 is titled "Data Lakes" and shows the Spark logo in the centre with ten arrows leading out to logos. The slide never defines the term.

Definition: data lake

Beyond the slides: a data lake is a central repository that keeps large amounts of data in its original (raw) format, structured and unstructured, from many different sources, to be processed later. Compare it with a data warehouse, which stores cleaned data in a fixed schema.

The picture's message: Spark is not tied to one storage system. It has connectors to all of these, so it can serve as the common compute layer over a company's data lake.

Kind of systemLogos on the slide
Relational databases (tables, SQL)PostgreSQL, MySQL, IBM DB2
NoSQL stores (flexible, scale out)MongoDB, Cassandra, HBase, Redis
Search engine"elastic" (Elasticsearch)
Messaging / streaming platform (not a database)Kafka
Distributed file system (Hadoop)HDFS

HDFS and HBase belong to the Hadoop ecosystem, which links to the bullet "Compatible with Hadoop" on the next slide. The slide draws the arrows one-way (from Spark to the system), but Spark both reads from and writes to these systems. You are not expected to know details of each product; know that the list shows variety.

Spark: the most popular data-flow system

Lecture 3 · Slide 10

Slide 10 collects the answer. Spark is described as an expressive computing system, not limited to the map-reduce model, and "the most popular data-flow system" (a claim with no source or date). Its additions to the MapReduce model are:

Addition on the slideMeaningWhich MapReduce weakness it fixes
Fast data sharing: avoids saving intermediate results to diskResults pass from one step to the next in memory.Performance bottleneck (Slides 5–6)
Fast data sharing: caches data for queries (e.g. for machine learning)Data that will be used again is kept in memory. Repeated queries and iterative learning algorithms re-read it from RAM, not from disk. (The slide mixes "queries" and "machine learning" in one bullet; they are two different uses.)Performance bottleneck, especially for iteration
General execution graphs (DAGs)Any acyclic graph of tasks, not just map then reduce. (The slide writes "DAGs=directed acyclic graph", a plural/singular mismatch.)"Does not compose": no more hand-built job chains (Slide 6)
Richer functions than just map and reduceMany operators are built in (filter, join, group, sort ...).Difficulty of programming (Slide 6)
Compatible with HadoopBeyond the slides: Spark can read data from HDFS and run on existing Hadoop clusters, so Hadoop data and infrastructure are reused.Not a fix; it makes adoption easy
Quick recap: problem → fix
  • Disk I/O between steps → fast data sharing in memory, plus caching.
  • Only map and reduce, jobs chained by hand → general DAGs and richer functions.
  • Existing Hadoop world → compatible with Hadoop.
Exam tip

"What does Spark add to MapReduce?" has a three-part model answer: fast data sharing (in-memory, no intermediate disk writes, caching), general execution graphs (DAGs), richer functions than map and reduce; and it stays compatible with Hadoop. Also be able to say why each addition helps.

Common mistake

Do not write "Spark is always faster because it does not use disk." Spark can use disk (for example when data does not fit in memory) and still reads its input from and writes its final result to disk-based storage. The gain comes from not touching disk between steps (Figure 3.2).

The key construct: the RDD

Lecture 3 · Slide 11

Slide 11 ("Spark Overview") gives the key construct/idea: the Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD). Its two sub-bullets: RDDs are a data abstraction in Apache Spark that allow in-memory processing of large datasets; and they provide transformations (e.g. map, filter) and actions (e.g. count, collect) through an API (application programming interface, the set of functions you may call), enabling distributed computation on data loaded into memory.

Definition: RDD

A Resilient Distributed Dataset is Spark's central data type: a large collection of records, split into partitions that live on different machines of the cluster and are kept, as far as possible, in memory.

The three words in the name

Lecture 3 · Slide 11

WordMeaning
DatasetA collection of records (lines of text, numbers, key-value pairs ...).
DistributedIts partitions are spread over many machines, so the machines work on their own pieces in parallel.
ResilientIt survives machine failures: a lost partition can be rebuilt. (The slide does not explain this word. Beyond the slides: Spark remembers how each RDD was derived from earlier ones, its lineage, and replays those steps for the lost partition only.)

Transformations and actions

Lecture 3 · Slide 11

You work with an RDD through two kinds of operations, both called through the API:

TransformationAction
Slide's examplesmap, filtercount, collect
What it doesBuilds a new RDD from an existing oneReturns a result to the driver program (the program you run); for example a number (count) or the data itself (collect)
Output typeAn RDDA value, not an RDD
Worked example — which is which? Lecture 3 · Slide 11

An RDD holds the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Apply filter keeping even numbers, then map doubling each, then count. (Practice example, not from the slides.)

  1. filter (transformation): gives a new RDD {2, 4, 6}.
  2. map (transformation): gives a new RDD {4, 8, 12}.
  3. count (action): returns the number 3 to the driver.

Answer: two transformations produce RDDs; one action produces the value 3.

Exam tip

The slide's own examples are the safest memory aid: map, filter = transformations; count, collect = actions. Rule of thumb: if it returns an RDD, it is a transformation; if it returns a result to you, it is an action.

Beyond the slides: what the slide leaves out

Three properties are not on Slide 11 but are central to how RDDs behave, and are the usual follow-up questions. RDDs are immutable: a transformation never changes an RDD, it creates a new one. They are fault tolerant through lineage (the recorded chain of transformations that produced them). Transformations are lazy: nothing is computed when you call them; Spark only records the plan, and the whole chain actually runs when an action asks for a result. Laziness is what lets Spark see the whole DAG before running it.

Not examined — code (understand, don't memorise)

The slides later show Spark code for these operations. In words: you load data as an RDD, call filter and map to describe the steps (nothing runs yet), then call count to trigger the work. You will not be asked to write such code.

Slide erratum

Slide 11's sentence "through API, enabling distributed computation on data loaded into memory" is missing an article ("through an API") but the content is right. "Resilient" is never explained on the slide (see the table above).

Higher-level APIs: DataFrames and Datasets

Lecture 3 · Slide 12

Slide 12 (still "Spark Overview") names the higher-level APIs: DataFrames and Datasets. They were introduced in more recent versions of Spark, and are different APIs for structured data, which allowed SQL support to be introduced (the slide's wording "allowed to introduce SQL support" is ungrammatical, not wrong).

Definition: DataFrame, Dataset, structured data

Structured data has a fixed shape: rows made of named, typed columns (a schema), like a database table or spreadsheet. A DataFrame is a distributed table of rows with named columns. A Dataset is a related typed interface for the same kind of data. Both are built on the Spark SQL engine (Slide 18) and can be converted back to an RDD. (The slide does not define "structured data"; this is the standard meaning.)

Beginner intuition

An RDD is a pile of sealed boxes: Spark can move them around but does not know what is inside, so you must say in code what to do with every box. A DataFrame is a spreadsheet: Spark can see the column names and types, so you can say "select the name column where age is over 30" (or write it in SQL) and Spark works out an efficient way to do it.

RDD (Slide 11)DataFrame / Dataset (Slide 12)
LevelLow-level, the core abstractionHigher-level, built on the core
Data it suitsAny records, Spark treats them as opaqueStructured data (rows with a schema)
Spark's knowledgeKnows nothing about the contentsKnows columns and types, so it can optimise
SQLNoYes (the SparkSQL box of Slide 8)
IntroducedFrom the start"More recent versions"

Beyond the slides: DataFrames appeared in Spark 1.3 and Datasets in Spark 1.6, and the two were unified in Spark 2.0. The slide's "more recent versions" is vague; do not memorise version numbers for the exam.

Exam tip

Remember the one-line contrast: RDD is the low-level core; DataFrames and Datasets are higher-level, for structured data, and are what makes SQL support possible.

Part 1 in one table: problem and fix

Lecture 3 · Slides 3–12

MapReduce (Slides 3–7)Spark (Slides 8–12)
Intermediate results written to disk, read back by the next stepFast data sharing: results kept in memory; data cached for reuse
Exactly two ranks: Map then ReduceGeneral execution graphs (any DAG)
Only two functions; hand-chained jobs; "does not compose well"Richer functions; one program describes the whole graph
Separate systems for streaming, graphs, ML, SQLOne engine plus Spark Streaming, GraphX, MLlib, SparkSQL (Slide 8)
Hadoop file system as the data homeConnectors to many systems (Slide 9); compatible with Hadoop (Slide 10)
(no equivalent single type)RDD: partitioned, in-memory, transformations and actions (Slide 11); DataFrames/Datasets for structured data and SQL (Slide 12)
Quick recap
  • Big data forced scale out; MapReduce hid storage, coordination and data-locality problems and simplified programming.
  • Two limitations: performance (disk I/O between steps) and programmability (does not compose; chains of jobs).
  • Data-flow systems generalise MapReduce: any number of ranks, any functions, one-directional DAG.
  • Spark adds fast in-memory data sharing and caching, general DAGs, richer functions, and stays compatible with Hadoop.
  • Ecosystem: core engine plus Spark Streaming, GraphX, MLlib, SparkSQL; connectors to many data stores.
  • Key type: RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset), with transformations (map, filter) and actions (count, collect); higher-level DataFrames/Datasets for structured data and SQL.

The RDD: Spark's basic data container

Lecture 3 · Slides 13–14

Slides 1–12 explained why Spark exists: Hadoop MapReduce writes to disk after every step and composes badly, so Spark adds fast data sharing in memory, general DAGs (directed acyclic graphs: networks of steps with arrows and no cycles), richer functions, and Hadoop compatibility. Slide 13 now names the single idea that makes this possible.

Beginner intuition

Think of a huge deck of exam papers to mark. You cut the deck into piles and hand one pile to each of many markers. You never scribble on the original papers; each marker produces a new pile of marked sheets. That is an RDD: a big collection, cut into pieces, spread over many workers, never edited in place, only turned into new collections.

Definition: RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset), Slide 13

A partitioned collection of records (objects), spread across the cluster, read-only, which Spark can cache in memory (with fallback to disk). Distributed = its pieces live on many machines. Dataset = it is a collection of records.

Reading the slide's bullets one by one

Lecture 3 · Slide 13

Slide wordingPlain meaningWhy it matters
Partitioned collection of records/objectsThe dataset is chopped into partitions; a record is one item (a line, a number, a pair, any object).Each partition can be processed on a different machine at the same time: partitions = parallelism.
Generalizes (key-value) pairsMapReduce only allowed (key, value) pairs. An RDD's records may be any object; (key, value) pairs are just one special case.More natural programs; no need to force every item into a pair.
Spread across the cluster, read-onlyPartitions sit on many machines. Read-only (immutable): you never change an RDD; you create a new one.No update conflicts between machines, and a lost piece can be rebuilt (see "Resilient" below).
Caching dataset in memory; fallback to disk possibleSpark keeps partitions in RAM when it can, and uses disk only if RAM is too small.Re-using an RDD is then fast; this is the answer to MapReduce's disk-I/O problem.
Created from Hadoop, or by transforming other RDDs (you can stack RDDs)Two ways to get an RDD: load external data, or apply a transformation to an existing RDD. Steps can be chained ("stacked").Programs become pipelines of RDDs, each built from the previous.
Best suited for applying the same operation to all elementsBulk operations (map, filter-style) that treat every record alike.Not designed for fine-grained updates to one record at a time.
Common mistake

"Created from Hadoop" does not mean the data must come through MapReduce. It means data held in Hadoop-supported storage, typically files in HDFS (the Hadoop Distributed File System). Also, "read-only" does not mean you cannot compute with an RDD; it means each computation yields a new RDD.

Beyond the slides: why "Resilient"? The slide never explains this word. Because an RDD is read-only and every transformation is deterministic (same input, same output), Spark only needs to remember the recipe (the chain of transformations, called the lineage) that produced each RDD. If a machine fails and a partition is lost, Spark re-runs the recipe for that partition alone. Resilient = able to recover from failure this way.

Figure 3.7: data in, RDDs stacked, one action out

Lecture 3 · Slide 13

Read it top to bottom. The two clouds are the "external world": any source or sink such as HDFS or a local file. The figure has 5 RDD boxes, 3 transformations (two running in parallel on independent RDDs, one merging two RDDs into one, for example a join or union) and exactly 1 action. Notice that nothing leaves the Spark world until the action at the bottom.

Figure 3.8: one RDD, many partitions, memory backed by disk

Lecture 3 · Slide 14

Slide 14 shows the same RDD at three levels: logical (one blue box), split into partitions (orange), and physical (a green in-memory partition on the worker that processes it, filled from stored data, the blue cylinders). Both arrows point into the memory partition: one from the partition's definition and one from the data on disk. The slide does not label the arrows; this is the natural reading and it matches "cache in memory, fall back to disk". Each row is independent, so the number of partitions is the amount of parallel work.

Worked example: partitions and immutability Lecture 3 · Slides 13–14

Take the records 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 as one RDD R with 3 partitions: [1,2], [3,4], [5,6], on workers W1, W2, W3. Apply the transformation "multiply each record by 2".

  1. Each worker doubles its own partition independently: W1 gives [2,4], W2 gives [6,8], W3 gives [10,12]. No data moves between machines.
  2. The result is a new RDD R2 with 3 partitions; R is unchanged (still 1,2,3,4,5,6).
  3. If W2 crashes, Spark re-runs "double" on partition [3,4] only and recovers [6,8].
Exam tip

If asked "What is an RDD?", give five facts: partitioned collection of records; spread across the cluster; read-only; cached in memory with disk fallback; created from stored data or by transforming other RDDs. Add "best for applying the same operation to all elements" and, for extra credit, "recoverable through lineage".

RDD operations: transformations, actions, lazy evaluation

Lecture 3 · Slides 15–16

Spark offers exactly two kinds of operations on RDDs. Slide 15 defines them.

TransformationAction
PurposeBuild a new RDD from other RDD(s) through deterministic operationsReturn a value to the program or export data
Examples on slidemap, filter, join, union, intersection, distinctcount, collect, reduce, save
EvaluationLazy: only records the step; computes nothing yetForces the computation of every pending transformation it depends on
Output typean RDDa number, a list, a file (not an RDD)

The words, defined

Lecture 3 · Slide 15

  • Deterministic: the same input always gives the same output, so a lost piece can be recomputed exactly.
  • map: apply a function to every record, one output per input. filter: keep only records that satisfy a condition. union: all records of two RDDs. intersection: only records in both. distinct: remove duplicates. join: combine records of two RDDs that share a key.
  • count: number of records. reduce: combine all records into one value with a function (for example sum). collect: bring all records to the driver program as a list. save: write the records to storage.
Key idea: lazy evaluation (Slide 15)

Nothing is computed until an action requires it. A program made only of transformations does nothing; as soon as an action is called, the whole chain behind it runs. Why? Spark sees the entire chain first, so it can pipeline steps, avoid storing intermediate RDDs, and compute only what the action needs.

Worked example: lazy chain with numbers Lecture 3 · Slide 15

Start from the RDD 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

  1. map: double each record. Recorded only. (Nothing computed.)
  2. filter: keep values greater than 6. Recorded only.
  3. count: an action, so Spark now runs both steps. After map: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. After filter: 8, 10, 12.
  4. Answer: 3. Without step 3 the program would return nothing and read no data.
Common mistake

Thinking filter or map "runs" when written. They only extend the recipe. Also, collect is an action that pulls every record onto one machine (Beyond the slides: so use it only on small results). Slide 15's phrase "actions force calculations and return values" is a little circular; remember it as "an action triggers the computation and delivers a result".

Lineage graph (Slide 16)

Lecture 3 · Slide 16

Slide 16 draws a lineage graph (a DAG): stored data gives RDD1; RDD2 and RDD3 follow by successive transformations; RDD4 is a different transformation of RDD1. The slide has no text besides the labels; the take-aways below are the intended reading.

  1. While the arrows are being defined, nothing is computed (lazy).
  2. Calling Act1 runs only data → RDD1 → RDD4. Calling Act2 runs only data → RDD1 → RDD2 → RDD3.
  3. RDD1 lies on both paths. Unless it is cached (kept in memory, Slides 13–14), each action recomputes it. Count: with no cache, calling both actions computes RDD1 twice; with a cache, once.
Exam tip

Typical question: "Explain lazy evaluation and why it helps." Answer: transformations only record lineage; an action triggers execution; Spark can optimise the whole chain (pipelining, no intermediate storage, compute only what is needed), and lineage also enables recovery.

The task scheduler: general DAGs, stages and shuffles

Lecture 3 · Slide 17

When an action is called, the task scheduler turns the lineage into an execution plan. Slide 17 lists four properties: it supports general directed acyclic task graphs (not just map then reduce); it pipelines functions where possible; it is cache-aware (reuses data, respects locality); and it is partitioning-aware to avoid shuffles.

Terms the slide does not define (Beyond the slides: standard Spark vocabulary)
  • Narrow dependency: each output partition is computed from a small, fixed set of input partitions (typically one), as in map and filter. No data moves across the cluster; can be pipelined.
  • Wide dependency / shuffle: each output partition needs data from many input partitions (groupBy, join). Data is exchanged across the network and written to disk; this is expensive.
  • Stage: a group of pipelined narrow steps. A new stage starts at every shuffle.
  • Locality: running a task on the machine that already holds its data (in cache or on disk) so nothing is copied.

Reading the figure

Lecture 3 · Slide 17

StepArrowsTypeConsequence
A → B, groupBy3 × 3 = 9all-to-all (shuffle)Ends Stage 1
C → D, map4, one-to-onenarrowPipelined: each partition flows through map then filter on one machine (Stage 2)
D → E, filter4, one-to-onenarrow
B → F3, one-to-onenarrowB is already partitioned as the join needs, so it is not shuffled again
E → F, join4 × 3 = 12all-to-all (shuffle)Only E moves; Stage 3 produces F

Arithmetic check: 9 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 12 = 32 arrows in the picture. If B were not already partitioned for the join, B → F would also need 3 × 3 = 9 arrows, giving 38; this is what "partitioning-aware to avoid shuffles" saves. Likewise B is drawn grey (cached), so Stage 1 (A → B) does not run again when F is recomputed or reused.

The four bullets, matched to the figure: (1) a general DAG with six RDDs and two branches; (2) map and filter share Stage 2 (pipelining); (3) grey B partitions are reused (cache-aware); (4) one-to-one B → F avoids a second shuffle.

Slide erratum

(a) The legend explains only "RDD" and "cached partition"; the black and orange partitions of RDD D are unexplained on the slide. (Beyond the slides: in the Spark research paper this figure comes from, black marks partitions already in memory, which is why those need no recomputation.) (b) The large dashed "Stage 3" box visually encloses Stages 1 and 2 as well; logically Stage 3 is only the join that produces F from B and E. Figure 3.10 draws the logical version. On the slide B sits outside the small Stage 1 box; in Figure 3.10 we draw B inside Stage 1 because it is the output of the Stage 1 groupBy. (c) The slide says "task graphs" while it draws RDD partitions: same idea at a different level of detail.

Exam tip

Know the four bullets by heart and be able to say what a shuffle is and why stage boundaries sit at shuffles. A map/filter chain is cheap (pipelined); groupBy/join are costly (shuffle).

Higher-level APIs: DataFrame and Dataset

Lecture 3 · Slides 18–19

An RDD is a bag of objects whose contents Spark cannot see. Slide 12 said newer Spark versions added DataFrames and Datasets, which enabled SQL support. Slide 18 defines them.

DataFrame (Slide 18)

Unlike an RDD, data is organised into named columns, like a table in a relational database. It imposes a structure on a distributed collection, allowing a higher-level abstraction.

Dataset (Slide 18)

An extension of the DataFrame API providing a type-safe, object-oriented programming interface, with compile-time error detection (mistakes such as using a field that does not exist are caught before the job runs).

Both are built on the Spark SQL engine and both can be converted back to an RDD.

Beginner intuition

An RDD is a box of unlabelled items. A DataFrame is a spreadsheet: columns have names, so you can say "the age column" and Spark understands and can optimise. A Dataset is a spreadsheet where each row is also a checked object, so the compiler warns you about a wrong column or type before you waste a long run.

RDDDataFrameDataset
Structurenone; any objectsnamed columns (table)named columns plus object types
You describearbitrary functions (black boxes)what you want, by column namesame, with typed objects
Error detectionat run timemostly at run timecompile time (type-safe)
EngineSpark coreSpark SQL engine; convertible back to an RDD

Beyond the slides: typed Datasets exist in the compiled JVM languages (Scala, Java); PySpark (Python) uses DataFrames. A DataFrame is a Dataset of generic rows, and the SQL engine's optimiser plans the query for you. "Compile-time" only makes sense in compiled languages, which the slide does not say.

The one-line comparison (Slide 19)

Lecture 3 · Slide 19

Not examined — code (understand, don't memorise)

RDD style: rdd.map(lambda x: ...).filter(lambda x: ...)
DataFrame / Dataset style: df.select("age").filter(df.age > 30)

In words: the RDD line hands Spark arbitrary functions, applied record by record, which Spark cannot look inside. The DataFrame line states what is wanted: pick the column "age", keep rows where age is greater than 30. Because that is declarative, Spark can optimise it. Both lines are chains of transformations, so both are lazy. As written, neither ends with an action and the "..." is a placeholder, so neither would actually run.

Exam tip

Expected answer on "why DataFrame over RDD": structure (named columns), higher-level abstraction, SQL support and optimisation by the engine. Dataset adds type safety and compile-time errors. Both convert to an RDD.

Spark's libraries

Lecture 3 · Slide 20

Spark is a platform: the core (RDDs plus the DAG scheduler) and four libraries for common jobs.

LibrarySlide's one-linerWhat it means
Spark SQLscalable processing of relational dataQuery structured data with SQL or DataFrames across a cluster.
Spark Streamingstream processing of live data streamsHandle data that arrives continuously, not stored files.
MLlibscalable machine learningML algorithms on a cluster; they loop over the same data many times, so in-memory caching helps.
GraphXgraph manipulationGraph computation (Beyond the slides: for example PageRank-style algorithms).
GraphX graph (Slide 20)

GraphX extends the Spark RDD with a Graph abstraction: a directed multigraph with properties attached to each vertex and edge. Directed: every edge has a direction. Multigraph: several parallel edges may join the same pair of vertices. Properties: user-defined attributes on every vertex and every edge. Example: vertices = people (property: name), edges = "follows" or "emailed" (property: date); two edges A → B are allowed. Because it builds on RDDs, a graph is also distributed and immutable.

Slide erratum

Typo: "datastreams" should read "data streams".

Spark vs Hadoop MapReduce

Lecture 3 · Slide 21

Slide 21 compares the two along three dimensions.

DimensionHadoop MapReduceSpark
PerformancePersists back to disk after every map or reduce action; runs easily alongside other services with minor performance differences; works well for the 1-pass jobs it was designed for.Processes data in memory, so normally faster. Caveat: often needs lots of memory; if other resource-demanding services compete or the data cannot fit in memory, Spark degrades.
Ease of useLower-level programming model (Map and Reduce functions)Easier to program: higher-level APIs
Data processingMap then reduceMore general: general DAGs, many operators, SQL, streaming, ML, graphs

Counting the figure: 3 passes under MapReduce means 3 reads and 3 writes (6 disk operations) against 1 read and 1 final write (2 disk operations) for Spark, the 2k versus 2 pattern of Figure 3.2. This is an illustration of the principle, not a measured speed-up; the slide gives no "10x" or "100x" numbers and says nothing about fault tolerance or cost.

Common mistake

Writing "Spark is always faster". The slide says normally faster, with caveats: it needs lots of memory, and for a simple one-pass job on a shared cluster MapReduce is perfectly adequate.

Exam tip

"Compare Spark and MapReduce": answer on performance (with the memory caveat), ease of use, and generality, and name MapReduce's strengths (one-pass jobs, coexistence with other services).

Which problems suit MapReduce?

Lecture 3 · Slides 22–23

Slide 22 is a section divider titled "Problems Suited for Map Reduce"; it carries no printed number (it sits between printed slides 21 and 23). Slide 23, titled "Problems NOT suitable for MapReduce", answers both sides.

MapReduce is great forMapReduce is inefficient when random or irregular access is required
Sequential data access: scan the files start to end, each record handled independently (word count, filtering, simple aggregation). Splits easily across machines.
  • Interdependent data, for example comparisons of many pairs of items (every item must meet every other) and machine learning (many repeated passes over the same data).
  • Graphs: a vertex needs its scattered neighbours, and iterative algorithms need many passes.

Beyond the slides: each extra MapReduce round costs a shuffle and a disk write, so iterative or interdependent jobs pay that cost again and again; Spark's caching and general DAGs soften it. Number check: comparing all pairs among n items needs n(n−1)/2 comparisons: each of the n items is paired with the other n−1, and each pair is counted twice, so divide by 2 (1,000 × 999 / 2 = 499,500).

Slide erratum

The divider says "Suited" while the next slide is titled "NOT suitable"; the divider also writes "Map Reduce" with a space and has no number. Slide 23 has a grammar slip: "access to data required" should be "is required".

Decision checklist: MapReduce or Spark?

Lecture 3 · Slides 21, 23

This checklist combines Slides 21 and 23. It is a study aid, not a slide.

QuestionIf yes, lean to
One pass over the data, sequential scan, read-map-reduce-write once?MapReduce is fine
Must it coexist with other resource-hungry services, with little memory to spare?MapReduce
Does the job loop over the same data many times (machine learning)?Spark (cache in memory)
Graphs, or records that depend on each other, or comparisons of many pairs?Spark (DAGs, GraphX), though still costly
Need SQL, streaming, ML or graph libraries in one system?Spark
Want shorter programs with higher-level APIs?Spark
Is there enough memory for the working set?If no, Spark degrades; reconsider

Tutorial and further reading

Lecture 3 · Slide 24

Slide 24 only points to hands-on material, adds no new concepts, and no code from Lectures 1–5 is examined, so use it for practice only. It lists a Spark programming tutorial (a Google Colab notebook, which may become unavailable) and the official guides: the Spark RDD Programming Guide, the DataFrame and SQL guide, the MLlib Guide, the GraphX Guide, and Spark Streaming. They map onto Slides 13–20 in that order.

Slide erratum

The "DataFrame and SQL Guide" link points to the PySpark DataFrame API reference page, not to the Spark SQL programming guide the link text suggests.

Quick recap of Slides 13–24
  • RDD = partitioned, read-only collection spread over the cluster, cached in memory with disk fallback; made from stored data or from other RDDs; best for the same operation on every element.
  • Transformations (map, filter, join, union, intersection, distinct) are deterministic and lazy; actions (count, collect, reduce, save) trigger execution and return or export.
  • Scheduler: general DAGs, pipelining of narrow steps, cache-aware reuse and locality, partitioning-aware shuffle avoidance; shuffles (groupBy, join) end stages.
  • DataFrame = named columns; Dataset = type-safe with compile-time checks; both on Spark SQL and convertible to RDDs.
  • Libraries: Spark SQL, Streaming, MLlib, GraphX (directed multigraph with vertex and edge properties).
  • Spark vs MapReduce: faster in memory but memory-hungry; easier; more general. MapReduce suits sequential, one-pass work; it struggles with random access, interdependent data, ML and graphs.

Theory Q&A bank

Lecture 3 · Slides 1–24

Cover the answer, write your own, then compare. Numbered points are marking points. These questions are self-made practice except where a slide poses the question itself (for example "Scale up or scale out?").

Q1. Scale up or scale out? (the slide's own question)

Lecture 3 · Slide 3

  1. Scale out. Scale up means one bigger machine; scale out means many commodity machines in a cluster.
  2. Scaling up is costly and has a hard ceiling; a search engine crawling billions of pages cannot fit on one machine.
  3. Scaling out creates storage, coordination and programming problems, which the MapReduce model hides.

Q2. What did the MapReduce programming model give us?

Lecture 3 · Slide 3

  1. It handles persistent storage (distributed file system, replicated chunks).
  2. It handles distributed worker coordination (the master assigns tasks and restarts failed ones).
  3. It brings computation closer to the data (data locality).
  4. It is simpler for the programmer: only map and reduce functions are written.

Q3. Describe the execution of a MapReduce job (six steps).

Lecture 3 · Slide 4

  1. Fork: the user program starts a master and workers.
  2. Assign: the master gives map tasks and reduce tasks to idle workers.
  3. Read: a map worker reads its input split.
  4. Local write: it writes intermediate pairs to its own local disk.
  5. Remote read: each reduce worker pulls its share from every map worker (the shuffle).
  6. Write: the reduce worker writes an output file.

Q4. What are the two major limitations of MapReduce? Explain "does not compose well".

Lecture 3 · Slides 5–6

  1. Performance bottlenecks: mapper output is saved to disk and read again by reducers, and each job writes to HDFS; disk is much slower than memory.
  2. Programming difficulty: many problems are not easily described as one map plus one reduce.
  3. Many applications need several chained steps. Each step is a separate job linked only through files on disk, so each link pays the disk cost and the programmer must manage the chain by hand: MapReduce "does not compose well for all large applications".

Q5. What is a data-flow system, and how does it generalise MapReduce?

Lecture 3 · Slide 7

  1. MapReduce has exactly two ranks of tasks (Map, then Reduce).
  2. A data-flow system allows any number of ranks and functions other than Map and Reduce.
  3. Data flows in one direction only, so the task network is a DAG (directed acyclic graph: directed edges, no cycles).

Q6. What does Spark add to the MapReduce model?

Lecture 3 · Slide 10

  1. Fast data sharing: avoids saving intermediate results to disk, and caches data for repeated queries or machine learning (fixes the performance limitation).
  2. General execution graphs (DAGs) (fixes composability).
  3. Richer functions than map and reduce (fixes programming difficulty).
  4. It remains compatible with Hadoop, so existing data and clusters can be reused.

Q7. Draw and describe the Spark software stack. Why is it useful?

Lecture 3 · Slides 8–9

  1. Bottom: the Spark core, a fast memory-optimised execution engine with Python, Java and Scala APIs.
  2. On top: Spark Streaming (stream processing), GraphX (graph computation), MLlib (machine learning), SparkSQL (SQL API).
  3. One engine serves all workloads, and connectors (data lakes, slide 9: HDFS, HBase, Cassandra, MongoDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Kafka and others) let it read many stores.

Q8. What is an RDD? Why is it called resilient and distributed?

Lecture 3 · Slides 11, 13–14

  1. A Resilient Distributed Dataset: a partitioned collection of records, spread across the cluster, read-only.
  2. It can be cached in memory with fallback to disk, and is created from Hadoop-supported data or by transforming other RDDs.
  3. Distributed: its partitions live on many machines and are processed in parallel.
  4. Resilient (beyond the slides): Spark records the lineage of transformations, so a lost partition is recomputed from its recipe.
  5. It is best for applying the same operation to all elements.

Q9. Compare transformations and actions. What is lazy evaluation and why is it useful?

Lecture 3 · Slides 11, 15

  1. Transformation (map, filter, join, union, intersection, distinct): builds a new RDD through a deterministic operation. Action (count, collect, reduce, save): returns a value or exports data.
  2. Lazy evaluation: transformations only record the step; nothing is computed until an action requires it.
  3. Useful because Spark sees the whole chain first: it can pipeline steps, avoid storing intermediate RDDs and compute only what the action needs.

Q10. Explain the lineage graph of Slide 16: what runs when Act1 and Act2 are called?

Lecture 3 · Slide 16

  1. Defining the transformations computes nothing.
  2. Act1 runs stored data → RDD1 → RDD4. Act2 runs stored data → RDD1 → RDD2 → RDD3.
  3. RDD1 is on both paths: without caching it is computed twice; if cached, once.
  4. The lineage also lets Spark rebuild a lost partition.

Q11. What does Spark's task scheduler do? (four properties)

Lecture 3 · Slide 17

  1. Supports general directed acyclic task graphs.
  2. Pipelines functions where possible (map then filter in one pass, in one stage).
  3. Cache-aware: reuses cached data and respects locality.
  4. Partitioning-aware to avoid shuffles: if data is already partitioned as needed, it is not moved again. A shuffle (all-to-all, for example groupBy or join) ends a stage.

Q12. Compare RDD, DataFrame and Dataset.

Lecture 3 · Slides 12, 18–19

  1. RDD: low-level, unstructured collection of objects; you give functions Spark cannot look inside.
  2. DataFrame: data organised into named columns, like a relational table; imposes structure, higher-level abstraction, enables SQL support.
  3. Dataset: extension of the DataFrame API with a type-safe, object-oriented interface and compile-time error detection.
  4. Both are built on the Spark SQL engine and both convert back to an RDD.

Q13. Name the Spark libraries and describe GraphX's graph.

Lecture 3 · Slide 20

  1. Spark SQL (scalable relational data), Spark Streaming (live data streams), MLlib (scalable machine learning), GraphX (graph manipulation).
  2. GraphX extends the RDD with a Graph abstraction: a directed multigraph with properties attached to each vertex and edge.
  3. Directed = edges have direction; multigraph = parallel edges between the same two vertices allowed; properties = user-defined attributes.

Q14. Compare Spark and Hadoop MapReduce.

Lecture 3 · Slide 21

  1. Performance: MapReduce persists to disk after every map or reduce action and works well for 1-pass jobs and alongside other services; Spark works in memory so is normally faster, but needs lots of memory and degrades if memory is short or other services compete.
  2. Ease of use: MapReduce has a lower-level model; Spark has higher-level APIs.
  3. Data processing: MapReduce is map then reduce; Spark is more general (DAGs, SQL, streaming, ML, graphs).

Q15. Which problems are suited, and which not suited, to MapReduce?

Lecture 3 · Slides 22–23

  1. Suited: sequential data access, scanning files with each record handled independently (word count, filtering, simple aggregation).
  2. Inefficient where random or irregular access is needed: interdependent data (comparisons of many pairs of items, machine learning) and graphs.
  3. Reason: such jobs need many rounds, and each MapReduce round pays a shuffle and disk write (beyond the slides).

One-page cheat sheet

Lecture 3 · Slides 1–24

Definitions

TermOne-line meaning
Scale up / scale outOne bigger machine / many commodity machines (choose scale out)
Data-flow systemNetwork of tasks, any number of ranks, any functions, one direction (DAG)
DAGDirected acyclic graph: arrows, no loops
RDDPartitioned, read-only collection of records across the cluster; cached in memory, disk fallback
TransformationRDD to new RDD; deterministic; lazy
ActionReturns a value or exports data; forces computation
LineageRecorded chain of transformations; enables recovery (beyond slides)
Shuffle / stageAll-to-all data exchange / pipelined group of steps ended by a shuffle (beyond slides)

GraphX graphDirected multigraph with vertex and edge properties

Procedures in a few steps

  • MapReduce execution: fork; assign map/reduce; read split; local write; remote read (shuffle); write output.
  • Spark program: create RDD from stored data; chain lazy transformations; call an action; scheduler builds DAG, cuts stages at shuffles, pipelines, reuses cache.
  • Problem to fix (Slides 5–10): disk I/O to fast data sharing; two ranks to general DAGs; few functions to richer functions.
  • Stack (Slide 8): core + Streaming, GraphX, MLlib, SparkSQL.
  • Scheduler (Slide 17): general DAGs; pipelines; cache-aware and locality; partitioning-aware to avoid shuffles.

Numbers to recompute

  • k chained MapReduce jobs: 2k disk touches; minimum needed 2 (one read, one write).
  • Figure of Slide 17: 3 × 3 = 9 (groupBy), 4 + 4 + 3 one-to-one, 4 × 3 = 12 (join); total 32 arrows.
  • All pairs among n items: n(n−1)/2 (1,000 items: 499,500).

Common mistakes & traps

Lecture 3 · Slides 1–24

  • Writing "Spark is always faster". The slide says normally, with a memory caveat; one-pass jobs suit MapReduce fine.
  • Saying Spark never uses disk. Input and final output are on disk, and RDDs fall back to disk; the gain is no disk between steps.
  • Saying map output goes to HDFS. It goes to the mapper's local disk; only final reducer output goes to the distributed file system.
  • Mixing up control flow (fork, assign) with data flow (read, local write, remote read, write) on Slide 4.
  • Calling collect or count a transformation. They are actions; map and filter are transformations.
  • Believing a transformation runs when written. It only records the step (lazy); an action triggers it.
  • Thinking "read-only" means an RDD cannot be used. Each operation yields a new RDD; the old one is unchanged.
  • Assuming a DAG may contain loops. It is acyclic; iterations are written as a longer acyclic graph.
  • Treating DataFrames and Datasets as the same: only the Dataset is type-safe with compile-time error detection.
  • Describing a GraphX graph as undirected or simple: it is a directed multigraph with properties.

Lecture 4Frequent Itemsets & Association Rules (A-Priori, PCY, SON)

Roadmap — what this lecture is about
  • The problem (Slides 1–18): given a huge file of baskets (small sets of items), find itemsets that occur together in at least s baskets (frequent itemsets) and turn them into if-then association rules, judged by support, confidence and interest.
  • The hard part (Slides 19–28): finding frequent itemsets. The cost is the number of passes over a disk-resident file; the scarce resource is main memory; the bottleneck is counting pairs. The naive method needs about 4 bytes × n(n−1)/2 of memory.
  • Exact multi-pass algorithms (Slides 29–51): A-Priori (monotonicity, Ck/Lk), PCY (hash pairs into buckets in the idle Pass 1 memory, bitmap, 2/3 rule), and its refinements Multistage (3 passes) and Multihash (2 passes).
  • At most two passes (Slides 52–69): random sampling (approximate: false positives and false negatives) and SON (exact), with SON as two MapReduce rounds and a five-basket worked example.
  • Practice (Slides 70–84): the cat-and-dog baskets (pairs, triples, confidence, interest), A-Priori on integer baskets, the PCY bitmap, and the multistage idea. Slides 85–86 are the summary and the reading list.

Exam checklist — by the end you can:

  • compute support, list all frequent itemsets level by level for a given s, and state monotonicity;
  • compute confidence and interest of a rule, say when a rule is interesting, and generate all rules above a confidence threshold from the frequent itemsets (including the boundary case conf = c);
  • explain why passes and main memory are the cost model and why pairs are the bottleneck;
  • compute the memory of the naive method, the triangular matrix (4 bytes per pair) and the triples method (12 bytes per occurring pair), and state the 1/3 break-even;
  • run A-Priori by hand (Pass 1, frequent items, Pass 2, Ck, Lk) and explain the renumbering trick;
  • describe PCY Pass 1, the bit-vector, the Pass 2 candidate test (both conditions), why no frequent pair is lost, why a bitmap, and the 2/3 rule;
  • describe and compare Multistage and Multihash (passes, filters, risks, limits);
  • explain random sampling (scaled threshold, false positives vs false negatives) and SON (chunks, candidates, second pass, why it is exact) and contrast them;
  • describe SON in MapReduce (Map 1, Reduce 1, Map 2, Reduce 2) and work the five-basket example, including the correct list of 9 candidates.
