Where this lecture starts: finding what goes together

Lecture 4 · Slides 1–2

Slide 1 is the title card: "Large-Data Frequent Pattern Analysis, SON MapReduce" (instructor Dr. Jarek Szlichta). Read it as a one-line summary of the lecture. Frequent pattern analysis means finding things that occur together often. Large-data means the data is far too big to handle naively. SON MapReduce is the final algorithm of the lecture, a way to do the job on a cluster. The slide does not spell out "SON" (Beyond the slides: it stands for Savasere, Omiecinski and Navathe, the authors of the algorithm).

Slide 2 supplies the motivation, supermarket shelf management:

Slide 2 bulletPlain meaning
Goal: identify items that are bought together by sufficiently many customersFind product combinations that many shoppers buy in the same visit. "Sufficiently many" will become the support threshold (Slide 8).
Approach: process the sales data to find dependencies among itemsRead through the receipts and look for "if they buy this, they also buy that" patterns.
A classic rule: if someone buys diaper and milk, then they are likely to buy beerThe famous beer-and-diapers rule. Its message: such rules are surprising, so nobody would guess them, and a program must find them in the data. "Do not be surprised if you find six-packs next to diapers!"
Beginner intuition

Imagine you could read every receipt a supermarket printed this year. You would notice that some groups of products keep turning up on the same receipt. The shop can put those products next to each other, advertise them together, or discount one and not the other. Everything in this lecture is about finding such groups quickly when there are billions of receipts.

Common mistake

The beer-and-diapers story on Slide 2 is folklore. The slide gives no data to back it up, and the words "likely" and "sufficiently many" are informal. Do not quote it as a proven fact. What you must know are the precise definitions that replace these vague words: support, confidence and interest (Slides 8–11).

The market-basket model

Lecture 4 · Slides 3–4

Input: items and baskets

Lecture 4 · Slide 3

Definition: item, basket, market-basket model

The model has two ingredients. A large set of items (for example, everything a supermarket sells). A large set of baskets, where each basket is a small subset of items (for example, the things one customer buys on one day). The model is the picture "many small sets drawn from one big catalogue".

The slide shows the input as a table with columns TID (transaction ID, simply the basket number) and Items. This guide uses it as the 5-basket running table for Slides 3, 4 and 8:

TIDItems
1Bread, Coke, Milk
2Beer, Bread
3Beer, Coke, Diaper, Milk
4Beer, Bread, Diaper, Milk
5Coke, Diaper, Milk

Five baskets, five distinct items (Beer, Bread, Coke, Diaper, Milk). Three facts about baskets matter later:

  • A basket is a set. Order is irrelevant and an item appears at most once in it, so {Beer, Bread} = {Bread, Beer}.
  • Baskets are small compared with the item catalogue: a customer buys a handful of products out of tens of thousands.
  • "Basket" is only a name. Anything that groups things together can be a basket (Slides 5–6 show this).
Beginner intuition

One basket = one shopping receipt. The table is the pile of receipts, reduced to "which products were on each receipt". Prices, quantities and times are thrown away on purpose.

Output: association rules

Lecture 4 · Slide 4

On Slide 4 the same table is the Input, and the Output is a box titled "Rules Discovered" containing two rules: {Milk} → {Coke} and {Diaper, Milk} → {Beer} (the slide writes the arrow as "-->"). The text on the left says what a rule means: association rules are statements of the form "people who bought {x, y, z} tend to buy {v, w}".

You can check the two rules against the table. Milk is in baskets 1, 3, 4, 5 and Coke is in 1, 3, 5 of those, so Coke accompanies Milk in 3 of 4 baskets. {Diaper, Milk} is in baskets 3, 4, 5 and Beer is in 3 and 4 of those, so 2 of 3. (These two counts are our own check; the slide prints no numbers.) Slide 10 will turn "tend to" into a precise number called confidence.

Slide erratum

Slide 4 writes a rule as {x,y,z} → {v,w}, with a set on the right, but Slide 10 formally defines a rule with one item j on the right. Slides 17–18 then use several items on the right again (for example b → c,m). Treat "one item on the right" as the simple textbook case and "a set on the right" as the general case; the confidence formula is the same: support of the whole itemset divided by support of the left side.

Where the model is used

Lecture 4 · Slides 5–6

The model is abstract, so it fits many problems. The slides give four uses. The only thing that changes between them is what you call a "basket" and what you call an "item".

ApplicationBasket =Item =What a frequent pattern tells you
Real market baskets (Slide 5)the set of products bought in one tripa productHow shoppers move through a store (position tempting items), and tie-in "tricks", e.g. run a sale on diapers and raise the price of beer. The rule must occur frequently "or no $$'s", i.e. no money to be made.
"People who bought X also bought Y" (Slide 5, Amazon)one customer's purchasesa productRecommendations: if many baskets contain X and Y together, suggest Y to a buyer of X.
Plagiarism detection (Slide 6)a sentencea document that contains that sentenceTwo documents that appear together in many baskets share many sentences. "Items that appear together too often could represent plagiarism."
Drug side-effects (Slide 6)a patienta drug taken, or a side-effect sufferedA frequent itemset such as {drug A, drug B, side-effect X} flags a drug combination that leads to a particular side-effect.
Common mistake

In the plagiarism example the roles look reversed on purpose: baskets are sentences and items are documents. Read it as "this sentence appears in these documents". A basket then lists the documents containing one sentence. If you swap the roles you would be counting sentences that co-occur in documents, which answers a different question.

Key idea

Slide 5's last sub-bullet is the reason this lecture talks about frequent patterns, not just any pattern. A pattern seen in two receipts out of a million cannot change how a store is run or a recommendation is made. Only patterns that occur often enough are worth acting on. "Often enough" is the support threshold, defined next.

Roadmap of the lecture

Lecture 4 · Slide 7

The roadmap (Slide 7)

Lecture 4 · Slide 7

Slide 7 is a black "Outline" slide. It splits the lecture into two parts:

  1. First, define frequent itemsets and association rules (Slides 8–18, this part of the guide).
  2. Then, algorithms for finding frequent itemsets: the A-Priori algorithm, the PCY algorithm "+ 2 refinements", and MapReduce (SON, from the title slide).

The two PCY refinements are not named on the slide. (Beyond the slides: in the textbook Mining of Massive Datasets they are the Multistage and Multihash algorithms.)

Support and frequent itemsets

Lecture 4 · Slides 8–9

The definitions (Slide 8)

Lecture 4 · Slide 8

Slide 8 begins with the "simplest question": find sets of items that appear together "frequently" in baskets. A set of items is called an itemset (a basket is one particular itemset; so is {Beer, Bread}). The slide defines three terms.

Definition: support, support threshold, frequent itemset

Support of an itemset I: the number of baskets that contain all items of I. Written support(I).

Support threshold s: a number of baskets chosen by the analyst.

Frequent itemset: an itemset with support(I) ≥ s, i.e. it appears in at least s baskets.

Beginner intuition

Support is a tally. Go through the receipts. For the itemset you care about, make one tally mark for every receipt that has all its items. The final number of marks is the support. The threshold s is a cut-off line: "I only care about combinations seen at least this many times".

The slide's example uses the table above and states support of {Beer, Bread} = 2. The figure shows where the 2 comes from.

Method, in three steps: (1) for each basket ask "does it contain every item of the itemset?"; (2) make a tally mark for each yes; (3) the number of marks is the support. Baskets 2 and 4 contain both Beer and Bread, so the support is 2. With s = 2 the itemset would be frequent; with s = 3 it would not.

Common mistakes about support
  • Support is a count of baskets here, not a fraction or percentage. (Beyond the slides: many textbooks and tools divide by the number of baskets; if an exam gives a percentage threshold, convert with s = fraction × number of baskets.)
  • A basket may contain extra items and still counts: basket 4 has Diaper and Milk as well, and it still counts for {Beer, Bread}.
  • You count baskets, not purchases. Buying three Beers in one basket adds one, not three.
  • "At least s" means ≥. An itemset with support exactly s is frequent.
  • Always state s. The same data gives different frequent itemsets for different thresholds.

Worked example: eight baskets, s = 3 (Slide 9)

Lecture 4 · Slide 9

Slide 9 changes data and uses short letters: items = {milk, coke, pepsi, beer, juice}, written m, c, p, b, j. The support threshold is 3 baskets. In these letters b means beer (on Slides 3, 4 and 8 the letter B would suggest Bread).

BasketItemsBasketItems
B1{m, c, b}B2{m, p, j}
B3{m, b}B4{c, j}
B5{m, p, b}B6{m, c, b, j}
B7{c, b, j}B8{b, c}

The slide lists the answer: frequent itemsets: {m}, {c}, {b}, {j}, {m,b}, {b,c}, {c,j}. It does not show the counts, so here they are, level by level:

  1. Single items. m = 5 (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6); c = 5 (B1, B4, B6, B7, B8); b = 6 (B1, B3, B5, B6, B7, B8); j = 4 (B2, B4, B6, B7); p = 2 (B2, B5). Keep those ≥ 3: m, c, b, j. Pepsi is not frequent, although it is on the item list.
  2. Pairs. Only {m,b} = 4 (B1, B3, B5, B6), {b,c} = 4 (B1, B6, B7, B8) and {c,j} = 3 (B4, B6, B7) reach 3. Everything else has support 2 or less; for example {m,c} = 2 (B1, B6).
  3. Triples. No triple reaches 3. The best is {m,c,b} with 2 (B1, B6). So there are no frequent triples and nothing larger.

The slide's eleven coloured arrows say exactly what the dots say: red for {m,b}, green for {b,c}, dark blue for {c,j}. The slide does not explain the colours and the arrows overprint the text, so use the figure instead.

Key idea: a pattern you will see again

Every frequent pair above is made only of frequent single items (m, c, b, j), and pepsi, the one infrequent item, appears in no frequent pair. This is the monotonicity property: if a set is frequent, so are all its subsets. Equivalently, a basket that contains a bigger set also contains every smaller set, so the smaller set's support can only be larger. The A-Priori algorithm (later slides) is built on this one fact, and Slide 17 already uses it.

Common mistake

Do not assume two frequent items make a frequent pair. m and c are both frequent (5 each), but {m,c} has support only 2. The converse direction is the safe one: a frequent pair always has frequent members.

Exam tip

For "find all frequent itemsets" questions, build a tick table (rows = baskets, columns = items) and count level by level: singles, then pairs, then triples, until a level has no frequent set. Write each count with the basket numbers that support it; that earns the method marks even if one count is off. Quiz L4-Q1 does this in full.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution, verify that support({Beer, Bread}) = 2, then find every frequent itemset of the eight baskets with s = 3 and compare with the slide's list.

Quiz L4-Q1Support and frequent itemsets (two examples) Lecture 4 · Slides 8–9
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 8 — Frequent Itemsets. “Simplest question: find sets of items that appear together ‘frequently’ in baskets.” Support for an itemset I is the number of baskets containing all items in I. Given a support threshold s, the sets of items that appear in at least s baskets are called frequent itemsets. The slide shows the five baskets below (the same table as on Slides 3–4) and states: support of {Beer, Bread} = 2.

3Beer, Coke, Diaper, Milk

(a) Verify that the support of {Beer, Bread} is 2. Practice (not printed on the slide): compute the support of every single item, every pair and every triple of items in this table, and list the frequent itemsets. Slide 8 gives no threshold, so the practice uses s = 3 and s = 2 (our choice, not the slide’s).

Slide 9 — Example: Frequent Itemsets. Items = {milk, coke, pepsi, beer, juice} (written m, c, p, b, j). Support threshold = 3 baskets. The eight baskets are:

BasketItemsBasketItems

(b) Find all frequent itemsets. Show the full count table for all single items, all pairs and all triples (and say what happens for bigger sets). The slide’s answer: {m}, {c}, {b}, {j}, {m,b}, {b,c}, {c,j}.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

A basket is one shopping receipt. The support of a set of items is just a tally: go through the pile of receipts and make one tally mark for every receipt that has all the items of the set on it. Nothing else: no averages, no percentages, just a count. A set is frequent when its tally reaches the threshold s. Think of s as a cut-off line: “I only care about combinations that happen at least this many times”.

Formulas used in this quiz

Support: support(I) = number of baskets B with I ⊆ B (“⊆” = every item of I is also in B).   Frequent: I is frequent ⇔ support(I) ≥ s.   How many itemsets: from n items there are C(n, k) = n! ÷ (k!(n − k)!) itemsets of size k, and 2n − 1 non-empty itemsets in total.

Part (a) — the five baskets of Slide 8

  1. Formula / idea: support(I) = the number of baskets that contain every item of I. Three consequences that beginners often miss: (i) order does not matter, {Beer, Bread} = {Bread, Beer}; (ii) a basket may contain extra items and still counts (basket 4 also has Diaper and Milk); (iii) what is counted is baskets, not how many times an item is bought.

  6. Practice: apply the threshold rule “support ≥ s”. Slide 8 gives no s, so practise with two values:
    • s = 3: frequent = all five singles (Beer, Bread, Coke, Diaper, Milk) plus the pairs {Coke, Milk} and {Diaper, Milk}; no triple. That is 7 frequent itemsets. {Beer, Bread} (support 2) is not frequent here.
    • s = 2: frequent = the 5 singles; the 7 pairs {Beer, Bread}, {Beer, Diaper}, {Beer, Milk}, {Bread, Milk}, {Coke, Diaper}, {Coke, Milk}, {Diaper, Milk}; and the 2 triples {Beer, Diaper, Milk} and {Coke, Diaper, Milk}. That is 14 frequent itemsets (5 + 7 + 2). Now {Beer, Bread} is frequent.
    Lesson: the same data gives different frequent itemsets for different thresholds, so always state s. Also notice that every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent: {Beer, Diaper, Milk} is frequent at s = 2, and so are {Beer, Diaper}, {Beer, Milk}, {Diaper, Milk}, {Beer}, {Diaper} and {Milk} (this is the monotonicity property of Slide 30, used again in part (b)).
  7. Cross-check by counting the other way round (basket by basket). A basket with k items contains 2k − 1 non-empty sub-itemsets (basket 3 with 4 items has 24 − 1 = 15: 4 singles + 6 pairs + 4 triples + 1 four-set). Adding 1 to the counter of each of them, for every basket, gives exactly the supports above. For these five baskets that is (23 − 1) + (22 − 1) + (24 − 1) + (24 − 1) + (23 − 1) = 7 + 3 + 15 + 15 + 7 = 47 counter increments, which equals the totals by size, 16 singles + 19 pairs + 10 triples + 2 four-sets + 0 five-sets = 47. ✓ This basket-by-basket view is what a program does, and it shows why counting all itemsets explodes for big baskets (the reason for the clever algorithms later in Lecture 4).
Preview: why support matters (Slides 4 and 10)

The two rules on Slide 4 are built from these counts. Confidence (Slide 10) = support(I ∪ j) ÷ support(I). For {Milk} → {Coke}: support({Milk, Coke}) = 3 and support({Milk}) = 4, so confidence = 3/4 = 0.75. For {Diaper, Milk} → {Beer}: support({Beer, Diaper, Milk}) = 2 and support({Diaper, Milk}) = 3, so confidence = 2/3 ≈ 0.667. You do not need these for this quiz; they only show that every association rule starts from support counts.

We count singles, then pairs, then triples, then see what is left. The rule applied to every count is the one from Slide 8: frequent ⇔ support ≥ 3. None is frequent. We did not even need to count them: if a set appears in at least 3 baskets then every subset of it does too (monotonicity, Slide 30). No triple is frequent, so no 4-set or 5-set (each contains triples) can be frequent.

Exam tip: a shortcut that needs no triple counting (monotonicity, Slide 30)

Two facts save work. (1) Since {p} is not frequent, no pair containing p can be frequent (Slide 30, “contrapositive for pairs”), so only 6 of the 10 pairs even needed counting (those made of m, b, c, j). (2) A triple can be frequent only if all three of its pairs are frequent. The frequent pairs {m,b}, {b,c}, {c,j} form a chain m – b – c – j, never a “triangle”: {m,b,c} would need {m,c} (support 2) and {b,c,j} would need {b,j} (support 2). So there is no candidate triple and we could have stopped after the pairs. You will use exactly this reasoning in the A-Priori algorithm.

Reading the coloured arrows on Slide 9

The slide draws arrows from each frequent pair to the baskets that contain it: red arrows from {m,b} to B1, B3, B5, B6 (4 baskets); green arrows from {b,c} to B1, B6, B7, B8 (4 baskets); blue arrows from {c,j} to B4, B6, B7 (3 baskets). The number of arrows ending at baskets is the support. These match the pair table above (the slide has no colour legend; the colour-to-itemset reading is ours).

Common mistakes
  • Counting baskets with Beer or Bread (4 baskets) instead of Beer and Bread (2), or adding the two single supports (3 + 3 = 6). Only baskets with both count.
  • Counting only baskets that are exactly {Beer, Bread} (basket 2 only, giving 1). A basket with extra items, like basket 4, still counts.
  • Using “> s” instead of “≥ s”. {c,j} has support exactly 3 = s and is frequent.
  • Assuming two frequent items make a frequent pair. m and c are both frequent, but {m,c} has support 2 and is not.
  • Mixing up count and fraction. On the slides support is a count of baskets (support 2, threshold “3 baskets”). Beyond the slides: some textbooks divide by the number of baskets (here 2/5 = 0.4); when a question gives the threshold as a number of baskets, compare counts.
  • Forgetting that order does not matter and that you must state s: the frequent list changes with the threshold (7 itemsets at s = 3 but 14 at s = 2 in part (a)).
Final answer:
(a) support({Beer, Bread}) = 2 (baskets 2 and 4), as the slide says. Singles: Beer 3, Bread 3, Coke 3, Diaper 3, Milk 4. Pairs: Coke–Milk 3 and Diaper–Milk 3; Beer–Bread, Beer–Diaper, Beer–Milk, Bread–Milk, Coke–Diaper 2 each; Beer–Coke, Bread–Coke, Bread–Diaper 1 each. Triples: {Beer, Diaper, Milk} 2, {Coke, Diaper, Milk} 2, six triples 1, and {Beer, Bread, Coke}, {Bread, Coke, Diaper} 0. Practice thresholds: s = 3 gives 7 frequent itemsets (5 singles + {Coke, Milk}, {Diaper, Milk}); s = 2 gives 14 (5 singles, 7 pairs, 2 triples).
(b) Supports: m 5, b 6, c 5, j 4, p 2; pairs mb 4, bc 4, cj 3, mc 2, mj 2, mp 2, bj 2, bp 1, jp 1, cp 0; no triple above 2; no 4- or 5-itemset above 1. Frequent itemsets (s = 3): {m}, {c}, {b}, {j}, {m,b}, {b,c}, {c,j}: 7 of the 31 possible itemsets.
Where the marks come from: (1) state the definition: support = number of baskets containing all items of the set, and frequent = support ≥ s; (2) show the check for {Beer, Bread} by naming baskets 2 and 4; (3) correct single-item counts (the tick table), discarding {p} in part (b); (4) correct pair counts, with the baskets named, in particular {m,b} = 4, {b,c} = 4, {c,j} = 3 and rejecting {m,c}, {m,j}, {b,j} (each 2); (5) correct triple counts, or a valid monotonicity argument that no triple can be frequent; (6) apply the “≥ 3” threshold correctly, including the boundary case {c,j} = 3; (7) state the final list of 7 frequent itemsets. Even with a counting slip, a clearly stated method keeps most of the marks.

Association rules and confidence

Lecture 4 · Slide 10

Frequent itemsets say which items occur together. They do not say which item leads to which. A rule adds direction, in the form "if you see this, expect that".

Definition: association rule and confidence (Slide 10)

An association rule is an if-then rule about the contents of baskets. The rule {i1, i2, …, ik} → j means: "if a basket contains all of i1, …, ik, then it is likely to contain j". Write I = {i1, …, ik} for the left side.

The confidence of the rule is the probability of j given I:

Formula

conf(I → j) = support(I ∪ {j})support(I)

Numerator: baskets containing all of I and also j. Denominator: baskets containing I. The slide writes "support(I ∪ j)"; it means the itemset I with the item j added.

Beginner intuition

Pick out only the receipts that contain the "if" items. Of those, what fraction also contain the "then" item? That fraction is the confidence. The left side defines the population you look at, which is why it is the denominator.

Facts to remember:

  • Confidence lies between 0 and 1 (0 = never together, 1 = always together).
  • It is not symmetric: conf(I → j) and conf(j → I) have the same numerator but different denominators. Slide 4's {Milk} → {Coke} has 3/4, whereas {Coke} → {Milk} has 3/3 = 1 (Coke is in baskets 1, 3, 5 and all three have Milk).
  • Slide 10 warns: "in practice there are many rules; we want to find the significant/interesting ones!" Confidence alone is not enough, as the next slide shows.
Common mistake

Putting the wrong support in the denominator. The denominator is the support of the left side only (the "if" part), never of the whole rule and never of the right side.

Interesting rules and the interest measure

Lecture 4 · Slides 11–15

Why high confidence can mislead (Slide 11)

Lecture 4 · Slide 11

Slide 11's headline: not all high-confidence rules are interesting. The example: the rule X → milk may have high confidence for many itemsets X, "because milk is just purchased very often (independent of X) and the confidence will be high".

Beginner intuition

Suppose 95% of all receipts contain milk. Then "if the basket has batteries, it has milk" is true about 95% of the time, and so is the same rule for shoelaces, tyres and anything else. High confidence, zero information: milk would be there anyway. To find a real association, ask whether knowing the "if" part improves on the baseline chance of the "then" item.

Definition and formula: interest (Slide 11)

The interest of a rule I → j is the difference between its confidence and the fraction of baskets that contain j:

Interest(I → j) = conf(I → j) − Pr[j], where Pr[j] = (number of baskets containing j) ÷ (total number of baskets).

The slide says interesting rules are those with high interest values (usually above 0.5). How to read the number:

InterestMeaning
≈ 0Knowing I tells you nothing about j: the rule just reflects how popular j is.
large positiveI makes j much more likely than usual: a real association.
negativeI makes j less likely than usual.
Slide erratum / omission

Slide 11 mentions only high interest. Beyond the slides: the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets) counts a rule as interesting when the interest is high in absolute value, positive or negative, because a strongly negative value is also informative. The slide also never gives a formula for Pr[j]. The threshold "usually above 0.5" is only a rule of thumb.

Example: confidence and interest of {m,b} → c (Slides 12–15)

Lecture 4 · Slides 12–15

Slides 12–15 are one slide built up in four steps, on the same eight baskets as Slide 9, for the rule {m, b} → c ("if milk and beer, then coke"). Each step reveals one more line:

SlideWhat it showsHow to get it
12Question: Confidence = ?conf = support({m,b,c}) / support({m,b})
13Answer: 2/4 = 1/2Numerator 2 (B1, B6 hold m, b and c); denominator 4 (B1, B3, B5, B6 hold m and b)
14Question: Interest = ?Interest = conf − Pr[c]
15Answer: 1/2 − 5/8 < 0.5; "item c appears in 5/8 of the baskets"; "rule is not very interesting!"c is in B1, B4, B6, B7, B8, so Pr[c] = 5/8 = 0.625

Reading the figure: confidence uses only the green row (baskets that satisfy the "if" part); the baseline Pr[c] uses the orange row (all baskets). Coke appears in 50% of the baskets that have milk and beer, but in 62.5% of all baskets. Milk and beer do not help predict coke; they slightly hurt. The rule has respectable confidence (0.5) and is still not interesting. That is exactly the situation Slide 11 warns about.

Slide erratum

Slide 15 writes "Interest = 1/2 − 5/8 < 0.5" and never evaluates the difference. The value is 1/2 − 5/8 = 4/8 − 5/8 = −1/8 = −0.125. The "< 0.5" is trivially true for a negative number; the meaningful statement is that |−0.125| = 0.125 is far below 0.5. The same slides also contain the typo "B4=" (missing space). Neither changes the conclusion.

Exam tip

Write the three counts (support of the left side, support of the whole itemset, number of baskets containing the right-hand item) before dividing. Then give confidence, Pr[j], the signed interest, and one sentence of interpretation. Each is a separate mark.

Try it yourself first: compute the confidence and the interest of {m,b} → c from the eight baskets, then decide whether the rule is interesting.

Quiz L4-Q2Confidence and interest of an association rule Lecture 4 · Slides 10–15
Question (as on the slides)

There are eight shopping baskets over the items m = milk, c = coke, p = pepsi, b = beer, j = juice (the item list and the same baskets as on Slide 9; they are repeated on Slides 12–15):

B1{m, c, b}B2{m, p, j}
B3{m, b}B4{c, j}
B5{m, p, b}B6{m, c, b, j}
B7{c, b, j}B8{b, c}

Consider the association rule {m, b} → c (“if a basket contains milk and beer, it is likely to contain coke”).

(a) What is the confidence of the rule? (Slide 12: “Confidence = ?”)
(b) What is the interest of the rule? (Slide 14: “Interest = ?”)
(c) Is the rule interesting? Justify your answer with the interest value. (Slide 15 states the conclusion; Slide 11 says interesting rules have high interest, usually above 0.5.)

The slides ask only “Confidence = ?” and “Interest = ?”. Part (c) is added from the closing remark of Slide 15 (“Rule is not very interesting!”) so that you also practise justifying the verdict.

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Imagine a school lunch line in which almost everybody takes a water bottle. The rule “if you took a sandwich, then you took water” is right nearly every time (high confidence), yet it is useless, because water would have been taken anyway. Interest removes that illusion by subtracting how often water is taken anyway. Equivalently, ask: “does learning that the basket has milk and beer improve on a blind guess about coke?” Blind guess: coke is in 62.5% of all baskets. After learning about milk and beer: only 50%. So no, it does not help. Coke is fairly common (62.5% of baskets), and baskets with milk and beer contain it even less often (50%), so the rule does worse than a blind guess. The same logic as the water-bottle case of Slide 11, with a milder base rate.

Formulas used (Lecture 4 · Slides 8, 10, 11)

Support of an itemset S: support(S) = the number of baskets that contain every item of S (Slide 8).

Confidence of the rule I → j (Slide 10; it is the probability of j given I): conf(I → j) = support(I ∪ {j})support(I). Here I ∪ {j} means the itemset I with the item j added, so a basket must contain all of those items.

Baseline probability of the right-hand item (Slide 11): Pr[j] = (number of baskets containing j) ÷ (total number of baskets).

Interest (Slide 11): Interest(I → j) = conf(I → j) − Pr[j]

  1. Name the pieces of the rule. In {m, b} → c the “if” part (left side) is I = {m, b}, the “then” item (right side) is j = c, so I ∪ {j} = {m, b, c}, and the total number of baskets is 8. Why: every formula above is written in terms of I and j, so we must say which is which before we count anything.
  2. Check every basket once. Support is only counting, so go through B1 to B8 and record three yes/no questions: does the basket contain both m and b? does it contain c? does it contain all of m, b and c? Why: the three totals at the bottom of the table are exactly the three numbers we need.
    BasketItemscontains m and b?contains c?contains m, b and c?
    B1{m, c, b}✓✓✓
    B2{m, p, j}✗ (no b)✗✗
    B3{m, b}✓✗✗
    B4{c, j}✗ (no m, no b)✓✗
    B5{m, p, b}✓✗✗
    B6{m, c, b, j}✓✓✓
    B7{c, b, j}✗ (no m)✓✗
    B8{b, c}✗ (no m)✓✗
    Total4 (B1, B3, B5, B6)5 (B1, B4, B6, B7, B8)2 (B1, B6)
  3. Count the “if” part: support(I) = support({m, b}) = 4. The baskets containing both milk and beer are B1 = {m, c, b}, B3 = {m, b}, B5 = {m, p, b} and B6 = {m, c, b, j}. B2 has milk but no beer, and B7, B8 have beer but no milk, so they do not count (all items of I must be present). Why: this is the denominator of confidence: “in how many baskets does the ‘if’ part happen?”.
  4. Count the “if and then” part: support(I ∪ {c}) = support({m, b, c}) = 2. Look only at the four baskets of step 3 and keep those that also contain coke: B1 and B6. B3 and B5 have no coke. Why: this is the numerator: “in how many of those baskets did the ‘then’ part happen too?”.
  5. (a) Confidence. conf({m, b} → c) = support({m, b, c}) ÷ support({m, b}) = 2/4 = 1/2 = 0.5. Meaning: among the baskets that already contain milk and beer, exactly half also contain coke.
  6. Count the baseline: Pr[c] = 5/8 = 0.625. Count the baskets containing coke among all eight baskets, ignoring milk and beer: B1, B4, B6, B7, B8 = 5 (B2, B3, B5 have none). So Pr[c] = 5/8 = 0.625. Why: interest compares the rule with “how often does coke appear anyway, whatever else is in the basket?”. This is the “Item c appears in 5/8 of the baskets” line of Slide 15. Note that here we count over every basket, not just the four that contain {m, b}.
  7. (b) Interest. Interest({m, b} → c) = conf − Pr[c] = 1/2 − 5/8. Use the common denominator 8: 4/8 − 5/8 = −1/8 = −0.125. Meaning: knowing that the basket has milk and beer moves the chance of coke from 62.5% down to 50%, a change of −12.5 percentage points.
  8. (c) Decide. Slide 11 says interesting rules have a high interest value, usually above 0.5. Here the interest is −0.125, far below 0.5 (and even its size, |−0.125| = 0.125, is below 0.5), so the rule {m, b} → c is not interesting. Reason in words: coke is fairly common (in 5 of the 8 baskets, 62.5%), so a confidence of 0.5 is no better than what we would get without looking at the left side; the rule does even slightly worse than the baseline. This agrees with the slide’s “Rule is not very interesting!”.
  9. Side note: the support of the rule (Slide 16). Slide 16 defines the support of an association rule as the support of the set of items on the left side, so here it is support({m, b}) = 4. That is at least the threshold s = 3 of Slide 9, so the rule passes the support filter; it is the interest test that rejects it. Beyond the slides: many other books define a rule’s support as support(I ∪ {j}) (here 2). In this course, use the Slide 16 convention.
Slide erratum (minor omission, no answer changes)

Slide 15 stops at “Interest = 1/2 − 5/8 < 0.5” and never evaluates the subtraction. The value is −1/8 = −0.125, and it is negative (the inequality on the slide is true, so the conclusion stands). Slide 11 also says interesting rules have “high interest values (usually above 0.5)” without saying how large negative values are treated. Beyond the slides: in the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets, Section 6.1.3) a rule is interesting when its interest is large positive or large negative, i.e. when the absolute value is large; a strongly negative interest means the left side makes the right side much less likely. For this rule |−0.125| = 0.125 < 0.5, so the verdict is the same under both readings.

What each number means in plain English

QuantityValuePlain-English meaning
support({m,b})44 of the 8 baskets contain both milk and beer: the “if” part occurs in half of the baskets.
support({m,b,c})22 baskets contain milk, beer and coke together.
conf({m,b} → c)2/4 = 0.5“If a basket has milk and beer, it also has coke” is true for 50% of such baskets, i.e. the rule is right half of the time.
Pr[c]5/8 = 0.625Coke is in 62.5% of all baskets: the chance that a random basket has coke, with no other information.
Interest−1/8 = −0.125Confidence minus baseline. Zero would mean “the left side tells us nothing about coke”; a large positive value would mean the left side strongly boosts coke. −0.125 is a small drop in the chance of coke: the rule is not a useful signal.
Key idea — a popular right-hand item caps the interest

Confidence can be at most 1, so Interest ≤ 1 − Pr[j]. For j = c this bound is 1 − 5/8 = 3/8 = 0.375, already below 0.5, so no rule ending in c could pass the “above 0.5” rule of thumb on these baskets. Our own exhaustive check (not on the slides): of the 60 rules with 1 to 4 items on the left, one item on the right, and a left side that occurs in at least one basket, the largest interest is 3/8 (for example {b, j} → c, whose confidence is 1), so on this tiny data set no rule reaches 0.5. The 0.5 of Slide 11 is only a rule of thumb meant for large data.

Common mistakes
  • Wrong denominator for confidence. Divide by support(I) = 4 (baskets with the left side), not by 8 (all baskets). 2/8 = 0.25 is wrong.
  • Wrong Pr[c]. Pr[c] = 5/8 counts every basket with coke. It is not 2/8, and it is not computed only inside the four {m, b} baskets (that would just give the confidence again, and the interest would always be 0).
  • Reading I ∪ {j} as “or”. It is the itemset {m, b, c}: a basket must contain all three items, so support({m, b, c}) = 2, not the number of baskets containing m, b or c.
  • Direction matters. conf({m, b} → c) = 2/4 = 0.5, but conf(c → {m, b}) = support({m,b,c}) ÷ support({c}) = 2/5 = 0.4. The denominator is always the support of the left side.
  • Do not call a rule interesting just because the confidence looks fairly high. Always subtract Pr[j] and compare with the threshold.
  • Keep the sign. The result is −1/8, not +1/8. A negative interest says the left side makes the right side less likely than normal.
Exam tip

Write the answer in this order so that every step earns marks: (1) both formulas, (2) support(I), (3) support(I ∪ {j}), (4) conf = (3) ÷ (2), (5) Pr[j], (6) interest = conf − Pr[j], (7) one sentence of conclusion that mentions the 0.5 threshold and why the rule is or is not interesting. List the basket numbers you counted, so a counting slip can still earn the method marks. Writing the slide’s own line “Interest = 1/2 − 5/8 < 0.5” is acceptable, but evaluating it to −1/8 is better.

Final answer: (a) confidence = 2/4 = 1/2 = 0.5, from support({m, b}) = 4 and support({m, b, c}) = 2. (b) Pr[c] = 5/8 = 0.625, so interest = 1/2 − 5/8 = −1/8 = −0.125. (c) −0.125 is far below 0.5 (and |−0.125| < 0.5 too), so the rule {m, b} → c is NOT interesting: coke is simply a very common item.
Where the marks come from: (1) correct confidence formula support(I ∪ {j}) ÷ support(I); (2) support({m, b}) = 4 with the right baskets (B1, B3, B5, B6); (3) support({m, b, c}) = 2 (B1, B6); (4) conf = 2/4 = 1/2; (5) correct interest formula conf − Pr[j]; (6) Pr[c] = 5/8 (c is in B1, B4, B6, B7, B8); (7) interest = 1/2 − 5/8 = −1/8 with the sign kept; (8) the conclusion “not interesting” with the reason (well below 0.5, because c appears in 5/8 of all baskets). The exact split of marks on a real exam may differ.

The mining problem and the two-step recipe

Lecture 4 · Slides 16–17

The problem statement (Slide 16)

Lecture 4 · Slide 16

Problem (Slide 16)

Find all association rules with support ≥ s and confidence ≥ c.

Two thresholds are chosen by the analyst: s (a count of baskets: how common must the pattern be?) and c (a number between 0 and 1: how reliable must the if-then be?). The rules that pass both tests are the output.

The slide's Note: "Support of an association rule is the support of the set of items on the left side." The slide's second bullet gives the focus of the whole lecture: "Hard part: finding the frequent itemsets!"

Slide erratum / flag: support of a rule

The slide's note is non-standard. Beyond the slides: the usual definition (Agrawal et al.; the textbook) takes the support of a rule A → B as support(A ∪ B), the whole itemset, which is also what Slides 17–18 effectively do (they start from frequent itemsets I = left ∪ right). The two definitions can give different rule sets in general; on the Slide 18 data with s = 3 and c = 0.75 they happen to give the same six rules. If an exam asks "what is the support of a rule on these slides", quote the slide (support of the left side); when you compute rules, follow Slides 17–18: find frequent itemsets first.

Common mistake: two meanings of the letter c

On Slides 16 and 18, c is the confidence threshold, but "c" is also the item coke in the baskets, and "c=4/6" on Slide 18 means "confidence = 4/6". Read each c from its context. This guide writes the item as c inside baskets and rules and the threshold as c = 0.75 with its value.

Step 1 and Step 2 (Slide 17)

Lecture 4 · Slide 17

Slide 17 splits the problem into two steps:

  1. Step 1: find all frequent itemsets I ("we will explain this next": the rest of Lecture 4).
  2. Step 2: rule generation. For every subset A of I, generate the rule A → I \ A (where "\" means "set minus": everything in I except A). Compute its confidence and output the rules above the confidence threshold.
Formula (Slide 17)

confidence(A, B → C, D) = support(A, B, C, D)support(A, B)

General form: conf(A → I \ A) = support(I) / support(A). Here A, B, C, D are individual items: the left side is {A, B}, the right side {C, D}, and their union is the frequent itemset I.

The two sub-bullets under Step 2 explain why this step is cheap:

  • "Since I is frequent, A is also frequent." Every basket that contains I also contains A, so support(A) ≥ support(I) ≥ s. This is monotonicity again. It means the denominator support(A) was already counted in Step 1 (when all frequent itemsets and their counts were found).
  • "Single pass to compute the rule confidence." Our reading: at most one extra pass over the data is needed to fetch any count that is missing; no repeated searching is required. In the worked example (Quiz L4-Q3) every needed count is already in the Step 1 table, so no extra pass is needed.

How many rules to try? From a frequent itemset of size k there are 2k − 2 candidate rules (every non-empty proper subset can be the left side): 2 rules for a pair (A → B and B → A), 6 for a triple, 14 for a set of 4.

Slide erratum

(1) "For every subset A of I" should read "every non-empty proper subset": A = ∅ or A = I gives meaningless rules. (2) The letters A, B, C, D in the formula are items, while A in "A → I \ A" is a set: do not mix them. (3) The right side may now hold several items, a generalisation of Slide 10's single j.

Beyond the slides: pruning idea

The Stanford CS246 slides this lecture is adapted from add a shortcut that this slide omits: if A,B,C → D fails the confidence test, then so does A,B → C,D. The numerator support(A,B,C,D) is the same, but the denominator support(A,B) can only be as large or larger than support(A,B,C), so the confidence can only drop. You can see it on Slide 18: b,c → m has 3/5, and moving c to the right gives b → c,m with 3/6, which is lower.

Why the hard part is Step 1

Step 2 divides numbers that Step 1 already produced. Step 1 must count how often every candidate itemset occurs in a huge file, and the number of candidate itemsets grows explosively with basket size. That is why A-Priori, PCY and SON exist.

Final answer for the Slide 18 data

Exactly six rules pass: b → c, c → b, m → b, b,m → c, c,m → b, j → c. Slide 18 shows only three of them as kept (b → c, m → b, b,m → c) and hides the other three behind "…".

Slide erratum / what the slide leaves out

(1) The "…" hides three accepted rules (c → b, c,m → b, j → c), so do not copy the slide's list as the complete answer to "find all rules". (2) The three red strike-throughs are the only sign that a rule failed; the slide never says why (confidence below 0.75). (3) The frequent-itemset list omits single items, which are frequent here too, because rules need at least two items. (4) "c=4/6" uses c for confidence while "b→c" uses c for coke.

Exam tip

Organise rule generation by itemset: for each frequent set of size ≥ 2, list every split into left and right side, write support(I) / support(left) with the actual numbers, then compare with the threshold using "≥". Check the boundary case b,m → c: 3/4 = 0.75 passes. Quiz L4-Q3 gives the full, step-by-step version.

Common mistakes
  • Dividing by support(I) − or by the right side's support − instead of by the support of the left side.
  • Forgetting the reverse direction: each pair gives two rules, a triple gives six.
  • Rejecting a rule with confidence exactly equal to the threshold (the condition is ≥).
  • Skipping single-item left sides such as b → c,m (the left side may be one item with a two-item right side).

Try it yourself first: for the Slide 18 baskets with s = 3 and c = 0.75, find all frequent itemsets and all rules that pass, before opening the solution.

Quiz L4-Q3Generating association rules from frequent itemsets Lecture 4 · Slides 16–18
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 18 — Example. Eight baskets over the items m (milk), c (coke), p (pepsi), b (beer), j (juice) and one extra item n that occurs only once. (Careful: this is not exactly the data of Slides 9–15 — here B3 = {m, c, b, n}.)

B1{m, c, b}B2{m, p, j}
B3{m, c, b, n}B4{c, j}
B5{m, p, b}B6{m, c, b, j}
B7{c, b, j}B8{b, c}

Support threshold s = 3 baskets; confidence threshold c = 0.75. Task (Slides 16–17): find all association rules with support ≥ s and confidence ≥ c — Step 1: frequent itemsets; Step 2: for every subset A of a frequent itemset I generate the rule A → I \ A and output those above the confidence threshold.

(a) Step 1. Find all frequent itemsets and give their support counts.
(b) Step 2. For every frequent itemset I of size ≥ 2, generate every rule A → I \ A and compute its confidence.
(c) List the rules whose confidence is ≥ 0.75.
(d) Explain why every subset A of a frequent itemset I is itself frequent, and why the confidences therefore need only supports that were already computed in Step 1.

The parts (a)–(d) are our split of Slides 16–18. The slide itself prints only the start of the answer: its frequent itemsets of size ≥ 2 and six of the rules, the last line being “…”. The complete answer is worked out below.

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Picture a supermarket. Step 1 asks: which groups of products are bought together often enough to matter (here: in at least 3 of the 8 baskets)? Step 2 takes each such group, say {beer, coke}, and asks the question in both directions: “of the baskets that contain beer, what fraction also contain coke?” and “of the baskets that contain coke, what fraction also contain beer?”. Each answer is a fraction, the confidence. We keep a rule only if its fraction is at least 3/4. The expensive part is Step 1 (Slide 16: “Hard part: finding the frequent itemsets!”); once it is done, Step 2 is just dividing numbers we already have.

Formulas used (Lecture 4 · Slides 8, 10, 16, 17)

Support of an itemset S: support(S) = number of baskets that contain every item of S (Slide 8). Frequent means support ≥ s = 3.

Confidence of a rule A → B (Slides 10 and 17): conf(A → B) = support(A ∪ B)support(A). For a rule cut out of a frequent itemset I we have B = I \ A, so A ∪ B = I and conf(A → I \ A) = support(I)support(A). The left side goes in the denominator. Keep the rule if conf ≥ 0.75 (“≥”: exactly 0.75 passes).

Number of rules from an itemset of size k: 2k − 2 (every non-empty, proper subset A of I is a left side).

  1. Plan: the two-step recipe of Slide 17. Step 1 = find all frequent itemsets I, counting level by level (single items, then pairs, then triples …). Step 2 = for each such I cut it into a left side A and a right side I \ A, compute the confidence and keep the rule if it is ≥ 0.75. Why this order: first find which item sets occur often (support), then ask how reliable each “if … then …” is (confidence). Notation warning: on Slide 18 the letter c means both the item “coke” and the confidence threshold; here the item is written c and the threshold “0.75”.
  2. Part (a), Step 1a — count every single item. Tick each item in each basket (✓), then add up the row. We need these counts twice: to find the frequent items and, later, as denominators of confidences. Why: an item that is in fewer than 3 baskets can never be part of a frequent set (justified in the part (d) step below), so we can ignore it from now on.

So only the 4 frequent items need to be paired: C(4,2) = 6 pairs. (The other 9 pairs contain n or p and have support at most 2 — e.g. {m, p} is only in B2 and B5 — so they are infrequent anyway.)

So the search stops: no frequent itemset has size 4. (Beyond the slides: this “count only what could still be frequent” idea is the A-Priori algorithm that Slides 30–31 explain later; with 8 baskets we simply did it by hand.)

  6. Part (d) — why every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent (placed here because Step 2 relies on it). Let I be frequent, so support(I) ≥ s, and let A ⊆ I. A basket that contains all items of I automatically contains all items of A, because the items of A are among those of I. Hence the set of baskets that contain I is a subset of the set of baskets that contain A, and therefore
    support(A) ≥ support(I) ≥ s
    so A is frequent too (Slide 17: “Since I is frequent, A is also frequent”; Slide 30: monotonicity). Concrete check: {b,c,m} is in B1, B3, B6; its subset {b,m} is in B1, B3, B5, B6 — all three baskets reappear, plus B5 — so 4 ≥ 3. (The same argument read backwards says: an item or set with support below s can never be inside a frequent set, which is why p and n could be dropped.)
    Consequence for Step 2 (no new counting). Step 1 produces a table of every frequent itemset with its count (the table above). For a rule A → I \ A from a frequent I, the numerator support(I) is in the table because I is frequent, and the denominator support(A) is in the table because A is frequent by the argument above. So computing a confidence is one table look-up and one division (Slide 17 calls this a “single pass”). Two bonus facts: support(A) ≥ support(I) means every confidence is ≤ 1, and support(A) ≥ s ≥ 1 means we never divide by zero. Also, the rule’s own support (= support of its left side, Slide 16) is support(A) ≥ 3, so every rule cut from a frequent itemset already meets the support requirement; only the confidence test can reject a rule.

An itemset of size k gives 2k − 2 rules: every subset A except the empty set (a rule with nothing on the left says nothing) and I itself (nothing left to predict). The single items give no rules. Count: four pairs × 2 rules + one triple × 6 rules = 8 + 6 = 14 rules. A pair {x, y} gives x → y and y → x (two different rules with different denominators). The triple {b,c,m} gives three rules with one item on the left (b → c,m, c → b,m, m → b,c) and three with two items on the left (b,c → m, b,m → c, c,m → b).

The same idea gives a pruning rule: a smaller left side has a larger or equal support, so its confidence can only be lower or equal. Hence if b,c → m fails (3/5 = 0.6), then b → c,m and c → b,m (left sides inside {b,c}) must fail too, with no need to test them; conversely, moving items from the right side to the left side can only raise the confidence (c → b,m has 1/2, but c,m → b has 3/3 = 1). On an exam still write the fraction for every rule you consider, because each computed confidence is a mark.
Common mistake
  • Wrong denominator or direction. b → m and m → b share the numerator 4 but have different denominators (support of b = 6, of m = 5): 4/6 = 0.67 fails, 4/5 = 0.80 passes. Always divide by the support of the left side, never by the right side or by 8.
  • Dropping the boundary. 0.75 ≥ 0.75, so j → c and b,m → c are kept.
  • Stopping at the slide. The slide’s “…” hides three more valid rules: c → b (5/6), j → c (3/4) and c,m → b (3/3).
  • Using the counts of Slides 9–15. There B3 = {m, b}, so {b,m} → c had confidence 2/4 on Slide 13, and {c,m} and {b,c,m} had support 2 (not frequent). On Slide 18, B3 = {m, c, b, n}: confidence 3/4, and both sets have support 3.
  • Forgetting cases. Only itemsets of size ≥ 2 give rules; the left side must be a non-empty proper subset; every such subset (not just single items) must be tried; and do not leave out a rule just because its reverse failed.
Exam tip

Layout that earns marks: (i) a table of all frequent itemsets with counts; (ii) for each itemset, write down its 2k − 2 rules; (iii) show every confidence as a fraction support(I)/support(A) before the decimal; (iv) state the threshold test explicitly; (v) list the surviving rules at the end. Even if one count is wrong, the method marks remain.

Bonus (not asked on Slide 18) — are the six rules “interesting”?

Slide 11: Interest(I → j) = conf − Pr[j], where Pr[j] is the fraction of baskets containing j (all six rules have a single item on the right, so the definition applies); interesting rules are usually above 0.5. Passing the confidence filter does not make a rule interesting: b and c each occur in 6 of the 8 baskets, so even a confidence of 0.75 is no better than the baseline 6/8 = 0.75.

c → b5/6 ≈ 0.8336/8 = 0.750.08 (1/12)no
m → b4/5 = 0.86/8 = 0.750.05 (1/20)no
j → c3/4 = 0.756/8 = 0.750.00 (0)no
b,m → c3/4 = 0.756/8 = 0.750.00 (0)no
c,m → b3/3 = 16/8 = 0.750.25 (1/4)no

All six interest values are far below 0.5: the confidences are high mostly because b and c are in 75 % of all baskets anyway.

Final answer —
(a) Frequent itemsets (s = 3): size 1: {b}:6, {c}:6, {m}:5, {j}:4; size 2: {b,c}:5, {b,m}:4, {c,j}:3, {c,m}:3; size 3: {b,c,m}:3; none of size 4 (9 in all).
(b) 14 rules: {b,m}: b→m 4/6, m→b 4/5; {b,c}: b→c 5/6, c→b 5/6; {c,m}: c→m 3/6, m→c 3/5; {c,j}: c→j 3/6, j→c 3/4; {b,c,m}: b→c,m 3/6, c→b,m 3/6, m→b,c 3/5, b,c→m 3/5, b,m→c 3/4, c,m→b 3/3.
(c) The 6 rules with confidence ≥ 0.75: b → c (5/6 ≈ 0.83), c → b (5/6 ≈ 0.83), m → b (4/5 = 0.80), j → c (3/4 = 0.75), b,m → c (3/4 = 0.75), c,m → b (3/3 = 1). The other 8 fail.
(d) Every basket containing I also contains each subset A, so support(A) ≥ support(I) ≥ s; hence A is frequent, was counted in Step 1, and conf = support(I)/support(A) uses only stored counts.
Where the marks come from: (1) support counts of the single items, the rule “frequent = support ≥ 3”, dropping n and p; (2) the pair counts and the four frequent pairs (bc 5, bm 4, cj 3, cm 3); (3) the triple {b,c,m} = 3 and the statement that nothing larger is frequent; (4) the complete list of frequent itemsets with counts; (5) the formula conf(A → I \ A) = support(I)/support(A) with the left side in the denominator; (6) listing all 14 rules (2 per pair, 6 for the triple, both directions); (7) each correct confidence (the individual fractions are the marks if you slip somewhere); (8) the comparison with 0.75 including the boundary case, and the final list of six rules; (9) the part (d) explanation: baskets containing I ⊆ baskets containing A, so support(A) ≥ support(I) ≥ s, and the confidence reuses stored counts. (The course has published no rubric; this is the natural split.)
Slide erratum

No numerical error: every frequent itemset and every rule confidence printed on Slide 18 is correct. Three wording or completeness points: (1) Slide 17 says “for every subset A of I”; read literally this includes A = ∅ and A = I, which are not rules. The correct statement is “every non-empty proper subset A of I”. (2) Slide 18 lists only the frequent itemsets of size ≥ 2 (singletons are omitted although their counts are needed as denominators) and shows only 6 of the 14 rules, hiding the rest behind “…”; the crossing-out is not explained on the slide (it marks the rules with confidence below 0.75). (3) Slide 16 defines the support of a rule as the support of its left side. Beyond the slides: many textbooks use the support of the whole itemset I instead. Here it makes no difference: a rule with support(A) ≥ 3 and confidence ≥ 0.75 has support(I) ≥ 0.75 × 3 = 2.25, hence ≥ 3 because supports are whole numbers; all six rules also have support(I) ≥ 3.

Slide check: matches the slide’s answer. Slide 18’s frequent itemsets of size ≥ 2 are exactly ours. Its printed rules b → m 4/6, b → c 5/6, b,c → m 3/5, m → b 4/5, b,m → c 3/4, b → c,m 3/6 all agree with the table; the three crossed out (b → m, b,c → m, b → c,m) are below 0.75. The slide is incomplete rather than wrong: its “…” hides 8 rules, among them three more that qualify (c → b 5/6, j → c 3/4, c,m → b 3/3), so the full answer has 6 rules, not the 3 uncrossed ones visible. See the Slide erratum box above for wording points.
Quick recap of Slides 1–18
  • Model: items and baskets (small sets drawn from a big catalogue); input is a TID table, output is if-then rules. Applications: store layout, tie-in sales, recommendations, plagiarism (baskets = sentences, items = documents), drug side-effects (baskets = patients).
  • Support of an itemset = number of baskets containing all its items; frequent = support ≥ s.
  • Confidence of I → j = support(I ∪ {j}) / support(I); it is asymmetric.
  • Interest = conf − Pr[j]; removes the effect of a popular right-hand item. Example: {m,b} → c has conf 1/2, interest −1/8, not interesting.
  • Problem: find all rules with support ≥ s and confidence ≥ c. The slide defines rule support as the support of the left side; the textbook uses the whole itemset.
  • Recipe: Step 1 find frequent itemsets (the hard part); Step 2 for every non-empty proper subset A of each frequent I, test A → I \ A with conf = support(I) / support(A). Monotonicity guarantees support(A) is known.

How frequent itemsets are found at scale: the computation model

Lecture 4 · Slides 19–22

Slide 19 is a black divider titled "Finding Frequent Itemsets" (it has no printed number). Everything before it said what we want: itemsets that occur in at least s baskets, and the association rules built from them. From here to slide 28 the lecture asks how to find them when the data are huge. Before any algorithm, it fixes three things: where the data live, what a computation costs, and what is scarce.

Where the data live: flat files, basket by basket

Lecture 4 · Slide 20

Beginner intuition

Picture a very long roll of till receipts. Each receipt (basket) is short, but the roll is kilometres long and sits in a warehouse (the disk), not on your desk. You can only read it from one end to the other. To find which pairs of products appear on many receipts, you must walk along the roll, and for each receipt write down every pair of products printed on it.

Definition: flat file

A plain file on disk with no index and no database structure. Here it stores the baskets one after another ("basket-by-basket"); each basket is a short list of items, and every item is a positive integer (Milk = 1, Beer = 2, ... on the slide; the names are only for human readers). Integers matter because they can later be used as array positions (Slides 25–27).

The slide's key points:

  • Baskets are small (a handful of items), but there are many baskets and many different items.
  • As each basket is read, expand it into pairs, triples, ... The slide says to use nested loops to generate all sets of size k: two loops for pairs, three for triples, k loops for k-sets.
  • Green note: "We want to find frequent itemsets. To find them, we have to count them. To count them, we have to generate them." Counting and generating are the same bottleneck.
Worked example: how many pairs does a scan generate? Lecture 4 · Slide 20

A basket with m items contains m(m−1)/2 pairs (choose 2 of m). Basket 1 has 5 items: 5·4/2 = 10. Basket 2 has 3 items: 3·2/2 = 3. Basket 3 has 4 items: 4·3/2 = 6. Total: 10 + 3 + 6 = 19 pair-occurrences. The pair {Milk, Beer} = {1,2} occurs in all three baskets, so its count is 3. Because ids are sorted inside a basket, "smaller id first" generates each pair exactly once.

Slide erratum (minor)

The green caption under the figure, "Items are positive integers,", ends in a comma and is cut off. Beyond the slides: the original Stanford CS246 slide continues "and boundaries between baskets are −1"; here the thick horizontal lines in the figure play that role.

What a computation costs: passes over the data

Lecture 4 · Slide 21

Because the baskets sit on disk, and disk is far slower than memory, the real cost of mining disk-resident data is usually the number of disk I/Os (input/output operations). In practice, frequent-itemset algorithms read the data in passes.

Definition: pass

One sequential reading of the whole file, all baskets read in turn from first to last. Cost of an algorithm = number of passes it makes over the data. Fewer passes means a faster algorithm.

So the yardstick is "how many times do I have to read the file?", not "how many CPU operations?". Beyond the slides: whole-file sequential reads are far cheaper than random access, and CPU work on in-memory counters is cheap compared with disk reads, which is why this simple model works. Preview of what follows: A-Priori reads the file once per itemset size (two passes to get the frequent pairs); PCY also needs two passes for pairs but keeps fewer pair counters; SON needs two passes in total for all sizes.

What is scarce: main memory

Lecture 4 · Slide 22

For many frequent-itemset algorithms, main memory is the critical resource. While scanning, you must keep a counter for each itemset you are counting (for example, each pair). All those counters must sit in RAM at the same time, so memory limits how many different things you can count in one pass.

The slide asks: "Swapping in/out is a disaster (why?)" and leaves the answer to you.

Answer: why swapping is a disaster

If the counters do not fit in RAM, the operating system moves memory pages to and from disk ("swapping" or "paging"). Every basket increments counters at essentially random places, so almost every increment lands on a page that is currently on disk. Each such access costs milliseconds instead of about a hundred nanoseconds (thousands of times slower; this is called thrashing). In the worst case you pay one disk access for every pair occurrence, and the run time explodes. Design rule: count only as many things per pass as fit in memory, even if that costs extra passes.

Why frequent pairs are the hard part

Lecture 4 · Slide 23

Slide 23: "The hardest problem often turns out to be finding the frequent pairs of items {i1, i2}", followed by two "Why?" prompts: "Freq. pairs are common, freq. triples are rare" and "Probability of being frequent drops exponentially with size". The slide then says: concentrate on pairs first, then extend to larger sets.

  • Single items are few and cheap: one counter per item.
  • Pairs are the first level where the candidate space is huge (about n²/2 possible pairs) and many pairs really are frequent, so the counters strain memory.
  • Triples and larger are much rarer. For a k-set to be frequent, all k items must appear together in at least s baskets, and the more items you demand, the less likely that is.
Worked example: why the probability drops exponentially Lecture 4 · Slide 23

Beyond the slides, a toy model. Suppose each item appears in a random basket with probability p = 0.01 (1 %), independently. A pair appears together with probability about p² = 10−4; a triple about p³ = 10−6; a 4-set about 10−8. Each extra item multiplies the probability by 0.01: exponential decay in the size k (pk).

Common mistake

"Drops exponentially" is a heuristic about typical data, not a theorem. With strongly correlated items (for example, always-bought-together bundles) large frequent itemsets can exist. Also, do not say pairs are hard because they are "complicated": they are hard because there are so many of them to count in memory. The slide gives only the assertion; the memory argument is on Slides 24–27.

Beyond the slides: a triple can only be frequent if all three of its sub-pairs are frequent, so once the frequent pairs are known the triples to count are few. That is the idea of A-Priori (Slide 30).

Counting pairs in memory: the naive algorithm

Lecture 4 · Slides 24–28

The naive algorithm and its memory bill

Lecture 4 · Slide 24

Naive approach: read the file once; keep in main memory one counter for each possible pair; from each basket generate its pairs by two nested loops and add 1 to each pair's counter. With n items there are n(n−1)/2 possible pairs ({i,j} is the same as {j,i}, and an item is not paired with itself, hence not n²).

When the naive algorithm fails

It fails if (#items)² exceeds main memory. The slide reminds you that #items can be 100K (Wal-Mart) or 10B (Web pages).

Worked example: 105 items, 4-byte counters Lecture 4 · Slide 24
  1. Pairs: 105(105−1)/2 = 4,999,950,000 ≈ 5 × 109.
  2. Memory: 4 bytes × 4,999,950,000 = 19,999,800,000 bytes ≈ 20 GB (decimal gigabytes).
  3. That is more than a typical machine's RAM, so swapping (Slide 22) would follow.
  4. For 10B = 1010 items (our calculation): pairs ≈ 5 × 1019, memory ≈ 2 × 1020 bytes (200 exabytes): hopeless.

Memory grows with the square of the number of items: ten times more items means a hundred times more memory. The slide's rule "(#items)² exceeds memory" is a rule of thumb; the exact need is 4·n(n−1)/2 ≈ 2n² bytes.

Two ways to store the counters

Lecture 4 · Slides 25–27

Approach 1: triangular matrixApproach 2: triples [i, j, c]
What is storedOne counter for every possible pair {i,j} with i < j, in a flat array; the position of the cell tells you which pair it is.One record [i, j, c] ("the count of the pair {i,j} is c") for each pair that actually occurred (count > 0).
Bytes4 bytes per pair, for all n(n−1)/2 pairs, occurring or not.About 12 bytes per occurring pair (three 4-byte numbers); pairs that never occur cost nothing.
Total4·T, fixed, where T = n(n−1)/2.12·O, where O = number of distinct pairs that occur.
Extra needsItem ids must be 1..n with no gaps.A lookup structure (for example a hash table) to find a pair's record quickly.
Break-even rule (Slide 27)

Approach 2 is smaller when 12·O < 4·T ⇔ O < T/3. Triples beat the triangular matrix only if fewer than 1/3 of the possible pairs actually occur.

Worked example: the 1/3 rule with the Slide 24 numbers Lecture 4 · Slides 24–27

T = 4,999,950,000 ≈ 5 × 109; T/3 ≈ 1.67 × 109. Matrix: always 4·T ≈ 20 GB. Triples: if 109 distinct pairs occur, 12 × 109 = 12 GB (better); if 3 × 109 occur, 36 GB (worse). Real baskets are small, so usually far fewer than a third of all pairs occur, and triples win, but see Slide 28.

Slide erratum (omission): "matrix" means triangular matrix

Slide 25 says only "matrix", but "4 bytes per pair" holds only for a triangular matrix (each pair {i,j} stored once, i < j). A full n × n matrix stores every pair twice plus the diagonal, about 8 bytes per pair. Beyond the slides: with items numbered 1..n, the pair (i, j), i < j, goes to cell k = (i − 1)(n − i/2) + j − i of a one-dimensional array of n(n−1)/2 cells. For n = 4: (1,2)→1, (1,4)→3, (2,3)→4, (3,4)→6. The 12 bytes of Approach 2 also ignore the overhead of the lookup structure.

"Can we do better?"

Lecture 4 · Slide 28

Slide 28 states the problem: "Problem is if we have too many items so the pairs do not fit into memory. Can we do better?" Both storage schemes need memory proportional to the number of possible (or occurring) pairs, so with 105 items or more the one-pass naive algorithm fails. The answer, starting at Slide 29, is A-Priori: it avoids counting most pairs at the price of an extra pass.

Quick recap: Slides 19–28
  • Data: flat file on disk, basket by basket, items are positive integers; generate pairs/triples with nested loops. To find frequent sets you count them; to count them you generate them.
  • Cost = number of passes (disk I/Os). Critical resource = main memory; swapping is a disaster (random increments cause a disk access each).
  • Pairs are the bottleneck: frequent pairs are common, frequent triples rare (probability drops exponentially with size).
  • Naive: n(n−1)/2 counters; 105 items need about 5 × 109 counters = 20 GB. Triangular matrix = 4 bytes per possible pair; triples = 12 bytes per occurring pair; triples win only if fewer than 1/3 of the pairs occur.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution and answer the memory questions, the "why?" prompts of Slides 21–23, and the 1/3 break-even.

Quiz L4-Q4Memory needed to count pairs: matrix vs triples Lecture 4 · Slides 20–28
Question (as on the slides)

Slides 20–28 (“Itemsets: Computation Model”, “Computation Model”, “Main-Memory Bottleneck”, “Finding Frequent Pairs”, “Naïve Algorithm”, “Counting Pairs in Memory”, “Comparing the 2 Approaches” and two “Comparing the two approaches” slides) build up one story. They contain one calculation and several “why?” prompts. In the order they appear:

  • Slide 20. The data sit on disk in a flat file, stored basket by basket; items are positive integers. The picture shows three baskets, {Milk 1, Beer 2, Fanta 3, Diaper 4, Butter 5}, {Milk 1, Beer 2, Bread 6} and {Milk 1, Beer 2, Sprite 7, Mustard 8}, followed by “Etc.”. Baskets are small, but there are many baskets and many items. As baskets are read they are expanded into pairs, triples, etc. with nested loops. Slide note: “We want to find frequent itemsets. To find them, we have to count them. To count them, we have to generate them.”
  • Slide 21. The true cost of mining disk-resident data is usually the number of disk I/Os. Algorithms read the data in passes (all baskets read in turn). “We measure the cost by the number of passes an algorithm makes over the data.”
  • Slide 22. For many frequent-itemset algorithms main memory is the critical resource: we need to count something (e.g. occurrences of pairs of items) and the number of different things we can count is limited by main memory. “Swapping in/out is a disaster (why?)”.
