  • Slide 24 (naïve algorithm). Read the file once, counting in main memory the occurrences of each of the n(n−1)/2 possible pairs (generate each basket’s pairs with two nested loops). Fails if (#items)² exceeds main memory; #items can be 100K (Wal-Mart) or 10B (Web pages). Suppose 105 items and 4-byte integer counts: number of pairs 105(105−1)/2 = 5×109; therefore 20 gigabytes of memory are needed.
  • Slides 25–27 (two approaches). Approach 1: count all pairs using a matrix (a triangular matrix, 4 bytes per pair). Approach 2: keep triples [i, j, c] = “the count of the pair of items {i, j} is c”; if integers and item ids are 4 bytes we need approximately 12 bytes for each pair with count > 0. Slide 27: Approach 2 beats Approach 1 if less than 1/3 of the possible pairs actually occur. (Slide 26 is a picture only: a triangle labelled “4 bytes per pair” next to a triangle with a few dots labelled “12 per occurring pair”.)
  • Slide 28. “Problem is if we have too many items so the pairs do not fit into memory. Can we do better?”
(a) Naïve counting (slide 24). For n items, how many possible pairs are there? How much main memory does the naïve algorithm need for n = 105 items with 4-byte counts? (Slide answer: 5×109 pairs, 20 GB.)
(b) Matrix vs triples (slides 25–27). Write the memory needed by Approach 1 (triangular matrix) and by Approach 2 (triples). Show why Approach 2 wins only when fewer than 1/3 of the possible pairs occur, and evaluate both for 105 items.
(c) The “why?” questions (slides 21–23). Explain (i) why the cost is measured in passes over the data; (ii) why main memory is the bottleneck and why swapping in/out is a disaster; (iii) why finding frequent pairs is the hardest part, i.e. why frequent pairs are common but frequent triples are rare.
(d) Slide 28. “Can we do better?” What does the lecture do next?
(e) Practice (our own, not on the slides). Repeat (a) and (b) for n = 20,000 items; say which approach needs less memory if 30 million, and if 100 million, distinct pairs occur; and find the largest number of items whose triangular matrix of 4-byte counts fits in 8 GB.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Imagine n students and you want to know, for every two students, how many days they sat together. You need one tally box per pair of students, and the number of pairs grows with the square of the number of students (100 students: 4,950 pairs; 1,000 students: 499,500 pairs). In a data-mining run the “students” are items, the “days” are baskets and the tally boxes must live in main memory (RAM, random-access memory), because we add 1 to some box every time we see a pair — billions of times.

Approach 1 is a printed table with a pre-made box for every pair: boxes are small (4 bytes) and the box’s position tells you which pair it is, but boxes for pairs that never sit together are wasted. Approach 2 is a notebook where you write a line “student i, student j, count” only when a pair really occurs: a line is bigger (three numbers, 12 bytes, because you must write down who the pair is), but pairs that never occur cost nothing. Which is smaller depends on how many pairs actually occur — the break-even is exactly one third.

Formulas used in this quiz

Number of possible pairs: N = n(n−1)/2 = C(n, 2).   Approach 1 memory: 4 × N bytes.   Approach 2 memory: 12 × x bytes, where x = number of distinct pairs that occur at least once (0 ≤ x ≤ N).   Break-even: 12x = 4N ↔ x = N/3.   Units: 1 GB = 109 bytes, 1 TB = 1012, 1 EB = 1018 (the slide’s “20 gigabytes” uses decimal GB).

Part (a) — the naïve algorithm needs 20 GB for 105 items (slide 24)

  1. Formula / idea — count the possible pairs: a pair is an unordered set {i, j} of two different items. There are n choices for the first item and n−1 for the second, so n(n−1) ordered pairs; but {i, j} and {j, i} are the same pair, so every pair was counted twice and we divide by 2: N = n(n−1)/2. Why we need it: the naïve algorithm reads each basket once, generates all its pairs with two nested loops, and adds 1 to a counter for each pair. Before it knows which pairs will occur, it must keep one counter for every possible pair, all in main memory. So the number of counters is N.
  2. Substitute n = 105: N = 105 × (105 − 1)/2 = 100,000 × 99,999 / 2 = 4,999,950,000 ≈ 5×109 (the slide rounds because 105−1 ≈ 105, and 105 × 105 / 2 = 5×109).
  3. Convert counters to bytes: memory = (number of counters) × (bytes per counter) = 4,999,950,000 × 4 = 19,999,800,000 bytes ≈ 2×1010 bytes = about 20 GB. Why ×4: the question says counts are 4-byte integers. (In binary units, 1 GiB = 230 bytes, it is 18.6 GiB; either way it is far more than the 8–16 GB of RAM of a typical machine — Beyond the slides: typical RAM sizes.) So the naïve algorithm fails (slide 24).
  4. See how fast it grows: memory = 4 × n(n−1)/2 = 2n(n−1) ≈ 2n² bytes. It grows with the square of the number of items: 10 times more items means 100 times more memory (this is the slide’s “(#items)² exceeds main memory”; the slide drops the constant 2). All values below were computed with Python:
    Items nPairs n(n−1)/2Memory at 4 bytes per pair
    10,000 (104)49,995,000 ≈ 5×107≈ 0.2 GB
    50,0001,249,975,000 ≈ 1.25×109≈ 5 GB
    100,000 (105, Wal-Mart, slide 24)4,999,950,000 ≈ 5×109≈ 20 GB
    1,000,000 (106)499,999,500,000 ≈ 5×1011≈ 2,000 GB = 2 TB
    1010 (Web pages, slide 24)≈ 5×1019≈ 2×1020 bytes = 200 EB
Common mistake

(1) Forgetting the “÷ 2”: using n² pairs gives 40 GB instead of 20 GB. (2) Forgetting “× 4 bytes”: answering “5×109” for the memory (that is the number of counters, not bytes). (3) Writing n(n−1)/2 but then using 105 × 105 without the 1/2.

Part (b) — triangular matrix (Approach 1) versus triples (Approach 2) (slides 25–27)

  1. Approach 1 — triangular matrix (4 bytes per possible pair): a table with one 4-byte counter per pair. We keep only the cells with i < j, because {i, j} = {j, i} and {i, i} is not a pair. A full square n × n table would store every pair twice plus a useless diagonal: for n = 105 that is 4n² = 40 GB, twice as much. Memory = 4 × N = 4 × n(n−1)/2 bytes — the same for every dataset, even if most pairs never occur. The counter’s position tells us which pair it belongs to, so no item ids are stored. Items are positive integers (slide 20), so they can be used directly as positions.
    Not examined — how the triangle is stored (understand, don’t memorise)

    Beyond the slides: with items numbered 1…n, the triangle is stored as one long array and the pair {i, j}, i < j, sits at position k = (i−1)(n − i/2) + j − i. For n = 5 the ten pairs {1,2}, {1,3}, {1,4}, {1,5}, {2,3}, …, {4,5} land in positions 1, 2, …, 10 without gaps (checked with Python).

  2. Approach 2 — triples [i, j, c] (12 bytes per occurring pair): there is now no fixed position, so each entry must say which pair it is. We store the item id i (4 bytes), the item id j (4 bytes) and the count c (4 bytes): 3 × 4 = 12 bytes per entry. An entry is created only when a pair is seen for the first time (so every stored count satisfies c > 0); pairs that never occur take no space. Let x = the number of distinct pairs that occur in the data. Memory = 12 × x bytes. It depends on the data. (The slide says “approximately”: a real program also needs a lookup structure such as a hash table to find the entry of a pair, which adds overhead.)
  3. Compare — derive the 1/3 rule: Approach 2 is smaller exactly when 12x < 4N. Divide both sides by 12: x < 4N/12 = N/3. Divide by N: x/N < 1/3. So Approach 2 beats Approach 1 if fewer than 1/3 of the possible pairs actually occur (slide 27); at exactly x = N/3 the two use the same memory, and above 1/3 the matrix wins. The threshold 1/3 does not depend on n: it is just the ratio 4 : 12 of the entry sizes.
  4. Evaluate for n = 105: N = 4,999,950,000. Approach 1 = 4 × 4,999,950,000 = 19,999,800,000 bytes ≈ 20 GB (fixed). Break-even x = N/3 = 1,666,650,000 ≈ 1.67×109 pairs, where Approach 2 also needs 12 × 1,666,650,000 = 19,999,800,000 bytes ≈ 20 GB. Other cases (Python):
    Share of pairs that occurOccurring pairs xApproach 2 = 12xApproach 1 = 4NSmaller
    1%49,999,5000.6 GB20 GBtriples
    10%499,995,0006.0 GB20 GBtriples
    20%999,990,00012.0 GB20 GBtriples
    1/3 (≈ 33.3%)1,666,650,00020.0 GB20 GBtie
    50%2,499,975,00030.0 GB20 GBmatrix
    100%4,999,950,00060.0 GB20 GBmatrix (triples 3× worse)
  5. Two sanity checks on when each approach wins (Practice, our own numbers). (1) Toy case from the slide-20 baskets. The three baskets {1,2,3,4,5}, {1,2,6}, {1,2,7,8} use items 1–8, so n = 8 and N = 8 × 7 / 2 = 28. They make 10 + 3 + 6 = 19 pair increments, but only x = 17 distinct pairs, because {1,2} (Milk, Beer) occurs in all three baskets and ends with count 3. Matrix = 4 × 28 = 112 B; triples = 12 × 17 = 204 B. Here x/N = 17/28 ≈ 61% > 1/3, so the matrix is smaller, as the rule predicts (the file continues with “Etc.” on the slide, so this is a toy only). (2) Realistic scale. Baskets are small, so x is limited by the pairs the baskets contain. 106 baskets of 10 items give at most 106 × C(10, 2) = 106 × 45 = 4.5×107 distinct pairs, i.e. at most 0.9% of the 5×109 possible pairs, so the triples need at most 12 × 4.5×107 = 540 MB instead of 20 GB. So on sparse data Approach 2 wins; on dense data (many pairs occur) the matrix wins.
Exam tip

To answer “when is Approach 2 better?” write the one-line inequality and then simplify: 12x < 4 · n(n−1)/2 ⇒ x < n(n−1)/6 ⇒ fewer than one third of all pairs. State the two per-entry sizes (4 B vs 12 B = three 4-byte numbers) first; that alone usually earns a mark. Always quote the slide numbers: 5×109 pairs and 20 GB for 105 items.

Common mistake

(1) Saying “triples are always 3 times worse (12 vs 4 bytes)”: the 12 bytes are paid only for pairs that occur, the 4 bytes for all possible pairs. (2) Mixing up x (pairs that occur) and N (pairs that could occur), or turning the inequality round: triples win when x is less than N/3. (3) Forgetting units (bytes vs GB). (4) Forgetting that the matrix cost is the same whatever the data.

Part (c) — the “why?” questions (slides 21–23)

(c)(i) Why the cost is measured in passes (slide 21)

  1. The data live on disk: the file of baskets is huge (gigabytes to terabytes) and cannot be held in main memory, so it stays on disk. Moving data from disk is far slower than computing on data already in RAM, so the time is dominated by disk I/Os (I/O = input/output, i.e. disk reads and writes), not by arithmetic. That is the slide’s statement: “the true cost of mining disk-resident data is usually the number of disk I/Os”.
  2. The data are read in passes: the efficient way to use a disk is to read it in order, big block after big block. One pass = reading all baskets once, in turn, from the first to the last. Every extra pass re-reads the entire file. Beyond the slides: an illustration, order of magnitude only. A 1 TB file read sequentially at 100 MB/s takes 1012 / (100×106) = 10,000 s ≈ 2.8 hours per pass.
  3. So we count passes: total I/O ≈ (number of passes) × (cost of one read of the file). What happens inside a pass — expanding a basket into pairs and adding 1 to counters in RAM — is cheap by comparison. Counting passes is simple and does not depend on the particular machine. Slide 21: “We measure the cost by the number of passes an algorithm makes over the data.”
  4. It is a trade-off with memory: the naïve algorithm uses 1 pass but needs 20 GB (part (a)); A-Priori uses 2 passes but far less memory (slide 30). Algorithms often spend an extra pass to save memory.

(c)(ii) Why main memory is the bottleneck, and why swapping is a disaster (slide 22)

  1. We must count while reading: as every basket is read we update counters (“occurrences of pairs of items”). An update (add 1) is fast only if the counter is in main memory. The number of counters we can keep is therefore (RAM size) ÷ (bytes per counter) — “the number of different things we can count is limited by main memory”. Part (a) showed that the table of pair counters needs about 2n² bytes, which quickly exceeds RAM.
  2. What swapping is: if the table is larger than RAM, the operating system keeps only some pages of it in RAM and parks the rest on disk (virtual memory). When the program touches a page that is not in RAM, the page must first be read from disk (a page fault) and often another page must be written out to make room.
  3. Why it is a disaster — (A) no locality: the pairs of one basket land in scattered cells of the table, and the next basket hits other scattered cells. The updates jump around the whole table at random, so a page just loaded is rarely used again soon. Illustration (our own numbers): with a 20 GB table and 4 GB of RAM, if updates were spread evenly, only about 1/5 of the table is in RAM at any moment, so about 4 of every 5 updates wait for the disk (Figure L4-Q4-3).
  4. (B) Disk is about 105 times slower than RAM per access (Beyond the slides: typical orders of magnitude for a hard disk, RAM ≈ 100 ns, random disk access ≈ 10 ms: 10 ms / 100 ns = 105). A solid-state drive (SSD) is faster, roughly 100 μs per random access, i.e. still 103 times slower than RAM; the conclusion does not change.
  5. (C) There are billions of updates. A basket of k items makes k(k−1)/2 pair updates. Illustration (our own numbers): 108 baskets of 10 items give 108 × 45 = 4.5×109 updates:
    SituationTime per updateTotal time for 4.5×109 updates
    Every counter is in RAM100 ns450 s = 7.5 minutes
    Every update goes to disk (worst case, hard disk)10 ms4.5×107 s ≈ 521 days ≈ 1.4 years
    80% of updates go to disk (20 GB table, 4 GB RAM)mixedstill ≈ 417 days
    Every update goes to an SSD100 μs4.5×105 s ≈ 5.2 days
    The machine spends its time moving pages instead of counting (thrashing). Moreover these are random I/Os, which the “number of passes” measure of slide 21 does not even see, so swapping silently ruins the cost model.
  6. The cure: design the algorithm so that every counter fits in RAM — use less memory per count (Approach 2 when few pairs occur) or count fewer things (A-Priori, slide 30) — even if it costs another pass.

(c)(iii) Why frequent pairs are the hard problem (slide 23)

  1. What the slide claims: “Freq. pairs are common, freq. triples are rare” because “probability of being frequent drops exponentially with size”. Frequent means support ≥ s: the set must appear together in at least s baskets.
  2. Why frequent sets get rarer as they grow: every extra item is an extra condition that a basket must satisfy. Beyond the slides: an illustration that assumes items are independent (real data are not exactly independent). If an item is in 10% of the baskets, a given pair is in about 0.1² = 1% of them, a triple in 0.1³ = 0.1%, a 4-set in 0.01%. Each added item multiplies by the same factor, so the chance falls exponentially with the size. Real data are correlated, so the decrease is slower, but the trend is the same.
  3. Monotonicity makes it a chain: if an itemset is frequent then every subset of it is frequent too (slide 30). So a frequent triple can only be built from frequent pairs, and a frequent pair only from frequent items: pairs are the necessary stepping stone to everything larger.
  4. Check on a real example — the 8 baskets of slide 18 with s = 3 (we counted them with Python; slide 18 lists the frequent itemsets of size 2 and 3):
    SizePossible sets (6 items)Sets that occur at least onceFrequent sets (support ≥ 3)Share of possible sets that are frequent
    1 (items)664: m, c, b, j4/6 ≈ 67%
    2 (pairs)15124: {b,m} {b,c} {c,m} {c,j}4/15 ≈ 27%
    3 (triples)2091: {m,c,b}1/20 = 5%
    415200%
    The share of possible sets that are frequent falls 67% → 27% → 5% → 0% as the size grows, as the slide says (the exponential drop is much clearer on large data; with only 8 baskets the numbers are tiny).
  5. Why that makes pairs the memory bottleneck: before any counting we cannot know which pairs will turn out frequent, so a naïve counter must be ready for all N = n(n−1)/2 pairs — 5×109 for 105 items. Single items are cheap: 105 counters × 4 B = 400 KB, about 50,000 times less than the 20 GB for pairs (slide 31: pass 1 needs “memory proportional to #items”). For triples and larger sets, monotonicity lets us count only sets whose smaller subsets are all frequent, and by step 2 there are few of those. (Counting every triple naïvely would be far worse: C(105, 3) ≈ 1.67×1014 counters, about 667 TB at 4 bytes — so the saving from pruning is essential.) Hence the pair-counting table is the largest table the algorithm has to hold, and slide 23 concludes: “Let’s first concentrate on pairs, then extend to larger sets.”
Key idea

Three facts, one story. (1) Only passes over the disk-resident file are charged (slide 21). (2) Everything that is counted must fit in RAM, otherwise swapping makes the run impossibly slow (slide 22). (3) The thing that threatens to overflow RAM is the table of pair counters, which grows like n² (slides 23–24). The two ways of storing it (matrix 4 B per possible pair, triples 12 B per occurring pair) only shift the problem by a constant factor, so we need a smarter algorithm (A-Priori, slide 30).

Part (d) — “Can we do better?” (slide 28)

  1. The problem: both approaches break down when there are too many items: the matrix needs 4N bytes (2 TB for 106 items, 200 EB for 1010, part (a)), and the triples may need up to 12N if many pairs occur. Counting every possible pair is simply too much.
  2. The answer the lecture gives: the two-pass A-Priori algorithm (Lecture 4 · Slides 30–33). It uses monotonicity (slide 30): if item i does not appear in s baskets, then no pair containing i can appear in s baskets. Pass 1 counts the individual items (memory proportional to #items) and finds the frequent items; pass 2 counts only pairs whose two items are both frequent (memory proportional to the square of the number of frequent items only; slide 31).
  3. The trade-off: one extra pass over the data buys a much smaller counting table. Slide 33 then reuses the triangular-matrix idea of this quiz with n = number of frequent items, after re-numbering the frequent items 1, 2, … .

Part (e) — Practice: n = 20,000 items (our own item count, not from the slides)

  1. Possible pairs: N = n(n−1)/2 = 20,000 × 19,999 / 2 = 199,990,000 ≈ 2×108.
  2. Approach 1 (matrix): 4 × 199,990,000 = 799,960,000 bytes ≈ 0.8 GB (800 MB), whatever the data.
  3. Break-even for Approach 2: x < N/3 = 66,663,333.3, i.e. at most 66,663,333 pairs (≈ 6.67×107, 1/3 of all pairs); at that point 12 × 66,663,333 = 799,959,996 bytes ≈ 0.8 GB, the same as the matrix.
  4. Scenarios (Python):
    Occurring pairs xShare of NTriples = 12xMatrixSmaller
    19,999,00010%239,988,000 B ≈ 0.24 GB≈ 0.8 GBtriples (3.3× smaller)
    30,000,00015%360,000,000 B = 0.36 GB≈ 0.8 GBtriples (55% less memory)
    66,663,3331/3799,959,996 B ≈ 0.8 GB≈ 0.8 GBtie
    100,000,000≈ 50%1,200,000,000 B = 1.2 GB≈ 0.8 GBmatrix (triples 1.5× larger)
    So with 30 million occurring pairs the triples need less memory; with 100 million the matrix does.
  5. Largest n whose triangular matrix fits in 8 GB: need 4 × n(n−1)/2 = 2n(n−1) ≤ 8×109 ⇒ n(n−1) ≤ 4×109 ⇒ n ≈ √(4×109) ≈ 63,246. Check with Python: n = 63,246 needs 7,999,986,540 bytes ≤ 8×109, but n = 63,247 needs 8,000,239,524 bytes > 8×109. So 63,246 items. Sanity check by scaling: memory grows like n², and 20 GB corresponds to 105 items, so 8 GB corresponds to 105 × √(8/20) ≈ 63,246 ✓. (If “8 GB” means 8 GiB = 233 bytes, the answer is exactly n = 65,536 = 216.)
Final answer:
(a) Number of pairs = n(n−1)/2. For n = 105: 4,999,950,000 ≈ 5×109 pairs × 4 bytes ≈ 2×1010 bytes = 20 GB (grows like 2n²).
(b) Triangular matrix = 4 bytes × n(n−1)/2 (fixed; 20 GB for 105 items). Triples = 12 bytes × x, with x = number of occurring pairs. 12x < 4·n(n−1)/2 ↔ x < n(n−1)/6, so triples win only if fewer than 1/3 of the possible pairs occur (for 105 items: x < 1.67×109; at 10% occurring 6 GB, at 50% 30 GB, at 100% 60 GB).
(c)(i) Cost = number of passes: the file is on disk, disk I/O dominates, and one pass reads every basket once, sequentially.
(c)(ii) Counters must fit in RAM; if swapped, almost every random update needs a disk access (about 105 times slower than RAM, times billions of updates), so the run thrashes.
(c)(iii) Pairs are the bottleneck: there are n(n−1)/2 of them to count (5×109 for 105 items), while the chance of being frequent drops exponentially with set size (monotonicity), so far fewer triples and larger sets need counting.
(d) It leads to the two-pass A-Priori algorithm (slides 30–33): pass 1 finds the frequent items, pass 2 counts only pairs of frequent items; one extra pass to save memory.
(e) n = 20,000: 199,990,000 pairs; matrix ≈ 0.8 GB; break-even x ≈ 6.67×107 pairs (1/3); 30 million occurring pairs: triples 0.36 GB win; 100 million: triples 1.2 GB lose; largest n that fits 8 GB = 63,246.
Where the marks come from: (1) formula n(n−1)/2 for the number of pairs, with the reason (÷2 because {i,j} = {j,i}); (2) substitution to 5×109; (3) ×4 bytes to reach 20 GB, with units; (4) triangular matrix = 4 bytes per possible pair, triples [i, j, c] = 3 × 4 = 12 bytes per occurring pair; (5) the inequality 12x < 4·n(n−1)/2 and the conclusion “fewer than 1/3 of the possible pairs”; (6) the passes argument: data on disk, disk I/O dominates, a pass = one sequential read of all baskets; (7) main memory limits what can be counted; swapping means random accesses to disk (very slow) for billions of updates; (8) pairs are hardest: n(n−1)/2 candidates, and frequency drops exponentially with set size (monotonicity), so triples are rare; (9) slide 28 leads to the two-pass A-Priori algorithm that counts only pairs of frequent items; (10) the practice numbers (199,990,000 pairs, 0.8 GB, 1/3 threshold, 63,246 items).
Slide check: matches the slide’s answers — 105(105−1)/2 = 4.99995×109 ≈ 5×109 pairs, 19.9998 GB ≈ 20 GB, 4 bytes vs 12 bytes, break-even 1/3 (all verified with Python). No numerical erratum. Omissions and loose wording on the slides (none changes an answer): (i) slide 24’s “fails if (#items)² exceeds main memory” is shorthand — the exact need is 2n(n−1) bytes, the constant 2 is dropped; (ii) slide 25 says “count all pairs using a matrix” before slides 26–27 make it a triangular matrix, and “4 bytes per pair” means per possible pair; (iii) slide 25’s “approximately 12 bytes” ignores the lookup-structure (hash table) overhead of a real implementation, which would lower the 1/3 threshold a little; (iv) slides 22 and 23 pose “why?” but print no answer — the answers above are standard course background (textbook Mining of Massive Datasets, Chapter 6), with the order-of-magnitude timings marked “Beyond the slides”; (v) slide 20’s last line “Items are positive integers,” is cut off on the slide (Beyond the slides: the usual version continues “and boundaries between baskets are −1”); this does not affect any answer.

The A-Priori algorithm

Lecture 4 · Slides 29–36

Slide 29 is another black divider ("A-Priori Algorithm", no printed number). Slides 30–36 give the algorithm for pairs, then for all itemset sizes. The name is Latin for "from what comes before": use what you already know about smaller sets to decide what to count among bigger ones.

The key idea: monotonicity and its contrapositive

Lecture 4 · Slide 30

Beginner intuition

A band cannot fill a stadium more often than any single member fills a stadium. In the same way, a bundle of products cannot be bought together more often than each product is bought at all. So if a product is rarely bought, every bundle containing it is rarely bought, and you can stop worrying about all of those bundles.

Definition: monotonicity (Slide 30)

If a set of items I appears at least s times, so does every subset J of I.

Contrapositive for pairs (the form you actually use)

If item i does not appear in s baskets, then no pair including i can appear in s baskets. (Read "s baskets" as "at least s baskets", as in the first statement.) The same holds for any set that contains an infrequent subset.

Why it is true: every basket containing I also contains each subset J of it, so support(J) ≥ support(I). Support can only go down as sets grow.

Worked example: monotonicity on the Slide 9 baskets (s = 3) Lecture 4 · Slides 9, 30

Slide 9's baskets: B1={m,c,b}, B2={m,p,j}, B3={m,b}, B4={c,j}, B5={m,p,b}, B6={m,c,b,j}, B7={c,b,j}, B8={b,c}. Item p appears only in B2 and B5: support 2 < 3. So {p,m}, {p,b}, {p,j}, {p,m,b}, ... cannot reach 3 and need never be counted. (Check: support{m,p} = 2.)

Slide erratum (wording)

Slide 30 calls A-Priori a "two-pass approach". That is true for finding frequent pairs. For larger itemsets A-Priori needs one pass per itemset size (Slide 36).

Pass 1 and Pass 2

Lecture 4 · Slides 31–32

  1. Pass 1. Read the baskets and count the occurrences of each individual item. Memory needed: proportional to the number of items (one counter per item).
  2. Between passes. Items with count ≥ s are the frequent items. Keep a list of them; drop the item counters.
  3. Pass 2. Read the baskets again. For each basket, keep only its frequent items, generate all pairs among them, and add 1 to each pair's counter. These pairs are the candidate pairs: both elements are frequent. Memory needed: proportional to the square of the number of frequent items (counters), plus the list of frequent items so that you can test membership.
  4. End. Pairs whose counter is ≥ s are the frequent pairs.
Slide erratum (omission)

"Memory proportional to square of frequent items" means the square of the number of frequent items. The slide also never states the final filter after Pass 2 (keep pairs with count ≥ s); it appears on Slide 34.

Slide 32's picture carries two messages: Pass 2 needs far more memory than Pass 1, and Pass 1 leaves most of memory empty (PCY will use that, Slide 38).

Detail: triangular matrix and renumbering

Lecture 4 · Slide 33

Slide 33: you can use the triangular-matrix method with n = number of frequent items (note: here n no longer means all items, as on Slide 24). This may save space compared with storing triples. The catch: a triangular matrix needs items numbered 1..n with no gaps, but frequent items keep their original ids (say 5, 17, 903, 12004).

Trick (Slide 33)

Re-number the frequent items 1, 2, ... and keep a table relating the new numbers to the original ("Old item #s" in the figure). Then the triangular array has only n(n−1)/2 cells for the frequent items.

Worked example: the saving Lecture 4 · Slide 33

Beyond the slides, illustrative numbers. With 105 items the naive matrix needs about 20 GB (Slide 24). If only 104 items are frequent: 104(104−1)/2 = 49,995,000 pairs × 4 bytes ≈ 200 MB. With 1000 frequent items: 4 × 1000·999/2 = 1,998,000 bytes ≈ 2 MB. If instead all 106 items were numbered: about 2 × 1012 bytes (2 TB).

General k: candidates Ck and frequent sets Lk

Lecture 4 · Slides 34–35

Definition: Ck and Lk (Slide 34)

Ck = the candidate k-itemsets: those that might be frequent (support ≥ s) based on information from the pass for k−1. Lk = the set of truly frequent k-itemsets (the slide says "k-tuples"; they are sets).

Common mistake

A candidate has not been shown to be frequent; it only means no subset has been ruled out. Counting decides. Frequent means support ≥ s, not > s (the slide draws "≥" as an underlined ">").

C1 is all items; counting them (Filter) gives L1, the frequent items. Construct forms C2 = all pairs of items from L1. A second Filter counts those pairs and keeps the ones reaching s (L2). Slide 34 marks the second Construct "To be explained"; Slide 35 explains it.

Worked example: the hypothetical steps of Slide 35 Lecture 4 · Slide 35
StepSetSize
C1{b} {c} {j} {m} {n} {p}6
count, prune non-frequentL1 = {b, c, j, m} (n and p dropped)4
generate C2{b,c} {b,j} {b,m} {c,j} {c,m} {j,m} (all pairs of L1)6

The callout on the slide (green "**") says: generate Ck from Lk−1 and L1, i.e. take each frequent pair and add one frequent item. {b,m}+c = {b,m,c}; {b,m}+j = {b,m,j}; {b,c}+j = {b,c,j}; {c,m}+j = {c,m,j}. The other extensions ({b,c}+m, {c,m}+b, {c,j}+b, {c,j}+m) only repeat triples already listed. This reproduces exactly the slide's four triples (checked by computer).

Slide erratum (omission): the slide's rule over-generates

The slide's rule does not check that every 2-subset of a new triple is frequent. Beyond the slides (standard A-Priori, textbook Mining of Massive Datasets): a triple is a candidate only if all its (k−1)-subsets are in Lk−1. Here {b,m,c} has {b,m}, {b,c}, {c,m} all in L2 and stays; {b,m,j} lacks {b,j} and {m,j}; {b,c,j} lacks {b,j}; {c,m,j} lacks {m,j}. Those three can be pruned before counting, so C3 = {{b,c,m}} and L3 is unchanged. The slide's version is not wrong, only wasteful.

Also, the data are made up: no baskets or threshold are given, so supports cannot be recomputed. With Slide 9's baskets and s = 3, the true frequent pairs are {b,m}, {b,c}, {c,j} ({c,m} has support 2) and there is no frequent triple. Quiz L4-Q5 runs A-Priori with real counts on the Slide 18 baskets.

A-Priori for all frequent itemsets

Lecture 4 · Slide 36

  • One pass for each k (itemset size). Total passes = size of the largest itemset you ask for.
  • Needs room in main memory to count each candidate of the current size.
  • For typical market-basket data and reasonable support (e.g. 1 %), k = 2 requires the most memory: there are very many candidate pairs (quadratic in the number of frequent items), while frequent triples are rare (Slide 23), so from k = 3 on the candidate sets shrink sharply. This is exactly why PCY attacks the Pass 2 memory.
  • Extension: lower the support s as the itemset gets bigger. Big sets are naturally rarer, so a lower threshold keeps interesting large sets from being missed. (Beyond the slides: with a different s per level, monotonicity pruning must be applied carefully, since thresholds differ by level.)
Slide erratum (unit)

"1 %" is a fraction; elsewhere support is an absolute count (Slide 8). s = 1 % of the baskets means s = 0.01 × (number of baskets).

Exam tip

A-Priori answers to know cold: (1) the property used is monotonicity; (2) Pass 1 counts items, Pass 2 counts only pairs of frequent items; (3) memory in Pass 2 is about m(m−1)/2 counters for m frequent items; (4) it needs one pass per itemset size; (5) it is exact: no frequent set is lost, since every discarded set had an infrequent subset.

Try it yourself first: reproduce the whole run C1 → L3 with real counts, then do the integer-basket exercise.

Quiz L4-Q5A-Priori step by step: C1, L1, C2, L2, C3, L3 Lecture 4 · Slides 29–36
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 35 – “Example: Hypothetical steps of the A-Priori algorithm”. The slide runs A-Priori with support threshold s = 3 on the eight baskets of Slide 18 and prints only the sets C1, L1, C2, L2, C3, L3 (no counts, and it does not reprint the baskets). Reproduce the whole run yourself, with the support count of every candidate, and explain why each step is allowed. The baskets (single-letter item names, as on Slide 18):

BasketItemsBasketItems
B1{m, c, b}B2{m, p, j}
B3{m, c, b, n}B4{c, j}

B7{c, b, j}B8{b, c}
(a) Pass 1. Write C1, count the support of every item and give L1.
(b) Pass 2. Construct C2 from L1 (Slide 35 lists 6 pairs), count the support of every candidate pair and give L2.
(c) Pass 3. Construct C3 (Slide 35 note: “generate Ck from Lk-1 and L1”), count the supports and give L3. Practice add-on: which candidates would the monotonicity idea (Slide 30) remove from C3 before counting?
(d) Practice follow-up: what must main memory hold in Pass 1 and in Pass 2 (Slides 31–33), and why may A-Priori ignore the items n and p from Pass 2 onwards?

Slide 35 is a worked example, not a question: parts (a)–(c) restate the slide’s run as a task; the last sentence of (c) and all of (d) are our own Practice questions on Slides 30–33. Careful with the data: here B3 = {m, c, b, n} (Slide 18), whereas Slides 12–15 use B3 = {m, b}. Slide 35 does not reprint the baskets, but its C1 contains n, and only the Slide-18 version of B3 contains n.

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
  1. Tools 1 – support and the threshold. The support of an itemset I is the number of baskets that contain every item of I. With s = 3, an itemset is frequent exactly when support(I) ≥ 3 (Slide 31: “appear ≥ s times”). “At least” matters: a support of exactly 3 is frequent. (Slide 34 prints the symbol as an underlined “>”, which means ≥; the data of Slide 35 confirm it, because {c,j}, {c,m} and {b,c,m} have support exactly 3 and are kept.)
  2. Tools 2 – Ck, Lk and the loop (Slide 34). Ck = the candidates: size-k sets that might be frequent, decided only from the information of the pass for k-1. Lk = the size-k sets that are truly frequent, i.e. the candidates whose counted support is ≥ s. The pipeline of Slide 34 is repeated for k = 1, 2, 3, …: Construct Ck (no data needed) → one pass over all baskets counts every candidate → Filter (keep count ≥ s) → Lk → construct Ck+1 from Lk. For k = 1 the candidates are simply “All items”; C2 = all pairs of items from L1; for C3 the slide only says “To be explained” and gives the footnote of Slide 35 (“generate Ck from Lk-1 and L1”).
  3. Tools 3 – monotonicity (Slide 30). If an itemset I appears in at least s baskets, then every subset J ⊆ I also appears in at least s baskets, because every basket that contains I also contains J: support(J) ≥ support(I). We use the contrapositive: if some subset of I is not frequent, then I cannot be frequent. For pairs (Slide 30): if item i is in fewer than s baskets, no pair containing i can be in s baskets.
    Beginner intuition

    Three friends can have lunch together 3 times only if every two of them have had lunch together at least 3 times (each shared lunch of the three also counts for every pair inside the group). So you never need to check a group of three unless all of its pairs have already passed the test. A-Priori builds bigger groups only from groups that already passed, level by level; the shortlist at each level is Ck, the ones that pass are Lk.

  4. Part (a), Pass 1 – C1 = every item that occurs. Nothing has been learned yet, so every single item is a candidate (Slide 34: “All items” feeds the first Filter). Scanning B1–B8 gives six items:

    C1 = { {b}, {c}, {j}, {m}, {n}, {p} }  (Slide 35, line 1).

  5. Count the support of each item (read the baskets once; keep one counter per item – memory proportional to the number of items, Slide 31). Add 1 to an item’s counter for every basket that contains it:
    ItemBaskets that contain itSupport≥ 3 ?
    bB1, B3, B5, B6, B7, B86yes
    cB1, B3, B4, B6, B7, B86yes
    jB2, B4, B6, B74yes
    mB1, B2, B3, B5, B65yes

    Sanity check: every basket entry is counted once, so the six supports must add up to the total number of items in all baskets: 6 + 6 + 4 + 5 + 1 + 2 = 24 = 3 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 ✓.
  6. Filter → L1 = the items with support ≥ 3. b (6), c (6), m (5) and j (4) pass; n (1) and p (2) fail.

    L1 = { b, c, j, m }  (Slide 35: “Prune non-frequent”).

  7. Why dropping n and p is safe (monotonicity). Any pair containing n occurs only in baskets that contain n, so its support is ≤ support(n) = 1 < 3; any pair containing p has support ≤ 2 < 3. The data confirm it: {b,n}, {c,n}, {m,n}, {b,p}, {j,p} occur once, {m,p} twice, and {c,p}, {j,n}, {n,p} never. The same bound holds for every larger set that contains n or p, so these two items never have to be looked at again.
  8. Part (b), Pass 2 – construct C2 = all pairs of items from L1. With 4 frequent items there are n(n-1)/2 = 4·3/2 = 6 pairs (the pair-counting formula of Slide 24):

    C2 = { {b,c}, {b,j}, {b,m}, {c,j}, {c,m}, {j,m} }  (Slide 35).

    The nine pairs that contain n or p ({b,n}, {b,p}, {c,n}, {c,p}, {j,n}, {j,p}, {m,n}, {m,p}, {n,p}) never get a counter. Without Pass 1 we would have to count all 6·5/2 = 15 pairs of the six items. This is the A-Priori saving.
  9. Count the candidate pairs (second pass over the baskets). For each basket, first ignore the items that are not in L1 (here n and p; the basket itself is not thrown away), then add 1 to every pair of the items that remain (Slide 31: count “only those pairs where both elements are frequent”; the pairs are generated by two nested loops, Slide 20).

  11. Part (c), Pass 3 – construct C3 the way Slide 35 does it. The footnote on the slide says: generate Ck from Lk-1 and L1. So take every frequent pair of L2 and add one frequent item of L1 that it does not contain. Why this reaches every frequent triple: if {x,y,z} is frequent, then by monotonicity {x,y} is in L2 and z is in L1, so the triple is produced from the pair {x,y} plus the item z. A triple can be reached from several pairs, so write each distinct triple once (the order inside a set does not matter):

Beyond the slides – the textbook A-Priori rule (Mining of Massive Datasets): keep a triple in C3 only if all three of its pairs are in L2 (in general: all its (k-1)-subsets are in Lk-1). In an exam write the slide’s 4 candidates and mention the prune (or the other way round); both are acceptable.

  15. When does A-Priori stop? The loop ends when a level has no candidates. Slide 35 stops at L3 and does not say what comes next. Beyond the slides: with the slide’s rule (extend each set of L3 by an item of L1), {b,c,m} + j gives the single candidate C4 = { {b,c,j,m} }. Counting it needs a fourth pass: it occurs only in B6, support 1 < 3, so L4 = ∅ and the algorithm stops after 4 passes. With the textbook prune, {b,c,j,m} is not even a candidate, because three of its four 3-subsets ({b,c,j}, {b,j,m}, {c,j,m}) are not in L3; then C4 = ∅ and 3 passes are enough (Slide 36: “one pass for each k”). Either way L4 = ∅. In total there are 4 + 4 + 1 = 9 frequent itemsets (4 single items, 4 pairs, 1 triple).

  17. Part (d), memory – Pass 1 (Slides 31–32). Main memory holds only the item counters: one per item (6 here), i.e. memory proportional to the number of items. When the pass ends, the counters are reduced to the list of frequent items {b, c, j, m}, and the rest of the memory is idle in Pass 1 (Slide 38 asks whether that idle memory can be used; that is the next topic of the lecture).
  18. Pass 2 memory (Slides 31–32). Main memory holds (i) the list of frequent items – “so you know what must be counted” – and (ii) counters only for pairs of frequent items: memory proportional to the square of the number of frequent items, not of all items. Here that is 6 pair counters instead of 15. Pairs containing n or p get no counter, because by the contrapositive of monotonicity (Slide 30, see “Why dropping n and p is safe” above) they can never reach support 3, so counting them would waste memory and could not change L2.
  19. The triangular-matrix trick (Slide 33) and the byte count. To store the pair counts in a compact triangular matrix, re-number the frequent items 1, 2, 3, … (here b → 1, c → 2, j → 3, m → 4) and keep a small table “new number → old item” (the “Old item #s” box on the slide). The matrix then has n(n-1)/2 = 6 cells for n = 4 frequent items, as in the figure. Slide 33 says this “may save space compared with storing triples” [i, j, count]. With the byte sizes of Slides 24–27 (4-byte counts, 12 bytes per occurring pair in the triples method) the toy numbers are:
    Memory for the pair countersCount all pairs of all 6 itemsA-Priori Pass 2 (4 frequent items)
    Triangular matrix, 4 bytes per possible pair15 × 4 = 60 bytes6 × 4 = 24 bytes
    Triples [i, j, count], 12 bytes per occurring pair12 occurring pairs × 12 = 144 bytes6 occurring pairs × 12 = 72 bytes
    (Slide 27: the triples method wins only if fewer than 1/3 of the possible pairs occur; here 12 of 15 and 6 of 6 occur, so the triangular matrix is the better choice both times.) These numbers are tiny, but the saving is the point for big data: with 105 items Slide 24 needs 5 × 109 pair counters = 20 GB if every pair is counted. A-Priori’s price is an extra pass over the data; its gain is memory.
  20. Cost summary (Slide 36). A-Priori makes one pass for each k (itemset size) and needs room in main memory to count every candidate of Ck (6 counters in Pass 2 here; 4, or 1 with the prune, in Pass 3). For typical market-basket data and a reasonable support (e.g. 1%), k = 2 requires the most memory, which is why Slides 31–33 concentrate on pairs. The slide lists one extension: lower the support s as the itemset gets bigger.
Common mistakes
  • Using > 3 instead of ≥ 3. {c,j}, {c,m} and {b,c,m} have support exactly 3 and are frequent; dropping them gives a wrong L2 and an empty L3.
  • Building C2 from all six items (15 pairs) or putting n or p into any pair: C2 must come from L1 only.
  • Mixing up Ck and Lk. Ck = “might be frequent, not yet counted”; Lk = “counted and passed”. Do not read the 4 triples of C3 as 4 frequent triples.
  • Building Ck+1 from Ck instead of from Lk.
  • Deleting a basket when one of its items is ignored. B3 = {m,c,b,n} still adds bc, bm, cm in Pass 2; it just adds nothing involving n.
  • Using B3 = {m, b} from Slides 12–15 instead of Slide 18’s {m,c,b,n}: that gives c = 5, {b,c} = 4, {c,m} = 2, {b,c,m} = 2, so L3 = ∅ – a different answer.
Exam tip

Lay your work out as the slide does: C1 → counts → L1 → C2 → counts → L2 → C3 → counts → L3. Write the count next to every candidate together with the test “count ≥ 3”, including the failing ones (2, 2, 2, 1, 1, …), and check each pass with a sum (24 for items, 19 for pairs, 7 for triples). If you slip on one count, the steps that are correct given your own earlier numbers can still earn partial credit, but only if the numbers are written down. Always say which pass builds which set: Pass k counts Ck, the Filter gives Lk, the Construct step turns Lk into Ck+1.

Final answer (s = 3): C1 = {b, c, j, m, n, p} with supports b 6, c 6, j 4, m 5, n 1, p 2, so L1 = {b, c, j, m}. C2 = {bc, bj, bm, cj, cm, jm} with supports 5, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, so L2 = {{b,m}, {b,c}, {c,m}, {c,j}}. C3 = {{b,m,c}, {b,m,j}, {b,c,j}, {c,m,j}} (Slide 35 method: L2 + L1) with supports 3, 1, 2, 1, so L3 = {{b,c,m}}; with the textbook monotonicity prune C3 = {{b,m,c}} only, same L3. L4 = ∅ (3 passes with the prune, 4 without). 9 frequent itemsets in total. Memory: Pass 1 = item counters only (6); Pass 2 = list of frequent items + counters only for pairs of frequent items (6 instead of 15); n and p are ignored because, by monotonicity, no pair containing them can reach support 3.
Where the marks come from: (1) Definitions: support = number of baskets containing the set; frequent iff ≥ s = 3 (ties kept); meaning of Ck and Lk; the construct → count → filter loop; monotonicity and its contrapositive. (2) Pass 1: C1 with all six counts (6, 6, 4, 5, 1, 2) and L1 = {b,c,j,m}. (3) C2 = the 6 pairs of L1, justified by monotonicity (no pair with n or p). (4) The six pair counts (5, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2) and L2 with {b,j} and {j,m} dropped. (5) C3 built from L2 and L1 (4 triples) and, if you add it, the “all pairs in L2” prune down to {b,c,m}. (6) The triple counts (3, 1, 2, 1) and L3 = {b,c,m}. (7) Part (d): Pass 1 = item counters; Pass 2 = frequent-item list + counters only for pairs of frequent items (memory ∝ square of the number of frequent items); the re-numbering trick; why n and p are ignored; one pass per k.
Slide check: matches the slide’s answer. Slide 35 prints C1, L1, C2, L2, C3 and L3; every set above is identical (only the order of the elements may differ), and every support count was recomputed by program (the slide prints no counts). No error in the results; slide notes: (i) Slide 35 does not reprint the baskets; they are those of Slide 18, whose B3 differs from Slides 12–15. (ii) The slide’s C3 (4 triples) is not reduced by the monotonicity test; the textbook version would keep only {b,c,m}. Both give the same L3. (iii) Slide 34 leaves the construction of C3 “to be explained”; the only explanation is the one-line footnote of Slide 35, which does not mention the prune. (iv) Slide 34 prints “support > s” with an underlined >, which must be read as ≥ (as on Slide 31).

Quiz L4-Q8A-Priori on integer baskets (threshold 3) Lecture 4 · Slides 78–80
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 78 — “Quiz: Apriori Algorithm”. Compute frequent pairs for the baskets below with the Apriori algorithm. Assume threshold s = 3.

BasketItems
a){1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9}
b){1, 4, 7, 8, 9}
c){1, 2, 5, 9}

Watch out: the letters a)–d) on the slide label the four baskets. They are not four separate sub-questions: there is one question about one data set of 4 baskets. (Slides 79 and 80 show the same slide again with the slide’s answer added step by step: Pass 1 on Slide 79, Pass 2 on Slide 80. We compare with it at the end, so try the question first.)

(a) Pass 1 — count every single item and find the frequent items.
(b) Pass 2 — count only the candidate pairs (both items frequent) and find the frequent pairs. This is what the slide asks for.
(c) Practice (our extension, not on the slides): show that no pair containing item 4 or item 7 is ever counted (the memory saving), then run pass 3: build the candidate triples from the frequent pairs, prune them with monotonicity, count the survivors and list the frequent triples.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Imagine a club that met 4 times, and you want to know which pairs of members turn up together at least 3 times. Before you tally every possible pair of members (there could be millions), ask one cheap question first: did this person even come to 3 meetings? Someone who came to only 2 meetings can never be seen with anybody at 3 meetings, so every pair containing that person can be thrown away without counting it. That is the whole idea of A-Priori: pass 1 asks the cheap question about single items, pass 2 tallies only the pairs made of items that passed the test.

Formulas and rules used in this quiz

Count (support) of an itemset I: the number of baskets that contain every item of I (Slide 8). Frequent: I is frequent ⇔ count(I) ≥ s; here s = 3 and there are 4 baskets, so an itemset must lie in at least 3 of the 4 baskets (Slide 79: “count greater or equal 3”).
Monotonicity (Slide 30): if an itemset appears in at least s baskets, so does every subset of it. Contrapositive for pairs: if item i appears in fewer than s baskets, no pair containing i can appear in s baskets.
A-Priori (Slide 31): pass 1 counts single items and keeps those with count ≥ s. Pass 2 counts only the pairs whose two items are both frequent.
Counting pairs (Slide 24): n items give C(n, 2) = n(n − 1) ÷ 2 pairs; a basket with k items generates C(k, 2) = k(k − 1) ÷ 2 pairs.
Notation (Slide 34): Ck = candidate k-itemsets (might be frequent), Lk = the truly frequent k-itemsets.

Part (a) — Pass 1: count the single items Lecture 4 · Slides 31, 79

  1. Formula / idea: for every item i, count(i) = the number of baskets that contain i. One counter per distinct item, so the memory needed is proportional to the number of items (Slide 31). The items that reach count ≥ 3 form L1, the frequent items.
  2. Read the baskets once and tick the items. One row per basket, one column per item; the column sum is the count of that item. The distinct items in the data are 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 (seven items).

With n = 5 frequent items there are C(5, 2) = 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 candidate pairs (Slide 31: memory proportional to the square of the number of frequent items only). The ten candidates are {1,2}, {1,5}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,5}, {2,8}, {2,9}, {5,8}, {5,9}, {8,9}. A pair is only a candidate: it “might be frequent”. Its real count decides.
