Common mistake

Both items frequent does not mean the pair is frequent. Items 8 and 9 are each frequent (count 3), but {8,9} appears together only in baskets a and b (count 2). The 10 candidate pairs are only the pairs that might be frequent; pass 2 exists to find out which ones really are. The same happens for {2,8}, {2,9}, {5,8} and {5,9}.

Part (c) — Practice: why 4 and 7 are never counted, and pass 3 Lecture 4 · Slides 24–27, 30–36

  1. Idea (monotonicity, Slide 30): if an item appears in fewer than 3 baskets, then every pair containing it appears in fewer than 3 baskets too, because a pair can only be in a basket where each of its items is. Item 4 is in 2 baskets (a, b), so any pair with 4 is in at most 2 baskets. Item 7 is in 2 baskets (b, d), so any pair with 7 is in at most 2 baskets. Hence these pairs cannot be frequent and A-Priori never spends memory on them.
  2. Find the pairs that A-Priori never counts. There are 7 distinct items, so C(7, 2) = 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 pairs exist in principle. Only C(5, 2) = 10 of them have two frequent items. The other 21 − 10 = 11 pairs contain 4 or 7 (or both). Check by counting: 6 pairs contain 4, 6 pairs contain 7, and {4,7} is in both lists, so 6 + 6 − 1 = 11. The figure shows all 21 pairs as cells: green and orange cells get a counter, grey cells do not. The number in brackets in a grey cell is that pair’s true count, computed separately (by program) only to prove that skipping it was safe. The largest is 2, which is below 3, exactly as monotonicity predicts.
  3. Measure the saving on this tiny data set.
    Count every pairA-Priori pass 2
    Pair counters that must exist2110
    Counter increments while reading the 4 baskets (C(6,2) + C(5,2) + C(4,2) + C(5,2) = 15 + 10 + 6 + 10)4125 (10 + 3 + 6 + 6)
    Memory at 4 bytes per counter (triangular-matrix method, Slides 25–27 and 33; the frequent items renumbered 1–5)21 × 4 = 84 bytes10 × 4 = 40 bytes
    More than half of the counters are saved even here. On real data (Slide 24: 105 items give 5 × 109 pairs, about 20 GB) the saving is what makes pass 2 fit in main memory: the number of pairs grows with the square of the number of items, so removing infrequent items shrinks the pair table quadratically. The trick from Slide 33 for the compact triangular matrix: re-number the frequent items 1, 2, 5, 8, 9 as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and keep a table of the old numbers.
  4. Pass 3: build the candidate triples C3. Idea (Slide 35: “generate Ck from Lk−1 and L1”): take each frequent pair and add one frequent item that is not already in it. L2 has 5 pairs and 3 items can be added to each, which gives 15 additions; they collapse to 8 different triples (for example {1,2} + 5 and {1,5} + 2 are the same triple {1,2,5}): {1,2,5}, {1,2,8}, {1,2,9}, {1,5,8}, {1,5,9}, {1,8,9}, {2,5,8}, {2,5,9}. (Of the C(5,3) = 10 triples of frequent items, the two missing ones, {2,8,9} and {5,8,9}, contain no frequent pair at all.)
  5. Prune with monotonicity (Slide 30, applied to triples). If a triple is frequent, all three of its 2-element subsets must be frequent. So look up the three sub-pairs of each candidate in L2 = { {1,2}, {1,5}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,5} } and cross out any triple with a sub-pair that is not there:
    Candidate tripleIts three sub-pairs (✓ = in L2)Verdict
    {1,2,5}{1,2} ✓   {1,5} ✓   {2,5} ✓keep: counted in pass 3
    {1,2,8}{1,2} ✓   {1,8} ✓   {2,8} ✗ (count 2)pruned
    {1,2,9}{1,2} ✓   {1,9} ✓   {2,9} ✗ (count 2)pruned
    {1,5,8}{1,5} ✓   {1,8} ✓   {5,8} ✗ (count 2)pruned
    {1,5,9}{1,5} ✓   {1,9} ✓   {5,9} ✗ (count 2)pruned
    {1,8,9}{1,8} ✓   {1,9} ✓   {8,9} ✗ (count 2)pruned
    {2,5,8}{2,5} ✓   {2,8} ✗   {5,8} ✗pruned
    {2,5,9}{2,5} ✓   {2,9} ✗   {5,9} ✗pruned
    Only C3 = { {1,2,5} } survives. Pass 3 therefore needs just one counter. The candidate list shrinks step by step: 35 possible triples among the 7 items → 10 among the 5 frequent items → 8 that extend a frequent pair → 1 after pruning. Beyond the slides: textbooks call this “all sub-pairs frequent” test the prune step of A-Priori candidate generation, and a textbook-style join that combines only pairs sharing their first item produces 6 candidates ({1,2,5}, {1,2,8}, {1,2,9}, {1,5,8}, {1,5,9}, {1,8,9}); the same pruning leaves the same single survivor. Slide 35’s own example (for instance {b,m,j}) shows only the looser extension step.
  6. Count the survivor. Read the baskets a third time and count the baskets containing 1, 2 and 5 together: basket a {1,2,4,5,8,9} ✓; basket b {1,4,7,8,9} ✗ (no 2, no 5); basket c {1,2,5,9} ✓; basket d {1,2,5,7,8} ✓. Count({1,2,5}) = 3 ≥ 3, so it is frequent: L3 = { {1,2,5} }.
  7. Stop, and check. A candidate 4-itemset needs all four of its 3-element subsets to be frequent, which would need at least four frequent triples; we have only one, so C4 = ∅ and A-Priori stops after 3 passes (one pass per itemset size, Slide 36). Sanity checks by program: (i) the 7 pruned triples really have count 2 (nothing was lost); (ii) no 4-itemset reaches even 3 (the best have count 2); (iii) every subset of {1,2,5} is frequent, as monotonicity demands.
    Frequent itemsets overall: 5 single items + 5 pairs + 1 triple = 11.
Exam tip

Write the answer in the same two-pass layout as the slide: (1) a table of item counts and the list L1; (2) the list of candidate pairs (say how many: C(n, 2)); (3) a table of their counts; (4) L2. Always write the counts, not just the final list, so partial marks are available if one count is wrong. State “frequent means count ≥ 3” once at the top. A neat sentence to earn the “why” mark: “items 4 and 7 occur in only 2 baskets, so by monotonicity no pair containing them can be frequent and they need no counters.”

Common mistakes
  • Treating a)–d) as four sub-questions. They are the four baskets of one data set; the support of an itemset is counted over all four.
  • Using “> 3” instead of “≥ 3”. With “> 3” only item 1 (count 4) would survive pass 1 and no pair at all would be frequent. The slide says “greater or equal 3”.
  • Counting pairs with 4 or 7 in pass 2. The final list of frequent pairs would still be correct, but the point of A-Priori (the memory saving) is lost and the method mark for pass 2 may be lost with it.
  • Listing the 10 candidate pairs as the answer. Candidates are what you count; the answer keeps only those with count ≥ 3, i.e. 5 pairs (see the warning after part (b)).
  • Forgetting a basket while counting pairs, for example missing that basket b contributes {1,8}, {1,9} and {8,9}. Use the sum check (25 increments) to catch this.
  • Treating {1,2} and {2,1} as different pairs. Itemsets are unordered, so each pair is counted once per basket.
Final answer:
Pass 1: counts 1→4, 2→3, 4→2, 5→3, 7→2, 8→3, 9→3. Frequent items L1 = {1, 2, 5, 8, 9} (items 4 and 7 are dropped).
Pass 2: the 10 candidate pairs have counts {1,2} 3, {1,5} 3, {1,8} 3, {1,9} 3, {2,5} 3, {2,8} 2, {2,9} 2, {5,8} 2, {5,9} 2, {8,9} 2. Frequent pairs L2 = {1,2}, {1,5}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,5} (this is the slide’s answer).
Memory saving (practice): the 11 pairs containing 4 or 7 are never counted (10 pair counters instead of 21; 25 increments instead of 41).
Practice, pass 3: C3 = { {1,2,5} } after pruning 7 of the 8 candidate triples; count({1,2,5}) = 3, so L3 = { {1,2,5} }; C4 = ∅, so the algorithm stops. All frequent itemsets for s = 3: 5 single items, 5 pairs, 1 triple (11 in all).
Where the marks come from: (1) state the rule “frequent = count ≥ 3” and the A-Priori idea (monotonicity: an item in fewer than 3 baskets cannot be in a frequent pair); (2) pass 1: correct single-item counts (1:4, 2:3, 4:2, 5:3, 7:2, 8:3, 9:3); (3) L1 = {1, 2, 5, 8, 9}, with 4 and 7 removed; (4) pass 2: use only pairs of frequent items, i.e. the 10 candidates (C(5,2) = 10); (5) correct counts of those pairs (five with 3, five with 2); (6) the final list of five frequent pairs; (7) the memory-saving remark (pairs with 4 or 7 are never counted); (8) for the practice: candidate triples built from L2, pruned by monotonicity to {1,2,5}, counted as 3, and the stop because C4 is empty. The slides give no mark scheme, so this split is our suggestion; a clearly shown method keeps most of the marks even if one count slips.
Slide check: matches the slide’s answer. Slide 79 (pass 1: frequent items 1, 2, 5, 8, 9) and Slide 80 (pass 2: frequent pairs {1,2}, {1,5}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,5}) are exactly what the full computation gives; every number here was recomputed by program. Notes (not errors): the slides print only the final lists, not the counts, so the count tables and the whole of part (c) (memory saving, pass 3) are our additions; the letters a)–d) on Slide 78 are the baskets; Slide 34 describes Ck with “support > s”, while Slides 8, 31 and 79 and this answer use “≥ s” (a minor wording slip on Slide 34).

The PCY (Park-Chen-Yu) algorithm

Lecture 4 · Slides 37–45

Slide 37 is the divider "PCY (Park-Chen-Yu) Algorithm" (no printed number). PCY is named after its three authors, Park, Chen and Yu. It is an improvement of A-Priori that makes Pass 2 smaller by using memory that A-Priori leaves idle in Pass 1.

The observation: idle memory in Pass 1

Lecture 4 · Slide 38

Observation: in Pass 1 of A-Priori most memory is idle: only the individual item counts are stored (compare Figure L4p2-4). Slide 38's question: can we use the idle memory to reduce the memory required in Pass 2? Slides 39–45 answer yes.

Pass 1: hash pairs into buckets, keeping only counts

Lecture 4 · Slides 39–40

Beginner intuition

You cannot give every pair its own tally sheet, so you set out, say, 100 million mailboxes. A fixed rule (the hash function) drops every pair into one mailbox, and the mailbox only keeps a tally of how many pairs were dropped in, not which pairs. Many different pairs share a mailbox. Later, a mailbox whose tally is small proves that none of the pairs in it can be popular.

Definitions (Slide 39)

Hash function h: a fixed rule that maps a pair {i,j} to a bucket number 0 ... B−1; the same pair always lands in the same bucket. Bucket: just a counter (a few bytes, typically a 4-byte integer). Collision: two different pairs in the same bucket. A bucket count is the sum of the counts of all pairs that hash to it.

Pass 1 of PCY: in addition to the item counts, maintain a hash table with as many buckets as fit in memory. For each pair of items in each basket, hash the pair to a bucket and add 1 to that bucket's count. For each bucket, keep just the count, not the actual pairs that hash to the bucket.

Not examined — code (understand, don't memorise)

Slide 40 gives the Pass 1 pseudo-code, explained in words: for each basket, for each item in the basket add 1 to the item's count; then for each pair of items in the basket, hash the pair to a bucket and add 1 to that bucket's count. The last loop is the part marked "New in PCY"; the rest is A-Priori's Pass 1. The slide's note: pairs must be generated from the input file, because the file stores baskets, not pairs. A basket with b items produces b(b−1)/2 pairs: extra CPU work, but no extra disk pass.

Slide erratum (drawing)

On Slide 40 the green curly brace marked "New in PCY" is misaligned: it touches the old line "add 1 to item's count" and stops short of the new line "add 1 to the count for that bucket". The new code is the pair loop and both lines of its body.

Worked example: PCY Pass 1 on the Slide 9 baskets (s = 3) Lecture 4 · Slides 9, 39–40

Beyond the slides, a toy hash with 5 buckets. Number the items b=1, c=2, j=3, m=4, p=5 and use h({i,j}) = (i + j) mod 5. Baskets: B1={m,c,b}, B2={m,p,j}, B3={m,b}, B4={c,j}, B5={m,p,b}, B6={m,c,b,j}, B7={c,b,j}, B8={b,c}. The 8 baskets contain 3+3+1+1+3+6+3+1 = 21 pair-occurrences.

  1. Item counts: b=6, m=5, c=5, j=4, p=2. With s = 3, frequent items = {b, c, j, m}; p is out.
  2. True pair counts: {b,c}=4, {b,m}=4, {c,j}=3, {c,m}=2, {j,m}=2, {b,j}=2, {m,p}=2, {b,p}=1, {j,p}=1.
  3. Hash: bucket 0 gets {b,m} and {c,j} (1+4=5→0, 2+3=5→0); bucket 1 gets {c,m} and {b,p}; bucket 2 gets {j,m}; bucket 3 gets {b,c} and {j,p}; bucket 4 gets {m,p} and {b,j}.
  4. Bucket counts (sum of its pairs): bucket 0 = 4+3 = 7; bucket 1 = 2+1 = 3; bucket 2 = 2; bucket 3 = 4+1 = 5; bucket 4 = 2+2 = 4. Total 21, as expected.

Observations about buckets

Lecture 4 · Slide 41

This slide is the whole logic of PCY. A bucket's count is the sum of the counts of all pairs that share it, so it is at least as large as the count of any single pair in it.

Slide 41 statementWhyExample above
If a bucket contains a frequent pair, the bucket is surely frequent (count ≥ s).bucket count ≥ that pair's count ≥ s.Bucket 0 (7) holds {b,m}=4 and {c,j}=3.
Even without any frequent pair, a bucket can still be frequent (sad face).Many infrequent pairs collide and their counts add up.Bucket 1 = 3 ≥ s, but {c,m}=2 and {b,p}=1 are both infrequent. Bucket 4 = 4, pairs {m,p}=2, {b,j}=2.
For a bucket with total count < s, none of its pairs can be frequent (smiley).Each pair's count ≤ bucket count < s. This is the useful direction.Bucket 2 = 2 < 3: {j,m} is eliminated, even though j and m are both frequent items.

Pairs that hash to such an infrequent bucket "can be eliminated as candidates (even if the pair consists of 2 frequent items)". Pass 2: only count pairs that hash to frequent buckets. No truly frequent pair is ever lost (no false negatives); frequent buckets may only cause some unnecessary counting (false positives). Here a false negative means a truly frequent pair that gets wrongly thrown away, which must never happen, and a false positive means a pair that looks like a candidate but is not frequent, which is harmless because it is simply counted and later discarded; see also Slide 55 in the sampling section.

Between the passes: buckets become a bit-vector

Lecture 4 · Slide 42

  • Replace the buckets by a bit-vector (bitmap): 1 means the bucket count reached the support s (a frequent bucket); 0 means it did not.
  • A 4-byte integer is 4 × 8 = 32 bits, so the bit-vector needs 1/32 of the memory of the counters it replaces (1/32 = 0.03125). For 108 buckets: 400 MB as 4-byte integers, 12.5 MB as bits (illustration, Beyond the slides).
  • Also decide which items are frequent (count ≥ s) and list them for the second pass, exactly as in A-Priori.
Slide erratum (boundary)

Slide 42 says 1 means the count "exceeded" s, which suggests > s. The correct rule, consistent with Slide 41 ("less than s" is eliminated) and the definition of frequent, is count ≥ s: a bucket with count exactly s gets bit 1, because one pair with exactly s occurrences would produce it. Also, "1/32" assumes 4-byte counters.

Pass 2: the candidate-pair test

Lecture 4 · Slide 43

Definition: candidate pair in PCY (Slide 43)

In Pass 2 count all pairs {i, j} that meet both conditions:
1. Both i and j are frequent items (from Pass 1's item counts);
2. The pair {i, j} hashes (with the same hash function as in Pass 1) to a bucket whose bit in the bit-vector is 1 (a frequent bucket).

Both conditions are necessary for the pair to have a chance of being frequent. Each condition can only discard pairs that cannot be frequent, so no truly frequent pair is lost. Pairs that pass are only candidates; their counts still decide. A-Priori uses condition 1 alone, so PCY counts fewer pairs.

Worked example: PCY Pass 2 on the same data Lecture 4 · Slides 41–43
  1. Frequent items: {b, c, j, m}. A-Priori would count all C(4,2) = 6 pairs: bc, bj, bm, cj, cm, jm.
  2. Bit-vector (buckets 0..4) = 1 1 0 1 1. Test each pair's bucket: bc→3 (1) keep; bj→4 (1) keep; bm→0 (1) keep; cj→0 (1) keep; cm→1 (1) keep; jm→2 (0) drop.
  3. PCY counts 5 pairs instead of 6. Their true counts: bc=4, bm=4, cj=3, bj=2, cm=2. Frequent pairs: {b,c}, {b,m}, {c,j}, the same answer as A-Priori.

With only 5 buckets and 21 increments the average bucket count is 4.2, close to s, so pruning is weak. Real PCY uses as many buckets as memory allows (millions), giving small average counts and strong pruning.

Common mistake

Applying only the bucket test. Slide 41 states only the bucket rule, but Slide 43 adds that both items must also be frequent. Also, do not store the pairs themselves in Pass 1: only counts.

Main-memory picture and memory details

Lecture 4 · Slides 44–45

Slide 45 gives two practical points.

  1. Buckets require a few bytes each; the number of buckets is O(main-memory size). A bucket is only a counter and holds no pair identity, so the number of buckets grows in proportion to the memory you have. Use all spare memory for as many buckets as possible: a small average count per bucket gives better pruning.
  2. On the second pass a table of (item, item, count) triples is essential. The surviving candidate pairs are scattered, so the compact triangular matrix (4 bytes per pair) no longer works: the matrix needs a cell for every pair, including the eliminated ones. You must store triples, about 12 bytes per candidate pair.
The 2/3 rule (Slide 45)

The hash table must eliminate approximately 2/3 of the candidate pairs for PCY to beat A-Priori. Reason: let C be the number of A-Priori's candidate pairs (matrix, 4 bytes each = 4C). If PCY keeps a fraction f, it stores 12·f·C bytes (triples). PCY wins when 12f·C < 4C ⇔ f < 1/3: it must keep fewer than one third, i.e. eliminate more than two thirds (the same 1/3 break-even as Slide 27). Check: 12 × (1 − 2/3) = 4 bytes per original candidate pair.

Worked example: the 2/3 rule with numbers Lecture 4 · Slide 45

Beyond the slides, illustrative. A-Priori has C = 109 candidate pairs: matrix 4 × 109 = 4 GB. PCY eliminates 50 %: 5 × 108 pairs × 12 = 6 GB, worse than A-Priori. PCY eliminates 80 %: 2 × 108 × 12 = 2.4 GB, better. The break-even is at 2/3 eliminated (about 3.33 × 108 pairs kept × 12 = 4 GB).

Slide erratum (precision)

"Approx. 2/3" is exact only for 4-byte vs 12-byte sizes, and it ignores the extra memory taken by the bitmap and the frequent-item list, so the correct reading of "to beat A-Priori" is "more than 2/3". The slide does not explain where 2/3 comes from; it is the 12-vs-4 byte ratio.

Quick recap: PCY
  • Pass 1: count items and hash every pair to a bucket counter (counts only).
  • Between: counters → bit-vector (1 = count ≥ s, 1/32 of memory); items → list of frequent items.
  • Pass 2: count a pair only if both items are frequent and its bucket bit is 1; store (i, j, count) triples.
  • Frequent pair ⇒ frequent bucket; frequent bucket ⇏ frequent pair; bucket count < s ⇒ none of its pairs is frequent.
  • Needs to eliminate more than 2/3 of A-Priori's candidates to win.
Exam tip

If asked "why is the hash table converted to a bitmap?" answer: after Pass 1 only the yes/no fact "count ≥ s" matters; a bit replaces a 32-bit counter (1/32 of the memory), freeing memory for the Pass 2 candidate counters. If asked "why can PCY not lose a frequent pair?" answer: a pair's count is at most its bucket's count.

Try it yourself first: explain how the bitmap is used and why the hash map becomes a bitmap.

Quiz L4-Q9PCY: the bitmap — how it is used and why Lecture 4 · Slides 81–82 (theory on Slides 39–45)
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 81 — “Quiz: PCY algorithm” (the slide’s own answer is on Slide 82). PCY = Park–Chen–Yu, the three authors of the algorithm; it is a smarter version of A-Priori for finding frequent pairs.

(a) Describe how the bitmap is used in PCY algorithm.
(b) Why is the hash map in main memory from Pass 1 transformed into a bitmap in PCY algorithm?

The slide also shows a main-memory figure. Pass 1 holds “Item names to integers”, a table 1 … n of “Item counts” and a large “Hash table for bucket counts”. Pass 2 holds “Item names to integers”, a table 1 … n of “Frequent items”, a thin “Bitmap” strip and a “Data structure for counts of pairs”. No numbers are given: this is a pure explain / theory question, so every correct idea you write earns part of the marks. (“Hash map” on the slide means the hash table of bucket counts.)

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition — mailboxes and yes/no flags

A library wants to know which pairs of books are borrowed together at least s times. There are far too many possible pairs to give each one its own tally, so the librarian uses a rule (a hash function) that drops every pair into one of a fixed number of mailboxes and keeps only a tally per mailbox — not the pairs themselves. A mailbox with fewer than s tally marks cannot contain even one pair that reached s, so all pairs of that mailbox are cleared without ever being counted one by one. When the day is over, the tally numbers have done their job: one yes/no flag per mailbox (“could something frequent be in here?”) is all that is needed. That row of flags is the bitmap. A tally needs a whole 32-bit number, a flag needs 1 bit — that is the “1/32”. In the second pass you look at the flag before you give a pair its own counter.

Definition — the words used in this answer
  • Hash function h: a fixed rule that turns a pair {i, j} into a bucket number 0, 1, …, B − 1. The same pair always lands in the same bucket. A bucket is just a counter; different pairs can share a bucket (a collision).
  • Frequent (Slides 8, 31): count ≥ s. A frequent bucket (Slides 42–43) is a bucket whose total count is ≥ s.
  • Bitmap (= bit-vector): one bit per bucket, in bucket order. Candidate pair (Slide 43): a pair that PCY will give a counter to in pass 2.
Formulas and rules used in this quiz

Bucket count (Slides 39–40): count(b) = number of pair-occurrences hashed to bucket b = ∑ count({i, j}) over all distinct pairs with h({i, j}) = b. Hence for every pair: count({i, j}) ≤ count(h({i, j})).
Bitmap (Slide 42): bit[b] = 1 if count(b) ≥ s, otherwise 0.
Candidate pair (Slide 43): {i, j} is counted in pass 2 ↔ (1) i and j are both frequent items and (2) bit[h({i, j})] = 1.
Space (Slides 42, 82): 1 bit ÷ 32 bits (a 4-byte integer) = 132.   Break-even (Slide 45): the hash table must eliminate about 23 of the candidate pairs for PCY to beat A-Priori.

  1. Idea — what problem does the bitmap solve? (Slides 36, 38, 46). Main memory is the bottleneck of frequent-itemset mining (Slide 46). In pass 1 of A-Priori only one counter per item is stored, so most of the memory sits idle (Slide 38), yet pass 2 needs a counter for every pair of frequent items, and for typical market-basket data the case k = 2 needs the most memory (Slide 36). PCY asks: can the idle memory of pass 1 reduce the memory needed in pass 2? Yes: it uses that memory for a hash table of buckets that acts as a cheap pre-filter on pairs, and the bitmap is the compact form in which this pre-filter is carried from pass 1 into pass 2.
  2. Pass 1 of PCY (Slides 39–40). Read every basket once and, for each basket, do two things (Slide 40 shows this as pseudo-code; here it is in words):
    • add 1 to the counter of every item in the basket (exactly as in A-Priori);
    • new in PCY: generate every pair of items of the basket (m items give m(m − 1)/2 pairs, e.g. 6 items give 15 pairs; the pairs are not in the input file, they must be generated), apply h to the pair and add 1 to the counter of that bucket.
    The hash table has “as many buckets as fit in memory”, and for each bucket we keep only the count, never the pairs that hashed there (Slide 39). All pairs are hashed because, during pass 1, we do not yet know which items will turn out to be frequent.
  3. Why a bucket count is useful: three observations (Slide 41). Because a bucket count is the sum of the counts of all pairs in it (see the formula box):
    StatementTrue?Why
    If a bucket contains a frequent pair, the bucket is surely frequent.alwaysBucket count ≥ that pair’s count ≥ s.
    If a bucket is frequent, it contains a frequent pair.not necessarily (the “sad face” on the slide)Several small pairs, each below s, collide and add up to ≥ s. Such a “false-alarm” bucket still gets bit 1.
    If a bucket’s total count is less than s, none of its pairs can be frequent (the “happy face”).alwaysContrapositive of the first row. Those pairs are eliminated as candidates, even if both items are frequent.
    Only the third statement is used to prune, so PCY errs only on the safe side: it may keep a pair that is not frequent, but it never throws away one that is.
  4. Between the passes: build the bitmap (Slide 42). Wait until the last basket of pass 1 has been read (a bucket count can still grow until then), then scan the hash table once and replace it by a bit-vector, one bit per bucket: 1 if count ≥ s (a frequent bucket), 0 if count < s. In the same scan, look through the item counters and write down the list of frequent items (count ≥ s) “for the second pass” (last bullet of Slide 42). The item counters and the 32-bit bucket counters can now be thrown away; only the frequent-item list and the bitmap travel to pass 2. (Slide 42 words the 1-bit as “exceeded the support”; the correct condition is “reached”, count ≥ s — see the erratum box.)
  5. (a) Pass 2 — how the bitmap is used (Slide 43). Read all baskets a second time. For every pair {i, j} in a basket, give it a counter and count it only if it is a candidate pair, i.e. only if both conditions hold:
    1. Condition 1: both i and j are frequent items (look them up in the list of frequent items);
    2. Condition 2: the pair hashes to a bucket whose bit is 1, i.e. compute b = h({i, j}) and test bit[b] = 1 (a frequent bucket). Pass 2 must use the same hash function as pass 1, otherwise the bits would describe different groups of pairs.
    So the bitmap is a constant-time look-up table (“is this pair’s bucket frequent?”) placed in front of the pair counters. A pair that fails either test gets no counter and uses no memory (Figure L4-Q9-1). At the end of pass 2 the counters of the candidates are exact, and the candidates with count ≥ s are the frequent pairs. “Both conditions are necessary for the pair to have a chance of being frequent” (Slide 43): a frequent pair has frequent items (monotonicity, Slide 30) and lies in a frequent bucket (statement 1 of step 3). They are not sufficient: a candidate can still end with a count below s, which is why pass 2 still counts candidates exactly.
  6. (b) Why the pass-1 hash table is turned into a bitmap (Slides 42, 82).
    • Only a yes/no fact is needed. After pass 1 the only question asked about a bucket is “was its count ≥ s?” (the pruning rule is statement 3 of step 3). The exact count is never used again, so one bit is enough and nothing that pass 2 needs is lost.
    • It shrinks the table 32 times. A bucket count is a 4-byte integer = 4 × 8 = 32 bits; its bit replaces it. With B buckets the counts need 32B bits, the bitmap needs B bits: B ÷ 32B = 132 (about 3.1 %; a saving of 31/32 ≈ 96.9 %). Example (our numbers): B = 108 buckets need 108 × 4 bytes = 400 MB as counts, but only 108 bits ÷ 8 = 12.5 MB as a bitmap (400 ÷ 12.5 = 32). The “1/32” assumes 4-byte counts, as on the slide.
    • Memory is the bottleneck, and pass 2 needs the room. In pass 2 main memory must hold the list of frequent items, the bitmap and — the big part — the counters of the candidate pairs (Slide 44). Keeping the full 32-bit table would take 32 times more memory for information that is no longer needed and would steal space from those counters. The freed memory is what lets PCY count pairs that A-Priori could not fit.
    • Why the table can be so large in pass 1 in the first place: the memory is otherwise idle (Slide 38) and a bucket needs only a few bytes, so the number of buckets is O(main-memory size) (Slide 45) — many buckets, few collisions, good pruning. The bitmap then compresses that big table to a size pass 2 can afford. Big table in pass 1 + tiny summary in pass 2 is the whole design.
  7. The memory picture (Slide 44, and the figure on Slide 81). Read it left to right: the item counts of pass 1 become the list of frequent items of pass 2; the big hash table becomes the tiny bitmap; and the space saved holds the counts of candidate pairs. (The figure on Slide 81 also shows a small “Item names to integers” table that turns item names into integers 1 … n so that they can index the arrays; it is present in both passes.) The bitmap is the only thing that carries information about pairs from pass 1 into pass 2.
    A-Priori (Slides 30–33)PCY (Slides 38–45)
    Pass 1count itemscount items and hash every pair into a bucket, counting buckets
    Between passeslist the frequent itemslist the frequent items and turn the bucket counts into a bitmap
    Pass 2: pair {i, j} is counted ifboth items are frequentboth items are frequent and its bucket bit is 1
    Pass 2 counterstriangular matrix possible (Slide 33)(item, item, count) triples are essential (Slide 45)
    Frequent pairs foundexactly the same set (PCY only counts fewer useless pairs)
  8. Memory details: triples and the “2/3” rule (Slide 45).
    • Why (item, item, count) triples are essential. A-Priori counts all pairs of the n frequent items, so it can use the triangular matrix (Slide 33): the slot of {i, j} is computed from i and j, so only the 4-byte count is stored. PCY’s candidates are an irregular subset picked by the hash function. A formula-based array would still reserve a slot for every eliminated pair and save nothing, so PCY stores only the surviving pairs, and each counter must say which pair it belongs to: (item, item, count).
    • Beyond the slides — where “2/3” comes from (4-byte integers). A triple costs 3 × 4 = 12 bytes, a triangular-matrix slot only 4 bytes, so a PCY counter is 3 times as expensive. Let P = number of pairs of frequent items (what A-Priori counts; this is what Slide 45 calls “candidate pairs”) and C = number left after the bitmap. A-Priori needs about 4P bytes, PCY about 12C bytes.
      Formula — when does PCY beat A-Priori?

      12C < 4P ↔ C < P3 ↔ fraction eliminated 1 − CP > 23. This is the slide’s “the hash table must eliminate approx. 2/3 of the candidate pairs for PCY to beat A-Priori”.

      Example: n = 10⁵ frequent items, so P = n(n − 1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10⁹ pairsCandidates leftPass-2 counter memory
      A-Priori, triangular matrix (4 bytes × P)5 × 10⁹≈ 20 GB
      PCY eliminates 0 % (12 bytes × 5 × 10⁹)5 × 10⁹≈ 60 GB (worse)
      PCY eliminates 50 %2.5 × 10⁹≈ 30 GB (worse)
      PCY eliminates 2/3 (break-even)≈ 1.67 × 10⁹≈ 20 GB (equal)
      PCY eliminates 90 %5 × 108≈ 6 GB (better)
  9. Correctness — the bitmap never loses a frequent pair. Suppose {i, j} is truly frequent (count ≥ s). Then i and j each appear in at least s baskets, so both are frequent items (condition 1 holds). Its bucket count is at least the pair’s own count, hence ≥ s, so the bit is 1 (condition 2 holds). So every frequent pair is a candidate: PCY has no false negatives. Candidates that are not frequent (“false alarms”, caused by collisions) are counted exactly in pass 2 and then discarded. The output is therefore exactly the A-Priori result.
Common mistakes
  • “The bit says the pair is frequent.” No. The bit belongs to a bucket: a 1 only says the bucket might contain a frequent pair (nothing is proved), a 0 proves that every pair in it is infrequent.
  • “Frequent bucket ⇒ frequent pair.” Only the opposite holds: frequent pair ⇒ frequent bucket (Slide 41). Collisions can make a bucket frequent with no frequent pair inside (Practice: buckets 0 and 4).
  • Using only one of the two conditions in pass 2. Counting every pair of a frequent bucket would count pairs with infrequent items; counting every pair of frequent items would ignore the bitmap. Slide 43 requires both.
  • Using a different hash function in pass 2; the bit positions only make sense for the function of pass 1.
  • Saying the bitmap stores the counts or the pairs, or “1/32 of the data”. It stores one bit per bucket, and it is 1/32 of the memory of the hash table of counts (32-bit counts → 1-bit flags), not of all main memory.
  • Thinking PCY needs fewer passes or finds different pairs. It still takes two passes for pairs and returns the same frequent pairs as A-Priori; only the memory (the number of counted pairs) changes.
Slide erratum

(1) Wording of the bit rule. Slide 42 says a bit is 1 when the bucket count “exceeded the support s”. Read literally this means count > s, which would wrongly give bit 0 to a bucket whose count equals s exactly, although such a bucket can hold a frequent pair of count exactly s (frequent means ≥ s: Slides 8, 31, 41). The correct rule is bit = 1 if and only if count ≥ s. (2) Shorthand. The last line of Slide 41 (“Pass 2: only count pairs that hash to frequent buckets”) is only half of the rule; the full candidate test has two conditions (Slide 43).

Exam tip

The question has two halves — how the bitmap is used and why it is made — and the slide’s own answer (Slide 82) covers mostly how it is built and the 1/32. For full marks write both halves: Use: built between the passes, 1 = frequent bucket (count ≥ s), and in pass 2 a pair is counted only if both items are frequent and its bucket bit is 1 (same hash function). Why: 32-bit count → 1 bit = 1/32 of the memory, which frees main memory (the bottleneck) for the counts of candidate pairs. Add one line on correctness (a 0 bit proves infrequency, so no frequent pair is lost). Use the exact words “frequent bucket”, “candidate pair” and “same hash function”.

(A poor hash function for real data, chosen because it is easy to evaluate by hand; see the last bullet below.)

What the example shows (tie each point to Slide 41 and Slide 43).

  • The five frequent pairs sit in buckets 1 and 2, whose bits are 1: frequent pair ⇒ frequent bucket.
  • Buckets 0 and 4 have bit 1 although none of their pairs is frequent (5 = 1 + 2 + 2 and 6 = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 are sums of small counts): a frequent bucket need not contain a frequent pair. Bucket 0’s bit lets the false alarms {5,8} and {5,9} through; the pairs of bucket 4 all contain item 4, so condition 1 stops them anyway.
  • Bucket 3 has count 2 < 3, so its only pair {8,9} is dropped even though 8 and 9 are both frequent items (and indeed count({8,9}) = 2).
  • Both conditions are needed. {8,9} passes condition 1 but fails condition 2. Conversely all 11 pairs containing item 4 or item 7 (for instance {1,4}, bucket 1) land in buckets with bit 1, so the bitmap alone would not remove them; condition 1 does.
  • The 2/3 test on this toy. Only 1 of 10 pairs (10 %) was eliminated, far below 2/3. With 4-byte integers A-Priori’s triangular matrix needs 10 × 4 = 40 bytes, PCY’s triples 9 × 12 = 108 bytes (plus 5 bits). So on this tiny input PCY does not win on memory: the example shows the mechanism, not the saving. The reason: 41 pair-occurrences fall into only 5 buckets, an average of 41/5 = 8.2 per bucket, far above s = 3. With the more mixing hash (i + j) mod 5 the bucket counts would be 9, 8, 8, 9, 7, the bitmap 1 1 1 1 1 and nothing would be eliminated. Beyond the slides: PCY pays off when there are so many buckets that most of them receive fewer than s pair-occurrences — which is why the table is made as large as memory allows (Slide 45) and why “halving the number of buckets doubles the average count” is a risk (Slide 49).
Final answer:
(a) How the bitmap is used. In pass 1 PCY counts the items and hashes every pair of every basket to a bucket, adding 1 to the bucket’s counter (counts only, the pairs are not stored). A frequent pair makes its bucket frequent; a frequent bucket need not contain a frequent pair (collisions); a bucket with count < s contains no frequent pair. Between the passes the hash table is summarised as a bitmap: one bit per bucket, 1 if the bucket count is ≥ s (frequent bucket), 0 otherwise, and the frequent items are listed. In pass 2 a pair {i, j} is counted only if it is a candidate: (1) both i and j are frequent items and (2) it hashes (same hash function as pass 1) to a bucket whose bit is 1; both conditions are necessary. A pair in a 0-bit bucket cannot be frequent and is never counted. The candidates are counted exactly, and the result is the same set of frequent pairs as A-Priori. Pass-2 memory = frequent items + bitmap + counts of candidate pairs, stored as (item, item, count) triples, so the bitmap must eliminate about 2/3 of the candidate pairs for PCY to beat A-Priori.
(b) Why a bitmap. Pass 2 needs only the yes/no fact “is the bucket frequent?”, not the count. Each 32-bit (4-byte) integer count is replaced by a single bit, so the bitmap takes 1/32 of the memory of the table of counts. This frees main memory (the bottleneck) for the counters of candidate pairs in pass 2, and nothing needed is lost, because every frequent pair lies in a frequent bucket.
(Practice result, not part of the exam question: with s = 3, 5 buckets and h = (smaller item) mod 5 the bucket counts are 5, 16, 12, 2, 6, the bitmap is 1 1 1 0 1, {8,9} is removed, 9 candidates are counted and the frequent pairs are {1,2}, {1,5}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,5}.)
Where the marks come from (our estimate — the slides give no mark scheme): (1) pass 1 of PCY: item counts plus a hash table of pair counts, counts only and no pairs stored; (2) the observations: frequent pair ⇒ frequent bucket, frequent bucket does not imply a frequent pair, bucket count < s ⇒ none of its pairs is frequent; (3) between the passes: the table becomes a bit-vector, one bit per bucket, 1 = frequent bucket (count ≥ s), 0 = not, plus the list of frequent items; (4) pass 2: count a pair only if both items are frequent and it hashes to a bucket with bit 1, both necessary, same hash function; (5) the memory picture: item counts + hash table in pass 1; frequent items + bitmap + counts of candidate pairs in pass 2; (6) why: 32-bit integer counts become single bits, so 1/32 of the memory; (7) what the saved memory is for: counters of candidate pairs, memory is the bottleneck; (8) extra credit: triples (item, item, count) are essential and the hash table must eliminate about 2/3 of the candidate pairs to beat A-Priori; no frequent pair is lost; a correct small example (bucket counts 5, 16, 12, 2, 6; bitmap 1 1 1 0 1). Points (1)–(2) and (4)–(5) are the “how it is used” half; (3) and (6)–(7) are the “why” half and are what Slide 82 asks for.

The bit is 1 if the bucket is frequent and 0 if not. Thus integers of 32 bits are replaced by single bits, and the bitmap shown in the second pass in the figure takes up only 1/32 of the space that would otherwise be available to store counts.” Everything in it is included above. It does not say how the bitmap is used in pass 2 (the two candidate conditions of Slide 43) nor what the saved memory is for; the answer above adds both, plus the observations (Slide 41), the memory picture (Slide 44) and the triples/“2/3” point (Slide 45). Refinements of PCY: Multistage and Multihash

Lecture 4 · Slides 46–51

PCY's weakness: if there are too many pairs and too few buckets, infrequent pairs collide and make many buckets reach s. Too many pairs then survive Pass 2 and use scarce memory. Both refinements below add a second, independent filter. Slide 46's reminder: memory is the bottleneck, so we limit the number of candidates to be counted.

Multistage: three passes, a second hash function

Lecture 4 · Slides 46–47

Beginner intuition

Airport security with two different sieves in a row. The first sieve (PCY's bitmap) lets some innocent pairs through only because they shared a mailbox with popular pairs. The second sieve re-sorts the survivors into new mailboxes using a different rule. An innocent pair is unlikely to be unlucky twice, so the second sieve catches many of the first sieve's mistakes. The price: one more trip through the data.

Key idea (Slide 46)

After Pass 1 of PCY, rehash the pairs with a different hash function. This requires 3 passes over the data.

  1. Pass 1 (as in PCY): count items; hash every pair into the first hash table. Between passes: items → list of frequent items; first table → Bitmap 1 (B1).
  2. Pass 2: memory holds the frequent items and B1. Read the data again and hash pairs {i,j} into a second hash table with a different (independent) hash function, Hash2. Between passes: second table → Bitmap 2 (B2).
  3. Pass 3: count pair {i,j} iff (a) i and j are both frequent, and (b) {i,j} hashes to a frequent bucket in B1, and (c) {i,j} hashes to a frequent bucket in B2. Memory holds the frequent items, B1, B2 and the counters of the (now fewer) candidate pairs.

Beyond the slides (textbook Mining of Massive Datasets, §6.3.2): in Pass 2 only the pairs that satisfy (a) and (b) are hashed into Hash2. So each Hash2 bucket receives fewer pairs and fewer buckets reach s: that is where the second round of pruning comes from. Slide 47's caption "Hash pairs {i,j} into Hash2" does not say this, and the three conditions in the Pass 3 caption are listed with no "and"; all three must hold (the word "iff").

Multihash: two passes, several tables at once

Lecture 4 · Slides 49–50

Key idea (Slide 49): use several independent hash tables on the first pass. A second opinion without an extra pass: split the spare memory into two (or more) tables, each with its own independent hash function, and hash every pair into every table during the same Pass 1. Between passes make one bitmap per table. In Pass 2, a pair is a candidate only if both items are frequent and the pair hits a frequent bucket in every table. (This Pass 2 rule is not written on Slides 49–50; it is only implied by the figure of Slide 50.)

Risk (Slide 49)

Halving the number of buckets doubles the average count. The total number of pair-increments is fixed, so with half as many buckets per table each bucket gets on average twice as many pairs. "We have to be sure most buckets will still not reach count s." If so, we get a benefit like multistage, but in only 2 passes.

Worked example: halving the buckets Lecture 4 · Slide 49

Beyond the slides, illustrative numbers. 109 pair-increments into 108 buckets: average 109/108 = 10 per bucket. Split the same memory into two tables of 5 × 107 buckets each: average 109/(5 × 107) = 20 per bucket. If s = 100, almost no bucket is frequent either way and the double filter prunes very well. If s = 20, a large fraction of buckets reach s and the filter barely filters.

Rough pruning arithmetic (assumes independence and ignores the shrinking of the second table in multistage): if a fraction f = 0.3 of buckets are frequent, an infrequent pair slips through one table with probability 0.3, through two independent tables with probability 0.3² = 0.09, through three with 0.3³ = 0.027.

Slide erratum (omissions)

Slide 49 claims "a benefit like multistage" without justification: it holds only if most buckets stay below s. Slide 50's connectors from the Item-counts and the First-hash-table boxes start at the same corner and look like one forked line; read them as two separate wedges (item counts → frequent items; each hash table → its bitmap).

Extensions and their limits

Lecture 4 · Slide 51

Either multistage or multihash can use more than two hash functions. Each extension has a cost that limits it:

  • Multistage: diminishing returns, since the bit-vectors eventually consume all of main memory. Every added stage adds another bitmap that must stay in memory for all later passes (and costs another pass, which the slide does not say), crowding out the counters.
  • Multihash: too many hash functions makes all counts ≥ s. Memory is split among more and more tables, so each has fewer buckets and a higher average count; eventually almost every bucket reaches s, every bucket is "frequent", and nothing is filtered. ("All" is true only in the limit; read "most or all".)

So there is an optimum number of hash functions, usually 2 or 3. Slide 52 is a black divider: "Frequent Itemsets in ≤ 2 Passes". All algorithms so far (A-Priori, PCY, multistage, multihash) need about one pass per itemset size or more; the next part (random sampling, SON; Slides 53 onward) reads the data at most twice for all sizes.

Exam tip

Memorise the pattern: PCY = A-Priori + one hash filter; Multistage = more passes, filters in sequence; Multihash = same pass, filters in parallel. Typical questions: "describe the key idea of multistage" (second independent hash of the pairs that survived the first test, third pass counts only pairs passing both bitmaps), "what is the risk of multihash" (halving buckets doubles the average count), "why diminishing returns".

Quick recap: Slides 19–52
  • Cost = passes over the disk-resident basket file; scarce resource = main memory; pairs are the bottleneck.
  • A-Priori: monotonicity; Pass 1 item counts; Pass 2 counts pairs of frequent items; renumber items for the triangular matrix; Ck → Lk one pass per k; k = 2 needs most memory.
  • PCY: hash pairs into bucket counters in Pass 1, bitmap (1/32) between passes, candidate = both frequent and frequent bucket; buckets O(memory); needs to remove more than 2/3.
  • Multistage: 3 passes, second hash function, B1 and B2. Multihash: 2 passes, several tables at once; halving buckets doubles the average count. Limits: bitmaps eat memory; too many tables makes everything frequent.

Try it yourself first: describe the key idea of multistage and compare it with multihash.

Quiz L4-Q10Multistage and Multihash: key ideas Lecture 4 · Slides 83–84 (theory: Slides 46–47, 49–51)
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 83 — “Quiz: Multistage Algorithm”. Describe the key idea behind the multistage algorithm. The slide also shows the textbook picture of main memory in three passes: Pass 1 = “Item names to integers” + a table 1 … n of “Item counts” + one big “Hash table for bucket counts”; Pass 2 = “Item names to integers” + “Frequent items” + a thin “Bitmap 1” + a “Second hash table for bucket counts”; Pass 3 = “Item names to integers” + “Frequent items” + “Bitmap 1” + “Bitmap 2” + a “Data structure for counts of pairs”.

Slide 84 — the slide’s own answer. “The Multistage Algorithm uses additional hash tables to reduce the number of candidate pairs.” (This sentence is the caption of the multistage figure in the textbook.)

No data is given: this is a pure explain / theory question, so the solution is a written answer. (Multistage is an improvement of PCY — Park–Chen–Yu, the three authors — which itself improves A-Priori for finding frequent pairs; s is the support threshold.) The slide’s answer is only a one-line headline, so the solution first gives the full-marks answer (part a). Because an examiner can ask any follow-up on the same slides, it then covers the neighbouring points as parts (b)–(d) (multihash, comparison, diminishing returns — Slides 49–51), and ends with a small Practice run (part e) so you can see the mechanism with real numbers.

(a) Describe the key idea behind the multistage algorithm — what each of its three passes does and which test decides whether a pair gets a counter.
(b) Multihash (Slides 49–50): the same idea in two passes — how it works and what its risk is.
(c) Compare PCY, multistage and multihash in a table (passes, memory, risk, when to use).
(d) Why do more than two stages / hash tables give diminishing returns (Slide 51)?
(e) Practice (our own, not on the slides): run PCY, multistage and multihash by hand on the baskets of Slide 78.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Finding the few really popular pairs among millions of possible pairs is like screening a huge crowd at an airport. PCY is one coarse sieve (the bitmap): it throws away every pair that obviously cannot be popular. But some innocent pairs slip through, simply because they were dropped into the same "mailbox" (bucket) as popular pairs — or because several unpopular pairs shared a mailbox and their tallies added up. Multistage puts a second sieve with a different hole pattern (a different hash function) behind the first one. An innocent pair that slipped through the first sieve only because of its mailbox-mates is very unlikely to have popular mailbox-mates again, so the second sieve catches it. Only the survivors of sieve 1 are poured onto sieve 2 — and you know the survivors only after the first trip through the data is finished — so you need one more trip (a third pass). Multihash puts two smaller sieves side by side in the very first trip: no extra pass, but each sieve is coarser (fewer mailboxes), so more mailboxes look popular.

Facts and formulas used in this quiz

Frequent (Slides 8, 31): an itemset is frequent ⇔ its count ≥ s.   Bucket count (Slides 39–40): count(b) = ∑ of the counts of all pairs hashed to bucket b; hence count({i,j}) ≤ count(its bucket).
Bitmap (Slide 42): bit[b] = 1 ⇔ count(b) ≥ s (a frequent bucket); a 4-byte counter becomes 1 bit, so the bitmap needs 132 of the memory of its hash table.
PCY candidate (Slide 43): {i,j} is counted ⇔ i, j both frequent and bit1[h1({i,j})] = 1.
Multistage / multihash candidate (Slides 47, 50): {i,j} is counted ⇔ i, j both frequent and bit1 = 1 and bit2[h2({i,j})] = 1.
Average bucket count = N / B, where N = number of pair-occurrences hashed in pass 1 (∑ over baskets of C(basket size, 2)) and B = number of buckets. Halving B doubles it (Slide 49).

Part (a) — The key idea of the multistage algorithm Lecture 4 · Slides 46–47, 83–84

Key idea in one sentence (what the examiner wants first)

The multistage algorithm uses additional hash tables — a second, different hash function applied only to the pairs that survived PCY's first filter — to reduce the number of candidate pairs that must be counted, so their counters fit in main memory; it needs 3 passes. The steps below give the detail that earns the remaining marks.

  1. Where it comes from: the weakness of PCY (Slides 38–45). In PCY, pass 1 hashes every pair into a bucket and keeps only a count per bucket; between the passes the buckets become a bitmap (1 = frequent bucket). In pass 2 a pair gets a counter only if both items are frequent and its bucket bit is 1. But a bucket can be frequent although it contains no frequent pair — unpopular pairs collide and their counts add up to ≥ s (the "sad face" of Slide 41), or an unpopular pair simply shares a bucket with a popular one. Every such false candidate still receives a counter, and each counter is an (item, item, count) triple (Slide 45), which is why the slide demands that the hash table eliminate about 2/3 of the candidate pairs for PCY to beat A-Priori. Beyond the slides: a triple costs about 12 bytes against 4 bytes per pair in A-Priori's triangular array, so PCY wins only if at most about 1/3 of the pairs survive. Memory is the bottleneck (Slide 46): if too many false candidates survive, their counters do not fit in main memory. Multistage is the fix when one filter is not strong enough: use a second one.
  2. The key idea (Slide 46). The slide says: "Limit the number of candidates to be counted" and "Key idea: After Pass 1 of PCY, rehash pairs with a different hash function". In other words: add a second hash table (and later a second bitmap) so that a pair must be "vouched for" by two independent buckets instead of one. A false candidate that was unlucky in table 1 is unlikely to be unlucky again in table 2. The price is 3 passes over the data (Slide 46). This is exactly the slide-84 answer: additional hash tables reduce the number of candidate pairs.
  3. Pass 1 — identical to PCY (Slide 47, left). Read all baskets once: count every item, and hash every pair {i,j} of every basket with the first hash function h1 into Hash table 1 (add 1 to the bucket's counter; only the count is stored, not the pairs). At the end of the pass: item counts → list of frequent items (count ≥ s); Hash table 1 → Bitmap 1 (1 bit per bucket, 1 = count ≥ s). The big counters are discarded, which frees the memory they occupied.
  4. Pass 2 — rehash the survivors with a different function (Slide 47, middle). Main memory now holds the list of frequent items, Bitmap 1 and a second hash table. Read the baskets a second time. For each pair {i,j}: apply the PCY test (both items frequent and its bit in Bitmap 1 is 1). If it passes, hash the pair with a second hash function h2 into Hash table 2 (add 1 to that bucket); if it fails, ignore the pair. Nothing is counted exactly yet — Hash table 2 holds only bucket counts. At the end of the pass, Hash table 2 → Bitmap 2 (1 = count ≥ s). Why does this second table help? (i) The function is different (independent of h1): pairs that shared a bucket under h1 are spread over different buckets under h2, so an innocent pair no longer has the same popular neighbours. (If h2 were the same function, the same pairs would collide again and little would be learned.) (ii) Only candidates are hashed into it, so table 2 is much less crowded than table 1 (in the practice example of part (e) table 1 receives all 41 pair-occurrences, table 2 only 21) and more of its buckets stay below s. Part (e), step 5, shows a pair that would survive if all pairs were hashed into table 2 but is removed because only candidates are.
  5. Pass 3 — count only the pairs that survive all tests (Slide 47, right). Memory holds the frequent items, Bitmap 1, Bitmap 2 and the counters of candidate pairs. Read the baskets a third time and count {i,j} if and only if
    • (1) i and j are both frequent items, and
    • (2) {i,j} hashes (by h1) to a frequent bucket in Bitmap 1, and
    • (3) {i,j} hashes (by h2) to a frequent bucket in Bitmap 2.
    These counters are now exact; the pairs with count ≥ s are the frequent pairs.
  6. Why the result is still exactly right (no false negatives). Let {i,j} be a truly frequent pair, i.e. it occurs in at least s baskets. Check the three tests of pass 3 one by one:
    • (1) Both items are frequent: each of i, j occurs in at least as many baskets as the pair does (monotonicity, Slide 30).
    • (2) Bit in Bitmap 1 = 1: a bucket count is the sum of the counts of all pairs hashed to it, so count(bucket) ≥ count({i,j}) ≥ s.
    • (3) Bit in Bitmap 2 = 1: because the pair passed (1) and (2), every one of its occurrences was hashed into Hash table 2 in pass 2; so that bucket count is also ≥ count({i,j}) ≥ s.
    So a frequent pair is never discarded. An infrequent pair may survive (a false positive), but then its exact count in pass 3 shows that it is below s and it is not reported. Hence multistage returns exactly the same frequent pairs as A-Priori and PCY; only the number of counters (the memory) changes. Why fewer false positives: an infrequent pair now has to be unlucky twice. Beyond the slides (simple model): if it lands in a frequent bucket with probability f1 in table 1 and f2 in table 2, independently, it survives with probability about f1 · f2, which is smaller than either one (e.g. 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04).
  7. The memory picture and the cost (Slide 47 = Figure 1; Slide 84). Pass 1 looks like PCY. Pass 2 trades the big first table for the tiny Bitmap 1 (1/32 of its size) and uses the space it freed for the second table. Pass 3 keeps both bitmaps and spends the rest of memory on the counters of the few remaining candidates. (The textbook figure on Slide 84 also shows the "item names → integers" table at the top of each pass: the renumbering trick of Slide 33.) The cost is the extra pass: the whole data file must be read three times instead of two. Beyond the slides: by the same logic, with m hash tables (stages) multistage needs m + 1 passes (PCY = 1 table = 2 passes; two tables = 3 passes, as on Slide 46).
Slide erratum (omission) — Slides 46–47

Slide 47 (pass 2) says only "Hash pairs {i,j} into Hash2", and Slide 46 says "rehash pairs with a different hash function". Read literally, this suggests that all pairs are rehashed. The correct version: in pass 2 only the pairs that already pass the PCY test (both items frequent and bit in Bitmap 1 = 1) are hashed into Hash table 2 (standard in Mining of Massive Datasets, §6.3.2). This is what makes table 2 less crowded, and it is why a multistage pass 2 needs the frequent-items list and Bitmap 1 in memory (as Slide 47's memory picture shows). Write the restriction in your answer.

Part (b) — Multihash: the same idea in two passes Lecture 4 · Slides 49–50

  1. Key idea (Slide 49). "Use several independent hash tables on the first pass." Instead of building the second filter in a second pass (multistage), build both filters at the same time in pass 1. If it works, "we can get a benefit like multistage, but in only 2 passes".
  2. Pass 1 (Slide 50, left). The spare memory that PCY gives to one hash table is shared by two tables (Hash table 1 and Hash table 2), each with B/2 buckets. Count every item; hash every pair twice — with h1 into table 1 and with h2 into table 2 (h1, h2 independent). Between the passes: each table → a bitmap (Bitmap 1, Bitmap 2), item counts → list of frequent items.
  3. Pass 2 (Slide 50, right). Memory holds frequent items, Bitmap 1, Bitmap 2 and the counters. Count {i,j} iff i and j are frequent and bit1 = 1 and bit2 = 1 — the same three-part test as multistage's pass 3, but reached after only 2 passes.
  4. The risk (Slide 49). "Halving the number of buckets doubles the average count." Every pair is hashed into both tables, so each table still receives all N pair-occurrences, but spread over only B/2 buckets: the average bucket count is N/(B/2) = 2N/B. "We have to be sure most buckets will still not reach count s." If too many do, both bitmaps are mostly 1s and almost nothing is filtered — multihash can then be worse than PCY with one big table. Slide 49 puts the condition the other way round: if most buckets still stay below s, “we can get a benefit like multistage, but in only 2 passes”. Numbers for both cases are in part (d) and part (e).
  5. Difference from multistage in one line. Multistage: the two filters are applied one after the other (stage 2 sees only survivors of stage 1, needs an extra pass, keeps full-size tables). Multihash: the two filters are applied side by side to all pairs (no extra pass, but each table is half-size, so each filter is weaker).

Part (c) — PCY, multistage and multihash compared Lecture 4 · Slides 38–50

Baseline, A-Priori (Slide 31): 2 passes; pass 1 stores only item counts (most memory idle); pass 2 counts every pair of frequent items. All three algorithms below are refinements that use the idle pass-1 memory to count fewer pairs in the last pass.

When to usespare memory in pass 1, and a large share of buckets stay below s; the table must remove about 2/3 of the candidate pairs to beat A-Priori (Slide 45)PCY alone still leaves too many candidates for the counters to fit, and one more pass over the data is affordableyou want a multistage-like reduction but cannot afford a third pass, and bucket counts are well below s even after halving (many buckets, large s)

The "when to use" row combines the conditions stated on Slides 45, 46 and 49 with ordinary engineering reasoning; the slides do not give a formal rule.

Part (d) — Why more stages / more hash tables give diminishing returns Lecture 4 · Slide 51

Slide 51 (“PCY: Extensions”) says three things: either multistage or multihash can use more than two hash functions; in multistage there is a point of diminishing returns, since the bit-vectors eventually consume all of main memory; for multihash, too many hash functions makes all counts ≥ s (the slide prints “>” with an underline, which means ≥). Here is the reasoning behind each statement.

  1. Multistage — the bitmaps eat the memory (Slide 51). Every extra stage leaves one more bitmap in memory for the last pass. A bitmap is 1/32 of the table it summarises (Slide 42): a table of 108 four-byte buckets is 4 × 108 bytes = 400 MB, its bitmap is 108 bits = 12.5 MB. With m stages the last pass keeps m bitmaps, about m/32 of one table's memory (table below). That memory is taken from the space for the pair counters — exactly what the extra stage was supposed to protect. Beyond the slides: if each table were as large as all of main memory, 32 bitmaps would fill it completely, and long before that there would be no room left for the counters.
  2. Multistage — each stage helps less than the previous one. The false candidates are removed by a fraction each time, so the absolute gain shrinks, while the cost of a stage (one more bitmap and, beyond the slides, one more pass) stays the same. Illustration with our own idealised numbers: suppose each independent table lets 20 % of the remaining false candidates through.
    Hash tables (stages) mPasses (m + 1)Bitmap memory kept in last pass (fraction of one table)False candidates still countedRemoved by the last table added
    1 (= PCY)21/3220 %80 percentage points
    232/324 %16 percentage points
    343/320.8 %3.2 percentage points
    454/320.16 %0.64 percentage points
    565/320.032 %0.128 percentage points
    The first table removes 80 % of the false candidates, the second only 16 more, the fifth only 0.128. The truly frequent pairs can never be removed, so there is a floor below which no stage can go; once almost all false candidates are gone, another stage has almost nothing left to remove but still costs a bitmap and a pass.
  3. Multihash — too many tables make every bucket frequent (Slide 51). With k tables sharing the memory of one PCY table (B buckets), each table has B/k buckets but still receives all N pair-occurrences, so the average bucket count is k·N/B — k times the PCY average. When this average reaches s, a typical bucket is frequent, every bitmap is almost all 1s, the test “bit = 1” removes (almost) nothing, and the bitmaps merely waste memory.
    Beyond the slides (the textbook's reasoning, with our numbers; k = 1 is plain PCY): the bucket counts of one table add up to N, so at most N/s of its buckets can have a count ≥ s, i.e. at most a fraction k·N/(s·B) of them. Take a typical case where the PCY average count is s/10 (so N/(s·B) = 1/10). If the k hash functions are independent, an infrequent pair passes all k tests with probability at most (k/10)k:
    Tables kBuckets per tableAverage count per bucketShare of buckets that can be frequent (at most)Chance that an infrequent pair passes all k tests (at most)
    1B0.1 s10 %10.0 %
    2B/20.2 s20 %4.0 %
    3B/30.3 s30 %2.7 %
    4B/40.4 s40 %2.6 %
    5B/50.5 s50 %3.1 %
    6B/60.6 s60 %4.7 %
    8B/80.8 s80 %16.8 %
    10B/101.0 sno guarantee (up to 100 %)no guarantee (up to 100 %)
    Reading the table: the second table helps a lot (10 % → 4 %), the third and fourth help only a little (2.7 %, 2.6 %), and from the fifth table on the guarantee gets worse, because, as on Slide 49, every extra table has fewer buckets and so raises the average count, until it reaches s — the slide's “too many hash functions makes all counts ≥ s”. (The bound is a worst-case model, not a measurement; real data behave better or worse depending on how the counts are spread.)
  4. Conclusion. Two (or a few) hash tables capture most of the benefit; beyond that, multistage runs out of memory (and costs passes) and multihash runs out of “empty” buckets. The best number depends on the data and the memory — the slide only states that a point of diminishing returns exists.
