With real data where bucket counts stay well below s, the halving does not hurt this much (Slide 49).
Exam tip

For "Describe the key idea behind the multistage algorithm" write, in this order: (1) the purpose — reduce the number of candidate pairs (memory is the bottleneck); (2) the idea — after PCY's pass 1, rehash the surviving pairs with a different hash function into a second hash table (and bitmap); (3) the three passes — pass 1 = PCY, pass 2 = rehash candidates, pass 3 = count; (4) the pass-3 test — both items frequent and frequent bucket in bitmap 1 and frequent bucket in bitmap 2. Add one line on multihash (same idea, several tables in pass 1, only 2 passes, risk = halved buckets double the average count) if the question asks for a comparison. A figure of the three memory layouts is worth drawing.

Common mistakes
  • Saying multistage saves passes. It needs 3; the two-pass relative is multihash.
  • Mixing up the names: multistage = filters in stages, one after another (extra pass); multihash = several hash tables at once in the first pass.
  • Forgetting that the second hash function must be different, or saying that all pairs go into the second table. Only the pairs that already passed the PCY test do.
  • Thinking the bitmap stores counts. It stores one bit per bucket (1 = count ≥ s).
  • Mixing up a frequent bucket (bucket count ≥ s) with a frequent pair. A frequent bucket may contain no frequent pair at all (several small pairs add up).
  • Forgetting one of the three pass-3 tests (items frequent, Bitmap 1 bit = 1, Bitmap 2 bit = 1); PCY has only the first two.
  • Believing that more stages or more hash functions are always better (Slide 51), or that the algorithm may miss frequent pairs. It cannot: it only removes pairs that provably cannot be frequent; the survivors are counted exactly.
Final answer: The key idea of the multistage algorithm is to use additional hash tables to reduce the number of candidate pairs, so that their counters fit in main memory. It needs 3 passes. Pass 1 = PCY: count items and hash every pair with h1 into Hash table 1; afterwards Hash table 1 → Bitmap 1 and the item counts → list of frequent items. Pass 2: rehash, with a different hash function h2 into a second hash table, only the pairs that pass the PCY test (both items frequent and bit in Bitmap 1 = 1); afterwards Hash table 2 → Bitmap 2. Pass 3: count {i,j} iff i, j are both frequent and {i,j} hashes to a frequent bucket in Bitmap 1 and to a frequent bucket in Bitmap 2. The result is exactly the frequent pairs of A-Priori (no false negatives), found with fewer counters.
Multihash = the same idea in 2 passes: several independent hash tables share the pass-1 memory (each one smaller) and both bitmaps are used in pass 2. Risk: halving the buckets doubles the average count, so many buckets may reach s and the filter fails.
Diminishing returns (Slide 51): multistage — the bitmaps (and, beyond the slides, the extra passes) eventually consume main memory while each stage removes fewer false candidates; multihash — too many tables make all counts ≥ s, so every bit is 1.
Practice (Slide 78 baskets): counters needed — A-Priori 10, PCY 8, multihash 7, multistage 5 (the five frequent pairs {1,2}, {1,5}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,5}).
Where the marks come from: (1) Purpose / headline — additional hash tables reduce the number of candidate pairs; memory is the bottleneck (this is the slide's own answer). (2) Key mechanism — after PCY pass 1, rehash with a different hash function into a second table. (3) Three passes, each described correctly (pass 1 = PCY with Bitmap 1; pass 2 = hash the surviving pairs into Hash table 2 → Bitmap 2; pass 3 = count). (4) The pass-3 condition with all three parts (items frequent, bucket frequent in B1, bucket frequent in B2). (5) Bitmaps replace the tables (1 bit per bucket, 1/32 of the memory). (6) Correctness / effect — no false negatives, fewer false positives, exact counts in the last pass. (7) Multihash — several independent tables in pass 1, 2 passes, risk (halved buckets double the average count). (8) Comparison — passes, memory, risk, when to use. (9) Diminishing returns — bitmaps consume memory (multistage), all counts ≥ s (multihash). (10) Optional extra: a small numeric run or a labelled figure.
Slide check: the slide's own answer (Slide 84: “uses additional hash tables to reduce the number of candidate pairs”) agrees with ours but is only the headline: it does not say that a different hash function is used, that a third pass is needed, or what the pass-3 test is. Our answer adds these from Slides 46–47. Slide erratum (omission): Slides 46–47 do not say that in pass 2 only the pairs that pass the PCY test (frequent items and frequent bucket in Bitmap 1) are hashed into Hash table 2; the correct version is given in the box above. Small notes: (1) printed slide 48 does not exist in the PDF, so the multihash slides are printed 49–51 and printed slide 52 is only the section divider “Frequent Itemsets in ≤ 2 Passes”; (2) Slide 51 prints “all counts > s” with an underlined “>”, which means ≥ s; (3) Slide 42 says a bit is 1 if the bucket count “exceeded” s, but the standard meaning (and the one used on Slide 31 for frequent items) is count ≥ s, which is what we use.

Fewer passes: the limited-pass idea

Lecture 4 · Slides 52–53

Slide 52 is a section divider titled "Frequent Itemsets in ≤ 2 Passes" (it carries no printed number; the "≤" is drawn as an underlined "<"). Slide 53 states the problem it solves.

Beginner intuition

A pass is one complete read of the basket file from disk. Reading terabytes from disk is slow, so the number of passes is the main cost. Imagine counting votes: A-Priori and PCY say "first count single items, then re-read everything to count pairs, then re-read again for triples ...". The slide asks: can we get the answer after reading the file at most twice, whatever the itemset size?

What Slide 53 says, in plain words:

  • A-Priori, PCY, etc., take k passes to find frequent itemsets of size k. Read this as "k passes to reach itemsets up to size k": 5 passes to find frequent 5-itemsets. Every pass is another slow scan of the whole file.
  • "Can we use fewer passes?" The slide's answer is "use 2 or fewer passes for all sizes, but may miss some frequent itemsets", with two methods listed: random sampling and SON (Savasere, Omiecinski and Navathe, the three authors).
Slide erratum

On Slide 53 the phrase "but may miss some frequent itemsets" (printed in pink) is true of random sampling only. SON is listed under the same bullet, but SON is exact: it misses nothing and, after its second pass, reports nothing false (Slide 57, explained below). Keep the two straight: sampling = approximate, SON = exact. Both use at most two passes.

Random sampling

Lecture 4 · Slides 54–55

The method

Lecture 4 · Slide 54

Beginner intuition

Pollsters do not ask every voter; they ask a random few thousand and scale the result. Random sampling does the same with baskets: read a small random subset that fits in RAM, mine that subset completely in memory, and treat the answer as the answer for the whole file.

Definition: random sampling for frequent itemsets (Slide 54)

Take a random sample of the market baskets and run A-Priori (or one of its improvements such as PCY) in main memory on that sample, with the support threshold reduced proportionally to the sample size.

  1. Sample: pick a random subset of the baskets small enough to fit in main memory together with the counters (the slide's figure shows exactly two memory blocks: "Copy of sample baskets" and "Space for counts").
  2. Scale the threshold: if the sample holds a fraction p of all baskets, use p × s as the threshold on the sample.
  3. Mine in memory: run A-Priori / PCY on the sample. Moving from pairs to triples to bigger sets now costs no disk I/O, because every pass is a scan of RAM. This is the saving the slide names: "save disk I/O each time we increase the size of itemsets".
  4. Output the itemsets found frequent in the sample (optionally verify them, next section).
Worked example — scaling the threshold Lecture 4 · Slide 54

Beyond the slides: an illustration (the slide gives no numbers). A file has 107 baskets and the support threshold is s = 1 % of the baskets = 105 baskets.

  1. Take a 1 % random sample: p = 0.01, so the sample has 0.01 × 107 = 105 baskets.
  2. Scaled threshold = p × s = 0.01 × 105 = 1 000 baskets of the sample.
  3. As a fraction it is still "1 %" of the sample (1 000 / 105 = 1 %), which is why the slide can write "threshold s = 1 %" for both. If you forgot to scale and used 105 on a sample of 105 baskets, an itemset would need to be in every sampled basket, and almost nothing would pass.
Common mistake

Slide 8 defines support as an absolute count of baskets, but Slide 54 writes "s = 1 %". When a threshold is a percentage, always convert to a count of the data set you are actually counting in (sample or chunk). "Reduce proportionally" is about that count. Also note the sample must be random; the first n baskets of a file (Beyond the slides: often sorted by date or customer) can be badly biased.

Two kinds of mistake

Lecture 4 · Slide 55

Slide 55 has two bullets, one for each kind of error a sample can make.

Definition: false positive and false negative

A false positive is an itemset that looks frequent in the sample but is not frequent in the whole data. A false negative is an itemset that is frequent in the whole data but is not frequent in the sample, so it is missed.

  • Bullet 1: "Optionally, verify that the candidate pairs are truly frequent in the entire data set by a second pass (avoid false positives)." One more pass over the full file counts only the itemsets the sample reported. Those that fall below s are discarded. This removes false positives. It is optional because it costs a second disk pass; the slide's "candidate pairs" really means candidate itemsets of any size.
  • Bullet 2: "But you do not catch sets frequent in the whole but not in the sample." These are the false negatives. The verification pass only recounts itemsets that already appeared in the sample, so it can never bring a missed itemset back. This is why Slide 53 says sampling "may miss some".
Exam tip

The classic one-line contrast: sampling can give false positives (fixable with a second pass) and false negatives (not fixable); SON gives neither after its second pass. If a question asks "how do you remove false positives?", the answer is "count the reported itemsets over the entire data in a second pass".

Beyond the slides: trading memory for fewer misses

Lecture 4 · Slide 55 (extension)

Beyond the slides: the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets, Section 6.4.1) notes that false negatives can be reduced, though not eliminated, by lowering the sample threshold a little below the proportional value, for example to 0.9 × p × s or 0.8 × p × s. In the example above that is 900 or 800 instead of 1 000. An itemset that is just above s in the whole file but unlucky in the sample then still has a chance. The price: more itemsets pass in the sample, so more memory is needed and more false positives appear (which the second pass can remove). Slide 55 itself does not mention this.

The SON algorithm

Lecture 4 · Slides 56–57

Beginner intuition

Instead of asking a few voters, SON asks everyone but in groups. A huge pile of exam papers is split into small piles that one marker can handle. Each marker lists the mistakes that are common enough in her own pile. Any mistake that is common in the whole pile must be common in at least one small pile, so the union of the lists contains every truly common mistake. A final recount over all papers removes the listed mistakes that were only common by chance. The data is read exactly twice.

Pass 1: find candidates chunk by chunk

Lecture 4 · Slide 56

Definition: SON, Pass 1 and candidate (Slide 56)

SON (Savasere, Omiecinski and Navathe) repeatedly reads small subsets of the baskets into main memory and runs an in-memory algorithm (A-Priori, PCY, ...) to find the frequent itemsets of each subset. An itemset becomes a candidate if it is found frequent in any one or more of the subsets.

  1. Cut the entire basket file into chunks, each small enough to fit in memory with its counters.
  2. For each chunk in turn: load it, run the in-memory algorithm with the local (lowered) threshold, and write out the itemsets that are frequent in this chunk.
  3. The candidate list is the union of all those outputs (an itemset reported by several chunks is listed once).
Common mistake

Slide 56 stresses: "we are not sampling, but processing the entire file in chunks that fit into the memory." Every basket is read and used; nothing is thrown away. That is the whole difference from Random Sampling, and the reason SON can be exact.

Pass 2: count the candidates over everything

Lecture 4 · Slide 57

On a second pass, SON counts all the candidate itemsets over the entire file and keeps those that are frequent in the entire set (count ≥ s). Only the candidates are counted, not every possible itemset, so memory stays small.

Key "monotonicity" idea (Slide 57)

An itemset cannot be frequent in the entire set of baskets unless it is frequent in at least one subset. Consequence: the candidate list can never leave out a truly frequent itemset (no false negatives), and the second pass removes the itemsets that were frequent only locally (no false positives in the final output). So SON gives the exact answer, for all itemset sizes, with two passes.

Common mistake

The word "monotonicity" here is a different property from Slide 30's A-Priori monotonicity ("every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent"). Slide 57's version is "frequent overall ⇒ frequent in at least one chunk". Beware of mixing them up when asked "what is the monotonicity idea in SON?".

Why it works: the pigeonhole argument

Lecture 4 · Slide 57 (proof sketch, Beyond the slides)

Beyond the slides: the slide states the idea without proof (the proof follows Mining of Massive Datasets, Section 6.4.3). Suppose the file is split into p equal chunks, and the global threshold is s. Use the local threshold s/p in each chunk. If an itemset has fewer than s/p occurrences in every chunk, its total is below p × (s/p) = s, so it cannot be globally frequent. Taking the contrapositive: a globally frequent itemset reaches s/p in at least one chunk, so some chunk reports it, so it is a candidate.

Formula: the local threshold

local threshold of a chunk = pchunk × s, where pchunk = (baskets in the chunk) ÷ (baskets in the whole file). For equal chunks this is s/(number of chunks). Because counts are whole numbers, use "count ≥ the next integer at or above" the value.

Slide erratum

Slides 56–57 never say which threshold is used inside a chunk. If the full threshold s were applied to each small chunk, an itemset spread evenly across the chunks would be below s in every one of them and would be missed, and the "no false negatives" claim would be false. The threshold must be scaled down (the SON example on Slide 63 uses a local support of 2 against a global support of 4). Quiz L4-Q6 (below) checks this against the example's numbers.

SON on a cluster: two MapReduce rounds

Lecture 4 · Slides 58–60, 65–66

Why SON suits distributed data

Lecture 4 · Slide 58

Slide 58: "SON lends itself to distributed big data analysis." The baskets are spread over many nodes (machines). The slide's two sub-bullets are the entire algorithm: (1) compute frequent itemsets at each node; (2) accumulate the counts of all candidates. The reason it parallelises so well is that each chunk is mined independently: no machine needs to see another machine's chunk during Pass 1, and in Pass 2 each machine only counts on its own chunk, then the counts are added.

Beginner intuition

Recall MapReduce from the earlier lectures: map workers each process their own piece of the data and emit key-value pairs; the system groups pairs by key; reduce workers combine all values of one key. SON is "two MapReduce jobs back to back". Job 1 produces the candidate list. Job 2 uses that list to produce exact counts.

Round 1: Map Phase 1 and Reduce Phase 1

Lecture 4 · Slides 59–60

PhaseWhat the slide saysPlain meaning
Map Phase 1: run algorithm on subsets (Slide 59)The entire dataset is split into chunk servers; a subset of chunks is processed independently by each mapper. On each mapper, run a frequent-itemset algorithm (Apriori, PCY, FP-growth etc.). Each mapper outputs the candidate frequent itemsets from its subset of chunks.Every mapper takes the chunks it is responsible for, loads them in memory, mines them with a single-machine algorithm and emits the itemsets that are frequent there. Together the mappers see all the baskets.
Reduce Phase 1: collect candidate itemsets (Slide 60)Aggregate the candidates found in Phase 1 into a global list of candidate itemsets, including elimination of duplicates.The same itemset may be frequent in several chunks. The reducers' only job is a union without duplicates. Output: one global candidate list.

Beyond the slides (Mining of Massive Datasets, Section 6.4.4): the map output is a key-value pair (F, 1) for each locally frequent itemset F (the value 1 is meaningless; only the key matters), and the reducer simply outputs each key it receives once. The local threshold in Map Phase 1 is p × s, as above.

"FP-growth" appears on Slide 59 as one more example of an in-memory algorithm. It is not taught anywhere in Lectures 1–5, so you only need to know it is an alternative to A-Priori and PCY for mining one chunk.

Slide erratum

Slide 60 says the candidates "will be optionally evaluated against the entire dataset in Phase 2". For SON that is wrong. The second round is required: without it the output contains false positives (in the example on Slides 68–69, five of the eight listed candidates are thrown away). The word "optionally" belongs to Random Sampling (Slide 55), where verification really is optional. Slide 57 correctly says "on a second pass, count all the candidate itemsets". Also on Slide 59, "split into chunk servers" should read "split into chunks stored on chunk servers", and "candidate frequent itemsets that appear in subsets of chunks" should read "that are frequent in the subsets of chunks".

Round 2: Map Phase 2 and Reduce Phase 2

Lecture 4 · Slides 65–66

PhaseWhat the slide saysPlain meaning
Map Phase 2: count the support of candidate itemsets (Slide 65)Take the global list of candidates from Phase 1 and broadcast it to all mappers. Each mapper checks the support of each candidate on its chunks.This is the "second pass". Every mapper receives the same candidate list and counts every candidate in its own chunks, including candidates that were not frequent there (a count of 0 is reported as 0).
Reduce Phase 2: aggregate global support counts (Slide 66)Aggregate the support counts for each candidate globally. Itemsets whose support meets the minimum threshold are considered frequent.Each reducer receives, for one candidate, the per-chunk counts and adds them. Chunks do not overlap, so the sum is the exact global support. Keep the candidate if the total is at least s.

Beyond the slides: the Phase 2 map output is (C, v), where C is a candidate and v is its count in that mapper's chunks. "Broadcast" means the (small) candidate list is copied to every mapper; it is not shuffled by key.

Exam tip

If asked to "describe SON in MapReduce", answer with the four phases in order and say what is emitted at each: (1) Map 1 emits locally frequent itemsets; (2) Reduce 1 removes duplicates to form the candidate list; (3) Map 2 counts every broadcast candidate on its own chunks; (4) Reduce 2 sums the counts and applies the threshold. Mention "two passes over the data, whatever the itemset size" and "exact".

The worked example (five baskets, two chunks)

Lecture 4 · Slides 61–69

Slides 61–69 run the four phases on a tiny data set so you can see each list. The setting:

  • Slide 61: five transactions T1–T5 over apple, banana, orange and pear, with global support 4 (an itemset must be in at least 4 of the 5 baskets).
  • Slide 62: Chunk 1 = T1–T3 (3 baskets), Chunk 2 = T4–T5 (2 baskets).
  • Slides 63–64: Map Phase 1 and Reduce Phase 1 with local support 2; the slide shows a list of 8 candidate itemsets.
  • Slide 65–66 restate the Phase 2 rules; Slide 67 shows each mapper's counts of the 8 candidates; Slide 68 adds them up per candidate; Slide 69 repeats Slide 68 with the failing itemsets struck through.

What to watch for as you work the example:

  • An itemset such as {pear} is frequent locally in Chunk 2 (count 2) but its global count is only 2, below 4. It enters the candidate list and is eliminated in Phase 2: a textbook false positive.
  • A chunk must count every candidate, not only the ones it found itself (for example Chunk 1 reports {pear} with count 0).
  • The final answer must equal what plain A-Priori on the whole file would give. It does.
Slide erratum

Slides 63–64 (and so Slides 65–69) leave out a candidate. In Chunk 2 the triple {banana, orange, pear} occurs in both T4 and T5, so it also has local count 2 and A-Priori with local support 2 would report it. The correct candidate list has 9 itemsets, not 8. The final answer is unchanged because its global count is 2, below 4 (it would simply be a sixth false positive). Slide 63 also has the typo "e.g," and writes "{banana, pear} = 2 times" with "=" where every other line has ":". Slide 67's second line is missing separators between entries, and Slide 68 never states the final answer in words (it appears only as strike-through on Slide 69): the survivors are {banana} (4), {orange} (5) and {banana, orange} (4).

Not examined — local threshold in the example

The rule "local threshold = p × s" would give 0.6 × 4 = 2.4 for Chunk 1 and 0.4 × 4 = 1.6 for Chunk 2. The slides simply use 2 for both, which is safe: it is no higher than needed for Chunk 2 and lower than needed for Chunk 1 (so it can only produce extra candidates, never miss one). Quiz L4-Q6 part (e) discusses this.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution of the quiz below, reproduce each of the four phases from the five baskets, then compare, including the missing ninth candidate and the three-part explanation of why SON is exact.

Quiz L4-Q6SON algorithm: the two-chunk MapReduce example Lecture 4 · Slides 56–69
Question (as on the slides)

SON (Savasere, Omiecinski and Navathe) MapReduce Example — Slides 61–69 (theory on Slides 56–60). The slides run the SON algorithm on a tiny data set of five baskets (transactions) split into two chunks. They present it as a worked example rather than a numbered question, so it is restated here as a task: reproduce every phase and explain why it works.

BasketItemsChunk
T1[apple, banana, orange]Chunk 1 (Slide 62)
T2[banana, orange]
T3[apple, orange]
T4[banana, orange, pear]Chunk 2 (Slide 62)
T5[banana, apple, orange, pear]

Global support = 4 (Slide 61): an itemset is frequent in the whole data set if it is contained in at least 4 of the 5 baskets. Local support = 2 in each chunk (Slide 63). Mappers run Apriori on their chunk.

(a) Map Phase 1: find the locally frequent itemsets of Chunk 1 and of Chunk 2 (local support 2), with their local counts.
(b) Reduce Phase 1: form the global list of candidate itemsets (duplicates removed).
(c) Map Phase 2: broadcast the candidates and let each mapper count every candidate on its own chunk.
(d) Reduce Phase 2: add up the counts and keep the itemsets whose global support is at least 4. What are the frequent itemsets?
(e) Explain (i) why SON can have no false negatives, (ii) why the second pass removes the false positives, and (iii) how the local threshold relates to the global threshold.
(f) Describe the MapReduce view of SON: what do Map Phase 1, Reduce Phase 1, Map Phase 2 and Reduce Phase 2 each do (Slides 58–60, 65–66)?
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Two markers, one big pile of exam papers. A pile of 100 exam papers is split into two piles of 50. You want every mistake that occurs on at least 40 papers overall. Suppose mistake X really is on 40 papers. Could X be on fewer than 20 papers in pile A and on fewer than 20 papers in pile B? No: at most 19 + 19 = 38, which is less than 40. So X must be on at least 20 papers in one of the piles.

That is the whole trick of SON. Pass 1: each marker (mapper) writes down every mistake that is "common enough" in her own pile; this list can never miss a mistake that is common overall. But some listed mistakes were only common in one pile by chance. Pass 2: everybody recounts only the listed mistakes over all papers and throws away the ones that do not reach 40. Result: the exact answer, after reading the data just twice.

Key idea

SON = two passes. Pass 1 (Map Phase 1 + Reduce Phase 1): find the frequent itemsets inside each chunk, using a lowered (local) threshold; every itemset found anywhere becomes a candidate. Pass 2 (Map Phase 2 + Reduce Phase 2): count only the candidates over the whole data and keep those with global support ≥ s. Note (Slide 56): this is not sampling — the entire file is processed, just in chunks that fit into main memory.

Step 0 — set-up and the numbers we will need

  1. Definitions (Lecture 4 · Slide 8): the support of an itemset I is the number of baskets that contain all items of I; I is frequent if its support is at least the threshold s. Here the thresholds are counts, not percentages.
  2. Data facts: N = 5 baskets; global threshold s = 4 (that is 80 % of the baskets); Chunk 1 holds 3 baskets (T1–T3), Chunk 2 holds 2 baskets (T4–T5). The chunks do not overlap and together contain every basket — a partition of the file, so per-chunk counts add up to the global count.
  3. Fraction of the file in each chunk: p1 = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6 and p2 = 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4, so p1 + p2 = 1. We will use these in part (e). The slides simply state local support = 2 for both chunks.
  4. Three words to keep straight: a candidate is an itemset found frequent inside at least one chunk (Slide 56); a false positive is a candidate that is not frequent in the whole file; a false negative is an itemset that is frequent in the whole file but is missing from the candidate list. Pass 1 is built to give no false negatives, Pass 2 removes the false positives.

Part (a) — Map Phase 1: frequent itemsets inside each chunk (Slides 59, 63)

  1. Formula / idea: local count of I in a chunk = number of baskets of that chunk containing every item of I; I is locally frequent if local count ≥ 2. Each mapper runs an ordinary in-memory algorithm on its chunk (the slide uses A-Priori; Slide 59 also names PCY and FP-growth). A-Priori works level by level: count single items, keep the frequent ones, build candidate pairs only from frequent items, count them, keep the frequent ones, build candidate triples only from frequent pairs, and so on.
  2. Chunk 1 (T1, T2, T3), level 1 — single items: apple is in T1, T3 → 2; banana is in T1, T2 → 2; orange is in T1, T2, T3 → 3; pear is in none → 0. Keep those with count ≥ 2: apple, banana, orange.
  3. Chunk 1, level 2 — pairs (all three items are frequent, so all three pairs are candidates): {apple, banana} is only in T1 → 1 (not frequent); {apple, orange} is in T1, T3 → 2 (frequent); {banana, orange} is in T1, T2 → 2 (frequent).
  4. Chunk 1, level 3 — triples: the only possible triple {apple, banana, orange} needs all three of its pairs to be frequent, but {apple, banana} is not, so A-Priori does not even count it (inside Chunk 1 its true count is 1, from T1). Chunk 1 output = 5 itemsets: {apple}:2, {banana}:2, {orange}:3, {apple, orange}:2, {banana, orange}:2. This matches Slide 63.
  5. Chunk 2 (T4, T5), level 1 — single items: apple is only in T5 → 1 (not frequent); banana in T4, T5 → 2; orange in T4, T5 → 2; pear in T4, T5 → 2. Frequent: banana, orange, pear.
  6. Chunk 2, level 2 — pairs built only from the frequent items banana, orange, pear (apple is dropped, so no pair containing apple is ever counted): {banana, orange} in T4, T5 → 2; {banana, pear} in T4, T5 → 2; {orange, pear} in T4, T5 → 2. All three are frequent.
  7. Chunk 2, level 3 — triples: the triple {banana, orange, pear} has all its pairs frequent, so it is a candidate; it is contained in T4 and in T5 → count 2 ≥ 2, so it is locally frequent. Level 4: only one frequent triple exists, so no 4-item candidate can be formed. Chunk 2 output = 7 itemsets: {banana}:2, {orange}:2, {pear}:2, {banana, orange}:2, {banana, pear}:2, {orange, pear}:2 and {banana, orange, pear}:2.

Slide erratum

Slide 63 leaves out {banana, orange, pear} from the Chunk 2 list. It appears in both baskets of Chunk 2 (T4 and T5), so its local count is 2 and it meets the local support of 2; A-Priori does not stop at pairs. (The slide's list would be exactly right only if the course restricted itself to itemsets of size 2 or less — the slide does not say so.) Chunk 1 on the slide is complete. Consequences: the candidate list on Slide 64 should have 9 itemsets, not 8, and the Map Phase 2 lines on Slide 67 should also show {banana, orange, pear}: 0 times (Mapper 1) and 2 times (Mapper 2). The final answer on Slide 69 does not change because the total support of this triple is 2, below 4 (shown in part (d)). This is exactly the point of Pass 2: an extra candidate is harmless, it is simply filtered out. In an exam, write the triple and mention that the slide leaves it out.

Beginner intuition

Why does a mapper never count {apple, banana} in Chunk 2? Because A-Priori's rule says: a set can only be frequent if all its smaller subsets are frequent. In Chunk 2 apple is only 1 (below 2), so any set containing apple must be below 2 as well — no need to look. This is the "monotonicity" used inside a mapper; SON's own "monotonicity" (Slide 57) is a different idea that works across chunks (see part (e)).

Part (b) — Reduce Phase 1: the global candidate list (Slides 60, 64)

  1. Idea: every locally frequent itemset is sent out by its mapper as a key. All copies of the same itemset arrive at the same reducer, which keeps it once (elimination of duplicates, Slide 60). The local counts are ignored here — they are only local facts. The output is the global list of candidate itemsets; Slide 60 calls them "potential frequent itemsets", to be checked against the entire data set in Phase 2.
  2. Count the outputs: Mapper 1 sent 5 itemsets, Mapper 2 sent 7, so 5 + 7 = 12 items arrive. Three itemsets were sent by both mappers — {banana}, {orange} and {banana, orange} — so 12 − 3 = 9 unique candidates.

Common mistake

Adding up only the counts from the chunks where the itemset was locally frequent. That undercounts. For {apple}, Chunk 2 contributes 1 (not 0), giving 2 + 1 = 3; for {pear}, Chunk 1 contributes 0, giving 0 + 2 = 2. In Pass 2 each mapper must report its exact count for every candidate, including small counts and zeros.

Part (d) — Reduce Phase 2: global support and the answer (Slides 66, 68–69)

  1. Formula: global support of a candidate C = count1(C) + count2(C). This sum is the true global count because the chunks are disjoint and cover every basket. C is frequent if the sum ≥ s = 4.

The other 6 candidates ({apple}, {pear}, {apple, orange}, {banana, pear}, {orange, pear}, {banana, orange, pear}) are false positives that Pass 2 removes. On Slide 69 these are the struck-through lines (five of them; the sixth is the omitted triple).
  2. Sanity check directly on the whole file (not part of SON, only to confirm): banana is in T1, T2, T4, T5 = 4; orange is in all five baskets = 5; apple in T1, T3, T5 = 3; pear in T4, T5 = 2; {banana, orange} in T1, T2, T4, T5 = 4; {apple, orange} in T1, T3, T5 = 3.
  3. Nothing was missed: over the four items there are 15 non-empty itemsets; 9 are candidates. The other six — {apple, banana} (1 + 1 = 2 in total), {apple, pear} (0 + 1 = 1), {apple, banana, orange} (1 + 1 = 2), {apple, banana, pear} (0 + 1 = 1), {apple, orange, pear} (0 + 1 = 1) and {apple, banana, orange, pear} (0 + 1 = 1) — have a count of at most 1 in each chunk, so none of them can be locally frequent, and all have totals far below 4. A brute-force count of all 15 itemsets on the five baskets (checked by computer) gives exactly the same three frequent itemsets. So SON returned the exact answer: no false negatives and no false positives.

Part (e) — why SON is correct

(e-i) No false negatives (Slide 57, "monotonicity" idea). A false negative would be an itemset that is truly frequent but never reaches the candidate list.

  1. Concrete argument with our numbers: an itemset that is not locally frequent in a chunk has a local count of at most 1 there (the local support is 2). If that happened in both chunks, its total would be at most 1 + 1 = 2, which is below 4. So an itemset with total ≥ 4 must have a local count ≥ 2 in at least one chunk, i.e. it is locally frequent there and is output by that mapper. Chunk 1 has 3 baskets (count ≤ 3) and Chunk 2 has 2 baskets (count ≤ 2), so there are only three ways to reach a total of 4 or more, and each is caught:
Chunk 1 countChunk 2 countTotalCaught by (local count ≥ 2)
224both chunks
314Chunk 1 only (3 ≥ 2)
325both chunks
  1. General claim: if an itemset I has global support ≥ s, then in at least one chunk i its local count is ≥ pi · s, where pi is the fraction of all baskets that lie in chunk i.
  2. Proof by contradiction: suppose counti(I) < pi · s in every chunk. Add over all chunks (the chunks partition the file, so the local counts add up to the global count): count(I) = ∑ counti(I) < ∑ pi · s = s · ∑ pi = s · 1 = s. So count(I) < s, which contradicts "I is frequent". Hence some chunk has count ≥ pi · s. This is the slide's wording: an itemset cannot be frequent in the entire set unless it is frequent in at least one subset. (It is the same pigeonhole argument as in the exam-paper story.)
  3. Consequence: if each mapper uses a local threshold that is at most pi · s, every truly frequent itemset is output by at least one mapper in Phase 1 (each mapper uses an exact in-memory algorithm, so it finds all itemsets that are frequent in its chunk). The itemset therefore lands on the candidate list; Pass 2 then counts it exactly and keeps it. Nothing frequent is ever lost.
  4. In our data (p1 · s = 2.4, p2 · s = 1.6): {banana} has local counts 2 and 2; 2 < 2.4 in Chunk 1 but 2 ≥ 1.6 in Chunk 2, so Chunk 2 catches it (2.4 + 1.6 = 4: it cannot be below the line in both). {banana, orange} (2 and 2) is caught the same way; {orange} (3 and 2) is caught by both chunks (Figure L4-Q6-1).
Key idea — two different "monotonicity" rules

(1) A-Priori monotonicity (inside a mapper): if an itemset is frequent, all its subsets are frequent. (2) SON "monotonicity" (Slide 57, across mappers): if an itemset is frequent in the whole file, it is frequent in at least one chunk. Rule (1) makes each mapper fast; rule (2) is what guarantees SON never misses anything.

(e-ii) Why Pass 2 removes false positives. A false positive is an itemset reported as frequent although it is not frequent in the whole data.

  1. Where false positives come from: a candidate only needs to be frequent in one chunk — a local property (Slide 56: "any one or more subsets of the baskets"). It can be popular in one chunk and rare elsewhere. Example: {pear} is in 100 % of Chunk 2 (count 2) but 0 in Chunk 1, total 2 < 4; {apple} is 2 in Chunk 1 and 1 in Chunk 2, total 3 < 4.
  2. How Pass 2 fixes it: Pass 2 computes the exact global support of each candidate (sum of exact chunk counts) and applies the global test "total ≥ 4". Here 6 of the 9 candidates fail it and are discarded. Without Pass 2 (Slide 60 says the candidates are "optionally evaluated"; skip it only if false positives are acceptable), SON would output all 9 itemsets, 6 of them wrong, with no true supports. So: Pass 1 guarantees completeness (no false negatives); Pass 2 guarantees correctness (no false positives).

(e-iii) Local threshold versus global threshold.

  1. Beyond the slides: the textbook rule (Mining of Massive Datasets, Leskovec–Rajaraman–Ullman, Section 6.4.3). A mapper whose data holds the fraction p of all baskets uses local threshold p · s (rounded up when counts are integers). With k equal chunks this is s ÷ k. (Slide 59 lets a mapper process a subset of chunks; then p is the share of baskets that this mapper gets.) The slide uses 2 in both chunks; 2 = 4 ÷ 2 is the right value for two equal halves, and here it is also safe for the unequal chunks (table below). The slides do not say how the 2 was chosen.
ChunkBasketsFraction pp · sSmallest integer count that reaches itSlide usesSafe?
Chunk 133/5 = 0.60.6 × 4 = 2.432Yes: 2 ≤ 2.4 (more candidates than needed)
Chunk 222/5 = 0.40.4 × 4 = 1.622Yes: exactly the tightest safe value
  1. Integer version of the guarantee: if the thresholds are t1 and t2, an itemset missed by both chunks has counts ≤ t1 − 1 and ≤ t2 − 1, so its total is ≤ (t1 − 1) + (t2 − 1). No false negatives are possible as long as this is below s = 4.
  2. What happens when the local threshold is changed (every row verified by running SON on the five baskets):

  1. Conclusion: a lower local threshold is always safe but produces more candidates (more memory and more counting in Pass 2); a higher local threshold than p · s can break the no-false-negative guarantee. Use exactly (or just below) p · s.
Common mistake

Using the global threshold 4 inside each chunk. A chunk is only part of the data, so its counts are smaller; with threshold 4 almost nothing would be found in a chunk of 2 or 3 baskets (row (4, 4) above). Also do not confuse "candidate" with "frequent": a candidate is only locally frequent in some chunk; only the global sum ≥ s makes it frequent.

Part (f) — the MapReduce view (Slides 58–60, 65–66)

  1. Setting (Slide 58, "SON — Distributed Version"): the baskets are spread over many nodes (chunk servers); each node computes frequent itemsets on its own data, and then the counts of all candidates are accumulated. SON is thus two MapReduce jobs in sequence: Job 1 = Map Phase 1 + Reduce Phase 1 (find candidates, Pass 1); Job 2 = Map Phase 2 + Reduce Phase 2 (count candidates, Pass 2).
  2. The four phases (Figure L4-Q6-2 shows the data flow for our example; the table after it says what each phase does, and its slide):
PhaseInputWhat it doesOutput
Map Phase 1
Slide 59, 63		one or more chunks of baskets per mapper (mappers work independently, in parallel)runs an in-memory frequent-itemset algorithm (A-Priori, PCY, FP-growth …) on its chunk with the local thresholdthe locally frequent itemsets (the "candidate frequent itemsets"). Beyond the slides: in the textbook (MMDS §6.4.4) they are emitted as key–value pairs (itemset, 1)
Reduce Phase 1
Slide 60, 64		all candidate itemsets from all mappersgathers equal itemsets together and eliminates duplicates; counts are ignoredthe global list of candidate itemsets (potential frequent itemsets)
Map Phase 2
Slide 65, 67		the candidate list (broadcast to every mapper) + the mapper's chunkeach mapper counts the support of every candidate in its own chunk, zeros included(candidate, local count) for each candidate and chunk
Reduce Phase 2
Slide 66, 68–69		all local counts of each candidateadds the local counts to get the global support and keeps those that meet the thresholdthe frequent itemsets with their global supports: {banana}=4, {orange}=5, {banana, orange}=4
  1. Why it suits big data: each mapper only needs its chunk to fit in main memory; chunks are independent, so the work parallelises over many nodes; the data is read exactly twice (once per job), independent of the itemset size, whereas A-Priori needs k passes for itemsets of size k (Slide 53).
CompareRandom sampling (Slides 54–55)SON (Slides 56–60)
Which data is mineda random sample onlythe whole file, chunk by chunk (Slide 56: "we are not sampling")
Threshold useds scaled to the sample sizes scaled to each chunk size (p · s)
False negativespossible: "you do not catch sets frequent in the whole but not in the sample"none (monotonicity argument)
False positivespossible unless a second pass verifies the candidatesremoved by Pass 2 (Reduce Phase 2)
Passes over the full datanone for mining (one optional pass to verify)exactly 2
Slide erratum (imprecision on Slide 53)

Slide 53 lists SON together with random sampling under "Use 2 or fewer passes for all sizes, but may miss some frequent itemsets". That description is true of random sampling, but SON with both passes does not miss any frequent itemset (proved in (e-i)); it is an exact algorithm. Write the correct statement in the exam: SON finds exactly the frequent itemsets in two passes.

Exam tip

For "explain SON" answers, write in this order: (1) split the file into chunks that fit in memory; (2) Pass 1: find frequent itemsets in each chunk with a lowered local support p·s, union them as candidates; (3) Pass 2: count the candidates over all data, keep those ≥ s; (4) why correct: frequent overall ⇒ frequent in at least one chunk (no false negatives); Pass 2 removes false positives; (5) MapReduce: Map 1 / Reduce 1 = candidates, Map 2 / Reduce 2 = counts. For a numeric example, show the table of local counts, the candidate list, the per-chunk counts and the sums — each is a mark.

Final answer:
(a) Map Phase 1 (local support 2). Chunk 1: {apple}:2, {banana}:2, {orange}:3, {apple, orange}:2, {banana, orange}:2. Chunk 2: {banana}:2, {orange}:2, {pear}:2, {banana, orange}:2, {banana, pear}:2, {orange, pear}:2, {banana, orange, pear}:2 (the last one is missing on Slide 63).
(b) Reduce Phase 1: 9 unique candidates = the 8 on Slide 64 plus {banana, orange, pear}.
(c)–(d) Map Phase 2 counts (Chunk 1 | Chunk 2) and Reduce Phase 2 totals: {apple} 2|1 → 3; {banana} 2|2 → 4; {orange} 3|2 → 5; {pear} 0|2 → 2; {apple, orange} 2|1 → 3; {banana, orange} 2|2 → 4; {banana, pear} 0|2 → 2; {orange, pear} 0|2 → 2; {banana, orange, pear} 0|2 → 2. Frequent itemsets (global support ≥ 4): {banana} = 4, {orange} = 5, {banana, orange} = 4. The other 6 candidates are false positives removed in Pass 2.
(e) No false negatives: frequent overall ⇒ local count ≥ p·s in some chunk (else total < s·∑p = s; here: not locally frequent in both chunks ⇒ total ≤ 1 + 1 = 2 < 4). Pass 2 gives exact counts, so no false positives. Local threshold ≤ p·s (2.4 and 1.6 here, i.e. 3 and 2 as integers; the slide uses 2 and 2); never the global 4.
(f) Map 1 = local frequent itemsets per chunk; Reduce 1 = union without duplicates; Map 2 = broadcast candidates, count them per chunk; Reduce 2 = sum the counts, keep ≥ s.
Where the marks come from: (1) stating the support definition and threshold s = 4 on 5 baskets, local support 2; (2) Chunk 1: 3 singletons + 2 pairs with correct counts and the triple correctly excluded; (3) Chunk 2: 3 singletons + 3 pairs and the triple {banana, orange, pear} (the slide's list leaves it out — you still get the final answer without it); (4) Reduce Phase 1: union with duplicates merged, 9 candidates (8 as on the slide is accepted); (5) Map Phase 2: every candidate counted in every chunk, including 0s and the small counts such as {apple}:1; (6) Reduce Phase 2: sums and comparison with 4; (7) the three frequent itemsets with supports 4, 5, 4; (8) no false negatives: argument that frequent overall ⇒ frequent in at least one chunk; (9) Pass 2 removes false positives, with an example such as {pear} or {apple}; (10) local threshold ≈ p·s and why not 4; (11) the roles of the four MapReduce phases.
Slide erratum: Slide 63 omits {banana, orange, pear} (local count 2 in Chunk 2), so Slide 64 lists 8 candidates instead of 9 and Slide 67 omits its counts (0 in Chunk 1, 2 in Chunk 2); Slides 68–69 lack its row (0 + 2 = 2, a false positive; the slide strikes out five lines, the corrected list has six). Everything else on Slides 63–69 re-computed correctly (Chunk 1 list, all counts on Slide 67, all sums on Slide 68, the struck-through lines on Slide 69) and the slide's final answer {banana}=4, {orange}=5, {banana, orange}=4 is correct and unchanged. Minor: on Slide 67 the Mapper 2 line lacks separators between items; Slide 69 is Slide 68 repeated with strike-throughs; Slide 53 wrongly groups SON with "may miss some frequent itemsets" (see the imprecision box above).

Sampling versus SON

Lecture 4 · Slides 53–60 (comparison)

Random sampling (Slides 54–55)SON (Slides 56–60)
Data usedOnly a random sample of the baskets.All baskets, in chunks that fit in memory (not sampling).
Passes over the file1 (read the sample); 2 with optional verification.Exactly 2: Pass 1 finds candidates, Pass 2 counts them.
Threshold inside memoryScaled to the sample size (p × s).Scaled to each chunk's share of the file (pchunk × s).
False positivesPossible; removed only by the optional second pass.Possible in the candidate list; always removed by the (required) second pass.
False negativesPossible, and not recoverable.None (monotonicity idea, Slide 57).
ResultApproximate.Exact: same as A-Priori on the whole file.
ParallelismThe slides do not present it as a distributed design (one in-memory sample); SON is the one built for MapReduce.Chunks mined independently: maps naturally onto MapReduce (Slides 58–66).
Cost / weak pointCheapest. Risk: unlucky sample.A second full pass; the candidate list can be large if the local threshold is low.
Exam tip

"Why does SON never miss a frequent itemset but sampling can?" Sampling looks at only part of the data, so a globally frequent itemset can look rare in the sample. SON looks at every chunk, and a globally frequent itemset must be locally frequent in at least one of them.

Putting it all together: the cat-and-dog baskets

Lecture 4 · Slides 70–77

Slides 70–77 are a pair-by-pair practice session on one data set: eight "baskets", each of which is a sentence (a list of words). The words are the items. It reuses everything from the first half of the lecture: support and frequent itemsets (Slides 8, 30), A-Priori (Slides 30–36), confidence (Slide 10) and interest (Slide 11). The questions are posed on Slides 70, 72, 74 and 76; the answers are on Slides 71, 73, 75 and 77.

SlidesQuestion (threshold s = 3)Tool you need
70–71Compute the frequent pairs.A-Priori: Pass 1 counts words, Pass 2 counts pairs of frequent words.
72–73Are there frequent triples, quadruples or larger sets?Monotonicity: a triple needs all three of its pairs frequent; a quadruple all four triples.
74–75Confidence of the rule {cat, dog} → and, and of the rule {cat} → kitten.conf(I → j) = support(I ∪ {j}) ÷ support(I).
76–77Interest of {dog} → cat and of {cat} → kitten; "interesting"?Interest = conf − Pr[j], Pr[j] = share of all baskets containing j.

Ground rules the slides leave unsaid

Lecture 4 · Slides 70–71

  • A basket is a set. A word repeated in one basket ("a ... a" in basket 2, "training ... training" in basket 4, "and ... and" in basket 5) counts once for that basket.
  • Capital letters are ignored: "Cat" and "cat" are the same item. Without this, the answer to Slide 70 would shrink to just two pairs.
  • The symbol "&" in basket 6 is just another item, not the word "and".
  • Support is a count of baskets, and a count of exactly 3 is frequent (≥ s).
Key idea

This is A-Priori in miniature. Pass 1 shrinks 46 distinct words to 5 frequent ones. Pass 2 only needs the 10 pairs among those 5 (not the roughly one thousand possible pairs of all 46 words). The pairs that survive decide which triples are even worth counting, and so on. Each level uses the previous level's survivors, which is the A-Priori pruning principle on Slide 30.

Errors on the answer slides

Lecture 4 · Slides 71 and 73

Slide erratum

Slide 71 prints a table of which baskets contain each pair. Two cells omit basket 7: {dog, and} should list baskets 1, 2, 7, 8 (support 4, slide: 1, 2, 8) and {cat, and} should list 1, 2, 5, 7 (support 4, slide: 1, 2, 5). The five frequent pairs the slide lists are still right, because both 3 and 4 are at least 3.

Slide 73 answers the triples question with only "{dog, cat, a} is a frequent triple". There are two frequent triples: the second, {dog, cat, and} (baskets 1, 2, 7), is missing, a knock-on effect of the Slide 71 table error. It also says "There are not frequent quadruples" (should be "no"); the conclusion, no frequent quadruple, is right. The slide shows no reasoning, so a copied answer would earn no method marks. Quiz L4-Q7 gives the full working.

Confidence and interest on real data

Lecture 4 · Slides 74–77

Two lessons come out of Slides 74–77, both worth remembering for the exam:

  • Confidence divides by the support of the left side only (the number of baskets containing everything on the left), not by 8 and not by the support of the right side. Slide 75 reads: of the five baskets with cat and dog, three also have "and".
  • A high-looking confidence can still be uninteresting. "Cat" is in three quarters of all baskets, so finding it in 5/7 of the "dog" baskets means that dog adds nothing. Interest, being confidence minus the baseline probability, exposes this. Slide 77 concludes that both rules have interest close to 0 and are therefore "not very interesting".

Beyond the slides: in the textbook an association rule counts as interesting if its interest is large in absolute value (strongly positive or strongly negative). Slide 11 only counts high positive values. Also, {cat, kitten} has support 1, below s = 3, so the lecture's pipeline (rules are built from frequent itemsets, Slides 16–18) would never even generate the rule cat → kitten. Slide 77 evaluates it anyway as a formula exercise.

Try it yourself first: with the eight baskets in front of you and the ground rules above, work out all four parts before opening the solution.

Quiz L4-Q7Cat-and-dog baskets: pairs, triples, confidence, interest Lecture 4 · Slides 70–77
Question (as on the slides)

Consider the following set of eight baskets. Each basket is a list of words (the words are the items). Assume we set our threshold at s = 3. (Slides 70, 72, 74 and 76 pose the questions; Slides 71, 73, 75 and 77 print the slide answers.)

BasketWords in the basket (exactly as on Slide 70)
1{Cat, and, dog, bites}
2{Yahoo, news, claims, a, cat, mated, with, a, dog, and, produced, viable, offspring}
3{Cat, killer, likely, is, a, big, dog}
4{Professional, free, advice, on, dog, training, puppy, training}
5{Cat, and, kitten, training, and, behavior}
6{Dog, &, Cat, provides, dog, training, in, Eugene, Oregon}
7{Dog, and, cat, is, a, slang, term, used, by, police, officers, for, a, male, female, relationship}
8{Shop, for, your, show, dog, grooming, and, pet, supplies}
(a) Compute the frequent pairs of items. Lecture 4 · Slides 70–71
(b) Are there any frequent triples, quadruples or larger sets? Lecture 4 · Slides 72–73
(c) What is the confidence of the rule {cat, dog} → and? What is the confidence of the rule {cat} → kitten? Lecture 4 · Slides 74–75
(d) What is the interest of the rule {dog} → cat? What is the interest of the rule {cat} → kitten? Are these rules “interesting”? Lecture 4 · Slides 76–77
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
  1. Tools: the definitions we need (Lecture 4 · Slides 8, 10, 11, 16, 30, 31).
    • Support of an itemset I = the number of baskets that contain all items of I (Slide 8). I is frequent if it appears in at least s baskets, i.e. support(I) ≥ 3. A support of exactly 3 is frequent.
    • Confidence (Slide 10): conf(I → j) = support(I ∪ {j})support(I), the probability of j given that the basket contains all of I. The denominator is the support of the left side (Slide 16 calls this the support of the rule).
    • Interest (Slide 11): Interest(I → j) = conf(I → j) − Pr[j], where Pr[j] = (number of baskets containing j) ÷ (total number of baskets, here 8). “Interesting” rules are those with high interest, usually above 0.5.
    • Monotonicity (Slide 30): if a set is frequent, every subset of it is frequent. Contrapositive: a set with an infrequent subset cannot be frequent. So a pair can be frequent only if both its words are frequent, and a triple only if all three of its pairs are frequent.
    • How to read the baskets. A basket is a set of words, so a word repeated inside one basket counts once. Capital letters are ignored (“Cat” = “cat”, “Dog” = “dog”). The symbol “&” in basket 6 is just another token, not the word “and”.
    Beginner intuition

    Think of each basket as one shopping trip and each word as an item bought on that trip. Support = “on how many trips did these words show up together?”. Frequent = “on at least 3 trips”. Confidence of “left side → right word” = “of the trips that had the whole left side, what fraction also had the right word?”. Interest asks whether that fraction beats the right word’s everyday popularity: if a word is in 75 % of all trips anyway, finding it in 71 % of the trips that contain another word tells you nothing new.

  2. Clean the data: each basket becomes a set of lower-case words. Why: support counts baskets (Slide 8), so a word written twice in one basket counts once, and “Cat”/“cat” (also “Dog”/“dog”) must be the same word. Repeats that disappear: “a” in baskets 2 and 7, “training” in basket 4, “and” in basket 5, “dog” in basket 6. The “&” in basket 6 stays as its own token (it is not “and”). After cleaning, the eight baskets contain 46 different words (checked by program).
  3. (a) Pass 1 of A-Priori: count every single word (Slide 31). Why: by monotonicity a pair can be frequent only if both of its words are frequent, so the single-word counts tell us which pairs are worth counting at all.
    WordBaskets containing itSupport≥ 3 ?
    dog1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 87frequent
    cat1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 76frequent
    and1, 2, 5, 7, 85frequent

    each of the other 39 words (e.g. kitten, bites, puppy, &)one basket each1no
    The frequent words are L1 = {dog, cat, and, a, training}; the nearest misses “for” and “is” have support 2. So we count only C(5, 2) = 10 candidate pairs instead of C(46, 2) = 1035.
  4. (a) Pass 2 of A-Priori: count the 10 candidate pairs (Slide 31). First, for every basket list which of the five frequent words it contains; a basket with n frequent words adds C(n, 2) pairs:

    Sanity check: the pairs added per basket total 26, and the supports 5 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 0 also total 26. Baskets 2 and 7 are the busiest: each contains dog, cat, and, a, so each counts for six pairs.
  5. (a) Keep the pairs with support ≥ 3. L2 = {dog, cat} (5; baskets 1, 2, 3, 6, 7), {dog, and} (4; baskets 1, 2, 7, 8), {cat, and} (4; baskets 1, 2, 5, 7), {dog, a} (3; baskets 2, 3, 7) and {cat, a} (3; baskets 2, 3, 7). The other five fail: {a, and} 2, {dog, training} 2, {cat, training} 2, {and, training} 1, {a, training} 0. Double-check: a brute-force count over every pair that occurs anywhere in the baskets (271 distinct pairs, not only pairs of frequent words) finds no other pair with support 3; the best misses, such as {dog, is} and {a, and}, have support 2. So there are exactly five frequent pairs.
  6. (b) Frequent triples. Idea: by monotonicity a triple can be frequent only if all three of its pairs are in L2. Of the four triples that can be made from {dog, cat, and, a}, two pass this test; we count all four to be sure. Note that {a, and} is not in L2 (support 2).
    TripleIts three pairs (in L2?)Baskets with all 3 wordsSupportVerdict
    {dog, cat, a}{dog,cat} ✓, {dog,a} ✓, {cat,a} ✓2, 3, 73frequent
    {dog, cat, and}{dog,cat} ✓, {dog,and} ✓, {cat,and} ✓1, 2, 73frequent
    {dog, and, a}{dog,and} ✓, {dog,a} ✓, {and,a} ✗ (2)2, 72pruned
    {cat, and, a}{cat,and} ✓, {cat,a} ✓, {and,a} ✗ (2)2, 72pruned
    the 6 triples containing trainingeach contains a pair with “training”, and no such pair is frequent–at most 1pruned
    So two triples are frequent: {dog, cat, a} (baskets 2, 3, 7) and {dog, cat, and} (baskets 1, 2, 7), each with support exactly 3 = s. A brute-force count over every possible triple of words confirms that these are the only two. The slide builds C3 a little more loosely (Slide 35: Ck from Lk−1 and L1, giving 9 distinct candidate triples); their supports are 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, so L3 is the same two triples. (Slide 73 lists only the first triple: see the Slide erratum below.)
  7. (b) Quadruples and larger sets. A quadruple needs all four of its sub-triples to be frequent. Among the five frequent words, four of the five 4-sets contain training (excluded as before), leaving only {dog, cat, and, a}. Its sub-triples are {dog,cat,and} ✓, {dog,cat,a} ✓, {dog,and,a} ✗ and {cat,and,a} ✗, so it is pruned. Counting it anyway: it is in baskets 2 and 7 only → support 2 < 3. No frequent quadruple, and therefore no frequent set of 5 or more words (such a set would contain a frequent quadruple, by monotonicity). The largest frequent itemsets have size 3. In total there are 5 + 5 + 2 = 12 frequent itemsets (5 words, 5 pairs, 2 triples).
  8. (c) Confidence of {cat, dog} → and. Formula: conf = support({cat, dog, and}) ÷ support({cat, dog}).
    • support({cat, dog}) = 5: baskets 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 contain both cat and dog.
    • support({cat, dog, and}) = 3: of those five, only baskets 1, 2, 7 also contain “and” (basket 3 has no “and”; basket 6 has only the symbol “&”).
    • conf = 35 = 0.6, i.e. 60 % of the baskets that contain cat and dog also contain “and”.
  9. (c) Confidence of {cat} → kitten. Here I = {cat} and j = kitten.
    • support({cat}) = 6: baskets 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7.
    • support({cat, kitten}) = 1: only basket 5 contains “kitten” (it appears in no other basket).
    • conf = 16 ≈ 0.167 (about 17 %).

    Link to Slides 16–17: because {cat, kitten} is not a frequent itemset (support 1 < 3), the two-step method of Slide 17 would never generate this rule; the quiz simply asks us to compute its confidence.

  10. Picture of the counts used in (a)–(c). Each row is a word or itemset; a filled square means that basket contains every word of the row. Support is the number of filled squares. Reading downwards, adding a word can only remove filled squares (monotonicity). Confidence will be a ratio of two rows.
  11. (d) Interest of {dog} → cat. Formula: Interest = conf − Pr[cat].
    • conf({dog} → cat) = support({dog, cat}) ÷ support({dog}) = 57 ≈ 0.714 (dog is in baskets 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8; five of them, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, also contain cat).
    • Pr[cat] = fraction of all 8 baskets containing cat = 68 = 34 = 0.75.
    • Interest = 57 − 34 = 2028 − 2128 = −128 ≈ −0.036.
  12. (d) Interest of {cat} → kitten.
    • conf({cat} → kitten) = 16 (from part (c)).
    • Pr[kitten] = 18 = 0.125 (only basket 5 of the 8 baskets contains kitten).
    • Interest = 16 − 18 = 424 − 324 = 124 ≈ 0.042.
    RuleConfidencePr[right side]InterestInteresting?
    {dog} → cat5/7 ≈ 0.7146/8 = 0.75−1/28 ≈ −0.036no
    {cat} → kitten1/6 ≈ 0.1671/8 = 0.1251/24 ≈ 0.042no
  13. (d) Are the rules “interesting”? Slide 11: interesting rules are those with a high interest value, usually above 0.5. Here the interest values are −0.036 and +0.042, both essentially 0 and far below 0.5, so neither rule is interesting (the slide says “not very interesting”). In words: {dog} → cat has a fairly high confidence (0.714), but cat is already in 75 % of all baskets, so learning that a basket has “dog” does not make “cat” any more likely (71 % versus 75 %). This is exactly the “high confidence is not enough” warning of Slide 11. For {cat} → kitten, “kitten” is rare (1 of 8 baskets) and having “cat” lifts its chance only from 12.5 % to 16.7 %, based on a single basket, which is no real evidence of a link.

    Beyond the slides: the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets) also counts a very negative interest (the left side makes the right side much less likely) as notable. −0.036 is not that either, so the conclusion is the same.

Common mistakes
  • Counting occurrences instead of baskets. “training” is written 4 times but lives in only 3 baskets (4, 5, 6); “a” is written 5 times but is in only 3 baskets; “dog” 8 times in 7 baskets; “and” 6 times in 5 baskets. Support counts baskets, so always use the set of words of a basket.
  • Treating “&” (basket 6) as “and”. That would give {cat, dog, and} support 4 and confidence 4/5 instead of 3/5. Likewise do not treat “Cat” and “cat” as different words.
  • Using “> 3” instead of “≥ 3”. {dog, a}, {cat, a}, {dog, cat, a} and {dog, cat, and} all have support exactly 3 and are frequent (Slide 8: “at least s”).
  • Calling {a, and} frequent: it appears together only in baskets 2 and 7, support 2. That is why {dog, and, a} and {cat, and, a} fail.
  • Stopping at the slide’s single triple {dog, cat, a} and missing {dog, cat, and} (see the Slide erratum).
  • Dividing by the wrong number. Confidence divides by the support of the left side (5 for {cat, dog}, 6 for {cat}), not by 8; Pr[j] divides by 8, the number of all baskets. And Interest = conf − Pr[j], not Pr[j] − conf.
Exam tip

Write the basket numbers next to every count (for example “baskets with both cat and dog: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 → 5; of these, the ones with the word and: 1, 2, 7 → 3”). It makes each step checkable, so partial marks are easy to award; method marks go to the formula, the two supports and the final fraction. For (b) name both triples and say why {dog, and, a} and {cat, and, a} fail ({and, a} is not frequent). For (d) always give the number, compare it with the “usually above 0.5” guide and add one sentence of reason (the base rate Pr[j]): “near 0, far below 0.5, so not interesting”.

Slide erratum
  • Slide 71, table of pairs: it lists {dog, and} in baskets 1, 2, 8 and {cat, and} in baskets 1, 2, 5. Basket 7 (“Dog, and, cat, …”) contains dog, and, cat, so the correct lists are 1, 2, 7, 8 and 1, 2, 5, 7, and both pairs have support 4, not 3. The slide contradicts itself, because Slide 75 uses basket 7 for “and”. The list of five frequent pairs is not affected, and every other cell of the slide’s table is correct.
  • Slide 73: it names only {dog, cat, a} as a frequent triple. {dog, cat, and} is also frequent (baskets 1, 2, 7 → support 3 = s; its pairs have supports 5, 4, 4). Slide 75 itself proves it: it says “and” appears with cat and dog in baskets (1), (2) and (7). A likely cause of the slip (our inference): with basket 7 missing from Slide 71’s table, {dog, cat, and} would look like it has support 2. “No frequent quadruples” on Slide 73 is correct.
Final answer: (a) five frequent pairs: {dog, cat} = 5, {dog, and} = 4, {cat, and} = 4, {dog, a} = 3, {cat, a} = 3 (frequent words: dog 7, cat 6, and 5, a 3, training 3). (b) Two frequent triples: {dog, cat, a} (support 3, baskets 2, 3, 7) and {dog, cat, and} (support 3, baskets 1, 2, 7); no frequent quadruples (the only candidate {dog, cat, and, a} has support 2), hence nothing larger. (c) conf({cat, dog} → and) = 3/5 = 0.6; conf({cat} → kitten) = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. (d) Interest({dog} → cat) = 5/7 − 3/4 = −1/28 ≈ −0.036; Interest({cat} → kitten) = 1/6 − 1/8 = 1/24 ≈ 0.042. Both are close to 0 (far below 0.5), so neither rule is interesting.
Where the marks come from: (1) Correct definitions: support counts baskets, frequent means support ≥ 3, baskets treated as sets and words case-insensitively. (2) Single-word counts and the five frequent words (dog 7, cat 6, and 5, a 3, training 3), with the monotonicity reason for counting only pairs of frequent words. (3) The ten pair counts and the list of the five frequent pairs. (4) Triples: candidates chosen by monotonicity, counted (baskets 2, 3, 7 and 1, 2, 7), both frequent triples named, {and, a} named as the reason the other two fail; quadruple {dog, cat, and, a} shown to have support 2, so none and nothing larger. (5) Confidence: formula, support({cat, dog}) = 5 and support({cat, dog, and}) = 3 giving 3/5; support({cat}) = 6 and support({cat, kitten}) = 1 giving 1/6. (6) Interest: formula conf − Pr[j]; conf 5/7 and Pr[cat] = 3/4 giving −0.036; conf 1/6 and Pr[kitten] = 1/8 giving 0.042. (7) Conclusion “not interesting” with the reason (values near 0, not above 0.5; base rate).
Slide check: (a) matches the slide’s five frequent pairs, but Slide 71’s table omits basket 7 for {dog, and} and {cat, and} (true supports are 4 and 4, not 3 and 3); the answer is unchanged. (b) Slide erratum: Slide 73 lists only {dog, cat, a}; {dog, cat, and} (baskets 1, 2, 7) is also a frequent triple. “No frequent quadruples” matches. (c) matches (3/5 and 1/6). (d) matches (−0.036 and 0.042; “not very interesting”). Every number above was recomputed by program from the eight baskets.

PCY: the bitmap, how it is used and why it exists

Lecture 4 · Slides 81–82

Worked solution: Quiz L4-Q9, .

Questions (Slide 81): (1) describe how the bitmap is used in PCY; (2) why is the Pass-1 hash table transformed into a bitmap? The slide shows PCY's two memory layouts.

QuestionFull-mark answer
How is the bitmap used?Between the passes the hash table is summarised as a bitmap with one bit per bucket: 1 if the bucket's count reached the threshold s (a frequent bucket), 0 if not. In Pass 2 a pair {i, j} is counted only if both i and j are frequent items and the pair hashes (with the same hash function as in Pass 1) to a bucket whose bit is 1 (Slide 43).
Why a bitmap?A counter is a 32-bit integer, but we only need to know "frequent or not". One bit replaces 32, so the bitmap takes 1/32 of the space and leaves the memory free for the counters of candidate pairs, which is PCY's bottleneck.
Slide erratum

The answer on Slide 82 explains how the bitmap is built (one bit per bucket, 1 if frequent) and how small it is (1/32), but never says how it is used in Pass 2. The use is the candidate-pair test of Slide 43 above. "The figure" mentioned in the answer is on Slide 81, not Slide 82. The question's "hash map" means the hash table. The slide's bitmap box is drawn much larger than 1/32 of the table; the figure is only schematic. See Quiz L4-Q9. Beyond the slides (a sanity check): 108 buckets need 4 × 108 bytes = 400 MB as 4-byte counters, but only 108 bits = 12.5 MB as a bitmap.

Multistage: the key idea

Lecture 4 · Slides 83–84

Worked solution: Quiz L4-Q10, .

Question (Slide 83): describe the key idea behind the multistage algorithm. The slide shows three memory layouts. Slide 84's answer: "The Multistage Algorithm uses additional hash tables to reduce the number of candidate pairs."

For full marks expand the one-line answer with what the figure shows:

  1. Pass 1 is PCY's Pass 1: count items and hash all pairs into hash table 1.
  2. Between passes: items become a list of frequent items; hash table 1 becomes Bitmap 1.
  3. Pass 2 (the extra pass): hash the candidate pairs again with a different hash function into a second hash table; afterwards it becomes Bitmap 2.
  4. Pass 3: count a pair only if both items are frequent and it hits a frequent bucket in Bitmap 1 and Bitmap 2.
  5. Why: memory for the pair counters is the bottleneck, and more filters mean fewer candidate pairs. Cost: one extra pass (three passes in total).
Slide erratum

The one-line answer on Slide 84 omits the "different hash function", the "frequent in every bitmap" condition and the extra pass. "Ans" there also lacks the colon used on the other answer slides. For Multihash (the other PCY refinement, Slides 49–51) the extra tables are built together in the first pass, so no extra pass is needed, at the price of smaller tables; Quiz L4-Q10 covers both.
