Quick recap
  • A-Priori and PCY need about k passes for size-k itemsets; sampling and SON need at most 2 (Slide 53).
  • Sampling: scaled threshold, in-memory run; false positives fixable with a second pass, false negatives not (Slides 54–55).
  • SON: not sampling; chunks, candidate = locally frequent anywhere; second pass counts candidates; frequent overall ⇒ frequent in at least one chunk (Slides 56–57).
  • SON MapReduce: Map 1 mines chunks; Reduce 1 unions candidates; Map 2 counts broadcast candidates; Reduce 2 sums and filters (Slides 58–60, 65–66). Phase 2 is required, not optional (Slide 60 erratum).
  • The worked SON example needs 9 candidates (the slides list 8) and ends with {banana}, {orange}, {banana, orange} (Slides 61–69).
  • Slide 71's table and Slide 73's answer have errors (basket 7, second frequent triple); confidence divides by the left-side support; interest = confidence − Pr[j] (Slides 70–77).

Theory Q&A bank

Lecture 4 · Slides 1–86

Cover the answer, write your own, then compare. Numbered points are marking points. These questions are self-made practice except where a slide poses the question itself (Q4, Q10 and Q12 come from Slides 22, 81–82 and 83–84). Lecture 4 contains no BFR material (BFR belongs to Lecture 5), so no BFR question appears here.

Q1. Define support, support threshold, frequent itemset and confidence.

Lecture 4 · Slides 8, 10

  1. Support of an itemset I = the number of baskets that contain all items of I.
  2. Support threshold s = a basket count chosen by the analyst; I is frequent if support(I) ≥ s ("at least", so equality counts).
  3. Confidence of the rule I → j = support(I ∪ {j}) ÷ support(I): of the baskets containing I, the fraction that also contain j.
  4. Example (Slide 9 data, s = 3): support({m,b}) = 4, so {m,b} is frequent.

Q2. Why is a high-confidence rule not necessarily interesting? What is the interest measure?

Lecture 4 · Slides 11–15

  1. If j is bought very often anyway (for example milk), X → j has high confidence for almost every X, although X tells us nothing about j.
  2. Interest(I → j) = conf(I → j) − Pr[j], where Pr[j] = fraction of all baskets that contain j. It measures how much knowing I changes the chance of j.
  3. Interest near 0 means no real association; large positive means a real one. The slide treats high values (usually above 0.5) as interesting. Beyond the slides: the textbook counts large negative interest as interesting too (the left side makes j much less likely), so judge by the size of |interest|.
  4. Example: {m,b} → c has conf 1/2, Pr[c] = 5/8, interest = −1/8: not interesting.

Q3. State the association-rule mining problem and the two-step recipe. Which step is hard and why?

Lecture 4 · Slides 16–17

  1. Problem: find all rules with support ≥ s and confidence ≥ c.
  2. Step 1: find all frequent itemsets I.
  3. Step 2: for every non-empty proper subset A of each frequent I, form A → I \ A, compute conf = support(I) ÷ support(A), and keep it if ≥ c. The needed supports are already known because A is a subset of a frequent set, hence frequent (monotonicity).
  4. Step 1 is the hard part: it must count a huge number of candidate itemsets over a file too large for memory; Step 2 only divides numbers Step 1 produced.

Q4. Swapping in and out of memory is a disaster. Why? (the slide's own question)

Lecture 4 · Slide 22

  1. Counting increments counters at essentially random positions, one per pair occurrence.
  2. If the counters do not fit in RAM, most increments hit a page that is on disk, so each costs a disk access (milliseconds) instead of a memory access (about 100 nanoseconds): thousands of times slower (thrashing).
  3. Design rule: only count as many things per pass as fit in main memory, even if that needs more passes.

Q5. Why is finding frequent pairs the hardest part of the problem?

Lecture 4 · Slide 23

  1. Frequent pairs are common; frequent triples are rare, because the probability that k items appear together drops exponentially with k.
  2. Single items need only n counters, but there are about n²/2 possible pairs, so pair counters are the first level that strains memory.
  3. Once the frequent pairs are known, only triples whose sub-pairs are frequent need counting, which is a small set. So algorithms concentrate on pairs first.

Q6. Compare the triangular matrix and the triples method for counting pairs. When is each better?

Lecture 4 · Slides 24–27

  1. Triangular matrix: a flat array with one 4-byte counter for each of the T = n(n−1)/2 possible pairs; needs items numbered 1..n; memory 4·T whether or not the pair occurs.
  2. Triples [i, j, c]: one 12-byte record for each pair that actually occurs (O of them); memory 12·O; needs a lookup structure such as a hash table.
  3. Break-even: 12·O < 4·T ⇔ O < T/3. Triples win only if fewer than 1/3 of all possible pairs occur.
  4. Example: n = 10⁵ gives T ≈ 5 × 10⁹ pairs and 4·T ≈ 20 GB for the matrix.

Q7. State the A-Priori property and explain the two passes for pairs.

Lecture 4 · Slides 30–32

  1. Monotonicity: if a set appears in at least s baskets, so does every subset. Contrapositive: if item i is infrequent, no pair containing i can be frequent.
  2. Pass 1: count each item (memory proportional to the number of items). Keep the items with count ≥ s.
  3. Pass 2: for each basket generate only pairs of frequent items and count them (memory about m(m−1)/2 counters for m frequent items). Pairs with count ≥ s are the frequent pairs.
  4. It is exact: every discarded pair had an infrequent item.

Q8. Explain Ck and Lk and how A-Priori finds all frequent itemsets. Why renumber the items?

Lecture 4 · Slides 33–36

  1. Ck = candidate k-itemsets (not yet ruled out by the pass for k−1); Lk = the truly frequent ones. C1 = all items → count → L1 → construct C2 → count → L2 → … until Lk is empty.
  2. Construct Ck+1 from Lk (and L1); the standard rule also requires every k-subset of a candidate to be in Lk.
  3. One pass for each k, so the number of passes equals the size of the largest itemset. k = 2 needs the most memory.
  4. Renumbering: the triangular matrix needs ids 1..n with no gaps. Renumber the m frequent items 1..m and keep a table new number → old item number; the matrix then has only m(m−1)/2 cells.

Q9. Describe the PCY algorithm. Why can it never lose a frequent pair?

Lecture 4 · Slides 38–43

  1. Observation: in A-Priori Pass 1 most memory is idle. PCY uses it for a hash table of buckets.
  2. Pass 1: count items and hash every pair of every basket to a bucket; each bucket stores only a count, not the pairs.
  3. Between passes: bucket → bit (1 if count ≥ s); items with count ≥ s are the frequent items.
  4. Pass 2: count a pair {i,j} only if (a) i and j are both frequent and (b) it hashes to a bucket with bit 1. Store counts as (i, j, count) triples.
  5. No loss: a bucket count is the sum of the counts of the pairs in it, so it is at least each pair's count. A frequent pair therefore sits in a frequent bucket. Buckets with count < s hold no frequent pair. (A frequent bucket may still contain only infrequent pairs; that only causes extra counting.)

Q10. How is the bitmap used in PCY, and why is the hash table transformed into a bitmap? (the slide's own questions)

Lecture 4 · Slides 42, 81–82

  1. Use: in Pass 2, hash each pair with the same function; if its bucket's bit is 0 the pair is not counted, if 1 (and both items are frequent) it is a candidate.
  2. Why: after Pass 1 only the yes/no fact "count ≥ s" matters. A 4-byte counter (32 bits) is replaced by 1 bit, so the bitmap takes 1/32 of the memory.
  3. The memory saved goes to the candidate-pair counters of Pass 2, which are the bottleneck. Example: 10⁸ buckets are 400 MB as counters and 12.5 MB as bits.

Q11. Explain the 2/3 rule for PCY.

Lecture 4 · Slide 45

  1. After PCY the surviving pairs are scattered, so the triangular matrix no longer works; they must be stored as triples of about 12 bytes, versus 4 bytes per pair in A-Priori's matrix.
  2. If A-Priori has C candidate pairs it needs 4C bytes; if PCY keeps a fraction f it needs 12·f·C bytes.
  3. PCY wins when 12f·C < 4C ⇔ f < 1/3, so the hash table must eliminate more than about 2/3 of the candidate pairs.
  4. The number of buckets is O(main memory), so use all spare memory for buckets: a smaller average bucket count gives better pruning.

Q12. Describe the key idea of the multistage algorithm. (the slide's own question)

Lecture 4 · Slides 46–47, 83–84

  1. Multistage adds a second hash filter to PCY, using a different hash function on the pairs, to reduce the number of candidate pairs.
  2. Pass 1 = PCY Pass 1 (item counts, hash table 1); between passes: frequent items list and Bitmap 1.
  3. Pass 2: rehash pairs (those passing items-frequent and Bitmap 1) with a second hash function into table 2; then Bitmap 2.
  4. Pass 3: count {i,j} only if both items are frequent and it hits a frequent bucket in Bitmap 1 and in Bitmap 2.
  5. Fewer candidates mean less counter memory; the cost is an extra pass (three passes in total).

Q13. Describe Multihash. Compare it with Multistage and give the risks and limits of each.

Lecture 4 · Slides 49–51

  1. Multihash: split the Pass 1 memory into two (or more) hash tables with independent hash functions and hash every pair into all of them in the same pass. A bitmap per table. Pass 2 counts a pair only if both items are frequent and it hits a frequent bucket in every bitmap. Two passes in total.
  2. Risk: halving the buckets per table doubles the average bucket count, so more buckets may reach s and the filter weakens; most buckets must still stay below s.
  3. Multistage vs Multihash: multistage = three passes, filters applied in sequence, each table gets the full memory; multihash = two passes, filters in parallel, each table is smaller.
  4. Limits: multistage has diminishing returns (bitmaps eventually use all memory); multihash with too many tables makes (almost) all buckets frequent. In practice 2 or 3 hash functions.

Q14. Explain random sampling for frequent itemsets. What are false positives and false negatives, and which can be removed?

Lecture 4 · Slides 53–55

  1. Take a random sample of the baskets that fits in memory, run A-Priori or PCY on it in memory, with the threshold reduced proportionally (sample fraction p, threshold p × s). Fewer disk passes: no extra disk I/O when moving to bigger itemsets.
  2. False positive: frequent in the sample but not in the whole data. False negative: frequent in the whole data but not in the sample.
  3. An optional second pass over the full data counts the reported itemsets and discards those below s: this removes false positives.
  4. False negatives cannot be recovered, since only itemsets that appeared in the sample are rechecked. So sampling is approximate.

Q15. Describe the SON algorithm and explain why it is exact (no false negatives, no false positives).

Lecture 4 · Slides 56–57

  1. Pass 1: split the whole file into chunks that fit in memory (this is not sampling: every basket is used). On each chunk run an in-memory algorithm with a threshold scaled to the chunk (pchunk × s). An itemset frequent in any chunk is a candidate; the candidate list is the union.
  2. Pass 2: count all candidates over the entire file; keep those with count ≥ s.
  3. No false negatives: an itemset cannot be frequent in the whole file unless it is frequent in at least one chunk (if it were below its scaled threshold in every chunk, its total would be below s), so it is in the candidate list.
  4. No false positives: Pass 2 counts exactly over everything.
  5. Two passes for itemsets of all sizes; result identical to A-Priori on the whole file.

Q16. Describe SON as two MapReduce rounds, and contrast SON with random sampling.

Lecture 4 · Slides 58–60, 65–66

  1. Map Phase 1: each mapper runs an in-memory frequent-itemset algorithm on its chunks and emits the locally frequent itemsets.
  2. Reduce Phase 1: union of all of them with duplicates removed: the global candidate list.
  3. Map Phase 2: the candidate list is broadcast to all mappers; each counts every candidate on its own chunks.
  4. Reduce Phase 2: add the counts per candidate; keep those with total ≥ s. The second round is required, not optional (Slide 60 says "optionally": erratum).
  5. Contrast: sampling uses only part of the data, is approximate (false negatives possible) and its second pass is optional; SON uses all the data, is exact, and always makes exactly two passes. SON also parallelises because chunks are mined independently.

Algorithms in a few steps

AlgorithmSteps
A-Priori(1) Pass 1: count items. (2) Keep items with count ≥ s (frequent items), renumber them 1..m. (3) Pass 2: count only pairs of frequent items. (4) Keep pairs ≥ s. (5) For size k: build Ck from Lk−1 (all subsets frequent), count in pass k, keep Lk. One pass per k.
PCY(1) Pass 1: count items and hash every pair to a bucket counter (counts only). (2) Between: buckets → bit-vector (1 iff ≥ s); list frequent items. (3) Pass 2: count {i,j} iff both items frequent and bucket bit = 1; store triples. (4) Keep pairs ≥ s.
Multistage(1) Pass 1 as PCY → Bitmap 1. (2) Pass 2: rehash surviving pairs with a second hash function → Bitmap 2. (3) Pass 3: count {i,j} iff both frequent and bit 1 in B1 and B2.
Multihash(1) Pass 1: item counts plus two or more hash tables (each about half size) with independent hash functions. (2) Between: one bitmap per table. (3) Pass 2: count {i,j} iff both frequent and bit 1 in every bitmap.
Random sampling(1) Pick a random sample that fits in RAM. (2) Run A-Priori/PCY in memory with threshold p × s. (3) Output the frequent itemsets of the sample. (4) Optional: second pass counts them in the full data to drop false positives.
SON(1) Split the whole file into chunks. (2) Pass 1: mine each chunk with a scaled threshold; candidates = union. (3) Pass 2: count all candidates over the entire file. (4) Keep count ≥ s. Exact.
SON MapReduceMap 1: locally frequent itemsets. Reduce 1: union, no duplicates = candidates. Map 2: counts of broadcast candidates on own chunks. Reduce 2: sum, keep ≥ s.

Common mistakes & traps

Lecture 4 · Slides 1–86

  • Wrong denominator for confidence. Divide by support of the left side only. Not by the number of baskets, not by the right side's support. Slide 75: 3 of the 5 baskets with cat and dog, so 3/5.
  • Confusing confidence with interest. A rule with confidence 1/2 can have negative interest (Slide 15: 1/2 − 5/8 = −1/8). Always give Pr[j] and the signed interest.
  • Strict versus non-strict. Frequent and "passes the confidence threshold" use ≥. Support exactly s is frequent; confidence exactly c is kept (b,m → c with 3/4 = 0.75 on Slide 18).
  • Missing rule directions. A pair gives two rules, a triple gives six; also a one-item left side with a two-item right side. Slide 18's "…" hides three accepted rules (c → b, c,m → b, j → c).
  • Counting purchases, not baskets. Support counts baskets. A word repeated inside one basket counts once; capital letters are ignored on Slides 70–77.
  • Assuming frequent items make a frequent pair. m and c are frequent but {m,c} is not. Monotonicity works downward only: frequent set ⇒ frequent subsets, never the reverse.
  • PCY: using only the bucket test. A pair must have both items frequent and a frequent bucket. A frequent bucket does not imply a frequent pair (collisions); an infrequent bucket proves none of its pairs is frequent. Bit = 1 means count ≥ s, not "greater than".
  • PCY: forgetting triples. After PCY the triangular matrix no longer works, so counters are 12-byte triples; hence the 2/3 rule (not 1/3: it is the fraction to eliminate).
  • Mixing up Multistage and Multihash. Multistage = 3 passes, one table per pass; Multihash = 2 passes, several smaller tables in the same pass. Multihash's risk is that halving the buckets doubles the average count.
  • Treating SON like sampling. SON reads every basket and is exact; Slide 53 lumps them together ("may miss some") and Slide 60 says "optionally": both misleading. SON's second pass is mandatory.
  • Not scaling the threshold. Using the full s inside a chunk or sample misses itemsets spread across chunks. Use p × s (percentages must be turned into counts). Two different "monotonicity" ideas exist: A-Priori's (subsets of a frequent set are frequent) and SON's (frequent overall ⇒ frequent in some chunk).
  • Trusting slide answers blindly. Known errata: Slide 15's interest value is never computed; Slide 71 and Slide 73 miss basket 7 and the second triple {dog, cat, and}; the SON example (Slides 63–69) misses the ninth candidate {banana, orange, pear}. Show your own counts.

Lecture 5Clustering (Hierarchical, k-means, CURE, BFR, k-means on Map-Reduce)

Roadmap — what this lecture is about
  • The problem (Slides 1–14): given points and a distance measure, group them into clusters so that members of a cluster are similar and members of different clusters are not. The measure (Euclidean, cosine, Jaccard, edit) defines "similar". Clustering is hard because real clusters have odd shapes and sizes, and because in 10 or 10,000 dimensions many pairs of points are about equally far apart. Two families exist: hierarchical and point assignment.
  • Hierarchical clustering (Slides 16–21, quiz Slides 69–75): repeatedly merge the two nearest clusters; a cluster is represented by its centroid (Euclidean) or its clustroid (non-Euclidean). It costs O(N³), too much for big data.
  • k-means (Slides 22–34, quiz Slides 76–77): choose k, pick k seeds, then assign, update, reassign until convergence; choose k at the elbow of the average-distance curve.
  • Scalable versions (Slides 35–67): CURE (sample, hierarchical clustering, representatives moved 20% toward the centroid, one rescan; any shape), BFR (read data in memory loads and keep only N, SUM, SUMSQ per cluster in the discard set, plus compression and retained sets; normal, axis-aligned clusters; theory only) and k-means on MapReduce (mapper assigns, combiner pre-sums, reducer averages).
  • Quizzes (Slides 69–84) are solved in this guide; Slides 86–88 are the summary and the reading list (book Chapter 7).

Exam checklist — by the end you can:

  • define clustering and name the four distance measures with the data each suits; explain why clustering is hard and what the curse of dimensionality means;
  • contrast hierarchical (agglomerative, divisive) with point assignment, and explain a dendrogram;
  • run agglomerative clustering by hand with centroids (weighted-average update, distances, stopping at k) and draw the dendrogram; explain the clustroid and why it is needed; explain why the cost is O(N³);
  • run k-means by hand (farthest-first seeds, two rounds with every distance and every new centroid), state convergence, and explain how to pick k (elbow, too few / too many);
  • describe CURE in both passes, apply the 20% move to representatives, and say why representatives allow any shape;
  • explain BFR conceptually: assumptions (normal, axis-aligned; which ellipses are allowed), DS / CS / RS, why N, SUM and SUMSQ suffice and are updated by addition, the five steps per memory load, the Mahalanobis test, and how two CS sets are merged (no BFR numericals are examined);
  • describe k-means on MapReduce (mapper, combiner, reducer, iteration) and work the small numeric examples;
  • compare k-means, CURE, BFR and MapReduce k-means in one table.

Where clustering fits, and what the lecture covers

Lecture 5 · Slides 1–2

Lecture 5 is called Scalable Clustering: BFR, CURE, MapReduce (Slide 1). The title promises three things: two algorithms for clustering data that is too big for memory (BFR and CURE), and a way to run clustering on a cluster of machines (MapReduce). This first part of the chapter builds the foundations: what clustering is, why it is hard, and the oldest family of methods, hierarchical clustering. The slides never expand the acronyms, so here they are once: BFR = Bradley–Fayyad–Reina (the three authors), CURE = Clustering Using REpresentatives. Both come later in the lecture.

Slide 2 is the course map. Its first column, "High dim. data", lists three topics: locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), clustering (the green box, this lecture) and dimensionality reduction. The other columns (graph data, infinite data, machine learning, apps) belong to other parts of the course. The message of the slide is simply that clustering is a tool for high-dimensional data, and that is exactly the difficulty that shapes the rest of the lecture.

Slide numbering

The printed slide numbers in this deck skip some values (3, 7, 10, 11, 13, 15, 19, 20 do not exist in the PDF; the deck jumps 2→4, 9→12, 12→14, 14→16, 18→21). That is how the instructor's deck is; nothing is missing from this guide. Always use the printed number in the bottom-right corner of a slide.

The problem of clustering

Lecture 5 · Slide 4

Beginner intuition

You are given a huge pile of unlabelled photos and asked to sort them into piles so that photos in one pile look alike and photos in different piles look different. Nobody tells you the pile names or even exactly how many piles there should be. That is clustering. The only thing you need is a way to say how "alike" two photos are, which is a distance.

Definition — clustering (Slide 4)

Given a set of points and a notion of distance between points, group the points into some number of clusters so that (i) members of a cluster are similar to each other (small distance) and (ii) members of different clusters are dissimilar (large distance).

The slide adds what is usually true in practice: the points live in a high-dimensional space (many coordinates per point), and similarity is defined by a distance measure. The slide lists four: Euclidean, cosine, Jaccard and edit distance. It does not define them (they come from earlier lectures), so here is a one-line refresher of each with a tiny example.

DistanceWorks onDefinitionTiny example
Euclideannumeric vectorsstraight-line distance: √(∑(xi − yi)²)(0,0) and (3,4): √(9+16) = 5
Cosinevectors (direction matters, length does not)1 − cos θ, where cos θ = (x·y)/(|x||y|); equivalently the angle θ itselfx=(1,0,1,1), y=(1,1,0,1): x·y=2, |x|=|y|=√3, cos θ=2/3, distance = 1 − 2/3 = 0.333 (θ ≈ 48.2°)
Jaccardsets1 − |A∩B| / |A∪B|A={a,b,c}, B={b,c,d}: |A∩B|=2, |A∪B|=4, distance = 1 − 2/4 = 0.5
Edit distancestringsminimum number of single-character insertions and deletions that turn one string into the other (some books also allow substitutions)"cat" → "cart": insert r, distance 1
Exam tip

The choice of distance is the definition of "similar". Euclidean for numeric measurements (height, weight), Jaccard or cosine for documents seen as sets of words, edit distance for strings such as names or DNA. Euclidean is special for this lecture because only in Euclidean space can you average points (Slides 16 and 18).

Notice two things the slide leaves open: it does not say how many clusters to look for ("some number"), and it gives no threshold for "similar". Different algorithms answer these differently, and choosing the number of clusters (called k) becomes an issue in the k-means part of the lecture.

Pictures of clusters, outliers and difficulty

Lecture 5 · Slides 5, 6 and 8

Example: clusters of dogs

Lecture 5 · Slide 5

Slide 5 is the "easy" picture of what clustering should find. Each dog is a point in a 2-D space with weight on the horizontal axis and height on the vertical axis. The dogs fall into three visibly separate groups, labelled Beagles, Chihuahuas and Dachshunds. The algorithm is never told the breed names; it only sees the coordinates and discovers that the three groups exist. Chihuahuas are low and light, dachshunds are as low but heavier, beagles are tallest and heaviest. Beyond the slides: this is the classic dog example of the textbook, Mining of Massive Datasets (MMDS), chapter 7.

Example: clusters and outliers

Lecture 5 · Slide 6

Real data is rarely this tidy. Slide 6 shows three clusters (dense groups of × marks, drawn as coloured ellipses; 15, 14 and 10 points) plus a few isolated points that belong to no ellipse. The slide labels one of them Outlier and one ellipse Cluster. (There are in fact two isolated points; only the lower one is labelled, the upper one is an outlier too.)

Definition — outlier

An outlier (noise point) is a point that is far from every cluster and does not belong to any of them. A cluster is a dense group of mutually close points.

Why outliers matter

A good algorithm must not let an outlier drag a cluster's centre towards it, and it should either give outliers a cluster of their own or leave them out. This returns in BFR, where a special "retained set" collects exactly such stragglers.

Clustering is a hard problem

Lecture 5 · Slide 8

Slide 8 contains only a picture: thousands of coloured dots forming about eleven groups. The groups have very different sizes, densities and shapes, they overlap and touch, stray dots of one colour sit inside the region of another, and there is no legend. Even a person could not draw the "right" boundaries. The point of the slide is that real clusters have fuzzy edges; it prepares the next slide.

Why clustering is hard: high dimensions

Lecture 5 · Slide 9

Slide 9 makes one argument in two steps. First: clustering in two dimensions looks easy, clustering small amounts of data looks easy, and in most cases looks are not deceiving, so your eyes find the right clusters. Second: many applications involve not 2 but 10 or 10,000 dimensions. You cannot look at 10,000-dimensional data, and its geometry behaves unlike the plane. The slide's key sentence:

Key idea — high-dimensional spaces look different

Many pairs of points are at about the same distance. When nearly all pairs are about equally far apart, "near" and "far" lose meaning, so distance-based clustering has little to grab on to. Beyond the slides: the textbook calls this the curse of dimensionality. It is why the course also has a topic called dimensionality reduction (Slide 2).

Beginner intuition

On a street (1-D) your neighbour is much closer than a person across town. With many independent coordinates, two random points differ a little in each coordinate, and those many small differences add up to nearly the same total for every pair. Nobody is clearly "close".

Beyond the slides: a quick numerical check. The table shows 100 random points with every coordinate drawn uniformly from [0,1] (a computer experiment with a fixed random seed; the exact numbers vary from run to run, the trend does not). For each dimension d it gives the smallest and the largest of the 4,950 pairwise Euclidean distances.

Dimensions dsmallest distancelargest distancelargest ÷ smallest
20.0161.12870
100.4042.0165.0
1003.125.061.6
10,00040.041.61.04

In 2-D the farthest pair is 70 times farther than the nearest. In 10,000-D every pair is within 4% of every other: all points look equally far apart.

Exam tip

If asked "why is clustering hard?", give both reasons: (1) real clusters differ in size, density and shape, overlap, and come with outliers (Slides 6 and 8); (2) in high dimensions many pairs of points are at about the same distance (Slide 9). Say that both make "nearest cluster" unreliable.

Application: clustering documents to find topics

Lecture 5 · Slide 12

To cluster documents you must first turn each one into a point. Slide 12 does it with the simplest scheme. Let the vocabulary have k distinct words. Represent a document by the vector (x1, x2, …, xk) where xi = 1 if and only if the i-th word appears in the document, and 0 otherwise. Then: documents with similar sets of words may be about the same topic. A cluster of documents is a topic.

Worked example — three tiny documents as 0/1 vectors Lecture 5 · Slide 12

Vocabulary (k = 6): goal, match, team, vote, party, law. Doc 1 "the team won the match" contains match, team (and the slide's scheme ignores everything not in the vocabulary). Doc 2 "goal in the match for the team" contains goal, match, team. Doc 3 "the party passed the law in a vote" contains vote, party, law.

goalmatchteamvotepartylaw
Doc 1011000
Doc 2111000
Doc 3000111

Jaccard distance (words as sets): d(Doc1, Doc2) = 1 − 2/3 = 0.333; d(Doc1, Doc3) = 1 − 0/5 = 1. Docs 1 and 2 cluster together (sport), Doc 3 is far away (politics).

Two remarks. A real vocabulary has tens of thousands of words, so this is exactly the high-dimensional situation of Slide 9. And the slide does not say which distance to use; Jaccard (sets) or cosine (vectors) from the Slide 4 list are the natural choices.

Overview: two families of clustering methods

Lecture 5 · Slide 14

Slide 14 splits all methods into two families.

FamilyIdeaOutput
Hierarchical
(a) Agglomerative (bottom-up)
(b) Divisive (top-down)		(a) Initially every point is its own cluster; repeatedly combine the two "nearest" clusters into one.
(b) Start with one cluster holding everything and recursively split it.		A tree of nested clusters, the dendrogram. Choose the number of clusters afterwards by cutting the tree.
Point assignmentMaintain a set of clusters; each point belongs to its nearest cluster.A flat partition into a fixed number of clusters.

Reading a dendrogram

Lecture 5 · Slide 14

The picture on Slide 14 (top right) is a dendrogram of 30 items, coloured into four groups. The leaves along the bottom are the individual points. Each horizontal bar joins two clusters, and the height of the bar is the distance at which they were merged: low bars are very similar items, the top bar joins the most different groups. Slide 14 does not label the vertical axis; read it (0.2 to 0.9) as merge distance. Cutting the tree with a horizontal line at some height leaves as many clusters as bars the line crosses; the four colours on the slide are one such cut. Because one tree contains the answer for every possible number of clusters, you can decide "how many?" after clustering.

Which family are BFR and CURE?

Slide 14 does not say, but the point-assignment family is where k-means, BFR and CURE belong (they keep clusters and put each point into the nearest). Hierarchical clustering is the subject of the next slides. Do not mix the two: hierarchical = build a tree of merges; point assignment = fixed set of clusters that points are assigned to.

Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering

Lecture 5 · Slides 16–17

The key operation and the two decisions

Lecture 5 · Slide 16

Key operation

Repeatedly combine the two nearest clusters. Key problem: after you merge clusters, how do you represent the "location" of a cluster of many points, so that you can tell which pair of clusters is now closest?

Slide 16 answers with two decisions for the Euclidean case (where averages make sense):

  1. How to represent a cluster of many points? By its centroid, the average of its (data)points, coordinate by coordinate.
  2. How to determine "nearness" of clusters? Measure the distance between clusters by the distance between their centroids.
Definition — centroid

The centroid of a cluster of n points is the point whose every coordinate is the average of that coordinate over the n members: centroid = (1/n) ∑ points. It need not be one of the data points.

The algorithm, step by step:

  1. Start with every point as its own cluster (its centroid is the point itself).
  2. Compute the distance between the centroids of every pair of clusters.
  3. Merge the pair with the smallest distance; compute the centroid of the new cluster.
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until the stopping rule is met (see below).
Formula — centroid after a merge

Clusters P (nP points, centroid cP) and Q (nQ points, centroid cQ) merge into a cluster with centroid nP·cP + nQ·cQnP + nQ, a weighted average. It equals the plain average of all the original member points.

Worked example — why the update is weighted Lecture 5 · Slide 16

Cluster P = {(0,0), (2,0)} has centroid (1,0) and nP = 2. Cluster Q = {(4,3)} has nQ = 1. Merge them.

  1. Correct (average of all three points): ((0+2+4)/3, (0+0+3)/3) = (2, 1).
  2. Same thing from the centroids: (2·(1,0) + 1·(4,3)) / 3 = (6,3)/3 = (2, 1). ✓
  3. Wrong (midpoint of the two centroids): ((1+4)/2, (0+3)/2) = (2.5, 1.5). This treats the pair as if it were one point and is the classic mistake.
Common mistake

Averaging the two centroids instead of averaging all the points (or using the weights nP, nQ). A big cluster must pull the new centroid harder than a single point.

When to stop, and other cluster distances

Lecture 5 · Slide 16

Slide 16 gives no stopping rule. Beyond the slides: common choices are (a) stop when k clusters remain (used in Quiz L5-Q2, "stopping point k = 6"; going from N clusters to k takes N − k merges, because every merge removes exactly one cluster); (b) stop when the closest pair is farther apart than a threshold; (c) merge until one cluster is left and keep the whole tree. Beyond the slides: other ways to measure the distance between clusters exist (smallest, largest or average distance between members, called single, complete and average linkage); they can give a different tree. In this course use only the centroid rule of Slide 16.

The slide's worked picture

Lecture 5 · Slide 17

Slide 17 shows a complete run on six points, drawn as o (data point) with centroids drawn as x. The points on the slide are (0,0), (1,2), (2,1), (4,1), (5,0), (5,3); the slide prints no letters, so Figure 4 and the quiz below use A–F in that order. Read the slide in this order:

  1. The closest pairs are (1,2)–(2,1) and (4,1)–(5,0), both at √2 ≈ 1.414 (a tie). Their centroids are the blue x (1.5, 1.5) and the green x (4.5, 0.5), and the small blue and green circles enclose them.
  2. Next (0,0) joins the blue pair; the new (dark red) centroid is the average of all three points, (1, 1). Likewise (5,3) joins the green pair, new centroid (14/3, 4/3) ≈ (4.7, 1.3). The slide prints it rounded.
  3. Finally the two big clusters merge. The dendrogram at the bottom right records the order: blue pair first, green pair, then the single points, then the root.
Exam tip

To find the closest pair by hand, compare squared distances and skip square roots; take a root only for the pair you merge. After each merge, only the distances involving the new cluster change, so recompute only those. When two pairs tie, break the tie arbitrarily and say so.

The non-Euclidean case: clustroid

Lecture 5 · Slide 18

Slide 18 asks: what if the space is non-Euclidean? Then the only "locations" you can talk about are the points themselves: there is no "average" of two points. What is the average of two strings, or of two sets? The slide's approach has the same two decisions as Slide 16.

  1. Representing a cluster: by a clustroid, the (data)point "closest" to the other points of the cluster.
  2. Nearness of clusters: treat the clustroid as if it were the centroid when computing inter-cluster distances.
Definition — clustroid

The clustroid of a cluster is one of its own data points, chosen as the one most central under the given distance. A centroid is generally not a data point; a clustroid always is.

The slide emphasises "closest" but never says what it means. Beyond the slides: the textbook (MMDS 7.2.3) lists the usual choices. The clustroid is the point that minimises (a) the sum of its distances to the other points, (b) its maximum distance to another point, or (c) the sum of the squares of its distances to the other points.

Worked example — the three rules can disagree Lecture 5 · Slide 18 (numbers are ours)

Four points P, Q, R, S with the distances shown in Figure 5 (they satisfy the triangle inequality). For each point, list its distances to the other three.

Pointdistances to the otherssummaximumsum of squares
P6, 6, 517697
Q6, 3, 514670
R6, 3, 312654
S5, 5, 313559

Minimum sum: R (12). Minimum sum of squares: R (54). Minimum maximum: S (5). So "closest" depends on the rule; always state which one you use. The sum of squares punishes a single large distance more than the plain sum does.

Two properties to remember: with a clustroid every inter-cluster distance is just a distance between two real points (so it works with any distance function, including Jaccard and edit distance), and the clustroid must be recomputed after every merge (Beyond the slides: you compare the member points of the merged cluster, not only the two old clustroids). The two parts of Slide 18 are tested together with Slide 17 in the quiz below.

Euclidean case (Slide 16)Non-Euclidean case (Slide 18)
Cluster representativeCentroid = average of the pointsClustroid = data point "closest" to the others
Is it a data point?Usually notAlways
Cluster distancedistance between centroidsdistance between clustroids
Needs an "average"?YesNo (works with any distance)

Try it yourself first: work through the six-point run of Slide 17, cover the solution, and compare. It also asks you to read a dendrogram and to explain the clustroid.

Quiz L5-Q1Hierarchical clustering example and dendrogram Lecture 5 · Slides 17–18
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 17 (Example: Hierarchical clustering) is a picture with no printed question. It shows six data points (drawn as o), four centroids (drawn as x), circles and ellipses round the clusters, and a dendrogram. It illustrates the two rules of Slide 16: a cluster is represented by its centroid (the average of its points) and the nearness of two clusters is the distance between their centroids. Slide 18 then asks what to do in the non-Euclidean case, where no average exists. The parts below turn the slides into an exam-style question.

Point (my label)ABCDEF
Coordinates (x, y)(0, 0)(1, 2)(2, 1)(4, 1)(5, 0)(5, 3)
Leaf colour in the slide's dendrogramdark redbluebluegreengreenred

The letters A–F are my own labels (the slide prints only coordinates). Centroids printed on the slide: (1.5, 1.5) blue, (4.5, 0.5) green, (1, 1) red on the left, (4.7, 1.3) red on the right.

(a) Run agglomerative hierarchical clustering on the six points, using the Euclidean distance between cluster centroids, until one cluster is left. Show every merge: which two clusters are merged, at what distance, and the new centroid.
(b) Explain how the four centroids printed on Slide 17 arise.
(c) Draw the dendrogram.
(d) What does a dendrogram show, and how do you cut it to obtain k clusters (for example k = 2, 3, 4)?
(e) Non-Euclidean case (Slide 18): what is a clustroid, how does it differ from a centroid, and how is the nearness of two clusters then measured?
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
  1. Formula / idea — what agglomerative clustering does (Slides 14 and 16).

    Slide 14 lists two families of clustering methods: hierarchical (agglomerative = bottom-up, divisive = top-down) and point assignment. This example is agglomerative: at the start every point is a cluster of its own; in every round the two nearest clusters are combined into one; repeat until one cluster is left (or until k clusters are left). By hand you only need the two rules of Slide 16: (1) a cluster is represented by its centroid = the average of its points; (2) the nearness of two clusters is the distance between their centroids.

    Formulas used

    Centroid of a cluster of n points: ∑ xn for the x-coordinate and ∑ yn for the y-coordinate (the average of each coordinate).
    Distance between clusters P and Q with centroids (xP, yP) and (xQ, yQ): d(P, Q) = √( (xP − xQ)² + (yP − yQ)² ).
    Centroid after a merge, P with nP points and Q with nQ points: cnew = (nP·cP + nQ·cQ) / (nP + nQ). This is a weighted average; it equals the average of all the original member points.

    Beginner intuition

    Six houses are marked on a map and you want neighbourhoods. First glue together the two nearest houses. The glued pair is now one blob whose location is pinned at its middle (the centroid). Next round look again for the two nearest things on the map (single houses or blobs) and glue them. Keep going until everything is one big blob. The written record of who was glued to whom, and at what distance, is the dendrogram.

  2. Part (a), start — distances between all pairs of single points. At the start each cluster is one point, so its centroid is the point itself. Use d = √((x1 − x2)² + (y1 − y2)²). Example: d(B, C) = √((1 − 2)² + (2 − 1)²) = √2 = 1.414. All 15 distances:
    dA
    (0,0)    		B
    (1,2)    		C
    (2,1)    		D
    (4,1)    		E
    (5,0)    		F
    (5,3)
    A (0,0)02.242.244.125.005.83
    B (1,2)01.413.164.474.12
    C (2,1)02.003.163.61
    D (4,1)01.412.24

    The smallest distance is 1.41 and it occurs twice: B–C and D–E (both √2). A tie is harmless here: the two pairs share no point, so merging one does not change the other, and both will be merged anyway (D–E is still the smallest distance after B–C is merged, see the round-2 row of the table below). Ties are broken arbitrarily (Slide 71 does the same in another example); I merge B–C first.

    Exam tip

    To find the closest pair quickly, compare squared distances and skip the square roots: B–C = 2, D–E = 2, C–D = 4, A–B = 5, A–C = 5, D–F = 5, E–F = 9, B–D = 10, C–E = 10, C–F = 13, A–D = 17, B–F = 17, B–E = 20, A–E = 25, A–F = 34. The square root keeps the order, so the smallest d² is the smallest d. Take the root only for the pair you actually merge.

  3. Part (a), merge 1 — B and C at distance √2 = 1.414. New centroid = average of the two points = ((1 + 2)/2, (2 + 1)/2) = (1.5, 1.5). This is the blue x and the small blue circle on Slide 17. Clusters now: A, {B,C}, D, E, F (5 clusters).

    5ABC (1, 1), DEF (4.67, 1.33)ABC–DEF: √(122/9) = 3.682ABC + DEF

    Work done in total: 15 + 10 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 35 distance computations for 6 points. This growth is why the naive method does not scale (see part (d), Slide 21).

  5. Part (a), merge 2 — D and E at distance √2 = 1.414. D–E is still the smallest distance in round 2 (next: A–{B,C} = 2.121). New centroid = ((4 + 5)/2, (1 + 0)/2) = (4.5, 0.5), the green x and the small green circle. If you had merged D–E before B–C the tree would be identical. Clusters now: A, {B,C}, {D,E}, F (4 clusters).
  6. Part (a), merge 3 — A joins {B, C} at distance √4.5 = 2.121. Round 3 has A (0,0), {B,C} (1.5,1.5), {D,E} (4.5,0.5), F (5,3). The smallest distance is A–{B,C}: d = √((1.5 − 0)² + (1.5 − 0)²) = √4.5 = 2.121 (the runner-up is F–{D,E} = 2.550). New centroid, weighted by the number of points (1 for A, 2 for {B,C}): x = (1·0 + 2·1.5)/3 = 1 and y = (1·0 + 2·1.5)/3 = 1, so (1, 1). Check with the raw points: ((0 + 1 + 2)/3, (0 + 2 + 1)/3) = (1, 1). This is the red x on the left of Slide 17. Clusters now: {A,B,C}, {D,E}, F (3 clusters).
    Common mistake

    Do not average the two centroids as if they counted equally: ((0, 0) + (1.5, 1.5))/2 = (0.75, 0.75) is wrong. The cluster {B,C} stands for two points, so it must count twice (weights 1 and 2), or simply re-average the original points.

    Beginner intuition

    Notice that A is closer to the middle of {B,C} (2.121) than to B or to C separately (2.236 each). Measuring to a centroid is not the same as measuring to the nearest member: the centroid sits between the members.

  7. Part (a), merge 4 — F joins {D, E} at distance √6.5 = 2.550. Round 4 has {A,B,C} (1,1), {D,E} (4.5,0.5), F (5,3). F–{D,E}: √((5 − 4.5)² + (3 − 0.5)²) = √(0.25 + 6.25) = √6.5 = 2.550. {A,B,C}–{D,E}: √(3.5² + 0.5²) = √12.5 = 3.536. {A,B,C}–F: √(4² + 2²) = √20 = 4.472. The smallest is F–{D,E}. New centroid: x = (2·4.5 + 1·5)/3 = 14/3 = 4.667 and y = (2·0.5 + 1·3)/3 = 4/3 = 1.333, so (14/3, 4/3) ≈ (4.67, 1.33). Slide 17 prints this red x as (4.7, 1.3), i.e. rounded to one decimal. Clusters now: {A,B,C}, {D,E,F} (2 clusters), exactly the state drawn on Slide 17.
    Common mistake

    F is merged with the cluster {D,E} (distance 2.550), not with D alone, although the point-to-point distance d(D, F) = 2.236 is smaller. Once D has been merged, D no longer exists as a separate cluster; the only "location" of that cluster is its centroid (4.5, 0.5).

  8. Part (a), merge 5 — the last two clusters at distance √(122/9) = 3.682. Only {A,B,C} with centroid (1, 1) and {D,E,F} with centroid (14/3, 4/3) remain: d = √((14/3 − 1)² + (4/3 − 1)²) = √((11/3)² + (1/3)²) = √(122/9) = 3.682 (using the rounded (4.7, 1.3) would give 3.71, so keep exact fractions). New centroid = (3·(1, 1) + 3·(14/3, 4/3))/6 = ((3 + 14)/6, (3 + 4)/6) = (17/6, 7/6) ≈ (2.83, 1.17), which is also the average of all six points: (0+1+2+4+5+5)/6 = 17/6 and (0+2+1+1+0+3)/6 = 7/6. Slide 17 stops one merge earlier (at two clusters), so this centroid is not drawn, but this merge is the root of the dendrogram.
  9. Part (a) summary and part (b) — how the slide's centroids arise.
    MergeClusters mergedDistance between centroidsPoints in new clusterNew centroidOn Slide 17
    1B (1,2) + C (2,1)√2 = 1.4142(1.5, 1.5)blue x, small blue circle
    2D (4,1) + E (5,0)√2 = 1.4142(4.5, 0.5)green x, small green circle

    5{A,B,C} + {D,E,F}√(122/9) = 3.6826(17/6, 7/6) ≈ (2.83, 1.17)not drawn (the root)

    Part (b). Every centroid on the slide is simply the average of the data points inside its circle: (1.5, 1.5) is the average of (1,2) and (2,1); (4.5, 0.5) is the average of (4,1) and (5,0); (1, 1) is the average of (0,0), (1,2), (2,1); (4.7, 1.3) is the average of (4,1), (5,0), (5,3), namely (14/3, 4/3) rounded to one decimal. The dashed lines on the slide join each centroid to the points it was averaged from. The picture shows the state after four merges, that is, the two clusters {A,B,C} and {D,E,F}. The colours tell the story: blue = merge 1, green = merge 2, red = the two 3-point clusters created by merges 3 and 4, each of which added one red "loner" point (A or F) to a pair. The same colours are used for the leaves of the slide's dendrogram.

  10. Part (c) — draw the dendrogram. Recipe: (i) put the six points as leaves along the bottom, ordered so that lines do not cross (A, B, C, D, E, F); (ii) take the merges in order and, for each, draw a horizontal bar at the height equal to the merge distance, joining the vertical lines of the two clusters merged (together they form a "U"); the vertical stem rising from the middle of the bar is the new cluster and is used by the next merge; (iii) the last bar is the root: all points in one cluster. Heights: 1.414, 1.414, 2.121, 2.550, 3.682.

    In bracket form the tree is ((A, (B, C)), ((D, E), F)): the left sub-tree (A with the pair B–C) is the left ellipse of the slide, the right sub-tree (the pair D–E with F) is the right ellipse.

    The slide's dendrogram (bottom right of Slide 17) has the same shape but no distance axis: the blue pair is joined first, then the green pair, then the red leaf (0,0) joins the blue pair, the red leaf (5,3) joins the green pair, and the two sub-trees meet at the root. Its bar heights are only schematic: the two bars of merges 1 and 2 are really at the same height, 1.41, although the slide draws the green one a little higher.

    Slide erratum (minor — presentation only, no numerical error)

    All four printed centroids agree with the computation; (4.7, 1.3) is (14/3, 4/3) = (4.67, 1.33) rounded to one decimal. What the slide leaves out or draws loosely: (1) it prints no question and no merge distances; (2) its dendrogram is not to scale (no axis; the two merges at √2 are drawn at different heights); (3) it stops at two clusters, so the last merge (distance 3.682, centroid (2.83, 1.17)) and the root height are not shown. Figure 2 supplies the correct to-scale version.

  11. Part (d) — what a dendrogram shows.
    • The whole merge history as a nested (hierarchical) structure: every cluster contains the smaller clusters below it. Leaves are the data points; each U is one merge.
    • The order of the merges (bottom to top) and the distance at which each happened (the height of the bar). Low bars = very similar points; a long vertical stretch without any merge means a big gap between groups.
    • You can read off a clustering for any number of clusters without re-running the algorithm. (Read top-down the tree looks like repeated splitting, the idea of the divisive methods of Slide 14; this example is agglomerative, built bottom-up.)
    Common mistake

    The left-to-right order of the leaves carries no meaning: at every U the two branches may be swapped, like a hanging mobile. Only the tree structure and the heights matter. Also, the height is the distance between centroids at the merge, not the size of the cluster.

  12. Part (d) — how to cut the dendrogram to get k clusters. Draw a horizontal line at a chosen height h. Every vertical line it crosses is one cluster, made of all the leaves hanging below that line; the number of crossings is k. A lower cut gives more, tighter clusters; a higher cut gives fewer, looser ones. Equivalent view: stop the algorithm after n − k merges (here n = 6).
    kCut height hMerges doneClusters obtained
    6h < 1.410A, B, C, D, E, F (every point alone)
    5no clean cut: merges 1 and 2 are tied at 1.41, so stop after merge 11{B,C}, A, D, E, F
    41.41 < h < 2.122A, {B,C}, {D,E}, F
    32.12 < h < 2.553{A,B,C}, {D,E}, F
    22.55 < h < 3.684{A,B,C}, {D,E,F}: exactly the two big ellipses of Slide 17
    1h > 3.685all six points

    Unlike k-means (Slide 23: "start by picking k"), hierarchical clustering does not need k in advance: you build the whole tree and choose k afterwards.

    Beyond the slides: a common rule for choosing the cut is to look for the longest vertical stretch with no merge, i.e. the biggest jump between successive merge heights. Here the jumps are 0.71 (1.41 to 2.12), 0.43 (2.12 to 2.55) and 1.13 (2.55 to 3.68); the largest is just below the root, so k = 2 is the natural choice, in agreement with the slide. Other stopping rules in the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets, chapter 7, hierarchical clustering): stop at k clusters, or stop when the next merge would create a cluster that is too spread out (for example its diameter exceeds a threshold).

    Why this method does not scale (Slide 21)

    The naive implementation computes the pairwise distances between all pairs of clusters at every step and then merges, which costs O(N³) for N points (Slide 21), too expensive for big data sets that do not fit in memory. Beyond the slides: keeping the distances in a priority queue reduces this to about O(N² log N), which is still too slow for very large N. This is the motivation for the point-assignment methods (k-means and relatives) that follow.

  13. Part (e) — non-Euclidean case: why the centroid breaks down (Slide 18). In a Euclidean space the points are vectors of numbers, so we can add them and divide by n; the average is again a point of the space. In a non-Euclidean space the objects may be, say, words compared by edit distance or sets compared by Jaccard distance (Beyond the slides: these are examples, the slide names none). Then "the only locations we can talk about are the points themselves": there is no "average" of two words or two sets. Slide 18 therefore changes the two answers of Slide 16:
    • (1) Representing a cluster: use the clustroid = the data point of the cluster that is "closest" to the other points of the cluster.
    • (2) Nearness of clusters: treat the clustroid as if it were the centroid when computing inter-cluster distances, i.e. d(P, Q) = distance between the clustroid of P and the clustroid of Q. The rest of the algorithm is unchanged.

    Slide 18 leaves "closest" informal. Beyond the slides (textbook Mining of Massive Datasets, chapter 7): "closest" is usually made precise as the point with the smallest sum of distances to the other points of the cluster; two other common choices are the smallest maximum distance and the smallest sum of squares of distances. I use the sum of distances and show all three.

  14. Part (e) — worked demonstration of a clustroid. The Slide-17 data is Euclidean, so a centroid exists, but we can still compute the clustroids of the two final clusters to see the difference. For {D, E, F}:
    Candidate in {D, E, F}Distances to the other pointsSumMaxSum of squares
    D (4,1)d(D,E) = 1.414 + d(D,F) = 2.2363.6502.2367
    E (5,0)d(E,D) = 1.414 + d(E,F) = 3.0004.4143.00011
    F (5,3)d(F,D) = 2.236 + d(F,E) = 3.0005.2363.00014

    The clustroid is D (4, 1) under all three criteria (smallest sum 3.650, smallest max 2.236, smallest sum of squares 7). The centroid (4.67, 1.33) is not one of the data points; the clustroid always is. For {A, B, C}:

    Candidate in {A, B, C}Distances to the other pointsSumMaxSum of squares
    A (0,0)d(A,B) = 2.236 + d(A,C) = 2.2364.4722.23610
    B (1,2)d(B,A) = 2.236 + d(B,C) = 1.4143.6502.2367
    C (2,1)d(C,A) = 2.236 + d(C,B) = 1.4143.6502.2367

    B and C tie (sum 3.650 each, sum of squares 7 each; the maximum criterion cannot separate any of the three, all 2.236), so the clustroid is B (1, 2) or C (2, 1), chosen arbitrarily; the centroid (1, 1) is not a data point. Treating clustroids as the cluster locations, the distance between the two clusters would be d(C, D) = 2 or d(B, D) = √10 = 3.162, instead of the centroid distance 3.682. So the clustroid distance is only a stand-in for "where the cluster is", and the numbers (and in general the merge order) can differ from the centroid version. Beyond the slides (checked on this data): if the clustroids of the pairs {B,C} and {D,E} were chosen as C (2,1) and D (4,1), those two pairs would be only 2 apart and would merge before A joins (A is 2.236 from any of its candidates), whereas the centroids (1.5,1.5) and (4.5,0.5) are 3.162 apart.

    A truly non-Euclidean mini-example: words compared by edit distance (number of letters inserted or deleted). For the cluster {car, cart, carts}: d(car, cart) = 1, d(cart, carts) = 1, d(car, carts) = 2. Sums of distances: car 1 + 2 = 3, cart 1 + 1 = 2, carts 2 + 1 = 3. The clustroid is cart; there is no "average of car and carts" to use as a centroid.

  15. Part (e) — centroid versus clustroid at a glance.
    Centroid (Slide 16, Euclidean case)Clustroid (Slide 18, non-Euclidean case)
    Needspoints that can be averaged (vectors of numbers)only a distance between any two objects
    Definitionaverage of the points of the clusterthe data point "closest" to the other points (e.g. smallest sum of distances)
    A real data point?usually not, e.g. (1, 1) is not A, B or Calways, by definition
    Distance between clustersdistance between the two centroidstreat the clustroid as the centroid: distance between the two clustroids
    After a mergeweighted average of the two old centroids (cheap)Beyond the slides: no simple formula from the two old clustroids; the new clustroid has to be picked from the points of the merged cluster (needs distances, costlier)

    Beyond the slides: other definitions of cluster nearness exist (for example the smallest distance between any two members of the two clusters); this course uses centroid distance (Euclidean) and clustroid distance (non-Euclidean).

    Beginner intuition

    A centroid is the group's imaginary centre of gravity (it may fall in empty space, like the middle of a ring of people). A clustroid is the real person standing closest to everyone else: the group's "delegate". When you cannot compute a centre, you send the delegate instead.

    Exam tip

    For a "run hierarchical clustering" question: (1) state the rule (Euclidean distance between centroids); (2) write the pairwise distance table; (3) for each merge give the pair, the distance and the new centroid computed from all original points of the merged cluster; (4) say how you broke any tie; (5) stop at the required k or when one cluster is left; (6) draw the dendrogram with the heights written on it. If asked "what changes in the non-Euclidean case?", answer in two lines: no averages exist, so a cluster is represented by a clustroid (an actual data point closest to the others), and the distance between clusters is computed between clustroids "as if they were centroids"; add one example (strings with edit distance).

Final answer:
(a) Merges (centroid distance): 1) B + C at √2 = 1.414 → (1.5, 1.5); 2) D + E at √2 = 1.414 → (4.5, 0.5); 3) A + {B,C} at √4.5 = 2.121 → (1, 1); 4) F + {D,E} at √6.5 = 2.550 → (14/3, 4/3) ≈ (4.67, 1.33); 5) {A,B,C} + {D,E,F} at √(122/9) = 3.682 → (17/6, 7/6) ≈ (2.83, 1.17).
(b) Each printed centroid is the average of the points inside its circle; (4.7, 1.3) is (14/3, 4/3) rounded to one decimal.
(c) Tree ((A,(B,C)),((D,E),F)) with bars at 1.41, 1.41, 2.12, 2.55, 3.68 (Figure 2).
(d) A dendrogram records the merge order and the distance of every merge as a nested tree. Cut it with a horizontal line: k = number of vertical lines crossed (or stop after n − k merges). k = 2: {A,B,C} and {D,E,F}; k = 3: {A,B,C}, {D,E}, {F}; k = 4: A, {B,C}, {D,E}, F.
(e) Clustroid = the data point of the cluster that is closest to the other points (no averaging needed, always a real point); cluster distance = distance between clustroids, used as if they were centroids.
Where the marks come from: (1) stating the method: agglomerative = start with singletons and repeatedly merge the two nearest clusters; centroid = average of the points; cluster distance = Euclidean distance between centroids; (2) the distances at the start and at each round, identifying the closest pair (tie B–C / D–E noted and broken); (3) each of the five merges: the pair, its distance, and the correct new centroid (weighted, not the plain average of two centroids); (4) explaining that the slide's centroids are averages of the points in each circle, with (4.7, 1.3) rounded from (14/3, 4/3); (5) the dendrogram: correct nesting ((A,(B,C)),((D,E),F)), merge order, labelled leaves and heights; (6) saying what a dendrogram shows and the cutting rule (horizontal line, count the crossed vertical lines, or stop after n − k merges), with the clusters for k = 2, 3, 4; (7) the non-Euclidean variant: why no centroid exists, clustroid = data point closest to the others, and distances between clustroids used in place of centroid distances.
Slide check: matches the slide's answer. The slide prints no numeric answer, only the picture, and the computation reproduces all four printed centroids ((1.5, 1.5), (4.5, 0.5), (1, 1) exact; (4.7, 1.3) is 14/3 and 4/3 rounded to one decimal) and the same merge order as the slide's dendrogram (blue pair, green pair, then (0,0) joins the blue pair, (5,3) joins the green pair, then the root). Slide erratum (minor, presentation only, no answer changes): the slide's dendrogram is schematic (no distance axis; the two √2 merges are drawn at different heights), it does not show the last merge (distance 3.682, centroid (2.83, 1.17)) and it prints no distances or question; Slide 18 says "closest" without defining it (the three precise definitions above are Beyond the slides).

Why hierarchical clustering does not scale

Lecture 5 · Slide 21

Slide 21 describes the naïve implementation: at each step compute the pairwise distances between all pairs of clusters, then merge the closest pair. The slide states its cost as O(N³) and concludes it is too expensive for really big datasets that do not fit in memory. N is the number of points (the slide does not define it).

Where the N³ comes from Lecture 5 · Slide 21
  1. There are about N merges (N clusters down to 1).
  2. With m clusters left, a step looks at m(m−1)/2 pairs, about N²/2 at the start.
  3. Total work: ∑m=2..N m(m−1)/2 = (N+1)N(N−1)/6 ≈ N³/6, which is O(N³).
  4. Check with tiny numbers: N = 6 gives 15+10+6+3+1 = 35 distance computations (the table in Quiz L5-Q1 does exactly this). N = 12 gives 286 (the six rounds of Quiz L5-Q2 up to k = 6 use 251 of them). N = 106 gives about 1.7 × 1017.

There is a second problem besides time: the method needs all the data, and all pairwise distances, in memory at once. That is why the rest of the lecture introduces algorithms that read the data in chunks (BFR, CURE) and ones that run in parallel (MapReduce).

Beyond the slides: the faster version

Keep all pairwise distances in a priority queue (a heap). Building it costs O(N²). Each merge then deletes the entries of the two merged clusters and inserts the O(N) distances to the new cluster, each operation costing O(log N), so one merge costs O(N log N) and all N merges cost O(N² log N). This is better than O(N³) but still far too slow, and it still needs O(N²) memory, for really big data.

Common mistake

Writing "O(N²)" for the naïve method. The slide says O(N³): N rounds, each with about N² pairs. The priority-queue version is O(N² log N).

Worked example: hierarchical clustering of 12 points (k = 6)

Lecture 5 · Slides 69–75

These slides come later in the deck (they are the lecture's closing quiz), but they belong to the same topic, so the full worked solution is placed here. Slide 69, "Quiz: Hierarchical Clustering", gives twelve 2-D points and says: apply hierarchical clustering with Euclidean distance; assume the stopping point is k = 6. Slides 70–75 then walk through the answer: the starting state, the first merge (Slide 71), the next merges (Slides 72–74), the six final clusters (Slide 74) and the final tree (Slide 75).

What the solution needs from this chapter and what to watch for:

  • Stopping rule: k = 6 means stop when 6 clusters remain, so 12 − 6 = 6 merges.
  • Centroid rule: every merged cluster is represented by the average of all its points (use the weighted update), and the distance between clusters is the distance between centroids (Slide 16).
  • Ties: the slides break ties arbitrarily (Slide 71 says so). Several pairs are equally close at some rounds; any consistent tie-break is acceptable, but you must say you chose one.
  • Speed trick: compare squared distances and compute the full table only where points look close in the picture.

Try it yourself first: cover the solution, do the six merges on the twelve points, and only then compare with the worked answer below.

Quiz L5-Q2Hierarchical clustering of 12 points down to k = 6 Lecture 5 · Slides 69–75
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 69, "Quiz: Hierarchical Clustering": "Apply hierarchical clustering on the following data in a 2-dimensional Euclidean space. Assume stopping point is k = 6."

The data are a scatter plot of twelve points; every dot is printed with its coordinates and the slide gives no table. Read from the figure:

Region of the plotPoints (x, y)Count
upper left(4,10) (7,10) (4,8) (6,8)4
right(12,6) (10,5) (11,4) (9,3) (12,3)5
lower left(3,4) (2,2) (5,2)3

The slide asks one thing and then walks through the answer on slides 70–75 (every merge, the state at k = 6, and the final tree). The sub-tasks below follow that walk-through so that every step can earn partial marks; the letters (a) to (c) are ours, not the slide's.

(a) Run agglomerative hierarchical clustering (each cluster represented by its centroid, Euclidean distance between centroids). List every merge: the two clusters, their distance and the new centroid. Stop when k = 6 clusters remain.
(b) Give the six final clusters (members and centroids).
(c) Draw the tree (dendrogram) of the complete grouping (slide 75) and show where the k = 6 cut falls.
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
  1. Formula / idea: what "agglomerative hierarchical clustering with centroids" means (Lecture 5 · Slides 14 and 16).

    Slide 14 splits clustering methods into hierarchical (agglomerative = bottom-up, divisive = top-down) and point assignment. This quiz is agglomerative: at the start every point is a cluster by itself, and in every round the two nearest clusters are combined into one. Slide 16 gives the two rules you need to do this by hand: (1) in the Euclidean case a cluster is represented by its centroid = the average of its data points; (2) the nearness of two clusters is the distance between their centroids. (In a non-Euclidean space there is no average of points, so slide 18 uses a clustroid instead; not needed here.) The stopping point k = 6 means: stop as soon as 6 clusters are left.

    Formulas used

    Euclidean distance between centroids (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): d = √( (x1 - x2)² + (y1 - y2)² ).
    Centroid of a cluster with n points: ∑ xn and ∑ yn (the average of each coordinate).
    Centroid after a merge (cluster P with nP points and centroid cP, cluster Q likewise): cnew = (nP·cP + nQ·cQ) / (nP + nQ). It is a weighted average and equals the plain average of all the original points inside the new cluster.

    Beginner intuition

    Twelve pins on a map. Find the two closest pins and tie them together; from now on the tied pair is one blob that sits at its middle point (its centroid). Look for the closest two things again (single pins or blobs, always measured from centre to centre), tie them, and repeat until only six things are left. The record of who was tied to whom, and how far apart they were, is the tree on slide 75.

    Exam tip

    To find the closest pair, compare squared distances d² = (x1 - x2)² + (y1 - y2)² and skip the square root: the smallest d² belongs to the smallest d, and d² is a whole number for the raw points. Take the root only for the pair you actually merge. Keep centroids as exact fractions (14/3, 26/3) and round only at the end.

    Beyond the slides: this way of measuring the distance between clusters is usually called centroid linkage. Other rules (single, complete, average linkage) measure cluster distance differently and can give a different tree; in this course use only the centroid rule of slide 16.

  2. Data, initial state and number of merges (Lecture 5 · Slide 70). The 12 points are the ones read from the figure of slide 69. Initially each point is a cluster by itself and is the centroid of that cluster, so there are 12 clusters and their centroids are simply the 12 points: (2,2), (3,4), (4,8), (4,10), (5,2), (6,8), (7,10), (9,3), (10,5), (11,4), (12,3), (12,6). Every merge replaces two clusters by one, so the number of clusters drops by exactly 1 per merge. Going from 12 clusters to k = 6 needs 12 - 6 = 6 merges.
  3. Round 1: all distances between the 12 points (Lecture 5 · Slide 71). With 12 clusters there are 12·11/2 = 66 pairs. All 66 squared distances are in the table (a cell is d² between the row point and the column point; for example (10,5) and (11,4): (10 - 11)² + (5 - 4)² = 1 + 1 = 2).

    (6,8)53425416140
    (7,10)5334527441

    (12,3)9

    Reading the table: the smallest value is d² = 2 (green), which occurs twice: (10,5)–(11,4) and (11,4)–(12,3), each at d = √2 ≈ 1.414. This is exactly what slide 71 says. The next values are d² = 4 (bold; two pairs: (4,8)–(4,10) and (4,8)–(6,8)) and d² = 5 (bold; six pairs: (2,2)–(3,4), (6,8)–(7,10), (9,3)–(10,5), (9,3)–(11,4), (10,5)–(12,6), (11,4)–(12,6)). The other 56 pairs all have d² ≥ 8.

    Exam tip

    In the exam you do not have to compute all 66 distances. Look at the picture: only pairs that look close can be the minimum. Compute those few and compare; for every other pair just make sure it is clearly farther.

  4. Merge 1 (M1): (11,4) + (12,3) at d = √2 ≈ 1.414 (Lecture 5 · Slide 71). The two pairs at d² = 2 share the point (11,4), so there is a tie. Slide 71 says "let us break ties arbitrarily" and combines (11,4) with (12,3): d = √((11 - 12)² + (4 - 3)²) = √2. New centroid = average of the two points = ((11 + 12)/2, (4 + 3)/2) = (11.5, 3.5). We call the new cluster C1 = {(11,4), (12,3)}. 11 clusters are left.
  5. Merge 2 (M2): (4,8) + (4,10) at d = 2 (Lecture 5 · Slide 72). Only the distances to the new centroid (11.5, 3.5) are new; all the others are as in the table. Round 2, closest candidates:
    Pair of clusters (centroid)d² (squared distance)dVerdict
    (4,8) – (4,10)42.000merged (slide's choice)
    (4,8) – (6,8)42.000tie at the minimum, not chosen
    (10,5) – C1 (11.5, 3.5)9/2 = 4.52.121farther
    (2,2) – (3,4)52.236farther
    (6,8) – (7,10)52.236farther
    (9,3) – (10,5)52.236farther
    (10,5) – (12,6)52.236farther

    The smallest is d² = 4, i.e. d = 2, and it occurs for two pairs: (4,8)–(4,10) with d = √(0² + 2²) = 2 and (4,8)–(6,8) with d = √(2² + 0²) = 2 (this second tie is not mentioned on the slide, see the erratum at the end). Slide 72 combines (4,8) and (4,10). New centroid = ((4 + 4)/2, (8 + 10)/2) = (4, 9). We call it C2 = {(4,8), (4,10)}. 10 clusters are left.

  6. Merge 3 (M3): (10,5) + C1 at d = √4.5 ≈ 2.121 (Lecture 5 · Slide 72). Round 3:
    Pair of clusters (centroid)d² (squared distance)dVerdict
    (10,5) – C1 (11.5, 3.5)9/2 = 4.52.121merged (unique closest pair)
    (2,2) – (3,4)52.236farther
    (6,8) – C2 (4, 9)52.236farther
    (6,8) – (7,10)52.236farther
    (9,3) – (10,5)52.236farther
    (10,5) – (12,6)52.236farther
    (9,3) – C1 (11.5, 3.5)13/2 = 6.52.550farther
    (12,6) – C1 (11.5, 3.5)13/2 = 6.52.550farther

    Now there is a unique closest pair: (10,5) and the centroid of C1, (11.5, 3.5): d = √((10 - 11.5)² + (5 - 3.5)²) = √(1.5² + 1.5²) = √4.5 ≈ 2.121. This matches "the two closest centroids are (10,5) and (11.5, 3.5)" on slide 72. C1 has 2 points and (10,5) has 1, so the new centroid is a weighted average: x = (1·10 + 2·11.5)/3 = 33/3 = 11 and y = (1·5 + 2·3.5)/3 = 12/3 = 4, i.e. (11, 4). Check with the raw points: ((10 + 11 + 12)/3, (5 + 4 + 3)/3) = (11, 4). We call the new cluster C3 = {(10,5), (11,4), (12,3)}. 9 clusters are left.

    Common mistake

    Two traps in this merge. (1) Do not take the midpoint of the two old centroids. The midpoint of (10,5) and (11.5, 3.5) is (10.75, 4.25), which is wrong because C1 contains two points and must count twice; the weighted average (11, 4) is the same as averaging the three original points. (2) Measure to the centroid, not to a member. In round 1 the point (10,5) was only √2 ≈ 1.414 away from the single point (11,4), but (11,4) is no longer a cluster of its own: C1 sits at its centroid (11.5, 3.5), which is 2.121 away from (10,5). Distances between clusters can grow when clusters merge. (Beyond the slides: measuring to the nearest member would be a different method, called single linkage.)

  7. Merge 4 (M4): (6,8) + C2 at d = √5 ≈ 2.236 (Lecture 5 · Slides 73–74). Round 4, the state shown on slide 73:
    Pair of clusters (centroid)d² (squared distance)dVerdict
    (6,8) – C2 (4, 9)52.236merged (slide's choice)
    (2,2) – (3,4)52.236tie at the minimum, not chosen

    (12,6) – C3 (11, 4)52.236tie at the minimum, not chosen

    The smallest d² is 5 (d = √5 ≈ 2.236) and it is shared by five pairs: (6,8)–C2, (6,8)–(7,10), (2,2)–(3,4), (9,3)–C3 and (12,6)–C3. This is slide 73's "several pairs of centroids that are at distance √5". For example, (6,8) to the centroid (4,9) of C2: √((6 - 4)² + (8 - 9)²) = √(4 + 1) = √5. Slide 74 combines (6,8) with the cluster of two elements having centroid (4,9). Weights 1 and 2: x = (1·6 + 2·4)/3 = 14/3 and y = (1·8 + 2·9)/3 = 26/3, so the new centroid is (14/3, 26/3) ≈ (4.67, 8.67); the slide prints it rounded as (4.7, 8.7). Check with the raw points: ((6 + 4 + 4)/3, (8 + 8 + 10)/3) = (14/3, 26/3). We call it C4 = {(4,8), (4,10), (6,8)}. 8 clusters are left.

    Slides 73–74 show the three √5 merges together. In reality they happen one after the other, and you re-check the closest pair after each one (the next two tables do exactly that). We follow the slide's order: M4, M5, M6.

  8. Merge 5 (M5): (2,2) + (3,4) at d = √5 ≈ 2.236 (Lecture 5 · Slide 74). Round 5:

    Three pairs are still tied at d² = 5. The old tie (6,8)–(7,10) has disappeared because (6,8) is no longer a cluster of its own: (7,10) is now √(65/9) ≈ 2.687 from the centroid of C4. Slide 74 merges (2,2) with (3,4): d = √((3 - 2)² + (4 - 2)²) = √5. New centroid = ((2 + 3)/2, (2 + 4)/2) = (2.5, 3). We call it C5 = {(2,2), (3,4)}. 7 clusters are left.

  9. Merge 6 (M6): (9,3) + C3 at d = √5 ≈ 2.236 (Lecture 5 · Slide 74), and STOP. Round 6:
    Pair of clusters (centroid)d² (squared distance)dVerdict

    Two pairs are still tied at d² = 5: (9,3)–C3 and (12,6)–C3. Slide 74 merges (9,3) with the cluster of three elements having centroid (11,4): d = √((11 - 9)² + (4 - 3)²) = √5. Weights 1 and 3: x = (1·9 + 3·11)/4 = 42/4 = 10.5 and y = (1·3 + 3·4)/4 = 15/4 = 3.75, so the new centroid is (10.5, 3.75) (the slide prints (10.5, 3.8), which is 3.75 rounded to one decimal). Check with the raw points: ((9 + 10 + 11 + 12)/4, (3 + 5 + 4 + 3)/4) = (42/4, 15/4). We call it C6 = {(9,3), (10,5), (11,4), (12,3)}.

    Count the clusters: 12 - 6 merges = 6 clusters, which is the stopping point k = 6, so the algorithm stops here. (Had we continued, the next closest pairs would be at 2.687, 2.693 and 2.704, all larger than √5.)

    Common mistake

    "Stopping point k = 6" means stop when 6 clusters are left, not "do 6 merges". Here the two coincide only because 12 - 6 = 6. With the same data and k = 3 you would need 9 merges.

  13. Part (c): the tree (dendrogram) and the cut at k = 6 (Lecture 5 · Slide 75). A dendrogram records the merges: the leaves are the 12 points, every horizontal bar is one merge, and the height of the bar is the distance between the two centroids at that moment (the vertical axis below; slide 75 draws the same tree without a scale). A horizontal cut through the tree leaves as many clusters as vertical lines it crosses. A cut at about 2.46 (anywhere between 2.236, the last merge of the six, and 2.687, merge M7) crosses 6 lines, and these six lines are the six clusters of part (b). Merges M7 to M11 lie above the cut and are not performed when k = 6.

    Beyond k = 6 (not asked, but drawn on slide 75), carrying the same centroid method on with unique closest pairs gives (Cn = the cluster created by merge Mn):

    Slide 75's tree has exactly this shape, with the leaves in the same left-to-right order (2,2), (3,4), (5,2), (4,8), (4,10), (6,8), (7,10), (11,4), (12,3), (10,5), (9,3), (12,6). Left half: (2,2) and (3,4) join, then (5,2) joins them; (4,8) and (4,10) join, then (6,8), then (7,10) join them; these two groups meet at M10. Right half: (11,4) and (12,3) join, then (10,5), then (9,3), then (12,6). The left and right halves meet last (M11, the root). Merge distances only go up as you climb the tree (1.414, 2, 2.121, 2.236, 2.236, 2.236, 2.687, 2.693, 2.704, 6.617, 6.704), so there are no "inversions".

    Key idea: reading the heights

    The merges M1 to M9 all happen at small distances (1.41 to 2.70), while M10 and M11 happen at about 6.6 and 6.7. Beyond the slides: such a big jump in merge distance is the usual hint for where to cut a dendrogram, in the same spirit as looking for the "right k" in k-means (slide 31). Here the jump points to k = 3: the groups {(7,10), (4,8), (4,10), (6,8)}, {(5,2), (2,2), (3,4)} and {(12,6), (9,3), (10,5), (11,4), (12,3)}. This quiz asks for k = 6, which simply means that the three stragglers (7,10), (5,2) and (12,6) have not yet been absorbed into their groups (that would be M7 to M9). Also beyond the slides: with centroid distances the heights of a tree can in general go down at some merge (an inversion); that does not happen for this data.

  14. Ties: why the answer is not unique, and what to write in the exam (Lecture 5 · Slides 71–74). Ties occurred several times (M1: two pairs at √2; M2: two pairs at 2; M4 to M6: up to five pairs at √5), and the slides break them "arbitrarily". We tried every possible way of breaking the ties by computer. There are exactly four different sets of six clusters, and the slide's answer is one of them:
    #The six clustersWhat differs
    1{(4,8),(4,10),(6,8)}, {(7,10)}, {(2,2),(3,4)}, {(5,2)}, {(9,3),(10,5),(11,4),(12,3)}, {(12,6)}the slide's answer: (6,8) joins (4,9); (9,3) joins the cluster at (11,4)
    2{(4,8),(4,10),(6,8)}, {(7,10)}, {(2,2),(3,4)}, {(5,2)}, {(10,5),(11,4),(12,3),(12,6)}, {(9,3)}the 3-point cluster around (11,4) takes (12,6) instead of (9,3)
    3{(4,8),(4,10)}, {(6,8),(7,10)}, {(2,2),(3,4)}, {(5,2)}, {(9,3),(10,5),(11,4),(12,3)}, {(12,6)}(6,8) joins (7,10) instead of (4,9)
    4{(4,8),(4,10)}, {(6,8),(7,10)}, {(2,2),(3,4)}, {(5,2)}, {(10,5),(11,4),(12,3),(12,6)}, {(9,3)}both of the alternatives above

    The four results come from two independent √5 choices: does (6,8) join (4,9) or (7,10), and does the three-point cluster around (11,4) take (9,3) or (12,6)? The left group {(2,2),(3,4)} and the single point (5,2) are the same in all four. The tie at M1 changes nothing (all four results stay reachable); the tie at M2 matters only a little: if (4,8) + (6,8) were merged first, (4,10) would always end up in the same cluster, and results 3 and 4 would become impossible.

    Exam tip

    When two distances tie, say so ("(6,8) is √5 from both (7,10) and (4,9); I break the tie arbitrarily by ...") and continue consistently. Making the same choices as slides 71 to 74 is the safest way to match the marking key. Also remember that the naive method (recompute all pairwise distances at every step) costs O(N³) and is too expensive for really big data (slide 21); for these 12 points the six rounds already scan 66 + 55 + 45 + 36 + 28 + 21 = 251 pair distances.

    Slide erratum (omissions only; no number on the slides is wrong)

    (1) Slide 72 says the two closest clusters are (4,8) and (4,10); that is a correct minimum (d = 2), but (4,8) and (6,8) are also exactly 2 apart, which the slide does not say. (2) Slides 73 and 74 present three merges as if they all happened at once at √5. In fact five pairs are tied at √5, the merges happen one after the other (each changes a centroid), and two tied pairs, (6,8)–(7,10) and (12,6)–C3, are simply not chosen; other choices give the other three valid answers in the table above. (3) Slide 74 shows rounded centroids: (4.7, 8.7) is (14/3, 26/3) and (10.5, 3.8) is (10.5, 3.75). Every distance and centroid printed on slides 70 to 75 was recomputed in exact fractions and is correct.
