The merge distances are 2.687, 2.693 and 2.704.
Final answer: k = 6 is reached after 6 merges. Merges (distance between centroids): M1 (11,4) + (12,3) at √2 → centroid (11.5, 3.5); M2 (4,8) + (4,10) at 2 → (4, 9); M3 (10,5) + {(11,4),(12,3)} at √4.5 ≈ 2.121 → (11, 4); M4 (6,8) + {(4,8),(4,10)} at √5 → (14/3, 26/3) ≈ (4.67, 8.67); M5 (2,2) + (3,4) at √5 → (2.5, 3); M6 (9,3) + {(10,5),(11,4),(12,3)} at √5 → (10.5, 3.75). The six clusters: {(4,8), (4,10), (6,8)}; {(7,10)}; {(2,2), (3,4)}; {(5,2)}; {(9,3), (10,5), (11,4), (12,3)}; {(12,6)}.
Where the marks come from: (1) name the method: agglomerative = bottom-up, cluster = centroid (average of its points), cluster distance = Euclidean distance between centroids, and k = 6 means stop with 6 clusters (12 - 6 = 6 merges); (2) read all 12 points correctly and start with 12 single-point clusters; (3) find the closest pair by computing distances, note the tie at √2, and merge (11,4) with (12,3) into (11.5, 3.5); (4) merge (4,8) with (4,10) into (4, 9); (5) merge (10,5) with the centroid (11.5, 3.5) (d = √4.5) into (11, 4), using a weighted average; (6) the √5 round: (6,8) joins (4,9) giving (4.67, 8.67), (2,2) joins (3,4) giving (2.5, 3), and (9,3) joins (11,4) giving (10.5, 3.75); (7) stop at 6 clusters and list them with members and centroids (3 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 12 points); (8) the dendrogram with the cut at k = 6 (slide 75); (9) a remark that ties were broken arbitrarily, so other answers are possible.
Slide check: matches the slides' answer. The twelve points, all merges, all distances (√2, 2, √4.5, √5), all centroids ((11.5, 3.5), (4, 9), (11, 4), (4.7, 8.7), (2.5, 3), (10.5, 3.8, which is 3.75 rounded)), the six clusters on slide 74 and the tree on slide 75 were recomputed in exact arithmetic and agree. Slide erratum (omissions only, no wrong number): the second tie on slide 72 ((4,8)–(6,8) is also at distance 2), the five (not three) pairs tied at √5 on slides 73–74, and the fact that other tie-breaks give other valid 6-cluster answers (four in total); see the box in the last step.
Quick recap — Part 1
  • Clustering = group points so members are similar and different clusters are dissimilar, under a distance measure (Euclidean, cosine, Jaccard, edit); outliers belong to no cluster (Slides 4–6).
  • It is hard because clusters differ in size, density and shape, overlap, and in high dimensions many pairs of points are at about the same distance (Slides 8–9). Documents are clustered as 0/1 word vectors (Slide 12).
  • Two families: hierarchical (agglomerative bottom-up or divisive top-down, output a dendrogram) and point assignment (Slide 14).
  • Agglomerative: repeatedly merge the two nearest clusters; Euclidean: cluster = centroid (average), nearness = distance of centroids, new centroid = weighted average. Non-Euclidean: clustroid = actual point "closest" to the others (Slides 16–18).
  • Naïve cost O(N³) (priority queue O(N² log N), beyond the slides): too expensive for big data (Slide 21).

Next: from a tree of merges to k-means

Lecture 5 · Slide 22

Slide 22 is a black section divider titled k-means clustering; it carries no content and no number. It marks the switch from hierarchical clustering to the point-assignment family of Slide 14: you fix the number of clusters k in advance, keep k "centre" points and assign every point to the nearest centre. That material is the next part of this chapter.

k-means: point-assignment clustering

Lecture 5 · Slides 22–27

Slide 22 is a black divider titled "k-means clustering". It marks a change of family. The hierarchical methods you just met start with every point alone and merge clusters step by step. Point-assignment methods work differently: you decide in advance how many clusters you want, put that many "centre" points on the map, attach every data point to a centre, and keep adjusting the centres until nothing changes. k-means is the standard example, and the building block that CURE and BFR extend later in this lecture.

Beginner intuition

Think of opening k pizza shops in a city. Every household orders from the nearest shop. After a week each shop manager notices that the customers are not centred on the shop, so the shop is moved to the middle of its own customers. Now some households are closer to a different shop, so they switch. Repeat until nobody switches. The shops are the centroids, the households are the data points.

Setup: Euclidean space, choosing k, choosing the seeds

Lecture 5 · Slide 23

Slide 23 lists three things k-means needs before it can start:

  1. Euclidean space and distance. Points must have coordinates so that "the middle of a group of points" (their average) exists and distance is the straight-line distance.
  2. The number k of clusters, picked by you. (How to choose it well is the topic of Slides 31–34, below.)
  3. One starting point per cluster, called a seed. Slide 23 gives two ways: pick k points at random, or pick one point at random, then k−1 other points, each as far away as possible from the previous points.
Definitions

Euclidean distance between p = (x1, y1) and q = (x2, y2): d(p, q) = √((x1 − x2)² + (y1 − y2)²); in more dimensions add one squared difference per coordinate.

Centroid of a cluster: the coordinate-wise average (mean) of its points. It is generally not one of the data points.

Seed (initial centroid): the starting position of a centroid; with the methods of Slide 23 each seed is one of the data points.

Why "Euclidean" matters. The slide only says "assumes Euclidean", but the reason is the centroid: an average of points exists only where points can be added and divided by a count. For non-Euclidean data (for example sets or strings) there is no average; Slide 18 handled that for hierarchical clustering with a clustroid, an actual data point chosen to represent the cluster.

Spreading the seeds out (farthest-first)

Lecture 5 · Slide 23

Random seeds can land in the same natural group, which wastes a centroid. The second recipe avoids this. Slide 23 says "as far away as possible from the previous points".

Farthest-first rule, made precise (Beyond the slides:)

Seed 1: any point (random, or given). To choose each further seed: for every candidate point compute its distance to each seed already chosen and keep the smallest of those distances (its "score": how close it is to the nearest existing seed). Pick the candidate with the largest score. This is the same rule that Quiz L5-Q3 below uses and the one the answer on Slide 77 follows.

Worked example — farthest-first on six points in one dimension Practice, Slide 23 rule

Points on a line: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10. Suppose seed 1 is the point 1 and k = 3.

StepCandidates and their score (distance to nearest chosen seed)Choice
Seed 22: 1   3: 2   6: 5   9: 8   10: 910
Seed 32: min(1, 8) = 1   3: min(2, 7) = 2   6: min(5, 4) = 4   9: min(8, 1) = 16

The seeds 1, 6, 10 are spread over the line. Choosing 9 as seed 3 (largest distance to seed 1 only) would be wrong: it sits next to seed 10.

Common mistake

With k > 2, do not measure "far away" from the last seed only, and do not add distances. Use the smaller of the distances to all chosen seeds, then take the largest.

Slide erratum (omissions)

Slide 23 is titled "k-means Algorithm(s)" in the plural but shows one algorithm with two initialisation options. It also never says that the final clusters depend on the seeds. Beyond the slides: k-means always stops, but it can stop at a local optimum, a stable clustering that is not the best possible one. Different seeds can give different answers; that is why spread-out seeds (or several runs) are preferred.

The loop: assign, update, reassign

Lecture 5 · Slide 24

Slide 24 ("Populating Clusters") is the whole algorithm. Note that the slide numbers its steps 1, 2, 3 and then says "repeat 2 and 3". Steps 1 and 3 are the same operation (send each point to its nearest centroid); step 1 uses the seeds, step 3 uses the updated centroids.

  1. Assign. For each point, find the centroid it is nearest to and place the point in that cluster.
  2. Update. After all points are assigned, move each of the k centroids to the mean of the points now in its cluster.
  3. Reassign. Send all points to their closest (new) centroid. The slide notes this "sometimes moves points between clusters": a point near a boundary can be captured by the other centroid once the centroids have moved.
  4. Repeat 2 and 3 until convergence.
Definition: convergence (Slide 24)

Convergence means that points do not move between clusters and the centroids stabilise. The two conditions go together: if no point changes cluster, the means cannot change, and if the means do not change, no point will change cluster.

Worked example — the loop on six points, with deliberately bad seeds Practice, Slide 24 loop

Points 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10 (one dimension, so distance = |difference|). k = 2, seeds 1 and 2.

1. Assign to seeds1 and 2{1} and {2, 3, 6, 9, 10}3 is 1 away from 2 but 2 away from 1, and so on: seed 2 grabs almost everything.
2. Update1 and 6mean of {2, 3, 6, 9, 10} = 30/5 = 6
3. Reassign1 and 6{1, 2, 3} and {6, 9, 10}2: distance 1 to centroid 1, 4 to centroid 6, so it moves. 3: 2 against 3, so it moves too.
2. Update2 and 8.336/3 = 2 and 25/3 = 8.33
3. Reassign2 and 8.33{1, 2, 3} and {6, 9, 10}nobody moves (for example 6: 4 from 2 but 2.33 from 8.33)

Exam tip

For every point write the distance to every centroid (compare squared distances if you like; the square root never changes which is smallest) and underline the smallest. Then compute each new centroid as (∑x/n, ∑y/n) with the count n written out. State clearly which round your answer refers to. Quiz L5-Q3 below does exactly this.

Not examined — why it always stops (Beyond the slides:)

Each assign step and each update step can only keep or reduce the sum of squared distances from points to their centroid, and there are finitely many ways to split the points, so the loop must stop. The slide itself states no iteration cap, tie-breaking rule or proof.

The three-snapshot picture

Lecture 5 · Slides 25–27

Slides 25, 26 and 27 show one data set of 11 points (marked "x") in three snapshots, captioned "Clusters after round 1", "Clusters after round 2" and "Clusters at the end". The legend marks data points as "x" and centroids as hollow squares; the shaded ovals show which points belong together. The slides do not print k, but there are two centroids, so k = 2. The points form an "L": six lie along a flat row on the left (P1–P6), five climb diagonally to the right (P7–P11).

  • Slide 25, round 1. The seeds sit on two data points, P1 and P7. Each point joins the nearer seed: P1–P3 are pink, P4–P11 are blue. The split is lopsided (3 against 8), and neither seed is in the middle of its group, so the algorithm must continue.
  • Slide 26, round 2. The centroids have slid to the middle of their groups: pink moved right, blue moved up and to the right. Because of that, P4 (the point at the junction) is now closer to pink and switches. This is the sentence "sometimes moves points between clusters" on Slide 24 in action.
  • Slide 27, at the end. The centroids moved again and two more junction points, P5 and P6, joined pink. Final clusters: pink {P1–P6}, blue {P7–P11}. When no point changes cluster in a pass, the algorithm has converged (Slide 24).

Two lessons: points near the boundary can migrate over several rounds, and the final split (flat group, diagonal group) is the natural one even though the seeds were poor.

Slide erratum (minor, figure only)

The legend square on Slides 25–27 is green, but the centroids are drawn pink and blue. More importantly, the squares are drawn only roughly at the cluster means, and the slides do not say how many rounds lie between "round 2" and "the end". Do not compute from this figure. (Beyond the slides: measuring the 11 point positions from the picture (P5 is almost equidistant from the two centroids, so this depends on reading accuracy) and running k-means exactly from the same two seeds gives the round-1 and round-2 clusters shown above but then stops with {P1–P4} and {P5–P11}, which is also a stable state. The "at the end" picture is a different stable state with a smaller total squared distance. This is a small example of the local-optimum remark above: the end result depends on the exact centroid positions.)

Quick recap: k-means
  • Needs Euclidean points, a chosen k, and k seeds (random, or farthest-first).
  • Loop: assign each point to its nearest centroid; recompute each centroid as the mean of its points; reassign; repeat.
  • Stops when no point changes cluster and the centroids stabilise.
  • Centroid = mean, so it may not be a data point. Result can depend on the seeds.

Try it yourself first. Cover the solution and choose the two farthest seeds for the twelve points below, then carry out two rounds of the loop on paper.

Quiz L5-Q3k-means on 12 points (k = 3): farthest-point start, then two rounds Lecture 5 · Slides 76–77
Question (as on the slides)

Let us consider the twelve points presented below. K-Means clustering algorithm for k = 3 is used. Assume the initial choice of point is (6,8). What are the other two initial points? Pick points that are as far away as possible. Provide result of K-Means alg. after 2nd round.

Data (slide 76 draws the twelve points as a scatter plot with each point's coordinates printed beside it; read from that figure): (4,10) (7,10) (4,8) (6,8) (12,6) (10,5) (11,4) (3,4) (9,3) (12,3) (2,2) (5,2). Distances are Euclidean.

(a) The initial choice of point is (6,8). What are the other two initial points? Pick points that are as far away as possible.
(b) Provide the result of K-Means after the 2nd round.

Slide 77 prints the answer to (a) only and ends with “Note: compute the result of K-Means after 2nd round on your own.” So part (b) is solved in full below and carried on to convergence.

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition — k-means as three pizza shops

Think of the 12 points as 12 houses and the 3 centroids as 3 pizza shops. Start: open the three shops at three starting spots (here: at three of the houses). Assign: every house orders from its nearest shop. Update: every shop moves to the average position of the houses it serves. Reassign: every house re-checks which shop is now nearest. Repeat until nobody switches shop and the shops stop moving. Part (a) asks where to open the shops at the start (far apart from each other); part (b) asks what the map looks like after the second round.

Formulas used (Lecture 5 · Slides 23–24)

Euclidean distance between p = (x1, y1) and q = (x2, y2): d(p, q) = √( (x1 − x2)² + (y1 − y2)² ).
Shortcut: to decide which centroid is nearest it is enough to compare the squared distances d² (the square root never changes which number is smallest); take √ only when you report a distance. In the tables below each cell shows d² and, in brackets, d.
Centroid of a cluster of n points = coordinate-wise mean = (∑x / n, ∑y / n).
k-means loop (slide 24): (1) place each point in the cluster whose current centroid is nearest; (2) after all points are assigned, update the centroids of the k clusters; (3) reassign all points to their closest centroid; repeat 2 and 3 until convergence = points do not move between clusters and the centroids stabilise.

[Part (a): choosing the two other initial points] Idea (Lecture 5 · Slide 23): “Pick one point at random, then k−1 other points, each as far away as possible from the previous points.” The first point (6,8) is given. When more than one point is already chosen, “as far away as possible from the previous points” means: for every candidate compute its distance to each already-chosen point, keep the smaller of these (the distance to its nearest chosen point; slide 77 calls it the candidate’s “score”), and pick the candidate with the largest score. (This is the farthest-point or “max–min” rule.) We apply it twice: first for seed 2 (only one chosen point so far, so the score is just the distance to (6,8)) and then for seed 3.

    Beginner intuition — why the smaller of the two distances?

    Imagine placing three coffee shops so that they do not compete. The first is at (6,8); the second goes as far from it as possible, at (12,3). The third must be far from both. A site like (4,10) is √113 = 10.63 from the shop at (12,3) but only √8 = 2.83 from the shop at (6,8): it would sit right next to a shop that already exists, so its score is only 2.83. Taking the smaller distance catches this; looking at one shop only would not. (For this data, adding the two distances, 7.21 + 10.05 = 17.26, would also pick (2,2), but the rule on slide 77 is the smaller-distance score.)

Why did it converge so fast?

The data form three obvious blobs: a top group (y ≥ 8), a right group (x ≥ 9) and a bottom-left group. The farthest-point rule put exactly one seed in each blob, so the first assignment was already the “natural” grouping and the means merely moved to the middle of each blob. With a poor start (for example two seeds in the same blob) k-means usually needs more rounds and may end in a worse clustering. This is why slide 23 asks for seeds that are as far apart as possible.

Exam tip — what is a “round”?

Write a table of distances for every point and every centroid (squared distances are fine), mark the smallest in each row, list the resulting clusters, then show ∑x, ∑y and n for each new centroid. State the convergence test in words (“no point moved and the centroids did not change, so stop”). State your round convention in one line. Here it does not matter: whether round 1 means “assign only” or “assign + update”, the clusters never change after the first assignment and the centroids never change after the first update, so the state after round 2 is the same under every reading. If a point were ever exactly equidistant from two centroids (it does not happen here), the slides give no rule; say which tie-break you use.

Common mistakes in this question
  • Choosing seed 3 as the point farthest from the latest seed only: that gives (4,10), which is just 2.83 from (6,8). Always take the minimum over all chosen seeds, then the maximum of those minima.
  • Reusing the starting centroids (6,8), (12,3), (2,2) for the round-2 assignment instead of the updated ones (5.25, 9), (10.8, 4.2), (3.33, 2.67).
  • Stopping after the assignment and forgetting to recompute the centroids, or taking the centroid to be the “middle” data point instead of the average.
  • Saying k-means runs a fixed number of rounds: the stopping rule on slide 24 is convergence (nothing moves), not a round count.
  • Rounding too early, for example 3.3 and 2.7 for centroid 3: keep fractions (10/3, 8/3) or at least two decimals.
Not examined — optional self-check (beyond the slides)

Beyond the slides: the standard k-means objective is the sum of squared distances from each point to its own centroid. With the seeds as centres and the round-1 clusters it is 17 + 28 + 14 = 59; with the updated centroids it is 43/4 + 68/5 + 22/3 = 1901/60 = 31.68, and it stays 31.68 in round 2. Every assignment step and every update step can only keep this number the same or lower; if your own value ever goes up, you have an arithmetic error. The average distance from a point to its centroid (the quantity slide 31 uses to choose k) is 1.55 for this final clustering. Different starting seeds can end in a different (local) result, which is why the choice of seeds matters.

Final answer:
(a) The other two initial points are (12,3) (farthest from (6,8): √61 = 7.81) and then (2,2) (score = min(√52, √101) = min(7.21, 10.05) = 7.21, the largest). Starting centroids: (6,8), (12,3), (2,2).
(b) After the 2nd round: Cluster 1 = {(4,10), (7,10), (4,8), (6,8)} with centroid (5.25, 9); Cluster 2 = {(12,6), (10,5), (11,4), (9,3), (12,3)} with centroid (10.8, 4.2); Cluster 3 = {(3,4), (2,2), (5,2)} with centroid (3.33, 2.67) = (10/3, 8/3). The clusters and centroids are the same as after round 1: no point moved in round 2 and the centroids are unchanged, so k-means has converged and this is also the final clustering.
Where the marks come from: (1) rule for the starting points stated (first given, each next as far as possible from the already-chosen ones, using the nearest-chosen-point score) and Euclidean distance and centroid-as-mean formulas stated; (2) seed 2 = (12,3), justified as the farthest from (6,8) with d = √61 = 7.81; (3) seed 3 = (2,2), justified with the score min(√52, √101) = 7.21 and the remark that every other point scores less; (4) round 1: all 12 points assigned correctly, with distances shown; (5) centroids after round 1 computed as means: (5.25, 9), (10.8, 4.2), (3.33, 2.67); (6) round 2: all 12 points reassigned using the new centroids, with distances shown; (7) clusters and centroids after round 2 stated; (8) convergence criterion stated and applied (no point moved, centroids stable).
Slide check: part (a) matches slide 77 exactly: seeds (6,8), (12,3), (2,2); √52 = 7.21; √101 = 10.05; score 7.21; and its claim that every other point is closer than 7.21 to at least one of (6,8) and (12,3) is correct (the strongest competitor is (5,2) with score √37 = 6.08). Slide 77 gives no answer for part (b) (“compute … on your own”), so there is nothing to compare with; the clusters, centroids and convergence above were computed from scratch with exact fractions and checked by a program. No slide erratum. Two clarifications: the slide’s phrase “the one whose distance to (6,8) and (12,3) is the furthest” means “the largest score”, i.e. the largest value of the smaller of the two distances, and the slides do not define exactly what one “round” contains (see the Exam tip). The twelve coordinates were read from the labels on the slide-76 figure.

Choosing k

Lecture 5 · Slides 31–34

The printed numbering jumps from slide 27 to slide 31 in the lecture PDF (slides 28–30 are not in the file; nothing is missing from the sequence of ideas). Slide 31, "Getting the k right", answers the obvious question: k-means needs k, but how do you know it?

Average distance to the centroid versus k

Lecture 5 · Slide 31

Definition: average distance to centroid

For a clustering, take each point's distance to the centroid of its own cluster and average these distances over all points. It measures how tight the clusters are: small means points sit close to their centre.

The slide's recipe: try different k and watch how this average changes as k grows. It falls rapidly until the right k, then changes little. The slide's picture is a curve (vertical axis "Average distance to centroid", horizontal axis k) with an arrow labelled "Best value of k" pointing at the bend.

Beginner intuition

Adding a centroid always helps a little, because some point gets a closer centre. In the extreme, k = number of points gives distance 0, so you cannot just minimise the average. But while you are adding centroids that the data really need, the gain is large. Once every natural group has its own centroid, extra centroids only split groups that were already tight, and the gain is tiny. The bend is where the big gains stop.

Worked example — an elbow with numbers Practice, Slide 31 idea

Nine points on a line forming three tight groups: 1, 2, 3, then 10, 11, 12, then 24, 25, 26. For each k the best split into k groups (found by trying all ways to cut the sorted list) and its average distance to centroid:

kBest clustersAverage distanceDrop from the previous k
1all nine points (centroid 12.67)74 / 9 = 8.22—
2{1,2,3,10,11,12} and {24,25,26}3.225.00
3{1,2,3} {10,11,12} {24,25,26}6 / 9 = 0.672.56
4{1} {2,3} {10,11,12} {24,25,26}0.560.11
5{1} {2} {3} {10,11,12} {24,25,26}0.440.11

The drops are 5.00, 2.56, then only 0.11 and 0.11: the curve bends at k = 3, matching the three obvious groups.

Key idea: the elbow

Beyond the slides: this technique is commonly called the elbow (or knee) method; the slide does not name it. Its curve is schematic (no numbers on the axes), so the "best k" is read off visually as the bend, not computed. "Average" here is the mean distance to the centroid; some books use the sum of squared distances, which usually shows a bend at a similar k.

Too few, just right, too many

Lecture 5 · Slides 32–34

The three slides "Example: Picking k" use the same 41 points that fall into three natural groups (15 on the left, 15 on the upper right, 11 at the bottom). The short lines inside each cluster are samples of the distances from points to their centroid. The slides never print k; count the shapes.

SlidekSlide's wordsWhat the picture showsPosition on the Slide 31 curve
322"Too few; many long distances to centroid."The left and upper-right groups are lumped into one big cluster whose centroid is in empty space between them.steep part (large average)
333"Just right; distances rather short."One centroid in the middle of each natural group.the elbow
344"Too many; little improvement in average distance."The 15-point upper-right group is split into 10 + 5 although it had no gap.flat part

Measured from the slides' own picture (distances in pixels of the rendered slide, so only the ratios matter): average distance to centroid is about 280 for one cluster, 205 for k = 2, 85 for k = 3 and 72 for k = 4. Going 2 to 3 removes about 120; going 3 to 4 removes only about 13. That is the elbow, numerically.

Exam tip

"How would you pick k?" Model answer: run k-means for k = 1, 2, 3, …; plot average distance to centroid against k; it drops rapidly until the right k and changes little afterwards; choose k at the bend. Give the reasons: too few = clusters merge natural groups and distances are long; too many = clusters split tight groups for little gain.

Common mistake

Choosing the k with the smallest average distance. That is always the largest k tried (distance reaches 0 when every point is its own cluster). Look for where the improvement stops, not for the minimum.

The CURE algorithm: clusters of any shape, large data

Lecture 5 · Slides 35–42

Slide 35 is a black divider: "The CURE Algorithm — Extension of k-means to clusters of arbitrary shapes and large data". It promises two upgrades over k-means: (1) clusters need not be round blobs, and (2) the data may be too large for main memory. The next slides show how.

What CURE is, and why one centroid is not enough

Lecture 5 · Slide 36

(Printed Slide 37 is absent from the PDF; Slide 38 follows Slide 36 directly.)

Definition: CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives)

A clustering algorithm that (Slide 36) assumes a Euclidean distance, allows clusters to assume any shape, and uses a collection of representative points to represent clusters. A representative is one of several stand-in points, spread over a cluster, that together describe it.

The picture in the corner of Slide 36 shows two interlocking half-moons of dots, one blue and one red. It is the motivating example: with one centroid per cluster the centre of each moon falls in empty space, and the "nearest centroid" boundary slices straight through both moons. Describing each moon by several points lying along it lets a point find the right moon.

In the illustration above (built for this guide, 24 dots per moon) nearest-centroid assignment gives the wrong label to 10 of the 48 points (about one in five); with representatives along each moon, a point is assigned to the moon whose representative is nearest, which follows the curve.

Why Euclidean? Representatives are moved toward a centroid (an average), so CURE needs a space where averages exist, just like k-means. Beyond the slides: "any shape" means non-spherical shapes such as ellipses and crescents; very complicated or touching shapes can still fail.

Pass 1: build clusters and representatives from a sample

Lecture 5 · Slide 38

Slide 38 ("Starting CURE") says CURE is a 2-pass algorithm (one pass = one full read of the data from disk). Pass 1 works only on a small sample, so it fits in memory:

  1. Step 0, sample. Pick a random sample of points that fits in main memory.
  2. Step 1, initial clusters. Cluster these points hierarchically: start with every sampled point as its own cluster and repeatedly group (merge) the nearest points or clusters. Hierarchical clustering is affordable here because the sample is small (it is expensive on the whole data: Slide 21 gives its cost as O(N³)). The slide does not say when to stop merging; stop when the wanted number of clusters is left. Beyond the slides: the textbook suggests that two clusters are close if they contain a close pair of points, which lets clusters follow curved shapes.
  3. Step 2, representatives. For each cluster, pick a sample of points as dispersed as possible (far apart, tracing the outline of the cluster). From that sample, pick the representatives by moving them (say) 20% toward the centroid of the cluster.

"(say)" means the numbers 4 points and 20% are examples, not fixed constants. The slide leaves open how many dispersed points to take (the next slides use 4), and "20%" means 20% of the distance to the centroid.

The salary-versus-age example

Lecture 5 · Slides 39–41

Slide 39, "Example: Initial Clusters". A scatter plot with axes "age" (right) and "salary" (up) and no numbers. 24 points are drawn as the letters "h" and "e"; the slide never explains these letters, they are just two kinds of point and play no part in the algorithm. The result of Pass 1 steps 0–1 is three clusters: a round peach circle (upper right, 10 points, a mix of h and e), a gold ellipse (middle left, 6 points) and a long thin purple ellipse (bottom, 8 points). The two ellipses are elongated and lie side by side. This is the point of the picture: clusters can have different shapes and sizes, which a single-centroid method handles badly.

Slide 40, "Example: Pick Dispersed Points". The green note says "Pick (say) 4 remote points for each cluster." Four pink circles mark four points on the rim of the peach cluster: top, top right, left and bottom right. "Remote" and "dispersed" mean the same thing: far from each other and from the middle, so that together they outline the cluster. Only one cluster is shown, but the rule is applied to every cluster. The slide does not say how to choose them; Beyond the slides: take the point farthest from the centroid first, then repeatedly the point whose distance to the nearest chosen point is largest (the farthest-first idea of Slide 23).

Slide 41. Same title, new note: "Move points (say) 20% toward the centroid." The four pink circles slide inward. These moved points are the cluster's representatives. They are artificial: generally not data points.

Formula: moving a point toward the centroid

For a chosen point p and the centroid c of its cluster:   new position = p + 0.2 × (c − p) = 0.8 p + 0.2 c, applied to each coordinate. The point moves 20% of its distance to the centroid, so it ends up at 80% of its old distance from the centroid.

Worked example — one representative Practice, Slide 41 rule

Chosen point p = (10, 2), centroid c = (4, 6). c − p = (−6, 4); 0.2 × that = (−1.2, 0.8); new = (10 − 1.2, 2 + 0.8) = (8.8, 2.8). Check: old distance √(36 + 16) = 7.21; new distance = 0.8 × 7.21 = 5.77. Quiz L5-Q6 below applies the same rule to a whole picture of representatives.

Why move inward at all? (Beyond the slides, standard reasoning.) A rim point can be an outlier; pulling every chosen point a fixed fraction toward the centroid lessens the effect of such points, while a small fraction keeps the spread, and so the shape information. Moving 100% would collapse all representatives onto the centroid, which is just k-means.

Slide erratum (minor)

On Slide 41 the circles are drawn about one third of the way to the middle, not 20%. Measured from the picture, the drawing is only roughly to scale; use the 20% rule. Also, Slides 40 and 41 share a title, and the slides do not say that the representatives are new, synthetic points.

Pass 2: rescan and assign every point

Lecture 5 · Slide 42

After Pass 1 only the sample has been clustered; the representatives describe the clusters. Slide 42, "Finishing CURE", defines Pass 2: rescan the whole data set and visit each point p, and place it in the "closest cluster". The slide's definition: find the closest representative to p and assign p to that representative's cluster. Its picture shows one peach cluster with four representatives and a point p outside it.

  1. Read the next point p from the data on disk.
  2. Compute the distance from p to every representative of every cluster (Euclidean).
  3. Find the nearest representative; give p that representative's cluster label.
  4. Go to the next point. When the file is finished, every point has a label.

Only the few representatives (plus one point at a time) have to be in memory. Total data reads: two passes (one to take the sample, one to label everything).

Key idea

"Closest cluster" is defined through the representatives, not through the centroid. The figure's elongated cluster B has its centroid far to the right, so p is nearer the centroid of A, yet it is nearer to a representative of B and belongs to B. Slide 42 calls this the "normal definition of closest" (closest representative); it implies that other definitions exist but gives none.

CURE versus k-means

Lecture 5 · Slides 23–27, 35–42

k-meansCURE
DistanceEuclideanEuclidean
Cluster summaryone point, the centroid (mean)a collection of representative points
Cluster shapecompact, roundish blobsany shape (ellipses, rings, crescents)
Needs k up frontyes, picked by the user (elbow method)number of clusters at which Pass 1 stops merging (the slides do not give a rule)
Startk seeds: random or farthest-firsta random sample clustered hierarchically
Data handledthe whole data set, re-read in every rounda memory-sized sample for the hard work, then one rescan
Assigning a pointto the nearest centroidto the cluster of the nearest representative
Outliersa mean is pulled by them (Beyond the slides)representatives moved 20% inward damp them (Beyond the slides)
Iterationrepeat until convergenceno iteration: two passes
Quick recap: CURE
  • CURE = Clustering Using REpresentatives; Euclidean; any shape; large data.
  • Pass 1: random sample that fits in memory → cluster hierarchically → per cluster pick (say) 4 dispersed points → move them (say) 20% toward the centroid = representatives.
  • Pass 2: rescan all data; each point joins the cluster of its closest representative.
  • Next in this lecture: BFR, the other scalable extension of k-means (it assumes normal clusters instead).
Exam tip

"Describe how CURE works": give Pass 1 steps 0, 1, 2 (sample, hierarchical clustering, dispersed points moved 20% to the centroid) and Pass 2 (rescan, nearest representative). Mention why: any shape (representatives) and large data (sample plus one rescan).

Try it yourself first. Write the steps of CURE from memory, then move a set of representatives 20% toward the centroid and compare with the solution.

Quiz L5-Q6CURE: steps, and moving the representatives 20% toward the centroid Lecture 5 · Slides 82–83 (method: Slides 35–42, 87)
Question (as on the slides)

Quiz: Initialization in CURE (question on Slide 82; the slide’s answer is on Slide 83). CURE = Clustering Using REpresentatives.

(a) Describe in steps how CURE algorithm works.
(b) Assuming following selection of representative points from each cluster move the representative points 20% of the distance to the cluster’s centroid.

Data (the picture on Slide 82; it has no numbers). Two clusters in a 2-D plane: a small round cluster (a disc) in the middle and a ring-shaped cluster (a grey band) around it, with an empty gap (the hollow) in between. The selected representative points are the black dots: 5 dots on the small disc and 14 dots on the ring (7 along its outer edge and 7 along its inner edge, alternating) — 19 in all. Slide 83 repeats the picture with the dots moved; its only written answer is “Moving the representative points 20% of the distance to the cluster’s centroid”. Because the slide gives no numbers, part (b) first reads the dot positions off the picture (Figure L5-Q6-2).

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Picture two countries on a map: a round island, and a ring-shaped island (an atoll) around it. To describe a country you could plant one flag in its middle (that is what k-means does with a centroid). For the atoll that fails: its middle is open water, and it is exactly the same spot as the round island’s middle. CURE instead posts a handful of border guards (the representatives) spread around each country’s edge. A newcomer simply asks “which guard is nearest to me?” and joins that guard’s country. The “20% move” pulls every guard one fifth of the way back toward his country’s centre, so a guard who wandered out to a far-off hamlet (an outlier) cannot stretch the country.

Words you need

Centroid = the average (mean) of all the points of a cluster, coordinate by coordinate (Lecture 5 · Slide 16); it need not be a data point. Representative point = one of a few stand-in points that together describe a cluster. Euclidean distance = ordinary straight-line distance, d(p, q) = √((p1 − q1)² + (p2 − q2)²) in 2-D. Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering = start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the two nearest clusters (Slides 14 and 16).

Part (a) The steps of CURE Lecture 5 · Slides 35–42, 87
  1. What CURE is Lecture 5 · Slides 35–36 CURE is an “extension of k-means to clusters of arbitrary shapes and large data” (Slide 35). It assumes a Euclidean distance, allows clusters to have any shape and uses a collection of representative points to represent each cluster instead of one centroid (Slide 36). It is a 2-pass algorithm: Pass 1 builds the clusters and their representatives from a small sample; Pass 2 places every point of the whole data set (Slides 38 and 42).
  2. Pass 1, step 0 — pick a random sample of points that fits in main memory Lecture 5 · Slide 38 Why: the full data set is too big for memory, but a sample can be clustered in memory by a method that would be far too slow on all the data; being random, the sample tends to show the same overall shapes.
  3. Pass 1, step 1 — initial clusters: cluster the sample hierarchically Lecture 5 · Slides 38–39 Start with every sampled point as its own cluster and repeatedly “group nearest points/clusters” (merge the two closest clusters; Slide 14) until the wanted clusters are left; Slide 39 shows three initial clusters in a salary-versus-age plot. Why hierarchical: merging nearby points can follow a curved or elongated group, so clusters are not forced to be round blobs. Beyond the slides: merging stops when the wanted number of clusters is left (the slides give no stopping rule for CURE; compare “stopping point k” on Slide 69), and the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets) suggests merging clusters that contain a close pair of points, which lets clusters follow curved shapes.
  4. Pass 1, step 2a — in each cluster pick a sample of points that is as dispersed as possible Lecture 5 · Slides 38, 40 Slide 40: “pick (say) 4 remote points for each cluster”. Why: points spread over the cluster outline its shape and extent: for a ring, points all around the ring; for a long cluster, points at both ends and in between. Beyond the slides: a standard way is “farthest first” (the idea of Slide 23 for starting k-means): take one point, then repeatedly add the point whose distance to the nearest already-chosen point is largest, until you have (say) 4. The quiz picture uses 14 dots for the ring and 5 for the disc; “4” is only an example.
  5. Pass 1, step 2b — move each chosen point (say) 20% toward the centroid of its cluster; the moved points are the representatives Lecture 5 · Slides 38, 41 Slide 38: “pick representatives by moving them (say) 20% toward the centroid of the cluster”; Slide 41: “Move points (say) 20% toward the centroid”. The moved points are artificial positions (not necessarily data points), and the data points themselves are not moved. A Euclidean space is needed, otherwise there is no centroid and no “straight line” to move along (this is why Slide 36 says CURE assumes a Euclidean distance). This is the step part (b) asks you to carry out.
  6. Pass 2 — rescan the whole data set and put every point in its “closest cluster” Lecture 5 · Slides 42, 87 Read the entire data set once from disk. For each point p, find the closest representative to p (smallest Euclidean distance, over the representatives of all clusters) and assign p to that representative’s cluster (Slide 42). Only the few representatives and one point at a time have to be in memory, and no further iterations are needed. Beyond the slides: the textbook inserts an optional merge before this pass: two clusters are merged if a pair of their representatives (one from each) is closer than a user-chosen threshold.
Why representatives allow arbitrary shapes (Slide 36)

A cluster is described by several points spread over its outline, and a point belongs to the cluster of its nearest representative. So a cluster’s territory is the union of the neighbourhoods of its representatives, which can bend along a ring or a crescent (Slide 36 shows two interlocking crescents). One centroid can only describe a compact blob. In this quiz the ring’s centroid sits exactly where the small disc’s centroid is, so no centroid-only method can tell the two clusters apart, but the ring’s representatives lie on the ring and the disc’s lie in the disc, so every point finds the right cluster (checked numerically in part (b), step 9). BFR (Bradley–Fayyad–Reina, Slide 44), by contrast, assumes normally distributed, axis-aligned elliptical clusters; CURE has no such assumption.

CURE compared with k-means, in three bullets (k-means: Slides 23–27)
  • Shape. k-means summarises each cluster by ONE point (the centroid) and sends every point to the nearest centroid, so it finds compact, roundish blobs. CURE summarises each cluster by SEVERAL spread-out representatives, so a cluster can be a ring, a crescent or a long ellipse.
  • Data size and passes. k-means repeats “assign all points, recompute centroids” until convergence (Slide 24), so it needs the whole data set again and again. CURE clusters only a memory-sized sample in Pass 1 and then needs just one more scan (Pass 2), which is why Slide 35 says “large data”.
  • Start, summary and outliers. k-means starts from k chosen points (Slide 23) and its centroid, a mean, is dragged by outliers. CURE starts from a hierarchical clustering of the sample, pulls its representatives 20% toward the centroid (Beyond the slides: this damps the pull of outlying points) and defines “closest cluster” as the cluster of the closest representative. Both assume a Euclidean distance.
Part (b) Move the representatives 20% toward the centroid Lecture 5 · Slides 82–83 (method: 38, 41)
  1. Formula (write it down first). For a representative p and the centroid c of its own cluster, applied to each coordinate:
    Move 20% toward the centroid

    new position = p + 0.2 × (c − p) = 0.8 × p + 0.2 × c
    distance moved = 0.2 × d(p, c)    and    new distance to the centroid = 0.8 × d(p, c)

    Why it works: (c − p) is the arrow from the point to the centroid; adding one fifth of that arrow to p slides the point one fifth of the way along the straight line to the centroid. “Move 20% of the distance to the centroid” means move by 20% of that distance (the point stays far out), not “move to a place 20% of the distance away” (that would be 80% of the way in). Slide 83’s picture agrees: the dots only shift a little.
  2. Tiny numeric check of the formula. For p = (8, 6) and c = (4, 2): new = (8 + 0.2 × (4 − 8), 6 + 0.2 × (2 − 6)) = (8 − 0.8, 6 − 0.8) = (7.2, 5.2). The old distance √(4² + 4²) = 5.657 shrinks to √(3.2² + 3.2²) = 4.525 = 0.8 × 5.657.
  3. Find the centroids. The centroid is the average of all points of the cluster (not of the representatives only). Both clusters are symmetric about the same middle of the picture, so both centroids are at that middle. The ring’s centroid is therefore an empty spot in the hollow, not a data point; this is why CURE needs a Euclidean space, where averages exist. The slide marks no centroids, so we put the origin (0, 0) at the middle: c = (0, 0) for both clusters.
    Common mistake

    Do not average the representatives to get the centroid. The 14 ring dots average to about (1.4, −7.3) only because they are unevenly spaced; the true centroid of the whole ring is its middle.

  4. Read the coordinates off Slide 82. Slide 82 is a picture without numbers, so we measured it: x to the right, y upward, and the unit chosen so that the outer radius of the ring is 100 (the ring band runs from radius about 74 to 100, so the hollow’s edge is at about 74; the small disc has radius about 25). Readings are accurate to about ±1–2 units; any consistent reading earns the marks. Name the dots O1–O7 (ring, outer edge), I1–I7 (ring, inner edge), D1–D5 (small disc). The small disc is drawn about 2.7 units left of the ring’s middle; that is below reading accuracy (taking the disc’s own middle as its centroid would change each new disc position by only 0.2 × 2.7 = 0.5 units), so both centroids are taken at (0, 0).
  5. Worked rows, in full. With c = (0, 0) we have c − p = −p, so new = p − 0.2p = 0.8p.
    • O1 (ring, outer edge), p = (80, 58): c − p = (−80, −58); 0.2 × that = (−16, −11.6); new = (80 − 16, 58 − 11.6) = (64.0, 46.4). Check: old distance √(80² + 58²) = √9764 = 98.8; new distance √(64² + 46.4²) = √6248.96 = 79.1, i.e. 80% of the old distance; distance moved √(16² + 11.6²) = 19.8, i.e. 20% of the old distance.
    • I5 (ring, inner edge), p = (0, −78): c − p = (0, 78); 0.2 × that = (0, 15.6); new = (0 + 0, −78 + 15.6) = (0.0, −62.4). Check: old distance √(0² + 78²) = √6084 = 78.0; new distance √(0² + 62.4²) = √3893.76 = 62.4, i.e. 80% of the old distance; distance moved √(0² + 15.6²) = 15.6, i.e. 20% of the old distance.
    • D3 (small disc), p = (−23, 10): c − p = (23, −10); 0.2 × that = (4.6, −2); new = (−23 + 4.6, 10 − 2) = (−18.4, 8.0). Check: old distance √(23² + 10²) = √629 = 25.1; new distance √(18.4² + 8²) = √402.56 = 20.1, i.e. 80% of the old distance; distance moved √(4.6² + 2²) = 5.0, i.e. 20% of the old distance.
  6. All 19 representatives. Every row is new = 0.8 × old; the distances come from d = √(x² + y²).

  8. Sanity checks and what the numbers say. (i) Every new dot lies on the segment between its old position and the centroid (same direction, smaller radius). (ii) New distance = 0.8 × old; distance moved = 0.2 × old, so points farther out move farther. (iii) Ring, outer-edge dots: radius ≈ 98–101 becomes ≈ 79–80 (moved on average 19.8); they are still inside the grey band, whose inner edge is at about 74. Ring, inner-edge dots: ≈ 76–79 becomes ≈ 61–63 (moved on average 15.4), which is below 74, so they now lie inside the empty hollow. Small disc: ≈ 21–25 becomes ≈ 16.5–20.1 (moved on average 4.6), still inside the disc (radius about 25). (iv) The whole pattern is a shrunken copy (scaled by 0.8 about the same centre) of the old one. (v) No dot crosses the centroid, because each moves only 20% of the way. This is exactly the pattern of Slide 83: 7 dots in the band, 7 dots in the hollow, 5 dots pulled inward in the disc.
  9. Check that Pass 2 still works with the moved representatives. Take the 19 moved dots as the final representatives and assign data points p by the nearest representative (Euclidean distance, Slide 42).     (70, −45)83.2D5′   67.0O7′   6.6ring
    (Python check: of 300,000 random points in the ring band and 300,000 in the disc, none is closer to a representative of the other cluster.)
Why move the representatives toward the centroid?

Beyond the slides: the dispersed points are the most extreme points of their cluster, so they may be outliers or lie right at the fringe. Shrinking them toward the centroid pulls them in, and the farther out a point is, the more it moves (20% of a bigger distance). With a shrink of 100% every representative would collapse onto the centroid and CURE would behave like a centroid method such as k-means; with 0% it would use the raw boundary points. The slides only say “(say) 20%”, so treat 20% as an example value, not a law.

Practice (self-made, not from the slides): the same move with numbers given

A cluster has the five points (1, 1), (3, 7), (5, 1), (9, 3), (7, 3), so its centroid is c = (5, 3) (average of each coordinate; not (0, 0)). Pick the four dispersed points (1, 1), (3, 7), (9, 3), (5, 1) and move each 20% toward c with new = p + 0.2 × (c − p):

pc − p0.2 × (c − p)new position
(1, 1)(4, 2)(0.8, 0.4)(1.8, 1.4)
(3, 7)(2, −4)(0.4, −0.8)(3.4, 6.2)
(9, 3)(−4, 0)(−0.8, 0.0)(8.2, 3.0)
(5, 1)(0, 2)(0.0, 0.4)(5.0, 1.4)
Exam tip

Part (a) is “describe in steps”: write the numbered steps in this order with the key words: random sample that fits in main memory → hierarchical clustering of the sample (merge nearest points/clusters) → pick dispersed points in each cluster (say 4) → move them (say) 20% toward the centroid = the representatives → Pass 2: rescan all points, assign each to the cluster of the closest representative. For part (b), draw both clusters, mark the centroid, show new = p + 0.2(c − p) once, and put every new dot one fifth of the way in. A clearly shown formula and line earn marks even if a coordinate is slightly off.

Common mistake
  • Moving to 20% of the distance (i.e. 80% of the way) instead of moving by 20% of the distance; or moving by a fixed amount (“20 units”) instead of a fraction of each point’s own distance.
  • Using the wrong centroid (the middle of the whole data, the other cluster’s, or the average of only the representatives), or thinking the ring’s centroid must be a data point (it lies in the empty hollow).
  • Moving all data points, or the representatives of only one cluster. Every representative of every cluster moves, and only the representatives.
  • Forgetting Pass 2, or doing the final assignment by nearest centroid. In CURE a point goes to the cluster of its closest representative.
Slide erratum (minor: drawing and omissions only; no wrong rule)

(1) Slide 83 gives only a picture and one line of text, so the written steps of part (a) come from Slides 35–42 and 87. (2) The Slide 83 picture is hand-drawn and not to scale. Measured against Slide 82 (both pictures scaled to the same ring size), the ring dots moved only about 9–20% of their distance (outer edge from radius ≈ 99 to ≈ 80–90, inner edge from ≈ 77 to ≈ 62–68) and the disc dots about 30–45% (from ≈ 23 to ≈ 12–17), instead of exactly 20% for all. The direction (straight toward the common middle) and the pattern (7 dots in the band, 7 in the hollow, 5 in the disc) agree, so treat it as an imprecise drawing; for numbers use the exact rule above. (3) Omissions: the slides do not say when the hierarchical step stops, how “dispersed” points are chosen, or that the textbook merges close clusters before Pass 2 (Slide 87 omits it too); these are filled in above under “Beyond the slides”. (4) Slide 40 says “(say) 4” remote points per cluster while the quiz picture has 14 and 5; the number is a free parameter.

Final answer:
(a) CURE has two passes. Pass 1: (0) take a random sample of points that fits in main memory; (1) cluster the sample hierarchically (repeatedly merge the nearest points/clusters) to get the initial clusters; (2) in each cluster pick (say) 4 points that are as dispersed as possible and move each (say) 20% toward the cluster’s centroid, p′ = p + 0.2(c − p); the moved points are the representatives. Pass 2: rescan the whole data set and place each point in the cluster of its closest representative (Euclidean distance).
(b) Each representative moves straight toward the centroid of its own cluster by 20% of its own distance: new = p + 0.2(c − p), which with the centroid at the middle (0, 0) is 0.8 × p, i.e. to 80% of the old distance (outer radius of the ring = 100 units). Ring outer-edge dots: radius ≈ 99.1 → ≈ 79.3 (still in the band). Ring inner-edge dots: ≈ 77.1 → ≈ 61.6 (now in the hollow). Small-disc dots: ≈ 23.1 → ≈ 18.5 (still in the disc). All 19 coordinates are in the tables above, e.g. (80, 58) → (64, 46.4), (0, −78) → (0, −62.4), (−23, 10) → (−18.4, 8).
Where the marks come from: Part (a), roughly one mark per step: (1) CURE idea: Euclidean, representatives instead of one centroid, 2 passes; (2) random sample that fits in main memory; (3) hierarchical clustering of the sample (merge nearest points/clusters) gives the initial clusters; (4) in each cluster pick dispersed points (say 4); (5) move them (say) 20% toward the centroid, giving the representatives; (6) Pass 2: rescan all the data and assign each point to the cluster of its closest representative. Part (b): (7) correct formula or idea “one fifth of the way to the centroid”, new = p + 0.2(c − p); (8) correct centroid for each cluster (both at the middle; the ring’s is in the hollow); (9) every representative of both clusters moved straight toward its own centroid; (10) each move is 20% of that point’s own distance (new distance = 80% of old; outer dots move more than inner and disc dots). This split is a sensible guess, not the official mark scheme.
Slide check: matches the slide’s answer. Slide 83 shows every representative pulled toward the common middle, which is what “move 20% of the distance to the cluster’s centroid” gives; our exact positions (new = 0.8 × old) were recomputed with Python. Slide erratum (minor): the Slide 83 picture is not drawn exactly to scale (ring dots ≈ 9–20%, disc dots ≈ 30–45% instead of 20%) and the slides omit a stopping rule, the farthest-first rule and the merge step; see the erratum box above. The coordinates were measured from the raster picture on Slide 82 (accuracy about ±1–2 units), so your own readings may differ by that much without being wrong.

BFR: k-means for data that does not fit in memory

Lecture 5 · Slides 43–45

Slide 43 is a black divider titled "The BFR Algorithm" with the subtitle "Extension of k-means to large data". Two scalable clustering ideas are in this lecture. CURE (the section before) keeps a memory-sized sample, builds representative points from it and then rescans the data once. BFR takes the opposite route: it reads all the data, chunk by chunk, but keeps almost none of the points: it keeps running totals (N, SUM, SUMSQ) per cluster and per compressed group, plus a few raw retained points (RS).

Beginner intuition

A market-research firm interviews a billion people. It cannot keep a billion questionnaires on one desk. Instead, for each customer segment it keeps a tally sheet: how many people so far, the running total of their ages, and the running total of the squares of their ages. From those three numbers it can always say "the average age is 41, and ages are spread by about 9 years", and when a new questionnaire arrives it simply adds to the totals and throws the paper away. BFR is that tally-sheet trick applied to clusters.

What BFR is, and what it assumes

Lecture 5 · Slide 44

Definition: BFR (Bradley–Fayyad–Reina)

BFR is a variant of k-means designed to handle very large (disk-resident) data sets. It assumes that clusters are normally distributed around a centroid in a Euclidean space, and that the dimensions are independent, so each cluster is an axis-aligned ellipse (Slide 44). Its trick is an efficient way to summarise clusters: the memory required should be O(clusters), not O(data).

Take the three phrases one at a time.

  • "Very large, disk-resident". The data sit on disk because they do not fit in main memory (RAM). Reading from disk is the slow part, so the sensible plan is to read each point from disk only once and extract everything we need from it at that moment. (Beyond the slides: that is what BFR does: one pass over the data. The slides do not say "one pass" in words; they say points are read "in chunks".)
  • "Euclidean". A centroid is an average of points, and distances are straight-line distances. So BFR cannot be used with Jaccard, cosine or edit distance, exactly as for k-means itself (Slide 23).
  • "O(clusters), not O(data)". Memory grows with the number of clusters k (and the dimension d), not with the number of points n. Doubling the data size does not change the memory needed. The arithmetic: each cluster is stored with 2d + 1 numbers (Slide 49, explained below). For k = 50 clusters in d = 100 dimensions that is 50 × (2·100 + 1) = 10 050 numbers, whether the data hold 106 or 109 points. Keeping the 109 raw points would need 109 × 100 = 1011 numbers.

The normal-distribution assumption

Lecture 5 · Slide 44 (bell-curve figure)

The picture in the top-right corner of Slide 44 is the bell curve of the Gaussian (normal) distribution: the density of points is highest at the centre (the mean, 0 on the axis) and falls away symmetrically. The horizontal axis is measured in standard deviations σ (sigma): σ is the typical distance of a point from the centre, along that axis. The numbers on the slide are the share of all points in each strip between the dashed lines. Check that they add up: 2 × (0.3413 + 0.1359 + 0.0214 + 0.00135) = 0.9999, which is 1 up to rounding.

Why this matters for clustering: if a cluster really is normal, almost all of its points lie within 2 or 3 σ of its centroid. That fact is what makes the later "is this point close enough?" test (Slides 54–56) meaningful: "within about 2 standard deviations" has a precise probabilistic meaning only because of this assumption.

Definition: normal cluster in d dimensions (as BFR uses it)

Each coordinate of the points in a cluster is bell-shaped around the cluster mean, with its own standard deviation σ1, …, σd, and the coordinates do not influence each other. The cloud of points is then an ellipse (a stretched circle) whose long and short directions are along the coordinate axes.

Why "axis-aligned" ellipses?

Lecture 5 · Slide 44 (three clusters figure); shapes quiz Slides 78–79

The coloured picture on Slide 44 shows three clusters: a circle (blue), a wide horizontal ellipse (magenta) and a tall vertical ellipse (green). All three have their long and short directions parallel to the page axes. That is the BFR assumption. The standard deviations may be different in different dimensions (that makes an ellipse rather than a circle), but the axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space (Slide 79).

Why does BFR need this? (Beyond the slides for the full reasoning; the slides only state the rule.) A cluster is summarised by one mean and one variance per dimension (Slides 48–49). That describes spread along each coordinate axis separately. A tilted ellipse means that when x is large, y also tends to be large: the coordinates are correlated. Capturing that needs extra numbers (covariances, d(d − 1)/2 of them), which BFR does not store. A tilted cluster would be summarised by an axis-aligned ellipse that is too fat, and the closeness test would accept points that do not belong (see Figure 5 of Quiz L5-Q4 below).

Exam tip

The shape question is a standard one: horizontal ellipse OK, vertical ellipse OK, tilted ellipse not OK (circles are the special case of equal σ and are fine). Give the reason in one line: "standard deviations may differ along different axes, but the axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space".

Memory loads and the first k centroids

Lecture 5 · Slide 45

Slide 45 sets the stage for the whole algorithm in three bullets.

  1. Points are read from disk into main memory in chunks. One chunk is called a memory load. It is as many points as fit in RAM at once (together with the summaries).
  2. Most points from previous memory loads are summarised by simple statistics. They are not kept. The word is "most", not "all": some points (the retained set, next section) are kept exactly as they are.
  3. To begin, from the initial load we select the initial k centroids "by some sensible approach". The only one listed is "take k random points"; the second bullet is a literal "…".
Slide erratum (omission)

The "…" on Slide 45 stands for the other sensible approaches, which the slide never lists. Beyond the slides: (i) pick one random point, then repeatedly the point farthest from all points already chosen (the farthest-first rule of Slide 23, used in Quiz L5-Q3); (ii) cluster a small sample hierarchically and take the centroids. The slide also does not say how big a chunk is, and it takes k as known in advance, as in k-means.

The three sets of points: DS, CS and RS

Lecture 5 · Slides 46–47, 52

Slide 46 names the vocabulary that the rest of BFR is written in. At any moment each point that BFR has seen is in exactly one of three places (or has been merged into one of them).

Beginner intuition

A post office sorts letters. Letters for a known neighbourhood go in that neighbourhood's bin, where only a bundle count is recorded (DS). Letters from several senders in the same unknown town are tied into a bundle that waits to be assigned to a neighbourhood later (CS). A strange letter that fits nowhere stays loose on the table (RS).

Definitions (Slide 46)

Discard set (DS): points close enough to a centroid to be summarised. Only the summaries are kept in main memory; the points are discarded.

Compression set (CS): groups of points that are close together but not close to any existing centroid. These points are summarised, but not assigned to a cluster. Only the summaries are kept in main memory.

Retained set (RS): isolated points waiting to be assigned to a compression set. Held in main memory exactly as they are.

Read it like a night sky. The big blue ellipse is a real "galaxy": a cluster, whose size and shape reflect its standard deviations in each dimension. The small orange ellipses are tight little groups of stars that are not near a galaxy yet: they are summarised (each has its own centre, the +), but they do not belong to a cluster. The red dots are lone stars: neither near a galaxy nor near each other. Slide 52 is an exact repeat of Slide 47 (it is shown again just before the two "A few details" questions); nothing new is on it.

DSCSRS
What it holdspoints close to a cluster centroidsmall tight groups far from every centroidisolated points
In memory assummary per cluster (N, SUM, SUMSQ)summary per group (N, SUM, SUMSQ)the raw points
Assigned to a cluster?yesno (not yet)no
Points discarded?yesyesno
How many of themexactly k summariesa modest number of groupsa modest number of points
Fatestays; grows as points are addedmerged with other CS (step 4) or, in the last round, into the nearest cluster / outliermay join a new CS in a later load; last round: nearest cluster / outlier

Why bother with a CS? Suppose a group of 5 000 points lies far from every centroid. If we kept them as raw points, memory would grow with the data. If we threw them away, we would lose a possible cluster. Summarising them as one CS set costs only 2d + 1 numbers and keeps the option open. Why an RS? A single point, or two far-apart points, give no useful spread estimate (one point has variance 0). They are cheaper and safer to keep as they are until more points arrive.

Common mistakes
  • "The CS belongs to a cluster." No: the CS is summarised but not assigned to a cluster.
  • "All points are discarded." No: the RS points are kept exactly as they are.
  • "DS and CS are stored differently." Both are summaries; the difference is whether the group is attached to one of the k clusters.

(Slide 46 never says what the CS summary is. It is the same N, SUM, SUMSQ as for the DS; this is implied by Slides 48–51 and said outright on Slide 57.)

What is stored: N, SUM and SUMSQ

Lecture 5 · Slides 48–49

This is the technical heart of BFR, and it is short. The question: "what is the smallest thing we can keep about a cluster, so that we can still say where its centre is and how spread out it is, and so that we can add new points cheaply?"

Definition: the summary of a cluster (Slide 48)

For each cluster, the discard set (DS) is summarised by:

  • N: the number of points;
  • SUM: a vector whose i-th component is the sum of the coordinates of the points in the i-th dimension;
  • SUMSQ: a vector whose i-th component is the sum of the squares of the coordinates in the i-th dimension.

With d dimensions that is 1 + d + d = 2d + 1 numbers, whatever the size of the cluster (Slide 49). A cluster of 10 points and a cluster of 10 million points take the same space.

Formulas (Slide 49): reading the cluster back out of its summary

Centroid in dimension i: ci = SUMi / N

Variance in dimension i: σi² = SUMSQi / N − (SUMi / N)²

Standard deviation in dimension i: σi = √(SUMSQi / N − (SUMi / N)²)

Why the variance formula works. (Beyond the slides, three lines of algebra; you do not need to reproduce it.) Variance is the average squared distance from the mean c: (1/N) Σ (x − c)². Expanding the square gives (1/N) Σ x² − 2c · (1/N) Σ x + c². Since (1/N) Σ x = c, this is (1/N) Σ x² − 2c² + c² = SUMSQ/N − c². In words: mean of the squares minus the square of the mean.

Why this summary is so convenient

  • It is incrementally updatable. A new point x is absorbed by N ← N + 1, SUM ← SUM + x, SUMSQ ← SUMSQ + x² (coordinate by coordinate). The point can then be thrown away. This is exactly "Add Ns, SUMs, SUMSQs" on Slide 51.
  • Two summaries combine by addition (Figure 4). That is how CS sets are merged (step 4) and how a CS is folded into a cluster in the last round. No old points are consulted.
  • It supports the closeness tests. The centroid and the σi needed by the Mahalanobis test (Slide 55) come straight from N, SUM, SUMSQ.
  • It matches the axis-aligned assumption. Only per-dimension totals are stored, so only per-dimension variances can be recovered; that is why the clusters must be axis-aligned.

This also answers the question of Slide 80: the statistics do not have to be computed from scratch in each round; they are updated from their previous values (see Quiz L5-Q5 below).

Worked example (BFR numbers not examined; understand the idea only) — a tally card in one dimension Lecture 5 · Slides 48–49 (illustration added by this guide)

Points {1, 2, 3}. N = 3, SUM = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, SUMSQ = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. Centroid = 6/3 = 2. Variance = 14/3 − 2² = 4.667 − 4 = 0.667; σ = √0.667 = 0.816. Now the point 4 arrives: N = 4, SUM = 10, SUMSQ = 14 + 16 = 30, so the centroid is 2.5 and the variance is 30/4 − 2.5² = 7.5 − 6.25 = 1.25. Recomputing from {1, 2, 3, 4} gives the same answer, and no old point was needed.

Common mistakes
  • SUMSQ is not (SUM)². For {1, 2, 3}: SUMSQ = 14 but (SUM)² = 36. Square each coordinate first, then add.
  • SUM and SUMSQ are vectors (one entry per dimension), not single numbers; N is a single number.
  • The variance divides by N (not N − 1), as on Slide 49.
  • Don't average the standard deviations of two clusters to get the standard deviation of their union; add the N, SUM, SUMSQ and recompute.

Processing one memory load

Lecture 5 · Slides 50–51

Slide 49 ends with "Next step: actual clustering". Slides 50 and 51 give the loop that is run for each memory load (each chunk of points read from disk). There are five steps; the first four are repeated for every chunk and the fifth happens only once, after the last chunk.

  1. Step 1: add sufficiently close points to the clusters (DS). Find the points in the chunk that are "sufficiently close" to a cluster centroid, add them to that cluster and to the DS. They are so close to the centroid that they can be summarised and then discarded. (How "sufficiently close" is decided is question Q1 of Slide 53, answered by the Mahalanobis distance on Slides 54–56 below.)
  2. Step 2: cluster the rest. Use any main-memory clustering algorithm (for example k-means or hierarchical clustering; BFR treats it as a black box) on the remaining points together with the old RS. Clusters go to the CS; outlying points go to the RS. (Beyond the slides: in the textbook a group of two or more points counts as a cluster for the CS, and a point left alone stays in the RS.)
  3. Step 3: update the DS statistics. Adjust the statistics of the clusters to account for the new points: add the Ns, SUMs and SUMSQs. (The new CS groups from step 2 also get their own N, SUM, SUMSQ; the slide only mentions the DS.)
  4. Step 4: consider merging compressed sets in the CS. If two CS groups are close enough, combine them by adding their statistics. (How to decide is question Q2 of Slide 53, answered on Slides 57–58 below.)
  5. Step 5: last round only. If this is the last round (the last chunk of data), merge all compressed sets in the CS and all RS points into their nearest cluster, or treat them as outliers.
Key idea

After every memory load, the only things in memory are: the k cluster summaries, the CS summaries, the RS points and the next chunk. All the points that were absorbed into the DS or the CS are gone, yet nothing has been lost that BFR needs.

A feel for the dynamics

The table below is a made-up illustration (not from the slides) of how the three sets might develop over a run with k = 2.

MomentDS (two clusters)CSRS

Load 2N, SUM, SUMSQ grow by addition; centroids shift slightlya new group appears; two groups close together are mergedold strays are re-clustered with the new leftovers; two of them form a new CS group
Load 3, …samesamesame
