Slide erratum / omissions (Slides 50–51)
  • Slide 50 uses "sufficiently close" without defining it; the definition comes on Slides 54–56.
  • Step 5 gives two options, "nearest cluster" or "outliers", without a criterion. Beyond the slides: the same distance tests apply: a CS or RS point is merged into the nearest cluster only if it is close enough (for example within the threshold); otherwise it is an outlier.
  • On Slide 51 the legend overlaps the last line of step 5 ("as outliers)"); this is a layout flaw only. In practice the DS statistics are updated while points are absorbed in step 1, so "step 3" is bookkeeping done at that moment.

Q1: How close is "close enough"? The Mahalanobis distance

Lecture 5 · Slides 53–56

Slide 53, "A few details…", poses the two open questions of the loop:

  • Q1) How do we decide if a point is "close enough" to a DS cluster that we will add the point to that cluster?
  • Q2) How do we decide whether two compressed sets (CS) deserve to be combined into one?

Slide 54 answers Q1: BFR suggests that the Mahalanobis distance is less than a threshold. "Put into a cluster (and discard)" means: add the point's numbers into the cluster's N, SUM, SUMSQ, then throw the point away.

Why not ordinary Euclidean distance?

Lecture 5 · Slides 54–55

Consider a cluster that is long and thin: very spread out in x (σx = 4) and tight in y (σy = 1). A point 4 units away along the long direction is perfectly typical for this cluster. A point 4 units away along the thin direction is very unusual (4 standard deviations). Euclidean distance cannot tell them apart; both are at distance 4. The fix is to measure every direction in units of that direction's standard deviation.

Definition: Mahalanobis distance as used in BFR (Slide 55)

For a point (x1, …, xd) and a cluster centroid (c1, …, cd) ("normalised Euclidean distance from centroid"):

  1. Normalise in each dimension: yi = (xi − ci) / σi
  2. Take the sum of the squares of the yi
  3. Take the square root: d(x, c) = √( Σi=1..d ((xi − ci) / σi)² )

where σi is the standard deviation of the points in the cluster in the i-th dimension.

Reading it. A normalised difference yi = 1 means "one standard deviation away from the centre in dimension i". In one dimension the Mahalanobis distance is simply |x − c| / σ (how many standard deviations away you are). In several dimensions it is the Euclidean distance of the normalised point. A dimension in which the cluster is tight (small σi) counts a lot; a dimension in which it is spread out (large σi) counts little.

All the ingredients come from the summary: ci = SUMi/N and σi = √(SUMSQi/N − (SUMi/N)²) (Slide 49). So the test needs no raw points.

Worked example (BFR numbers not examined; understand the idea only) — Mahalanobis distance for understanding Lecture 5 · Slides 55–56 (numbers added by this guide)

Cluster centroid c = (10, 5), σ = (4, 1). (BFR numericals will not be asked; this only shows how the formula behaves.)

PointDifferences (x−c)Normalised yM.D. = √(y₁² + y₂²)EuclideanM.D. < 2 ?
P = (14, 5)(4, 0)(1, 0)14.00accept
Q = (10, 9)(0, 4)(0, 4)44.00reject
R = (13, 6)(3, 1)(0.75, 1)√1.5625 = 1.253.16accept
S = (17, 5)(7, 0)(1.75, 0)1.757.00accept
T = (10, 7)(0, 2)(0, 2)22.00reject (not < 2)

Point S is 7 units from the centroid in the ordinary sense but accepted; point T is only 2 units away but rejected. That is the point of the normalisation.

The acceptance rule and its threshold

Lecture 5 · Slide 56

Rule (Slide 56)

Accept a point for a cluster if its M.D. is < some threshold; common practice is to specify M.D. < 2.

The intuition behind "2" comes from the bell curve of Figure 1: roughly 2 standard deviations covers about 95% of a normal cluster's points. A point beyond that is unusual for this cluster. Points that fail the test for every cluster are not added to the DS; they go on to step 2 (they may become part of a CS or stay in the RS). (Beyond the slides: if more than one cluster passes the test, the point is given to the nearest one.)

Slide erratum (naming and a caveat)
  • Name. The slide's heading is "Mahalanobis distance", but its subtitle says "normalized Euclidean distance". They coincide here because BFR assumes axis-aligned clusters (no correlation between dimensions). The general Mahalanobis distance uses the full covariance matrix, √((x−c)T S−1 (x−c)). For BFR you use the slide's formula.
  • σ = 0. If a cluster has N = 1 or a constant coordinate, σi = 0 and the formula divides by zero. The slides do not address it.
  • Dimension (Beyond the slides). "M.D. < 2" is only sensible in low dimension. For a normal cluster the average squared M.D. of its members equals d, so a typical member has M.D. ≈ √d. The share of a true cluster's points that a fixed threshold of 2 would keep is 95.4% for d = 1, 86.5% for d = 2, 59.4% for d = 4 and only 5.3% for d = 10. A threshold that grows with the dimension, such as 2√d, keeps 95.4%, 98.2%, 99.7% and about 100% for those four cases. (Computed with the chi-square distribution.) In the exam, quote the slide's "M.D. < 2".

Q2: Should two compressed sets be combined?

Lecture 5 · Slides 57–58

Step 4 of the loop asks whether two CS groups (the slides call them "CS clusters", "CS subclusters" and "compression sets" interchangeably) actually belong together. Slide 57 gives two ways to decide.

Way 1: variance of the combined subcluster

Lecture 5 · Slide 57

"Compute the variance of the combined subcluster. N, SUM and SUMSQ allow us to make that calculation quickly." Add the two summaries (N = N1 + N2, SUM = SUM1 + SUM2, SUMSQ = SUMSQ1 + SUMSQ2) and read the variance with the Slide 49 formula. If the merged group is still tight (variance not much larger than the parts), merge them. The slide gives no numeric threshold for this variance.

Worked example (BFR numbers not examined; understand the idea only) — merge or not? Lecture 5 · Slide 57 (numbers added by this guide)

One dimension. CS1 = {9, 10, 11}: N = 3, SUM = 30, SUMSQ = 302 (σ = 0.816). Option A, CS2 = {11, 12, 13}: N = 3, SUM = 36, SUMSQ = 434. Merged: N = 6, SUM = 66, SUMSQ = 736; centroid 11; variance 736/6 − 11² = 122.667 − 121 = 1.667, σ = 1.29: still tight, so merge. Option B, CS2 = {19, 20, 21}: N = 3, SUM = 60, SUMSQ = 1202. Merged: N = 6, SUM = 90, SUMSQ = 1504; centroid 15; variance 1504/6 − 15² = 250.667 − 225 = 25.667, σ = 5.07: far more spread out than either part, so do not merge.

Way 2: Mahalanobis distance between the two centroids

Lecture 5 · Slides 57–58

"When merging compression sets you would typically use the Mahalanobis distance between the centroids of the two compression sets to decide whether or not they should be merged. A threshold like MD < 2 ensures that the compression sets are close enough." Because there are two clusters, each with its own σ, the distance needs a single σ per dimension; Slide 58 offers two choices for it (the two clusters are written with superscripts (1) and (2)).

Formulas (Slide 58)

(1) d(c1, c2) = √( Σi=1..d ((c1i − c2i) / σipool)² )

(2) σipool = √( ( (σi(1))² + (σi(2))² ) / 2 )   (the root of the average of the two variances)

or

(3) σipool = max( σi(1), σi(2) )   (the larger of the two standard deviations)

Merge if d(c1, c2) is below the threshold (e.g. 2). The root-mean-square in (2) is never larger than the max in (3), so option (3) gives the smaller distance and merges more readily. The slide does not remark on this.

Worked example (BFR numbers not examined; understand the idea only) — the two pooled σ choices Lecture 5 · Slide 58 (numbers added by this guide)

One dimension: CS1 has centroid 10 and σ(1) = 2; CS2 has centroid 13.5 and σ(2) = 1. Gap between centroids = 3.5.

Pooled σValueDistance = 3.5 / σpoolMerge at threshold 2?
(2) root of the average variance√((4 + 1)/2) = 1.5812.21no
(3) maximummax(2, 1) = 21.75yes
Slide erratum / omissions (Slides 57–58)
  • The first bullet of Slide 57 (variance of the combined set) and the last two (Mahalanobis distance of the centroids) are two different criteria; the slide does not say which to use or whether they are alternatives. State both in an answer.
  • No symbols on Slide 58 are defined in words (c1i, σi(1), σipool). Also, the pooled variance in (2) is a plain average of the two variances; it ignores the sizes N1, N2 (the textbook pooled variance would weight by size). The slide's version is the one to use.
  • σ = 0 (a CS with a single point or constant coordinate) is not handled, and "ensures … close enough" is loose wording: the threshold defines "close enough".

BFR in one page

Lecture 5 · Slides 43–58, 78–81, 87

BFR summary (theory only; no BFR numericals are examined)
  • What: Bradley–Fayyad–Reina, a variant of k-means for very large, disk-resident data. Memory O(clusters), not O(data).
  • Assumes: each cluster is normally distributed around its centroid in Euclidean space = an axis-aligned ellipse (σ may differ per axis; axes must line up with the space's axes; tilted ellipses and rings are not allowed).
  • Data flow: read the data in chunks (memory loads); choose k initial centroids from the first load (e.g. k random points); summarise old points by simple statistics.
  • Three sets: DS (close to a centroid: summary only), CS (tight groups far from every centroid: summary only, not assigned), RS (isolated points: kept raw).
  • Summary of a cluster: N, SUM, SUMSQ = 2d + 1 numbers. Centroid = SUMi/N; variance = SUMSQi/N − (SUMi/N)²; σ = √variance. Updated by addition, never from scratch.
  • Per memory load: (1) points close enough go to the DS; (2) cluster the rest + old RS: clusters → CS, outliers → RS; (3) update DS statistics (add Ns, SUMs, SUMSQs); (4) consider merging CS sets; (5) on the last load, merge CS and RS into the nearest cluster or call them outliers.
  • Q1 (close enough?): Mahalanobis distance = √Σ((xi − ci)/σi)²; accept if M.D. < threshold (common practice 2, about 2 standard deviations).
  • Q2 (merge two CS?): variance of the combined set (from N, SUM, SUMSQ) is small, or M.D. between their centroids (pooled σ = RMS of the two, or the max) is below a threshold.

Try it yourself first. Close the notes, write the BFR steps from memory as a numbered list, and decide for each of the three drawn ellipses whether BFR may handle it; then compare with the model answer.

Quiz L5-Q4BFR: steps of the algorithm and allowed cluster shapes (theory) Lecture 5 · Slides 78–79
Question (as on the slides)

Quiz: BFR Algorithm (BFR = Bradley–Fayyad–Reina clustering algorithm). Slide 78 asks two questions and draws three ellipses; Slide 79 (“Ans”) gives the slide’s short answer.

(a) Describe in steps how the BFR algorithm works.
(b) Which of the following three shapes are allowed for clusters in the BFR algorithm?

Slide 79 says only: “For steps of BFR see lecture slides” (these are Slides 44–58) and “The clusters in data for which the BFR algorithm may be used can have standard deviations that differ along different axes, but the axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space”; its picture labels the three shapes OK, OK, Not OK. Scope: this is a theory question (no code and no BFR numericals will be asked), so the answer below is written the way you should write it in the exam.

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition — sorting a billion photos with a small desk

Imagine sorting a billion photos into k albums when your desk holds only a few thousand photos at a time, so you work chunk by chunk. For each album you keep a tally card (how many photos, plus a few running totals) instead of the photos themselves. A photo that clearly fits an album is added to that album’s card and then thrown away (this is the DS). Photos that look alike but fit no album yet get their own “pile card” (the CS). Odd single photos stay loose on the desk (the RS). At the very end you decide where the pile cards and the loose photos go. That is BFR: the desk only ever holds the cards, a few loose photos and one chunk — never the whole collection.

Part (a) The steps of the BFR algorithm Lecture 5 · Slides 43–58

Plan of the answer: purpose and set-up (steps 1–4), then the loop that is run for every chunk (steps 5–9 are the slides’ own “steps 1–4”), then the last round (step 10, the slides’ “step 5”); steps 11–12 put it together and explain the memory saving.

  1. Purpose and assumptions (Slides 43–44). Idea: ordinary k-means (Slides 23–24) assigns every point to its nearest centroid, recomputes the centroids and repeats, so it must look at all the points again and again. If the data are so large that they sit on disk and do not fit in main memory (RAM), that is impractical. BFR (Bradley–Fayyad–Reina; Slide 43 is the section title “Extension of k-means to large data”) is “a variant of k-means designed to handle very large (disk-resident) data sets” (Slide 44). Say these things in your answer:
    • Assumption: clusters are normally distributed around a centroid in a Euclidean space, and the dimensions are independent, so each cluster is an axis-aligned ellipse (Slide 44; see part (b)).
    • Goal: an efficient way to summarise clusters so that the memory required is O(clusters), not O(data) (Slide 44).
  2. Read the data in chunks and choose the k initial centroids (Slide 45). Points are read from disk into main memory in chunks (one chunk = a memory load); most points from previous memory loads are summarised by simple statistics instead of being kept. To begin, from the initial (first) memory load select the initial k centroids “by some sensible approach”, for example take k random points (the “…” on the slide means that other approaches exist). Why: exactly as in k-means, the algorithm needs k starting centres; k is fixed in advance and each centre starts one cluster (in the DS, next step).
    Beyond the slides: another sensible choice is the farthest-point rule (pick one point at random, then k−1 others, each as far as possible from those already chosen: Slide 23, practised in the quiz on Slides 76–77); in practice the first load is often also clustered with an ordinary in-memory algorithm so that every cluster starts with real statistics (a single seed point has no spread yet). BFR makes one pass over the data: each point is read from disk once and, once absorbed into a summary, never needed again.
  3. Know the three sets of points: DS, CS, RS (Slides 46–47). BFR keeps track of three sets. Idea: a point is either clearly part of a known cluster (DS), or part of a tight little group that belongs to no known cluster yet (CS), or a loner (RS).
    SetMeaning (slide wording)What stays in main memoryAssigned to a cluster?
    DS — Discard setPoints close enough to a centroid to be summarised.Only the summary (N, SUM, SUMSQ) of each cluster; the points themselves are thrown away.Yes — to that cluster
    CS — Compression setGroups of points that are close together but not close to any existing centroid.Only a summary (N, SUM, SUMSQ) of each group.No — summarised but not assigned to any cluster
    RS — Retained setIsolated points waiting to be assigned to a compression set.The points themselves, exactly as they are (raw coordinates).No
    Figure 1 shows the three kinds of points in the style of the “galaxies” picture on Slides 47 and 52: the big ellipses are DS clusters (with their centroid +), the small ellipses are CS sets, the loose dots are RS points.
  4. What is stored: the summary statistics N, SUM, SUMSQ (Slides 48–49). For each DS cluster (and, in the same way, each CS group) BFR stores only: N, the number of points; the vector SUM, whose i-th component is the sum of the coordinates of the points in dimension i; the vector SUMSQ, whose i-th component is the sum of the squares of the coordinates in dimension i. That is 1 + d + d = 2d + 1 numbers (d = number of dimensions) for a cluster of any size (Slide 49). From them we get, without any raw point:
    Formula — what N, SUM, SUMSQ give us (Slide 49)

    Centroid in dimension i: ci = SUMi / N.   Variance in dimension i: σi² = SUMSQi / N − (SUMi / N)².   Standard deviation: σi = √(σi²).

    Why the variance formula is right: variance = average of (x − c)². Expanding, (1/N)∑(x − c)² = (1/N)∑x² − 2c·(1/N)∑x + c² = SUMSQ/N − 2c² + c² = SUMSQ/N − c², and c = SUM/N.
    Why these three numbers are enough: they tell us where the cluster is (centroid) and how spread out it is along each axis (σi) — exactly what BFR needs for its closeness test. And they are additive: adding a point adds 1 to N, its coordinates to SUM and their squares to SUMSQ; merging two groups just adds their Ns, SUMs and SUMSQs. So the statistics are never recomputed from scratch (this is what Slide 81 stresses, in the quiz on Slides 80–81).
    Sanity check of the idea (one dimension, not an exam numerical): group A = {1, 2, 3} has N = 3, SUM = 6, SUMSQ = 14; group B = {10, 12} has N = 2, SUM = 22, SUMSQ = 244. Adding the statistics gives N = 5, SUM = 28, SUMSQ = 258, so the merged centroid is 28/5 = 5.6 and the variance is 258/5 − 5.6² = 51.6 − 31.36 = 20.24 — exactly what the five raw numbers {1, 2, 3, 10, 12} give.
  5. Loop, slide step 1: absorb the points that are close enough into the DS (Slide 50). Now process the data one memory load (chunk) at a time. Slide step 1: find those points that are “sufficiently close” to a cluster centroid and add them to that cluster and to the DS. These points are so close to the centroid that they can be summarised and then discarded: their values are added into the cluster’s N, SUM, SUMSQ and the raw points disappear from memory. Why: this is how the data shrink — most points end here. (Natural reading: a point goes to the DS cluster with the smallest distance, provided that distance passes the test of the next step.)
  6. How “close enough” is decided: the Mahalanobis distance (Q1, Slides 53–56). Slide 53 asks (Q1): how do we decide that a point is close enough to a DS cluster? Slide 54: BFR suggests that the Mahalanobis distance (M.D.) is less than a threshold. Slide 55 gives the formula and calls it the normalised Euclidean distance from the centroid.
    Formula — Mahalanobis distance (Slides 55–56)

    For a point x = (x1, …, xd) and a cluster centroid c = (c1, …, cd): (1) normalise in each dimension, yi = (xi − ci) / σi; (2) take the sum of the squares of the yi; (3) take the square root.

    M.D.(x, c) = √( ∑i=1d ( (xi − ci) / σi )² )

    σi = standard deviation of the cluster’s points in dimension i; both ci and σi come from the stored N, SUM, SUMSQ (previous steps). Rule (Slide 56): accept the point for the cluster if M.D. < some threshold; common practice is M.D. < 2.

    A point that is not accepted by any DS cluster is not thrown away: it goes on to the next step.
    Why divide by σi? Clusters are not equally spread in every direction. M.D. measures the distance in units of that cluster’s own standard deviation, one dimension at a time, so “close” means “within about 2 standard deviations” on the cluster’s own scale. Figure 2 shows two points that are equally far from the centroid in plain Euclidean distance, yet only one is accepted — and that the accepted region (M.D. < 2) is itself an axis-aligned ellipse. How strict is “M.D. < 2”? In one dimension, Slide 44’s bell curve shows 34.13% + 13.59% = 47.72% of a normal cluster on each side of its centre up to 2σ, so about 95% of the cluster’s own points pass. Beyond the slides: in more dimensions fewer pass (M.D.² of a normal point follows a chi-square law with d degrees of freedom, so a typical point has M.D. around √d): about 86.5% for d = 2, 73.9% for d = 3 and only about 5% for d = 10. So “2” is a rule of thumb and the threshold is a tuning choice: larger = more points absorbed into the DS, smaller = more points left for the CS/RS. Also beyond the slides: the textbook Mahalanobis distance uses a full covariance matrix; with only the per-axis σi (no covariances) it reduces to the formula of Slide 55 — which is exactly why BFR needs axis-aligned clusters (part (b)).
  7. Loop, slide step 2: cluster the leftovers together with the old RS (Slide 50). Use any main-memory clustering algorithm (the slide leaves the choice open, e.g. hierarchical clustering or k-means) to cluster the remaining points (those not close enough to any DS centroid) and the old RS. Clusters go to the CS — each is summarised by N, SUM, SUMSQ and is not assigned to any of the k clusters — and outlying points go to the RS and are kept as raw points. Why: far-away points must not be forced into a wrong cluster, yet tight groups of them can already be compressed; and the old RS points get a fresh chance, because the new chunk may have brought their neighbours. Beyond the slides: a “cluster” of one single point is just an outlier (its variance is 0), so it stays in the RS; only groups of two or more points become CS sets.
  8. Loop, slide step 3: update the DS statistics (Slide 51). “DS set: adjust statistics of the clusters to account for the new points — add Ns, SUMs, SUMSQs.” Why: each DS cluster has just become bigger, so its N, centroid (SUM/N) and spreads σi change. Because the statistics are additive, the update only adds the new points’ contributions — no old point is needed. (In practice the addition is done as each point is absorbed in slide step 1; the slide lists it separately. New CS groups from slide step 2 are stored with their own N, SUM, SUMSQ in the same way.)
  9. Loop, slide step 4: consider merging compressed sets in the CS (Q2, Slides 51, 53, 57–58). Slide 53 asks (Q2): how do we decide whether two CS sets deserve to be combined? Small groups that now lie close together should become one group, otherwise the number of CS sets (and the memory used) would keep growing. How to decide (Slide 57): compute the variance of the combined subcluster; N, SUM and SUMSQ of the two sets simply add, so this can be done quickly without any raw point. In practice one typically uses the Mahalanobis distance between the centroids of the two compression sets, and a threshold like M.D. < 2 ensures that the sets are close enough. Because the two sets have different spreads, Slide 58 uses a pooled standard deviation in each dimension. If the sets are merged, the new set’s statistics are the sums of the two sets’ statistics.
    Formula — should two CS sets be combined? (Slide 58)

    d(c1, c2) = √( ∑i=1d ( (c1i − c2i) / σipool )² )

    σipool = √( ( (σi(1))² + (σi(2))² ) / 2 )   or   σipool = max( σi(1), σi(2) )

    c1, c2 = centroids of the two CS sets; σi(1), σi(2) = their standard deviations in dimension i. Merge if d(c1, c2) < threshold (e.g. 2). The pooled σ lets the two sets share one yardstick.

  10. Loop, slide step 5: the last round (Slide 51). “If this is the last round (last chunk of data), merge all compressed sets in the CS and all RS points into their nearest cluster (or treat them as outliers).” Why: after the last chunk no further points can arrive to give the CS sets and RS points new neighbours, so their fate must be decided: attach each to the nearest of the k clusters, or, if it is far from everything, declare it an outlier that belongs to no cluster. Beyond the slides: the points inside the DS were discarded, so the result of BFR is the k cluster summaries (N, SUM, SUMSQ, hence centroid and variance of each cluster); to find out which cluster each individual point belongs to, one more pass over the data would be needed.
  11. Putting the loop together (Slides 50–51). Figure 3 shows what happens to one memory load. The whole algorithm is: initialise (steps 1–2), then repeat the loop for every chunk (steps 5–9), then finish with the last round (step 10).
  12. Why the memory is O(clusters), not O(data) (Slide 44). After every memory load, main memory holds only the items in the table — none of which grows with the total number of points n, whereas plain k-means needs all n·d coordinates.
    What BFR keeps in main memoryHow many numbersGrows with n?
    DS: k clusters, each (N, SUM, SUMSQ)k × (2d + 1)no
    CS: m groups, each (N, SUM, SUMSQ)m × (2d + 1)no (merging keeps m small)
    RS: r isolated points, kept rawr × dno (r stays small)
    the memory load being processed: c pointsc × dno (the chunk size is our choice)
    The letters m, r, c are ours, not the slides’. Illustration with made-up sizes (not an exam numerical): k = 10 clusters, d = 100 dimensions: the DS needs only 10 × (2·100 + 1) = 2,010 numbers whether the data set has 10⁶ or 10⁹ points, whereas storing 10⁹ points of 100 numbers each would need 10¹¹ numbers. This relies on the RS staying small and on the CS sets being merged, which is exactly what steps 7 and 9 do.
Part (b) Which shapes are allowed? Lecture 5 · Slides 44, 78–79
  1. The rule (Slides 44 and 79). BFR assumes each cluster is normally distributed around its centroid. A normal distribution has ellipse-shaped contours, and its standard deviation may be different in every dimension (so the ellipse may be stretched), but the cluster’s axes must align with the axes of the space: clusters are axis-aligned ellipses. A circle (equal standard deviation in every dimension) is also allowed — it is the special case where the axes are equal (the picture on Slide 44 even shows a roundish cluster beside two stretched ones).
  2. Test each of the three drawings (Slide 78 → Slide 79). Look at the direction of the ellipse’s own long and short axes and compare them with the horizontal and vertical axes of the space (Figure 4).
    Shape on Slide 78Its own axes versus the axes of the spaceWhat it means for the dataAllowed?
    (1) wide (horizontal) ellipselong axis along x, short axis along y: both coincide with the axes of the spaceσx > σy; the dimensions are independentOK ✓
    (2) tall (vertical) ellipselong axis along y, short axis along x: both coincide with the axes of the spaceσy > σx; the dimensions are independentOK ✓
    (3) tilted ellipselong axis points diagonally: neither of its axes lines up with the axes of the spacex and y are correlated (one grows as the other shrinks)NOT OK ✗
  3. Why a tilted cluster is not allowed (the reason that earns the mark). The slide’s reason: the standard deviations may differ along different axes, but the axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space. Beyond the slides (why the algorithm needs this): the textbook (Mining of Massive Datasets, Chapter 7) says that the cluster’s dimensions must be independent: a cigar-shaped cluster is fine, but the cigar must not be rotated off the axes. Two reasons follow directly from the algorithm:
    • The stored summary cannot describe a tilt. N, SUM, SUMSQ hold one centre and one spread per dimension (2d + 1 numbers). A tilted ellipse means that the dimensions are correlated, and describing that would need extra sums of products xi·xj for every pair of dimensions (d(d − 1)/2 more numbers per cluster), which BFR does not keep.
    • The Mahalanobis test would use the wrong shape. The M.D. formula divides each coordinate by its own σi and has no cross terms, so its acceptance region is always an axis-aligned ellipse (Figure 2). Figure 5 shows what happens on a tilted cluster: the axis-aligned region is too “fat” and covers empty corners, so a point such as P is accepted (M.D. = 1.70) although it is 3.79 standard deviations away measured along the real tilted shape (fewer than 1 in 1000 genuine members lie that far out); and genuine members near the tips of the long axis fall outside the region and are wrongly rejected. The same argument holds in more dimensions: the ellipsoids must have their axes parallel to the coordinate axes.
Common mistake
  • Saying that all three sets are stored as raw points — only the RS is raw; DS and CS keep just N, SUM, SUMSQ.
  • Saying that CS points belong to a cluster — they are summarised but not assigned to any cluster until they are merged or until the last round.
  • Writing the variance as SUMSQ/N — you must subtract (SUM/N)²; and SUMSQi is ∑xi² (sum of squares), not (SUMi)².
  • Using plain Euclidean distance for “close enough” — BFR uses the Mahalanobis (normalised) distance; “M.D. < 2” means closer than 2 standard deviations, not 2 units.
  • Forgetting the last round (what happens to the CS and RS at the end), or thinking that k can change during the run.
  • Saying that BFR keeps all the points in memory or re-scans the data many times.
  • Part (b): answering “all ellipses are allowed” or “only circles are allowed”. Ellipses are allowed only if axis-aligned; circles are just the special case of equal spread.
Exam tip

For “describe in steps how BFR works” write a numbered list and use the lecture’s keywords: very large / disk-resident, chunks (memory loads), k initial centroids, DS / CS / RS, N, SUM, SUMSQ (2d + 1 numbers), Mahalanobis distance < threshold (e.g. 2), main-memory clustering of the remaining points + old RS, clusters to CS / outliers to RS, update statistics by adding, merge CS sets, last round: merge CS and RS into the nearest cluster or treat as outliers. For the shapes question give the verdict for each drawing (OK, OK, Not OK) and a one-line reason (axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space; standard deviations may differ per axis).

Slide erratum (wording on Slide 87)

The chapter summary on Slide 87 says BFR “assumes clusters are normally distributed about the axes”. That is loosely worded (it echoes the textbook’s chapter summary): the precise assumption (Slide 44) is that clusters are normally distributed around a centroid and are axis-aligned ellipses. Use the Slide 44/79 wording in the exam.

Final answer:
(a) BFR is a k-means variant for very large, disk-resident data; it assumes normally distributed, axis-aligned elliptical clusters in a Euclidean space and keeps only O(clusters), not O(data), in memory.
1. Read the data from disk in chunks (memory loads); take the k initial centroids from the first load (e.g. k random points).
2. Keep three sets: DS (points close enough to a centroid; only N, SUM, SUMSQ per cluster kept, the points are discarded), CS (tight groups far from every centroid; summarised by N, SUM, SUMSQ, not assigned to a cluster), RS (isolated points, kept raw). Each summary = 2d + 1 numbers: centroid = SUM/N, variance = SUMSQ/N − (SUM/N)².
3. For each memory load: (i) every point whose Mahalanobis distance to a centroid is below a threshold (e.g. 2) joins that cluster (DS) and is discarded; (ii) cluster the remaining points together with the old RS using any main-memory algorithm: clusters go to the CS, outlying points to the RS; (iii) update the DS statistics by adding Ns, SUMs, SUMSQs; (iv) consider merging CS sets (small variance of the combined set / M.D. between their centroids < 2).
4. After the last chunk: merge all CS sets and all RS points into their nearest cluster, or treat them as outliers.
(b) Wide ellipse: OK. Tall ellipse: OK. Tilted ellipse: NOT OK. Reason: the standard deviations may differ along different axes, but the axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space (BFR keeps only per-dimension statistics, no covariance).
Where the marks come from (our own breakdown of the separable ideas an examiner can credit; the course has not published a mark scheme): (a) (1) purpose and assumptions: k-means variant for very large data, normal / axis-aligned clusters, memory O(clusters); (2) chunk-by-chunk processing and the k initial centroids from the first load; (3) DS, CS and RS named and defined correctly; (4) the summary statistics N, SUM, SUMSQ, 2d + 1 numbers, centroid and variance formulas; (5) close points (Mahalanobis distance < threshold) go to the DS and are discarded; (6) remaining points plus old RS clustered with a main-memory algorithm, clusters to the CS, outliers to the RS; (7) DS statistics updated by adding; (8) CS sets merged (variance of the combined set / M.D. between centroids); (9) last round: CS and RS merged into the nearest cluster or treated as outliers. (b) (10) shape 1 allowed; (11) shape 2 allowed; (12) shape 3 not allowed; (13) the reason: axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space (standard deviations may differ per axis). A partly correct list still earns the marks for every idea it contains.
Slide check: part (b) matches Slide 79 exactly (OK, OK, Not OK, same reason; the three labels are in the picture, not in the slide text). Part (a): Slide 79 only says “For steps of BFR see lecture slides”, so the steps above are assembled from Slides 44–58; nothing on those slides is contradicted. Omissions on the slides, filled in above and labelled “Beyond the slides”: the other ways to pick the initial centroids (Slide 45 shows only “…”); which main-memory algorithm to use and that a one-point cluster stays in the RS (Slides 50–51); a numeric threshold for the combined variance (Slide 57; Slide 58 gives the pooled-σ M.D. test). Small notes: Slide 55 calls the formula “normalized Euclidean distance” while Slides 54 and 56 call it the Mahalanobis distance (the full Mahalanobis distance has covariance terms; BFR’s version has none); Slides 50–51 list the DS-statistics update as step 3 although in practice it happens while points are absorbed in step 1. Slide erratum: only the loose wording on Slide 87 (see the box above); there is no numerical error on these slides.

Try it yourself first. Compute N, SUM, SUMSQ, the centroid, the variance and the standard deviation of a three-point cluster, and say whether the statistics must be recomputed from scratch in each round (this quiz is flagged as not examined; the last question is theory).

Quiz L5-Q5BFR summary statistics: N, SUM, SUMSQ, centroid, variance, standard deviation Lecture 5 · Slides 80–81
Question (as on the slides)
Not examined — BFR numerical

BFR numerical — you were told this will NOT be asked; solved only so no quiz is missing. You can skip the arithmetic. Do read part (b) and the “Why this is conceptually valuable” box at the end: the idea that a cluster is stored as just N, SUM and SUMSQ, which are simply added together round after round, is theory and can be asked.

Quiz: SUM, SUMSQ, Variance (Slide 80; the slide’s own answer is on Slide 81). BFR is the Bradley–Fayyad–Reina clustering algorithm.

Suppose a cluster consists of the points (5, 1), (6, −2) and (7, 0).

(a) Compute each of the following statistics: N, SUM, SUMSQ, the centroid, the variance and the standard deviation.
(b) Do the statistics have to be computed from scratch in each round of the BFR algorithm?

Background (not part of the question; from Lecture 5 · Slides 48–49): BFR summarises the discard set (DS) of each cluster by N, SUM and SUMSQ. The variance in dimension i is SUMSQi / N − (SUMi / N)² and the standard deviation is its square root.

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition

Imagine a shopkeeper who, instead of keeping every receipt, keeps three running tallies: how many sales (N), the total of the amounts (SUM) and the total of the amounts each squared (SUMSQ). From just those tallies she can still say what the average sale was and how spread out the sales were. BFR does the same for a cluster of points: throw the points away, keep the tally card, and read the centre and the spread off the card. Our points have d = 2 coordinates, so the card holds only 2d + 1 = 5 numbers (Slide 49): N, two SUM entries and two SUMSQ entries. Here the cluster has just three points so that you can see every number.

Part (a) The statistics of the cluster Lecture 5 · Slides 48–49, 80–81
  1. Formulas to use (write these down first; they earn marks). The points live in d = 2 dimensions (first coordinate = dimension 1, second coordinate = dimension 2). Everything is computed per dimension.
    Formulas (Lecture 5 · Slides 48–49)

    N = number of points in the cluster
    SUMi = sum of the i-th coordinates of all points
    SUMSQi = sum of the squares of the i-th coordinates
    Centroidi = SUMi / N
    Variancei = SUMSQiN − (SUMiN)²
    Standard deviationi = √(Variancei)

  2. Set up: list every point with its squared coordinates. Squaring each coordinate is the only extra work needed for SUMSQ. Squaring happens before adding, and the square of a negative number is positive: (−2)² = 4.
    Pointdim 1 valuedim 2 valuedim 1 squareddim 2 squared
    (5, 1)515² = 251² = 1
    (6, −2)6−26² = 36(−2)² = 4
    (7, 0)707² = 490² = 0
    Column total18−11105
  3. N = the number of points. Count the rows: N = 3. (It is stored because it is the divisor in every average below.)
  4. SUM = the vector whose i-th entry is the sum of the coordinates in dimension i (Slide 48). Dimension 1: 5 + 6 + 7 = 18. Dimension 2: 1 + (−2) + 0 = −1. So SUM = [18, −1]. It is a vector with one entry per dimension, not a single number.
  5. SUMSQ = the vector whose i-th entry is the sum of the squares of the coordinates in dimension i (Slide 48). Square first, then add. Dimension 1: 25 + 36 + 49 = 110. Dimension 2: 1 + 4 + 0 = 5. So SUMSQ = [110, 5].
    Common mistake

    SUMSQ is the sum of the squares, NOT the square of the sum. The square of SUM would be [18², (−1)²] = [324, 1], which is a different thing from SUMSQ = [110, 5]. Square each coordinate first, then add.

  6. Centroid = SUMi / N in each dimension (Slide 49). The centroid is the average position of the points, and an average is “total divided by count”. Dimension 1: 18 / 3 = 6. Dimension 2: (−1) / 3 = −1/3 ≈ −0.333. So the centroid = [6, −1/3] ≈ [6, −0.333]. It is not one of the three given points; a centroid is just their average.
  7. Variance in dimension i = SUMSQi / N − (SUMi / N)² (Slide 49). In words: “the average of the squares minus the square of the average”. The second term is the square of the centroid coordinate from the previous step. Use exact fractions to avoid rounding errors.
    • Dimension 1: 110/3 − (18/3)² = 110/3 − 6² = 110/3 − 108/3 = 2/3 ≈ 0.667.
    • Dimension 2: 5/3 − (−1/3)² = 5/3 − 1/9 = 15/9 − 1/9 = 14/9 ≈ 1.556 (the slide rounds this to 1.56).
    Check from the definition (the variance is the average squared distance to the centroid). Dimension 1: distances to 6 are −1, 0, 1; squares 1, 0, 1; total 2; divided by 3 gives 2/3 ✓. Dimension 2: distances to −1/3 are 4/3, −5/3, 1/3; squares 16/9, 25/9, 1/9; total 42/9; divided by 3 gives 14/9 ✓. Both routes agree, so the shortcut built only from the tally card is trustworthy.

    Beyond the slides: why the shortcut works. The variance is the average of (x − μ)². Expanding the bracket, (x − μ)² = x² − 2μx + μ², and averaging gives (average of x²) − 2μ² + μ² = (average of x²) − μ². The average of x² is SUMSQ/N and μ = SUM/N.

  8. Standard deviation = the square root of the variance (Slide 49).
    • Dimension 1: √(2/3) = √0.6667 ≈ 0.816.
    • Dimension 2: √(14/9) = √14 / 3 = 3.742 / 3 ≈ 1.247 (the slide rounds this to 1.25).
    So SD = [0.816, 1.247]: the cluster is a little more spread out in dimension 2 than in dimension 1.
Part (b) Do the statistics have to be recomputed from scratch in every round? Lecture 5 · Slides 48–51, 57, 81
  1. Answer: No. They are updated incrementally from the previous values. The slide says this is “at the heart of BFR algorithm” (Slide 81).
  2. Why recomputing from scratch is impossible, not just slow. BFR reads the data one memory-load (chunk of points) at a time. A point that is close enough to a cluster is added to that cluster’s discard set (DS), summarised and then thrown away (Slide 50). The old points are therefore no longer available; the only way to know the new statistics is to start from the stored old ones.
  3. Why updating is easy: N, SUM and SUMSQ are plain totals, and totals can be added. When a new memory-load puts extra points into a cluster, BFR does step 3 of its loop, “Add Ns, SUMs, SUMSQs” (Slide 51): Nnew = Nold + Nadded; SUMnew = SUMold + SUMadded; SUMSQnew = SUMSQold + SUMSQadded. Afterwards the centroid, variance and standard deviation are read off the card again with the formulas of part (a). That costs a few operations per dimension, however many points have been seen so far.
  4. Practice — incremental update (my own illustration, not on the slides). Suppose a new point (8, −1) is found close enough to this cluster. Its own tiny card is N = 1, SUM = [8, −1], SUMSQ = [64, 1]. We only add:
    NSUMSUMSQcentroidvariance
    Old card (this quiz)3[18, −1][110, 5][6, −1/3][0.667, 1.556]
    New point (8, −1)1[8, −1][64, 1]——
    Updated card = old + new4[26, −2][174, 6][6.5, −0.5][1.25, 1.25]
    New centroid = [26/4, −2/4] = [6.5, −0.5]. New variances: 174/4 − 6.5² = 43.5 − 42.25 = 1.25 and 6/4 − (−0.5)² = 1.5 − 0.25 = 1.25. Recomputing from the four raw points gives exactly the same values, but the update never looked at the first three points again.
  5. The same addition merges two summaries. When BFR considers combining two compressed sets (CS), it adds their cards and gets the variance of the combined subcluster “quickly” from the merged card (Slide 57: “N, SUM, and SUMSQ allow us to make that calculation quickly”). In the last round the same addition folds a CS into its nearest cluster (Slide 51). Practice (my own numbers): add this card to the card of the two points (8, −1) and (9, 3), which is N = 2, SUM = [17, 2], SUMSQ = [145, 10]. The result is N = 5, SUM = [35, 1], SUMSQ = [255, 15], so the combined variances are 255/5 − 7² = 2 and 15/5 − (1/5)² = 2.96.
Why this is conceptually valuable

Because variance = SUMSQ/N − (SUM/N)², the stored 2d + 1 numbers are enough to recover both the centre and the spread of a cluster of any size, so BFR can discard the points and still run its distance test: the normalised (Mahalanobis) distance on Slides 54–56 divides each coordinate difference by the cluster’s standard deviation σi, which is exactly the square root of the variance computed in part (a). Means and variances cannot simply be added across chunks, but N, SUM and SUMSQ can; that is why the card stores these three quantities rather than the mean and variance themselves.

Exam tip

Even though this numerical will not be asked, be ready to say in words: (1) what N, SUM and SUMSQ are; (2) that 2d + 1 numbers describe a cluster of any size; (3) that the centroid is SUM/N and the variance in dimension i is SUMSQi/N − (SUMi/N)²; (4) that updates are done by adding N, SUM and SUMSQ, never by recomputing from old points.

Common mistake

Do not forget the “− (SUM/N)²” term: 110/3 = 36.67 on its own is only the average of the squares, not a variance. Beyond the slides: some statistics courses divide by N − 1 (sample variance), which would give 1.0 and 2.333 here. That is NOT the slide’s answer; the BFR formulas on Slide 49 divide by N, so always use SUMSQ/N − (SUM/N)².

Final answer:
(a) N = 3; SUM = [18, −1]; SUMSQ = [110, 5]; centroid = SUM/N = [6, −1/3] ≈ [6, −0.333]; variance = [2/3, 14/9] ≈ [0.667, 1.556] (110/3 − 6² and 5/3 − (−1/3)²); standard deviation = [√(2/3), √14/3] ≈ [0.816, 1.247].
(b) No. The statistics are not recomputed from scratch; they are updated incrementally by adding the new points’ (or merged sets’) N, SUM and SUMSQ to the stored values. This is at the heart of BFR.
Where the marks come from: (1) N = 3; (2) SUM = [18, −1], by adding coordinates dimension by dimension; (3) SUMSQ = [110, 5], by squaring before adding; (4) centroid = SUM/N = [6, −1/3] with the formula stated; (5) variance formula SUMSQ/N − (SUM/N)² stated and applied in both dimensions (2/3 ≈ 0.667 and 14/9 ≈ 1.556); (6) standard deviation = √variance (0.816 and 1.247); (7) part (b): “No” plus the reason (the statistics can be updated by adding N, SUM and SUMSQ of the new points to the previous values, so old points need not be revisited). Most of these marks survive an arithmetic slip in a later step, so show every line.
Slide erratum (notation and rounding only; no numerical result on the slide is wrong)

Slide 81 writes the first variance as “110/3 − 18/3²”. Read literally that is 110/3 − 18/9 = 34.67; the intended expression is 110/3 − (18/3)² = 36.667 − 36 = 0.667, as the slide itself writes for dimension 2, (−1/3)². The slide also rounds 14/9 = 1.556 to 1.56 and √(14/9) = 1.247 to 1.25, and prints √0.667 = 0.816: taking the square root of the rounded 0.667 gives 0.8167, so use the exact fraction 2/3 (√(2/3) = 0.8165) to get 0.816.

Slide check: matches the slide’s answer on every result (N = 3, SUM = [18, −1], SUMSQ = [110, 5], centroid [6, −1/3], variances 0.667 and 1.56, standard deviations 0.816 and 1.25, and “NO! They can be updated based on the previous values”). Slide erratum: notation and rounding only, as explained in the box above.

Three scalable ways to cluster: k-means, CURE and BFR

Lecture 5 · Slides 23–27, 35–42, 43–58, 86–87

Meaningpoint assignment to k centroidsClustering Using REpresentativesBradley–Fayyad–Reina: k-means for large data

Exam tip

"Why BFR, why CURE?" Both extend k-means to data that do not fit in memory. BFR gets there by summarising clusters (and so needs normal, axis-aligned clusters). CURE gets there by sampling and keeping representatives (and so handles any shape). When the question names a ring or crescent, answer CURE; when it names tilted ellipses, say BFR cannot, and that CURE can.

k-means on MapReduce

Lecture 5 · Slides 59–67, 84

Slide 59 is a divider titled "K-Means MapReduce" (it carries no printed number and no footer; 59 is inferred from the page order). The BFR and CURE part of the lecture is over. They cope with big data by summarising (BFR) or sampling (CURE). This last section shows the other standard way: leave k-means exactly as it is and spread the work over many machines with MapReduce.

Beginner intuition

Eight students stand in a corridor and two flags are planted in it. Every student walks to the nearest flag (each student can decide alone, so many helpers can work at the same time: this is the map step). Then each flag is moved to the average position of the students standing at it (to average a crowd you need the whole crowd in one place: this is the reduce step). Repeat until the flags stop moving.

The MapReduce vocabulary you need

Lecture 5 · Slides 61–63 (terms from the MapReduce lectures)

TermMeaning here
Nodeone machine of the cluster; the data are split across nodes (Slide 64: "on 3 nodes").
Mappera task that runs on a node over that node's share of the data and emits key–value pairs. "Emit" means "output one pair".
Shuffle (and sort)the system step between map and reduce that sends all pairs with the same key to the same reducer.
Reducera task that receives one key together with all its values and outputs a combined result.
Combineran optional mini-reducer that runs on each mapper's node before the shuffle, to shrink the data sent over the network. (Slide 63: "It can use combiners since the average can be decomposed into sum and count!")
Driver (Beyond the slides)the small program that starts one MapReduce job per iteration, hands the new centroids to the next job and decides when to stop.

The algorithm, step by step

Lecture 5 · Slides 60–63

Slides 60 to 63 are one slide built up in four steps (each slide adds a block to the previous one). Slide 63 shows the whole algorithm.

  1. Initialisation (Slide 60). Start with random initial centroids. (Beyond the slides: the k centroids are tiny, so the driver makes a copy available to every mapper.)
  2. Mapper (Slide 61). For each data point (x, y), find the nearest centroid and emit (centroidID, (x, y)). The key is the ID of the chosen centroid; the value is the point. This is the assignment step of k-means. A mapper needs no information from other mappers.
  3. Reducer (Slide 62). For each centroid, compute the new centroid by averaging the points assigned to it. The shuffle has put all points of one centroid at one reducer. This is the update step of k-means.
  4. Combiner (Slide 63). Because the average decomposes into a sum and a count, each node may first collapse its own pairs for a centroid into one pair (centroidID, (partial sum, count)). The reducer then adds up the partial sums, adds up the counts, and divides once.
  5. Iterations (Slide 63). Repeat the MapReduce process until the centroids stop moving (or for a predefined number of iterations).
k-means step (Slide 24)MapReduce rolePairs exchanged
assign every point to its nearest centroidMapperemits (centroidID, point)
(local pre-sum, optional)Combineremits (centroidID, (partial sum, count))
move each centroid to the mean of its pointsReduceroutputs (centroidID, new centroid)
repeat until nothing movesDriver starts the next jobnew centroids sent to the mappers

One MapReduce job is exactly one k-means iteration. The whole algorithm is a sequence of such jobs.

Common mistake: the average of averages

A combiner must not send a node's average. Suppose node A holds the points {2, 3, 5} for a centroid and node B holds {100}. The true mean is (2 + 3 + 5 + 100) / 4 = 27.5. The average of the two local averages is (3.33 + 100) / 2 = 51.67, which is wrong because the groups have different sizes. Sending (sum, count) = (10, 3) and (100, 1) gives (10 + 100) / (3 + 1) = 27.5, correct. This is why Slide 63 stresses "sum and count".

Why it scales

The mappers work on different parts of the data in parallel, and with combiners only a few small (sum, count) pairs per centroid cross the network, never the bulky data. The price: each iteration is a separate job that reads all the data from disk again, so many iterations are slow. (Beyond the slides: this is the main reason in-memory frameworks such as Spark became popular for iterative algorithms.) The slides do not mention this cost.

Slide erratum / omissions (Slides 59–63)
  • The slides write points as (x, y) but the example (Slide 64 onward) uses single numbers; the distance (Euclidean, in one dimension just |a − c|) is never named.
  • "Random initial centroids" and "stop moving" are not defined (exactly zero movement, or a small tolerance?). How the mappers receive the centroids is not stated.
  • The Reducer bullet on Slide 62 repeats its own heading ("Reducer: Reducer: …"); the slide's title on 59 says "K-Means" but on 60–63 "k-means". These are cosmetic.

The worked example (Slides 64–67)

Lecture 5 · Slides 64–67

Slide 64 sets the example: the data points (2, 21, 5, 8, 15, 3, 29, 25) with 2 clusters (k = 2) on 3 nodes (the parentheses are only a list of eight numbers, not a coordinate pair). Slide 65 gives the starting centroids (5 and 21) and the split of the data over the three nodes; Slide 66 ("Mapper Phase") lists the pairs each node emits; Slide 67 ("Reducer Phase") shows which points reach each reducer, the new centroids and the rule for iterating. The solved version, with every iteration, the combiner tables and the data-flow picture, is Quiz L5-Q7 below, so it is not repeated here.

What to look for in the quiz: (a) each mapper emits one pair per point it holds, with the ID of the nearest centroid as the key; (b) each reducer receives all points of one key and outputs their mean; (c) the driver compares the new centroids with the old and stops when they no longer change.

Try it yourself first. Without looking at the solution, work out what each of the three nodes emits in iteration 1 and what the new centroids are; then carry on until the centroids stop moving.

Quiz L5-Q7k-means with MapReduce — worked example (2, 21, 5, 8, 15, 3, 29, 25) Lecture 5 · Slides 59–67
Question (as on the slides)

k-means MapReduce example (Slides 64–67). Run k-means with MapReduce on the data points 2, 21, 5, 8, 15, 3, 29, 25 with 2 clusters (k = 2) on 3 nodes. Start with random initial centroids: Centroid 1 = 5 and Centroid 2 = 21. Assume the points are distributed over the nodes like this: Node 1: [2, 21, 5], Node 2: [8, 15], Node 3: [3, 29, 25].

(a) Mapper phase, iteration 1. What does each node (mapper) emit, as pairs (centroidID, point)?
(b) Reducer phase, iteration 1. Which points reach each reducer, and what are the new centroids? (Also show what the optional combiners would send.)
(c) Iterate. The slide says “repeat the MapReduce process with the updated centroids (4.5 and 22.5) until convergence”. Carry on, with the mapper, combiner and reducer tables of every iteration, until the centroids stop moving. State the final clusters and centroids.
(d) Roles. Explain what the mapper, the combiner, the reducer and the driver do, why the centroids are sent to every mapper, and draw the data flow of one iteration.

Slides 64–67 give the data and the answers to (a) and (b) only; Slides 60–63 give the algorithm (initialisation, mapper, reducer, combiner reminder, iterations). Parts (c) and (d) are our own completion of the example, written as practice for exam variants; every number was recomputed with Python.

Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
  1. Formula / idea: one k-means round = one MapReduce job. Ordinary k-means (Lecture 5 · Slide 24) repeats two things: (i) assign every point to the cluster whose centroid is nearest, then (ii) update every centroid to the average of the points assigned to it; it stops when the points no longer move between clusters and the centroids stabilise. The MapReduce version (Slides 60–63) does exactly one such round per job, so the Mapper is the assignment step and the Reducer is the update step.
    Formulas used in this quiz
    • Distance (1-dimensional Euclidean distance, because every point is a single number): d(x, c) = |x − c|. (For 2-D points (x, y), as the slides’ notation suggests, it would be √((x − cx)² + (y − cy)²).)
    • Mapper rule (Slide 61): centroidID(x) = the j with the smallest d(x, cj); emit (centroidID, x).
    • Reducer rule (Slides 62 and 67): new cj = ∑ x over the points of cluster jnj (how many points) = SUMjCOUNTj.
    • Combiner rule (Slide 63: “the average can be decomposed into sum and count”): each node sends (partial SUM, partial COUNT) per centroidID; the reducer adds all the sums, adds all the counts, then divides once.
    • Stopping rule (Slide 63): repeat until the centroids stop moving, or for a predefined number of iterations.
    Beginner intuition

    Picture 8 students standing in a long corridor at the positions 2, 3, 5, 8, 15, 21, 25, 29, and 2 flags planted at positions 5 and 21. Step A (mapper): every student walks to the nearest flag. Each student can decide alone, so three helpers (the 3 nodes) can each handle their own few students at the same time. Step B (reducer): each flag is moved to the average position of the crowd standing at it. To compute an average you need the whole crowd of that flag in one place, which is why everybody with the same centroidID is sent to the same reducer. Repeat A and B until the flags no longer move.

  2. Set-up (Slide 65). Number the centroids: ID 1 = 5 and ID 2 = 21; with k = 2 there are exactly two keys, 1 and 2. Every mapper receives a copy of this tiny list of k = 2 numbers (Beyond the slides: the “broadcast”, explained in step 10). Each node keeps only its own slice of the data, 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 points, each point exactly once, and the data never move:
    NodePoints stored on it (Slide 65)
    Node 12, 21, 5
    Node 28, 15
    Node 33, 29, 25
  3. Iteration 1 — Mapper (assignment step), answer to (a). For each point the mapper computes its distance to both centroids, finds the smaller one, and emits (centroidID, point). The smaller distance in each row is highlighted.
    NodePoint x|x − 5| (to ID 1)|x − 21| (to ID 2)NearestMapper emits (centroidID, point)
    12319ID 1(1, 2)
    121160ID 2(2, 21)
    15016ID 1(1, 5)
    28313ID 1(1, 8)
    215106ID 2(2, 15)
    33218ID 1(1, 3)
    329248ID 2(2, 29)
    325204ID 2(2, 25)

    So the three mappers emit: Node 1: (1, 2), (2, 21), (1, 5); Node 2: (1, 8), (2, 15); Node 3: (1, 3), (2, 29), (2, 25) — exactly Slide 66 (written there as “centroidID=1, 2” etc.; 8 pairs in total). Read (1, 2) as “centroid ID 1, data point 2”, not as a 2-D point. The only close call is 15: 10 away from 5 but only 6 away from 21, so it goes to ID 2. Shortcut for checking in one dimension: the half-way point of the two centroids is (5 + 21) / 2 = 13; everything below 13 is nearer to 5 and everything above 13 is nearer to 21 (no point is exactly on 13, so there are no ties).

  4. Iteration 1 — Combiner (optional local pre-aggregation). Slide 63 says a combiner may be used because an average is sum ÷ count. On each node the combiner merges that node’s pairs with the same key into one pair (partial SUM, partial COUNT). It runs on the node, before the network transfer, so it shrinks the data that has to be shuffled.
    NodeMapper output on that nodeKey 1: (sum, count)Key 2: (sum, count)
    1(1,2) (2,21) (1,5)(2 + 5, 2) = (7, 2)(21, 1)
    2(1,8) (2,15)(8, 1)(15, 1)
    3(1,3) (2,29) (2,25)(3, 1)(29 + 25, 2) = (54, 2)
    Totals after adding over the nodes(7 + 8 + 3, 2 + 1 + 1) = (18, 4)(21 + 15 + 54, 1 + 1 + 2) = (90, 4)

    With the combiner only 6 records leave the nodes instead of 8 (2 keys × 3 nodes); with a huge data set the saving is enormous, because each node sends at most k records.

    Common mistake

    Do not let the combiner send local averages. For key 1 the local averages are 3.5 (Node 1: points 2 and 5), 8 (Node 2) and 3 (Node 3). Averaging those three numbers gives (3.5 + 8 + 3) / 3 ≈ 4.83, but the true average is 4.5, because Node 1’s average stands for two points and the others for one. (Key 2 would give (21 + 15 + 27) / 3 = 21 instead of the true 22.5.) A sum and a count can be added safely in any order and grouping, an average cannot. This is why the slide says “sum and count”.

  5. Iteration 1 — Shuffle & sort, then Reducer (update step), answer to (b). The system routes every pair with key 1 to Reducer 1 and every pair with key 2 to Reducer 2 (“group by key”). Each reducer then takes the average of its points:
    Reducer forPoints that reach it (Slide 67 lists them sorted)SumCountNew centroid = sum ÷ count
    key 1 (old 5)2, 3, 5, 8 (arrive as 2, 5, 8, 3)184(2 + 3 + 5 + 8) / 4 = 18 / 4 = 4.5
    key 2 (old 21)15, 21, 25, 29 (arrive as 21, 15, 29, 25)904(15 + 21 + 25 + 29) / 4 = 90 / 4 = 22.5

    With the combiner the reducers receive (7,2) (8,1) (3,1) for key 1 and (21,1) (15,1) (54,2) for key 2, and get the same answer: (7 + 8 + 3) / (2 + 1 + 1) = 18 / 4 = 4.5 and (21 + 15 + 54) / (1 + 1 + 2) = 90 / 4 = 22.5. After iteration 1 the new centroids are 4.5 and 22.5 (Slide 67).

  6. Driver decision after iteration 1. Compare old and new centroids: ID 1 moved from 5 to 4.5 (change −0.5) and ID 2 moved from 21 to 22.5 (change +1.5). They moved, so we have not converged: start iteration 2 with the centroids 4.5 and 22.5 (Slide 67: “repeat the MapReduce process with the updated centroids … until convergence”).
  7. Iteration 2 — Mapper, with the NEW centroids (4.5 and 22.5). The data is the same, only the centroids changed. Every point is re-assigned from scratch (new half-way point (4.5 + 22.5) / 2 = 13.5):

    122.520.5ID 1(1, 2)

  8. Iteration 2 — Combiner and Reducer. Because the pairs are the same, the tables are the same:
    NodeCombiner key 1: (sum, count)Combiner key 2: (sum, count)
    1(7, 2)(21, 1)

    (Without a combiner Reducer 1 would again receive the points 2, 3, 5, 8 and Reducer 2 the points 15, 21, 25, 29.) The reducers output 4.5 and 22.5 again.

  9. Convergence check, answer to (c). New centroids (4.5, 22.5) = old centroids (4.5, 22.5): movement 0 and 0, and no point changed cluster. This meets the stopping rule of Slide 63 (“until the centroids stop moving”) and the convergence definition of Slide 24 (points do not move between clusters and centroids stabilise), so the driver stops. A third iteration would only repeat iteration 2, so two MapReduce jobs are needed: iteration 1 moves the centroids, iteration 2 confirms that they no longer move.

    24.5, 22.52, 3, 5, 815, 21, 25, 294.5, 22.5no (0, 0): STOP
    Exam tip

    Lay your answer out in the order the framework runs it: centroids → mapper pairs (key = centroidID, value = point) → combiner (sum, count) per node → shuffle → reducer total sum ÷ total count → new centroids → compare with the old ones → repeat or stop. Each iteration must use the centroids produced by the previous iteration (iteration 2 uses 4.5 and 22.5, not 5 and 21). In 1-D, find the midpoint of the two centroids first (13, then 13.5) and use it to check every assignment quickly. Always finish with an explicit sentence such as “centroids unchanged, so k-means has converged after 2 MapReduce iterations”. If the question only asks for “one iteration”, stop at 4.5 and 22.5 as the slide does. The order of the points inside a reducer’s list does not matter.

  10. Roles of every component, answer to (d).
    ComponentIts job in k-meansReceivesEmitsSlides
    Driver (the main program that submits the jobs; Beyond the slides)Loop control: picks the initial centroids, sends the current centroids to every mapper, runs one MapReduce job per iteration, reads the new centroids back, compares old and new, and stops at convergence or after a fixed number of iterationsnew centroids from the reducerscentroid list for the next job60, 63, 67
    MapperAssignment step: nearest centroid for each point. Works on one point at a time, so all nodes run in parallel on their own sliceone point + all k current centroids(centroidID, point)61, 66
    Combiner (optional)Local speed-up: partial (sum, count) per centroidID on one node, before the networkthe mapper output of one node(centroidID, (partial sum, partial count))63
    Shuffle & sort (done by the framework; Beyond the slides)Groups by key so that all values of one centroidID meet at one reducerall mapper / combiner pairs(centroidID, list of values)–
    ReducerUpdate step: new centroid = average of the points of that cluster = total sum ÷ total countone centroidID + all its points (or partial (sum, count) pairs)(centroidID, new centroid)62, 63, 67

    Why every mapper needs all the centroids: a mapper sees only its own few points but must compare each point with every centroid to find the nearest one. The k centroids are tiny (here 2 numbers), the data is huge, so it is cheap to copy the centroids to all mappers and never move the data (Beyond the slides: in Hadoop this is done with the distributed cache or the job configuration, in Spark with a broadcast variable). The mappers do not need to talk to each other. Every iteration the driver sends the newest centroids again.

    Why a reducer needs the whole cluster: a centroid is an average over all points of the cluster, and these points are spread over all nodes. The key (centroidID) tells the framework where to send each point. With k = 2 there are only 2 keys, so at most 2 reducers are busy; this is exactly why the combiner is valuable: with it each node sends at most k records, so the shuffle carries at most k × (number of nodes) = 2 × 3 = 6 records, however many points there are.

  11. Data-flow diagram of one iteration (iteration 1 with the real numbers), part of (d).

  12. Beyond the slides: extra facts that explain and check the result.
    • Combiner typing. A real combiner may run zero, one or several times, so it must produce the same kind of record that the reducer expects. That is why implementations let the mapper emit (centroidID, (point, 1)) and let the combiner and reducer just add the pairs. Slide 66 shows the simplified form without the “1”. The idea is identical. The combiner is only an optimisation: the centroids are the same with or without it.
    • Ties and empty clusters. A point exactly half-way between two centroids needs a fixed tie-break rule (for example the smaller centroidID); no ties occur here. If a centroid receives no point, its key never reaches a reducer; a common fix is that the driver keeps its old value.
    • Cost. Every iteration is a complete MapReduce job that re-reads the whole data set; this is why iterative algorithms such as k-means are the classic motivation for in-memory systems like Spark.
    • Quality check (sum of squared distances, SSE). The iteration-1 assignment has SSE 138 measured from the centroids 5 and 21 (22 + 116); the update to 4.5 and 22.5 lowers it to 128 (21 + 107); iteration 2 keeps 128. k-means never increases the SSE and there are only finitely many ways to split the points, so it always stops. For this tiny data set 128 is also the best possible split into two groups (all 7 ways of cutting the sorted list into a lower and an upper group were checked), but in general k-means only finds a local optimum.
    • Practice (not on the slides): the start matters (Lecture 5 · Slide 23). Same data, but initial centroids 2 and 29. Iteration 1: the points 2, 3, 5, 8, 15 go to ID 1 (15 is 13 from 2 but 14 from 29) and 21, 25, 29 to ID 2; the reducers give (2 + 3 + 5 + 8 + 15) / 5 = 33 / 5 = 6.6 and (21 + 25 + 29) / 3 = 75 / 3 = 25. Iteration 2 (centroids 6.6 and 25) gives the same clusters, so it stops with SSE 141.2, which is worse than 128 from the start 5 and 21. Different random starts can give different final clusters.
Common mistakes
  • Stopping after iteration 1 because the slide stops there. The slide ends with “repeat … until convergence”; run iteration 2 with 4.5 and 22.5 and show that nothing moves.
  • Re-using the old centroids (5, 21) in iteration 2 instead of the new ones (4.5, 22.5).
  • Dividing by the wrong number. Reducer 1 receives only 3 combiner pairs (one per node) but they stand for 4 points. Divide the total sum by the total count (4), not by the number of nodes or pairs.
  • Reading (1, 2) as a 2-D point. In (centroidID, point) the first number is the cluster key (1 or 2) and the second is the data point; the key is the centroid’s ID, not its value (5 or 21).
  • Putting 15 in cluster 1 because it “looks in the middle”. Use the numbers: 10 away from 5 but 6 away from 21; in iteration 2, 10.5 away from 4.5 and 7.5 away from 22.5.
Final answer:
(a) Mapper output, iteration 1 (Slide 66): Node 1 emits (1,2), (2,21), (1,5); Node 2 emits (1,8), (2,15); Node 3 emits (1,3), (2,29), (2,25).
(b) Combiners (optional): Node 1 → 1:(7,2), 2:(21,1); Node 2 → 1:(8,1), 2:(15,1); Node 3 → 1:(3,1), 2:(54,2). Reducer 1 receives 2, 3, 5, 8 and outputs (2+3+5+8)/4 = 18/4 = 4.5; Reducer 2 receives 15, 21, 25, 29 and outputs (15+21+25+29)/4 = 90/4 = 22.5 (Slide 67).
(c) Iteration 2 with centroids 4.5 and 22.5 sends every point to the same cluster and outputs 4.5 and 22.5 again, so the centroids stop moving: converged after 2 MapReduce iterations. Final clusters {2, 3, 5, 8} with centroid 4.5 and {15, 21, 25, 29} with centroid 22.5.
(d) Mapper = assignment step, emits (centroidID, point). Combiner = local partial (sum, count) per centroidID. Reducer = update step, new centroid = total sum ÷ total count. Driver = repeats the job until the centroids stop moving (or a fixed number of iterations). The k centroids are broadcast to every mapper because each point must be compared with all of them.
Where the marks come from: (1) The two rules: nearest centroid by distance |x − c| for the mapper, and new centroid = average = sum ÷ count for the reducer. (2) Mapper iteration 1: the correct nearest centroid for all 8 points (especially 15 → ID 2), written as (centroidID, point) pairs per node, with the distances or the midpoint 13 shown. (3) Grouping by key (shuffle) and, if asked, the combiner’s (sum, count) pairs, not partial averages. (4) Reducer iteration 1: the points reaching each reducer, the sums 18 and 90, the counts 4 and 4, the results 4.5 and 22.5. (5) Iteration 2 done with the new centroids 4.5 and 22.5, with the distances shown. (6) The convergence statement: centroids unchanged, so stop; the final clusters. (7) The roles: mapper = assignment, reducer = update, combiner = partial (sum, count), driver loops, centroids broadcast to all mappers. (8) The flow diagram: driver → mappers → (combiners) → shuffle → reducers → new centroids back to the driver.

The homework question (Slide 84)

Lecture 5 · Slide 84

Slide 84, "Quiz: K-Means MapReduce Homework" (the last letters of "Homework" run off the banner), asks you to compute clusters with k-means MapReduce for 17 numbers (2, 3, 5, 8, 15, 21, 23, 25, 29, 43, 45, 49, 62, 75, 76, 77, 85) with k = 3 on 3 nodes. The slide gives no answer, and it leaves three things open that your answer must state itself: the initial centroids, how the points are spread over the three nodes, and the stopping rule. A good answer fixes all three, then shows the mapper output, the combiner pairs and the reducer results of every round until nothing moves.

Exam tip

Because k-means can stop in different local optima for different starts, write down the starting centroids you chose (for example the farthest-first rule of Slide 23). The final clusters do not depend on how the points are split over the nodes; only the starting centroids matter.

Try it yourself first. Choose three starting centroids, split the 17 points over 3 nodes, and run rounds on paper until the centroids stop moving; then compare with the solution (and note what a different start does).

Quiz L5-Q8k-means MapReduce on 17 points, k = 3, on 3 nodes Lecture 5 · Slide 84
Question (as on the slides)

Slide 84, “Quiz: K-Means MapReduce Homework”. Compute clusters for the following data points using K-Means MapReduce: 2, 3, 5, 8, 15, 21, 23, 25, 29, 43, 45, 49, 62, 75, 76, 77, 85 (17 one-dimensional points). Assume there are three clusters (k = 3), on 3 nodes.

The slide gives no initial centroids, no distribution of the points over the nodes and no answer (the method is on Lecture 5 · Slides 60–67; Slides 60–63 only say “start with random initial centroids”). A complete answer therefore states its own start and then runs full rounds until convergence. This guide splits the work into the parts below. All slide numbers in the solution are Lecture 5 slides, and every number was checked with Python (exact fractions).

(a) Choose and state the initial centroids and the distribution of the points over the 3 nodes.
(b) Run k-means MapReduce round by round (Mapper output per node, Combiner (sum, count) per node, Reducer results) until the centroids stop moving.
(c) State the final clusters and centroids.
(d) Show that the answer does not depend on how the points are split over the nodes.
(e) Run a second, different initialisation. Does it give the same clustering? What does this teach?
Solution — every step is a potential partial mark
Beginner intuition — k-means in plain English

The 17 numbers are house numbers along one long street, and you want to open 3 pizza shops. (1) Put the 3 shops at three starting spots. (2) Every house orders from its nearest shop. (3) Each shop moves to the average address of its customers. Repeat (2) and (3) until nobody changes shop and the shops stop moving. That is k-means.

MapReduce only decides who does the work when the houses are stored on 3 different computers (nodes). Each node lets its own houses pick the nearest shop (Mapper), then writes one short note per shop, “total of the addresses and number of houses” (Combiner). One clerk per shop (Reducer) adds up the notes of all nodes and divides total by number to get the shop’s new position. A driver program checks whether any shop moved and, if so, starts another round. Only the tiny notes and the 3 shop positions travel over the network, never the bulky data.

  1. Formula / idea: one k-means round = one MapReduce job (Lecture 5 · Slides 60–63). Ordinary k-means (Slide 24) alternates (1) put every point into the cluster of its nearest centroid and (2) move every centroid to the average of its cluster, until points stop moving between clusters. MapReduce spreads these two steps over the machines. (The data-flow picture of one round is Figure L5-Q7-B in Quiz L5-Q7.)
    Formulas used in this quiz
    • Distance (Slide 23: “assumes Euclidean space/distance”). Every point is a single number, so d(p, cj) = |p − cj|. (For 2-D points (x, y) as written on Slides 61–63 it would be √((x − cx)² + (y − cy)²).)
    • Mapper (assignment step, Slide 61): for each of its own points find the nearest centroid j and emit (j, p).
    • Combiner (optional, Slide 63): on each node, for each key j add up the points and count them; emit (j, (sum, count)). Allowed because “the average can be decomposed into sum and count”: a mean cannot be added up, but a sum and a count can, in any order and any grouping.
    • Reducer j (update step, Slide 62): cjnew = ∑ of all partial sums for key j∑ of all partial counts for key j = average of the points of cluster j.
    • Driver / stop rule (Slides 24 and 63): repeat until the centroids stop moving (or for a fixed number of rounds).
    Tie convention (a point exactly midway between two centroids): give it to the lower key; no tie occurs in any run below. The data points never move between nodes; only the 3 centroids (to the mappers) and the small (sum, count) pairs (to the reducers) travel.
  2. Part (a) — what the slide leaves open, and our choices. Slide 84 gives only the data, k = 3 and “3 nodes”. The result depends on the start (see part (e)), so the start must be written down (examiners give marks for stating it).
    • Initial centroids by farthest-first (Slide 23: “pick one point at random, then k−1 other points, each as far away as possible from the previous points”). First pick: 2 (the first point of the list stands in for “random”). The point farthest from 2 is 85 (distance 83). For the third centroid take, for every remaining point, the distance to the nearest centroid already chosen, and pick the point where this is largest:
      candidate p358152123252943454962757677
      distance to 2136131921232741434760737475
      distance to 858280777064626056424036231098
      min of the two1361319212327414036231098

(“Far from all previous points” must mean the largest minimum distance: the plain sum of the two distances is 83 for every point between 2 and 85, so it could not choose.) Numbering them in increasing order (the numbering is arbitrary): c1 = 2, c2 = 43, c3 = 85.
    • Distribution over the 3 nodes: the sorted list cut into three blocks — Node 1 = [2, 3, 5, 8, 15, 21] (6 points), Node 2 = [23, 25, 29, 43, 45, 49] (6 points), Node 3 = [62, 75, 76, 77, 85] (5 points); 6 + 6 + 5 = 17, every point exactly once. (Slide 65 shows that a split may be any mix; part (d) tries another one.)
    • Reducers: one per centroid, i.e. 3 reducers (keys 1, 2, 3). Stop rule: the new centroids equal the old ones.

  7. Part (d) — the answer does not depend on how the points are split over the nodes.

    Why (the argument). (1) The Mapper’s decision for a point p uses only p and the 3 broadcast centroids, never the node that holds p. (2) The combiner and the reducer only add sums and counts, and addition is commutative and associative: (sum of the node-wise sums of key j) = (sum of all points of key j), whichever node each point sits on. So the reducers receive the same grand totals, produce the same new centroids, and by repeating the argument every round — and the final answer — is the same. The split only changes how much data crosses the network.

    Demonstration. A very different split (“round-robin”: the sorted points dealt out like cards, so every node holds small and large numbers): Node 1 = [2, 8, 23, 43, 62, 77], Node 2 = [3, 15, 25, 45, 75, 85], Node 3 = [5, 21, 29, 49, 76]. Same initial centroids (2, 43, 85). Round 1:

    Node 23, 15, 25, 45, 75, 85(1, 3), (1, 15), (2, 25), (2, 45), (3, 75), (3, 85)(1, (18, 2)), (2, (70, 2)), (3, (160, 2))
    Node 35, 21, 29, 49, 76(1, 5), (1, 21), (2, 29), (2, 49), (3, 76)(1, (26, 2)), (2, (78, 2)), (3, (76, 1))
    ReducerAdds up the partial (sum, count) pairsNew centroid
    Reducer 1(10, 2) + (18, 2) + (26, 2) = (54, 6)54 / 6 = 9
    Reducer 2(128, 3) + (70, 2) + (78, 2) = (276, 7)276 / 7 ≈ 39.43
    Reducer 3(77, 1) + (160, 2) + (76, 1) = (313, 4)313 / 4 = 78.25

    RoundReducer totals, split 1 (sorted blocks)Reducer totals, split 2 (round-robin)New centroids (both splits)

    Only the network traffic differs: split 1 shuffles 4 pairs per round, split 2 shuffles 9 pairs per round, and without any combiner both would shuffle all 17 points. (Python check: 20,000 random distributions of the 17 points over 2–5 nodes, with random sizes and order, for both starts of this quiz, always gave the same reducer totals in every round and the same final centroids.)

    Common mistake — combining averages instead of (sum, count)

    For key 2 in the round-robin split the three nodes send (128, 3), (70, 2), (78, 2), i.e. node averages 42.67, 35 and 39. The “average of the averages” is (42.67 + 35 + 39) / 3 = 38.89, which is wrong; the correct centroid is (128 + 70 + 78) / (3 + 2 + 2) = 276 / 7 = 39.43. An average cannot be merged without its count, which is exactly why the combiner emits (sum, count) (Slide 63). Two more traps: (1) every Mapper must use the same 3 global centroids in a round — a node must not cluster its own points with its own centroids; (2) after the centroids move, all points must be re-assigned.
