Even farthest-first, started from each of the 17 points in turn as the “random” first pick (ties in the farthest pick go to the smaller point), ends in all six clusterings, so it is a good heuristic, not a guarantee.

What this teaches — initialisation matters, so run k-means several times
  • k-means stops at a local optimum, not necessarily the best clustering. “Converged” only means “one more round changes nothing”. (Beyond the slides: every round can only keep or lower the SSE, so the algorithm must stop — but where it stops depends on the start.) Two sensible starts gave two different, equally “converged” answers (SSE 1168.8 and 1204.9), and even the farthest-first start did not find the best one (1122.5). Farthest-first likes extreme points such as 2 and 85, which are not typical members of a group.
  • Spread-out starting centroids are usually better than clumped ones (Slide 23 asks for centroids “as far away as possible”): the clumped start 2, 3, 5 needed 8 rounds, the most any of the 680 starts needs, against 3 for Run 1 and 2 for the start 8, 45, 76. In MapReduce every round is a full pass over all the data, so 8 rounds cost about 2.7 times as much as 3.
  • Practical rule: run k-means several times from different (random but well-spread) initial centroids and keep the run with the smallest SSE (or the smallest average distance to the centroid, the quantity Slide 31 uses for choosing k). This is why Slides 60–63 say “random initial centroids” and Slide 23 offers two ways to pick them. (Beyond the slides: the k-means++ rule is a smarter random choice that favours points far from those already chosen.) In MapReduce each extra run is simply another sequence of rounds.
  • What does not matter is the distribution of the points over the nodes (part (d)): that only changes who computes, never the result. The initial centroids do.
Exam tip — how to write this question

Because the slide leaves the start open, write your initial centroids and your node distribution first (marks for stating them). Then, for every round, show (1) the centroids sent to the mappers, (2) the (centroidID, point) pairs per node, (3) each node’s (sum, count) per key, (4) the reducer totals and the division, (5) “moved, so continue” or “unchanged, so stop”. Keep fractions exact (276/7) until the end and check that all sums add to 643 and all counts to 17 in every round. Finish with the final clusters and one sentence: “a different start may give a different local optimum, so run k-means several times”. If the question does give the initial centroids or the node split, use theirs; any correctly executed start should be accepted. Practice (self-made): redo Round 1 with the centroids 8, 45, 76 on the same nodes and compare with the reducer totals in the note above.

Final answer (our stated choices: farthest-first start {c1, c2, c3} = 2, 43, 85; Node 1 = [2, 3, 5, 8, 15, 21], Node 2 = [23, 25, 29, 43, 45, 49], Node 3 = [62, 75, 76, 77, 85]):
Run 1 converges after 3 MapReduce rounds: centroids 2, 43, 85 → 9, 276/7 ≈ 39.43, 78.25 → 11, 38.2, 75 → 11, 38.2, 75 (unchanged, stop).
Clusters: {2, 3, 5, 8, 15, 21, 23} with centroid 11 (= 77/7); {25, 29, 43, 45, 49} with centroid 38.2 (= 191/5); {62, 75, 76, 77, 85} with centroid 75 (= 375/5); SSE = 1168.8.
The result is the same for any distribution of the points over the nodes (sums and counts add up the same way).
Run 2 (start 2, 3, 5) needs 8 rounds and ends in a different local optimum: {2, 3, 5, 8, 15}, {21, 23, 25, 29, 43, 45, 49}, {62, 75, 76, 77, 85} with centroids 6.6, 235/7 ≈ 33.57, 75 (SSE 1204.9). The best clustering (start 2, 45, 85 or 8, 45, 76): {2, 3, 5, 8, 15, 21, 23, 25}, {29, 43, 45, 49}, {62, 75, 76, 77, 85} with centroids 12.75, 41.5, 75 (SSE 1122.5).
Lesson: initialisation matters, so run k-means several times from different, well-spread starts and keep the best result.
Where the marks come from: (1) stating the initial centroids (k = 3 of them) and how the points are distributed over the 3 nodes, since the slide gives neither; (2) the roles and formulas: Mapper = nearest centroid with |p − c|, Combiner = (sum, count) because average = sum / count, Reducer = total sum / total count, driver = repeat; (3) Mapper: distance of every point to every centroid and the emitted (centroidID, p) pair, per node, in every round; (4) Combiner: per node and key the (partial sum, count); (5) Reducer: total sum and count per key and the new centroid, in every round (9, 276/7, 313/4, then 11, 38.2, 75); (6) iterating with the updated centroids (Round 2 moves 23 and 62) until the centroids stop moving, with the convergence statement; (7) the final clusters and their centroids; (8) the argument that the node split does not change the result; (9) a second start, the observation that it ends in a different local optimum, and the lesson (initialisation matters, run several times). Marks are earned step by step even if a later round has an arithmetic slip.

Without those the clusters are not unique (part (e) shows six different stable clusterings for this data). The correct version of the question needs both: this guide stated its own and showed which results depend on it (the clusters do, the node split does not).

The method is identical: the distance is |p − c| and the average is a plain average; in 2-D the combiner would send (sum of x, sum of y, count). Summary: clustering and algorithm families (Slide 86)

Lecture 5 · Slide 86

  • Clustering: "Clusters are often a useful summary of data that is in the form of points in some space."
  • Clustering algorithms generally have one of two forms:
    • Hierarchical clustering algorithms begin with all points in a cluster of their own, and nearby clusters are merged iteratively.
    • Point-assignment clustering algorithms consider points in turn and assign them to the cluster in which they best fit.

Sort the lecture into these two forms: hierarchical = Slides 16–18 (and the quiz of Slides 69–75); point-assignment = k-means, BFR, and the second pass of CURE (each point goes to the cluster of the nearest representative). (Beyond the slides: hierarchical clustering must compare all pairs of clusters, which is expensive for huge data; that is why the big-data methods are point-assignment methods, and CURE uses hierarchical clustering only on a sample.)

Summary: BFR and CURE (Slide 87)

Lecture 5 · Slide 87

  • The BFR algorithm: "a version of k-means designed to handle data that is too large to fit in main memory. It assumes clusters are normally distributed about the axes."
  • Processing points in CURE: "After creating representative points for each cluster, the entire set of points can be read from disk and assigned to a cluster. We assign a given point to the cluster of the representative point that is closest to the given point."
Slide erratum (wording)

"Normally distributed about the axes" is loose. The precise assumption (Slides 44 and 79) is that clusters are normally distributed around a centroid and are axis-aligned ellipses. Use that wording in the exam.

Quick recap: this part
  • BFR keeps N, SUM, SUMSQ (2d + 1 numbers) per cluster, plus CS groups and raw RS points; it needs normal, axis-aligned clusters.
  • Each memory load: close points → DS; leftovers + old RS clustered → CS / RS; update by adding; merge CS; last round: merge CS and RS into the nearest cluster or call them outliers.
  • Close enough = Mahalanobis distance < threshold (about 2 σ); merge two CS by the variance of the union or the M.D. of their centroids.
  • k-means on MapReduce: Mapper = assign, Reducer = average, Combiner = (sum, count), Driver = iterate until the centroids stop moving.
  • BFR summarises, CURE samples, MapReduce parallelises; all three keep k-means usable on big data.

Theory Q&A bank

Lecture 5 · Slides 1–88

Cover the answer, write your own, then compare. Numbered points are marking points. Most questions are self-made practice; the ones the slides themselves pose are Q9 and Q12 (Slides 78 and 79: BFR steps and allowed shapes), Q8 (Slide 82: CURE steps), Q11 (Slide 80: are the statistics recomputed from scratch?), and Q13 (Slide 53: Q1 and Q2 of BFR). BFR questions here are theory only; no BFR numerical is examined.

Q1. Define clustering. What does the distance measure do, and which measures does the lecture name?

Lecture 5 · Slide 4

  1. Given a set of points and a notion of distance, group the points into clusters so that members of a cluster are similar (small distances) and members of different clusters are dissimilar (large distances).
  2. The distance measure defines what "similar" means; changing it changes the clusters. Points usually live in a high-dimensional space.
  3. Named measures: Euclidean (numeric coordinates, straight-line), cosine (vectors, direction), Jaccard (sets: 1 − |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|), edit distance (strings: minimum number of single-character edits).
  4. A distance is small when things are similar (Jaccard similarity 0.4 means Jaccard distance 0.6).

Q2. Why is clustering hard, especially in high dimensions?

Lecture 5 · Slides 8–9

  1. Real data is messy: clusters differ in size, density and shape, they overlap, and there is noise, so there is no clean gap between clusters (Slide 8).
  2. In 2 dimensions and with little data the eye can check a clustering. Applications often have 10 or 10,000 dimensions, which cannot be plotted (Slide 9).
  3. High-dimensional spaces look different: many pairs of points are at about the same distance. Then "near" and "far" no longer differ, and distance-based methods have little to grab (the curse of dimensionality, Beyond the slides: the name).
  4. Remedy mentioned by the course map (Slide 2): dimensionality reduction.

Q3. Compare hierarchical and point-assignment clustering. What are agglomerative and divisive methods and what is a dendrogram?

Lecture 5 · Slide 14

  1. Hierarchical methods build a tree of nested clusters. Agglomerative = bottom up: every point starts as its own cluster and the two nearest clusters are merged repeatedly. Divisive = top down: start with one cluster and split recursively.
  2. Point assignment keeps a set of clusters (their number fixed in advance) and assigns each point to the nearest one (k-means, BFR, CURE's second pass).
  3. A dendrogram is the tree of merges; leaves are points, the height of a bar is the distance at which the merge happened; cutting it at a level gives any number of clusters.
  4. Hierarchical needs all pairwise cluster distances (expensive); point assignment is the basis of the big-data methods.

Q4. Describe agglomerative clustering in Euclidean and non-Euclidean spaces. What are the centroid and the clustroid?

Lecture 5 · Slides 16–18

  1. Key operation: repeatedly combine the two nearest clusters. Two decisions: how to represent a cluster of many points, and how to measure nearness of clusters.
  2. Euclidean: a cluster is represented by its centroid = the average of its points (coordinate by coordinate); the distance between clusters is the distance between their centroids. After a merge the new centroid is the weighted average (nP·cP + nQ·cQ) / (nP + nQ), not the midpoint of the two centroids.
  3. Non-Euclidean (sets, strings): there is no average of two points, so use the clustroid = the data point "closest" to the other points of the cluster, treated as if it were the centroid. It is always an actual data point.
  4. Beyond the slides: "closest" is commonly the point with the smallest sum of distances (or smallest maximum, or smallest sum of squares) to the others; state the rule you use.

Q5. Why is hierarchical clustering not used for big data?

Lecture 5 · Slide 21

  1. Naive implementation: at each step compute the distances between all pairs of clusters, then merge the closest pair: cost O(N³).
  2. Reason: about N − 1 merges, each looking at up to about N²/2 pairs (for N = 12 the exact count is 286 distance computations, trivial; for N = 106 it is hopeless).
  3. Beyond the slides: a priority queue gives O(N² log N), still too slow, and the O(N²) pairwise distances do not fit in memory.
  4. Slide's conclusion: too expensive for really big data sets that do not fit in memory. That motivates CURE (hierarchical clustering only on a sample), BFR and MapReduce.

Q6. Describe the k-means algorithm: what it needs, how it starts, the loop, and when it stops.

Lecture 5 · Slides 23–27

  1. Needs: Euclidean space and distance (so that the centroid, an average, exists) and a chosen number of clusters k.
  2. Seeds: pick k starting points, either k random points, or one random point and then k − 1 points each as far as possible from the previous ones (farthest-first: choose the candidate whose smallest distance to the chosen seeds is largest).
  3. Loop: (a) assign each point to its nearest centroid; (b) after all points are assigned, move each centroid to the mean of its points; (c) reassign all points to the nearest (new) centroid, which sometimes moves points between clusters; repeat (b) and (c).
  4. Convergence: stop when points no longer move between clusters and the centroids stabilise.
  5. Beyond the slides: the result can depend on the seeds (local optimum), so spread-out seeds are better.

Q7. How do you choose k? What do "too few" and "too many" look like?

Lecture 5 · Slides 31–34

  1. Try different k and plot the average distance to the centroid against k.
  2. It falls rapidly until the right k, then changes little; choose k at the bend (Beyond the slides: the "elbow").
  3. Too few (Slide 32): natural groups are lumped together and many distances to the centroid are long.
  4. Just right (Slide 33): one centroid per natural group, distances rather short.
  5. Too many (Slide 34): a natural group is split and the average distance improves little.
  6. Do not pick the k with the smallest average distance: that is always the largest k tried.

Q8. Describe in steps how CURE works. Why does it use several representative points instead of one centroid?

Lecture 5 · Slides 35–42, 82–83, 87

  1. CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives): Euclidean distance, clusters of any shape, a collection of representative points per cluster; a 2-pass algorithm for large data.
  2. Pass 1: (0) take a random sample that fits in main memory; (1) cluster it hierarchically; (2) for each cluster pick a sample of points as dispersed as possible (say 4), then move each (say) 20% toward the cluster's centroid: new = p + 0.2 (c − p). These moved points are the representatives.
  3. Pass 2: rescan the whole data; assign each point p to the cluster of the closest representative.
  4. Why representatives: one centroid describes only a round blob; several points along a curved or elongated cluster (a ring, a crescent) let a point find the right cluster. Moving them inward damps the effect of outliers (Beyond the slides).

Q9. What is BFR, what does it assume, and which cluster shapes does it allow?

Lecture 5 · Slides 43–45, 78–79, 87

  1. BFR (Bradley–Fayyad–Reina) is a variant of k-means for very large, disk-resident data. Points are read in chunks (memory loads); most are summarised by simple statistics and discarded. Memory is O(clusters), not O(data).
  2. It assumes each cluster is normally distributed around a centroid in a Euclidean space and that the dimensions are independent, so it is an axis-aligned ellipse.
  3. Allowed (Slide 79): horizontal ellipse OK, vertical ellipse OK (circles too), tilted ellipse not OK.
  4. Reason: standard deviations may differ along different axes, but the axes of the cluster must align with the axes of the space. BFR stores per-dimension totals only, so it cannot capture correlation between dimensions (a tilt). Rings and other non-normal shapes are for CURE.

Q10. Define the discard set, compression set and retained set. What is kept in memory for each, and why have all three?

Lecture 5 · Slides 46–47, 52

  1. DS (discard set): points close enough to a cluster centroid; assigned to that cluster; only the summary (N, SUM, SUMSQ) is kept, the points are discarded.
  2. CS (compression set): groups of points that are close together but not close to any centroid; summarised (also N, SUM, SUMSQ) but not assigned to a cluster; points discarded.
  3. RS (retained set): isolated points waiting to be assigned to a compression set; kept in memory as they are.
  4. Why: DS keeps memory small; CS keeps a possible new cluster without storing its points; RS avoids summarising single points, which give no useful spread (one point has variance 0).

Q11. What does BFR store for a cluster, why is that enough, and must it be recomputed from scratch each round?

Lecture 5 · Slides 48–49, 80–81

  1. For each cluster: N (number of points), SUM (vector of per-dimension sums of coordinates), SUMSQ (vector of per-dimension sums of squared coordinates): 2d + 1 numbers whatever the cluster size.
  2. Centroid in dimension i = SUMi / N. Variance in dimension i = SUMSQi / N − (SUMi / N)²; standard deviation = its square root. So centre and spread can be read at any time.
  3. No: the statistics are not recomputed from scratch. A new point x is absorbed by N + 1, SUM + x, SUMSQ + x²; two summaries merge by adding their N, SUM and SUMSQ. This is at the heart of BFR (Slide 81).
  4. Because only per-dimension totals are kept, only per-dimension variances exist, matching the axis-aligned assumption.

Q12. Describe in steps how BFR processes the data.

Lecture 5 · Slides 45, 50–51, 78

  1. Start: choose k initial centroids from the first memory load by a sensible approach (e.g. k random points).
  2. Step 1: points sufficiently close to a cluster centroid are added to that cluster (DS) and discarded.
  3. Step 2: cluster the remaining points together with the old RS using any main-memory clustering algorithm; clusters go to the CS, outlying points to the RS.
  4. Step 3: update the DS statistics (add the Ns, SUMs and SUMSQs).
  5. Step 4: consider merging CS groups that are close enough (add their statistics).
  6. Step 5 (last round only): merge all CS groups and RS points into their nearest cluster, or treat them as outliers.
  7. Steps 1–4 repeat for each memory load.

Q13. How does BFR decide whether a point is close enough to a cluster (Q1), and whether two CS sets should be merged (Q2)?

Lecture 5 · Slides 53–58

  1. Q1: use the Mahalanobis distance (normalised Euclidean distance from the centroid): yi = (xi − ci) / σi, then d = √(Σ yi²). Accept the point if d is below a threshold; common practice is M.D. < 2 (about 2 standard deviations).
  2. Why not plain Euclidean distance: it ignores that a cluster is stretched more in some directions; dividing by σi measures each direction in units of that cluster's own spread. ci and σi come from N, SUM, SUMSQ, so no raw points are needed.
  3. Q2 (way 1): add the two summaries and compute the variance of the combined subcluster; if it stays small (still tight), merge.
  4. Q2 (way 2): compute the Mahalanobis distance between the two centroids using a pooled σ per dimension, either √(((σ(1))² + (σ(2))²) / 2) or max(σ(1), σ(2)); merge if below a threshold such as 2.

Q14. Describe k-means on MapReduce. Why must the combiner send (sum, count) and not an average?

Lecture 5 · Slides 60–67, 84

  1. Initialise with random centroids.
  2. Mapper: for each point find the nearest centroid and emit (centroidID, point). This is the assignment step.
  3. Combiner (optional): each node collapses its pairs per centroid into (centroidID, (partial sum, count)); allowed because the average decomposes into sum and count.
  4. Reducer: for each centroid add the sums, add the counts, divide: the new centroid = mean of its points (the update step).
  5. Iterate: one MapReduce job per k-means iteration, until the centroids stop moving (or a predefined number of iterations).
  6. An average of local averages is wrong when the nodes hold different numbers of points (nodes with {2, 3, 5} and {100}: true mean 27.5, average of averages 51.67); sums and counts add correctly.

Q15. Compare k-means, CURE, BFR and k-means on MapReduce. How does each cope with big data?

Lecture 5 · Slides 23–27, 35–67, 86–87

  1. k-means: Euclidean, one centroid per cluster, roundish blobs, many passes; the data must fit in memory.
  2. CURE: samples (memory-sized sample clustered hierarchically), keeps representatives, any shape, two passes, no iteration.
  3. BFR: summarises (N, SUM, SUMSQ per cluster; DS, CS, RS), reads each chunk once, assumes normal axis-aligned clusters.
  4. k-means on MapReduce: parallelises: the same clusters as ordinary k-means from the same start, spread over many machines; one job per iteration.
  5. All four are Euclidean (a centroid is an average). Hierarchical clustering is the contrast: it works with clustroids but costs O(N³).

Algorithms in a few steps

AlgorithmSteps
Agglomerative(1) Every point is a cluster. (2) Find the two clusters with the nearest centroids (clustroids). (3) Merge them; new centroid = weighted average. (4) Repeat until k clusters remain (or the whole dendrogram is built).
k-means(1) Choose k and k seeds (random or farthest-first). (2) Assign each point to its nearest centroid. (3) Move each centroid to the mean of its points. (4) Reassign; repeat 3 and 4 until nothing moves.
CUREPass 1: (1) random sample in memory; (2) cluster it hierarchically; (3) per cluster take (say) 4 dispersed points; (4) move them (say) 20% toward the centroid. Pass 2: rescan all data; each point goes to the cluster of the closest representative.
BFR (per memory load)(1) Close points to DS (add to N, SUM, SUMSQ). (2) Cluster the rest plus the old RS: clusters to CS, outliers to RS. (3) Update DS statistics. (4) Merge close CS groups. (5) Last load: merge CS and RS into the nearest cluster or call them outliers.
MapReduce k-means(1) Random centroids. (2) Mappers emit (nearest centroid ID, point). (3) Combiner: (ID, (partial sum, count)). (4) Reducer: sums, counts, divide, giving new centroids. (5) Repeat until they stop moving.

Common mistakes & traps

Lecture 5 · Slides 1–88

  • Midpoint instead of weighted average. A point joining a two-point cluster with centroid (1.5, 1.5): the new centroid is (1·p + 2·(1.5, 1.5)) / 3, not the midpoint of p and (1.5, 1.5) (Slide 17: (1, 1), not (0.75, 0.75)).
  • Centroid for strings or sets. Under Jaccard or edit distance there is no average; use a clustroid, which must be an actual data point.
  • Farthest-first with k > 2. Use the smallest distance to all chosen seeds, then take the largest; not the distance to the last seed only, and not a sum.
  • Skipping steps in k-means by hand. Show the distance of every point to every centroid, underline the smallest, recompute each centroid with its count, and state the round. Do not stop after the update without reassigning.
  • Picking k with the smallest average distance. It is always the largest k; choose the bend where the drop stops.
  • CURE: centroids as representatives. Representatives are dispersed points moved 20% toward the centroid (generally not data points); a point goes to the cluster of the nearest representative, not the nearest centroid. CURE needs two passes and no iteration.
  • BFR shapes. Horizontal and vertical ellipses are allowed; tilted ones are not. Rings and crescents are not BFR clusters either (use CURE).
  • BFR sets. The CS is summarised but not assigned to a cluster; the RS is kept as raw points; "all points are discarded" is false.
  • BFR statistics. SUMSQ is the sum of squares, not (SUM)²; SUM and SUMSQ are vectors; variance = SUMSQ/N − (SUM/N)² (divide by N); statistics are updated by adding, never recomputed from old points; do not average two standard deviations to get the union's.
  • Mahalanobis versus Euclidean. Divide each coordinate difference by σi of that cluster before squaring; a point can be far in Euclidean terms yet accepted (and the reverse).
  • MapReduce combiner. Send (sum, count), not a local average. One job is one k-means iteration; on Slide 84 state your own initial centroids, node split and stopping rule, as the slide gives none.
  • Trusting slide answers blindly. Known slide quirks: Slide 6 labels only one of the two outliers; Slide 41 draws the move as about one third, not 20%; Slide 81 prints "110/3 − 18/3²", which needs brackets: 110/3 − (18/3)² = 0.667; Slide 87 says "normally distributed about the axes", loosely.

Divisive clusteringTop-down hierarchical clustering: start with one cluster containing all points and split it recursively.L5 · Slide 14
Does not compose wellMapReduce jobs can only be chained through files on disk, so multi-step applications are slow and awkward.L3 · Slide 6
Duplicate document detectionFinding near-identical documents or pages.L1 · Slides 19–20
Dynamic programmingSolving a problem by reusing answers to smaller sub-problems.L1 · Slide 19
EC2, S3, EMRAmazon's Elastic Compute Cloud (rentable machines), S3 storage, and Elastic Map Reduce (hosted Hadoop).L2 · Slide 77
Edit distanceThe minimum number of single-character edits needed to turn one string into another.L5 · Slide 4

Fine granularityCutting a job into many small tasks, with far more map tasks than machines.L2 · Slides 58, 69

NThe number of points in a cluster summary.L5 · Slide 48

Spam detectionRecognising spam emails or link/web spam.L1 · Slides 19–20

Spark coreThe fast, memory-optimised execution engine underneath all Spark libraries.L3 · Slide 8
Spark SQL / SparkSQLSpark library providing a SQL API for scalable processing of relational (structured) data.L3 · Slides 8, 12, 20

Store, manage, analyzeThe three stages of working with data; this class focuses on analysis.L1 · Slide 8

UsefulA discovered pattern that it is possible to act on.L1 · Slide 10
ValidA discovered pattern that holds on new data with some certainty.L1 · Slide 10

Vertex and edge propertiesUser-defined attributes attached to every vertex and every edge in GraphX.L3 · Slide 20
WorkerA process that runs map or reduce tasks assigned by the master.L3 · Slide 4
